Oṃ.
In the Śrī Pāñcarātra, the Jayākhyasaṃhitā,
the first chapter, titled "The Purpose of Commencing the Scripture."
Salutations to the wielder of the discus, the bestower of all auspiciousness, who is the cause for the upliftment of those submerged in the ocean of sense-objects. (1)
[The Introduction to the Treatise] In a place well-established and honored, frequented by gods and brahmin seers, crowded with ascetics, and inhabited by those who perform meritorious deeds; (2)
Indeed, at Prabhāsa, the most excellent of sacred fords, the Lord Viṣṇu— the soul of the universe, the sovereign who bestows grace upon the worlds— is eternally present.
Therein, intent on serving the lineage of elders beginning with his father, always seeking liberation, free from passion, and devoid of envy; (4)
Seeing his own body submerged, Saṃvartaka, a treasury of splendor,
bowed with palms joined in reverence and spoke to his father Aurva.
Saṃvartaka said:
"Tell me the means for one submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra,
by knowing which there would be no further birth for me or for anyone else."

Aurva said: "O child, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, my ancestors— sages who were established in self-restraint, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and whose wealth was their asceticism— " || 7 ||
Indeed, this was envisioned by someone who, after performing most severe austerities for many thousands of years, [attained it]. (8)
(Endowed with the discipline of contentment and accompanied by the practice of vows),
through the attainment of the supreme good, the great seers felt a sense of renunciation;
indeed, at the conclusion of their asceticism over time, we have taken our stand upon the True Dharma.
Not having attained the sphere of accomplishment, they heaved sighs again and again.
We do not know what we shall become even now in this dense cycle of existence;
there is no eternal stability in the self-abiding state, nor is there the destruction of bondage.
"Enjoyments here are certainly not stable; what indeed can we do in this calamity?
Thus, having fallen into such a profound crisis, our ascetic practice remains unsettled. (11)
Then, having fallen into a state of confusion, a great voice arose,
prompted by those intent on meditation who were desirous of knowing the Dharma of the Blessed One.
[The knowledge of the supreme reality as the cause of the highest good:
Neither by the study of sacrifices and the Vedas, nor by gifts alone, nor by manifold ritual acts, nor by vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and others; || 13 ||
Indeed, there would be no stability even in heaven; and how could there be bondage or liberation if the supreme reality—which is eternal, imperishable, and immutable—is not known? (14)
But while the Lord of the World is all-pervading, eternally satisfied, stainless,
assuming forms by His own will, eternal, pure, awakened, and perfectly immaculate— (15)
O twice-born ones, as long as this supreme deity is not thus known,
liberation remains difficult to attain even in tens of millions of ages.

Therefore, strive so that the Teacher of the World—who dwells within the heart, whose nature is pure consciousness, who is both the possessor of qualities and devoid of qualities—may quickly [be realized]. (17)
"Without doubt, he quickly attains grace toward those who are helpless.
Having heard this unprecedented account, they remained there with delighted minds. (18)
At that very auspicious moment, O dear son, as soon as it was heard:
"What is this? By whom was it spoken? What is that Brahman which is indeed nameless? (19)
"How shall we know that correctly?"—thus they spoke to one another;
and when they remained immersed in doubt for a long time, [they said: (p. 3) 20.
Once again, a voice like nectar arose from the sky:
"That which is the syllable, unshakeable, the supreme Brahman, eternal—[this is the discernment of the ultimate reality]. (21)
O twice-born ones, know that Acyuta is the supreme goal of all;
by taking refuge in him, the sages who are deeply versed in Brahman cross the ocean of worldly existence.
They cross over by means of that lotus-eyed god, Nārāyaṇa himself—
Viṣṇu, who bears the conch and the discus and is overflowing with the vehicle of bliss.
Those contemplators of the inner self who take refuge in Him with devotion go indeed to the station of Viṣṇu, freed from old age and death. || 24 ||
Having spoken thus, when that voice subsequently ceased,
we were then joyful and satisfied, for the most part freed from our distress.
The Lord, whose body bears the Śrīvatsa mark, protects and rules the three worlds;
having established a state of mental composure, he is praised by sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
Then he thought further: "How shall we know that Lord?

Who in these three worlds truly knows the God of gods, who possesses the means for attaining the supreme reality? (27) [Thus, desiring to know the means for realizing the supreme principle, he approached Śāṇḍilya.]
"Whom has the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, even Adhokṣaja, become pleased with?
By the power of his asceticism, everything that was contemplated in his mind has then [been fulfilled]. || 28 ||
Afterwards, when this was correctly understood by all those of purified souls,
Śāṇḍilya was heard of on earth in this world as one who had accomplished his purpose.
And thus, all of them, with their hands raised carrying fruits and flowers from their own labor,
proceeded to where that sage remained, having accomplished his purpose.
Seated comfortably on Mount Gandhamādana, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga, he was possessed of ascetic merit and splendor, together with the twice-born.
It was endowed with various wonders, adorned with various flowers,
filled with fruit-bearing trees, and variegated with various minerals.
It was a delightful and charming place, inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas) and frequented by gods,
where those of disciplined conduct, great self-control, and devoted to the vows of yoga performed their austerities.
Surrounded by excellent disciples full of wisdom like the moon by the planets, he—who was rich in knowledge and action—was beheld by the sages standing with palms joined in reverence. (34)
He was saluted by all of them in turn, and they were likewise honored by him with fruits, roots, and the like, along with water and flowers.
When the Dharma had returned and arrived, the Blessed Sage Śāṇḍilya, who is worshipped by the gods and rich in asceticism, was questioned with great eagerness by all those ascetics.

[The Question Concerning the Reality of the Blessed One and the Manner of His Worship] O Blessed One, we desire to hear about the nature of the worship and the ritual acts of Viṣṇu, whose deeds are marvelous; please tell us out of your grace. (37)
For we have heard something most wonderful from the midst of the sky; since the true nature of the Blessed One was unknown to us, the supreme goal would have been difficult to attain. (38)
Likewise, even when not propitiated by sattvic action, [he remains] for the sake of our own deliverance as well as that of other living beings. (39)
"You ought to explain the Dharma of the Blessed One exactly as it is in every respect.
[Regarding the sequence of the commencement of this treatise, Śāṇḍilya says:
"Listen all of you, being self-restrained, to [the account] of Viṣṇu of wondrous splendor. (40)
This treatise is the very essence, a great secret Upaniṣad of knowledge; it is unrevealed, containing the womb of Brahman, and eternal.
And in former times, that was told to Nārada for the sake of his grace;
likewise, because of its extreme secrecy, it has not been revealed in this world.
Nor was he questioned by anyone out of reverence for the Dharma;
thus addressed, at the end of many days, he vanished from sight.
Furthermore, that which was indeed spoken again by Viṣṇu, the source of all power, who had descended once more, to the sage who was his own partial incarnation; || 44 ||
O best of beings, by the Lord who brings forth the worlds, while residing at Badarikāśrama, this vow was undertaken for the purpose of establishing the path of dharma. (45)
And likewise for the Siddhas who hear it, as well as for those who move through the sky—for the gods, the ṛṣis, and similarly for humans and others. (46)
Of the high-souled Ādityas, beginning with Mṛkaṇḍu and Tārkṣya;
of the Kinnaras, the Daityas, and the Vasus of purified souls. || 47 ||
[The promise to teach this scripture, as it was received from the teacher Nārada, to the sages who are followers of Sāṅkhya, perfected in Yoga, and knowers of theoretical and practical knowledge.]
Listen to that, O best of sages: the Dharma which delivers one from saṃsāra. || 48 ||
Just as it was previously obtained by me from the satisfied Nārada—
endowed with all knowledge and ritual action, and the means for accomplishing all perfections.
"Having understood that which is concise yet of great significance, likewise correctly bestowing discernment, and being the very essence—this indeed was studied by me in the past. (50)
For it is that which brings about the swift accomplishment of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation;
and having studied it, one subsequently attains the supreme knowledge among all forms of knowledge. (51)
I shall declare to you, according to the traditional teaching (āmnāya) and as it truly exists, that grace by which indeed I shall no longer be born again in this world.
Only one who has approached with faith and devotion is a fit vessel for the instruction of this scripture;
for it is only when a scripture has been understood in its proper sequence through the lineage of teacher and disciple, and is free from all doubts, that it bestows its fruit. (53)
Therefore, O twice-born ones, resort to this system with great effort from the very beginning, endowed with devotion and faith, and adorned with the conviction of its reality. 54.

Even if one were to give away all one's possessions, if that person is devoid of devotion and faith, is bereft of right conduct, is arrogant, and is a subverter of the meaning of the scriptures; || 55 ||
The scripture should not be spoken to one who goes to his downfall, nor should he speak it;
both he who speaks it and he who listens to it [commit a fault] unless they do so with proper conduct.
May they both go to the abode of the Source of the World, due to the terrible reversal [of their state].
[This section contains a description of the greatness of the Guru, interspersed with a description of devotion to the Guru as the means for attaining the highest good.]
For all things, O twice-born ones, such as worldly enjoyment and liberation, are dependent upon the scriptures. (57)
One should know that the teacher who expounds Vaiṣṇava knowledge is like Viṣṇu himself;
he who knows the scriptures should worship him with speech, mind, and body—he indeed is a true Vaiṣṇava. (58)
Since even one who merely recites a single quarter-verse of a śloka is always worthy of worship, how much more so he who explains the true nature of Lord Viṣṇu? (59)
And the teacher of the scripture as well, whose mind is absorbed in that very state;
by worshipping this triad—the All-pervading Lord, the scripture, and the Guru—[one attains success]. (60)
The fruit is indeed unfailing both in this world and in the next;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, who is attained through the knowledge of Him.
The scripture is the means for attaining knowledge, and that scripture resides in the mouth of the Guru;
therefore, because of this reason, the attainment of Brahman is always dependent upon the Guru.
O Brahmins, for this very reason, the Guru is remembered as the supreme teacher;
because the Lord, the Master of the World, having assumed a mortal body, [bestowed this knowledge]. (63)
Out of compassion, he uplifts the great worlds with the scripture in his hand;
therefore, one who fears the terror of saṃsāra should cultivate devotion toward the guru. 64.
He who would dispel the darkness of ignorance with the collyrium of the scriptures—[for] the scripture removes sin, is meritorious, purifying, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (65)
"He who speaks that which grants peace and great purpose, the Teacher of the World"—
having been addressed thus by that sage who knows Brahman, the sages assumed the state of disciples out of a desire to hear the truth. (66)
Then they all left their seats and became tranquil in mind;
falling at the base of his feet, their hearts were fixed on him and he was their sole refuge.
[Now begins the instruction:
Then, Viṣṇu’s hand was placed upon the heads of those sages of purified souls by the gratified sage who knows Brahman. (68)
Then that best of Brahmins, having prostrated before Acyuta Hari,
spoke of the great scripture handed down through tradition, which bestows the fruit of the nectar of knowledge.
[The determination of the time of the commencement of this treatise, the specific person who initiated it, and its particular title:
O best of sages, when a certain Kṛta Yuga had begun...
In the Pauṣkara Brahmakalpa, even though Aghokṣaja was present before their very eyes. (70)

When the Grandfather (Brahmā) had increased, being entirely free from desire and anger, and remained established throughout the three worlds—including all things mobile and immobile—without any adversaries; ||| 71 ||
When the Dharma had thus flourished and Adharma had come to destruction,
the lotus-eyed Lord was questioned by Nārada as follows.
For the sake of the victory of devotees and for the sake of his own welfare, [he spoke] this auspicious work, the most essential of the essential, composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter. (73)
This was proclaimed by the Teacher of the Three Worlds to the inquiring Nārada;
having extracted the very essence, it is a compendium containing the nectar of truth.
Having understood everything in its true nature through the very quality of omniscience,
he [perceived] the expansion of the knower and knowledge to the extent of one and a half crores.
The Jayāvyaya Niṣadatantra has issued forth from the root of Brahman,
just as a thunderclap arises spontaneously from the formless sky.
In the same way, from that which is peaceful and consists of pure consciousness, the scripture arises as the nature of sound;
yet that form of the All-pervading Lord remains changeless and free from conceptual construction.
That which is the modification of the source of the world is remembered as Śabdabrahman;
from that time onwards, O best of sages, it has existed in this world. (78)
"Victory!"— thus was the name Vimala bestowed by Viśvakarman;
Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra.
Thus, the venerable authority of the Blessed One’s teaching is renowned everywhere. || 1 ||
The Sāttvata, the Pauṣkara, and the excellent tantra known as the Jayākhya—these are celebrated as the "Three Jewels" (Ratnatraya); their specific characteristics are now described here.
This triple jewel is the essence of the Sāttvata scripture, its secret doctrine esteemed by the wise; it has issued directly from the mouth of the Blessed One.
In that very same way, this has been set forth without deficiency or excess;
however, other tantras have issued from the mouth of the Blessed One. (4)
Relying precisely upon that essence, through various methods of concise and detailed retention,
they have been pervaded accordingly by means of commentaries, amplifications, and logical principles.
Their authority is firmly established by the fundamental principle of exegesis;
likewise, in the Tantra consisting of one hundred and eight [verses], there is the Pārameśvara-saṃhitā.
The *Īśvaratantra*, the supreme scripture, has been introduced as a commentary for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the *Pauṣkara* and for the purpose of explaining the *Sāttvata*.
The commentary on this Jayākhyatantra is said to be the Pādma;
it was [revealed] upon the earth at those self-manifested sites where the Blessed One appeared.
Among the one hundred and eight principal [shrines], there is a quartet that is like a jewel:
Śrīraṅgam, Veṅkaṭādri, Hastiśaila, and thereafter [the next].
Then Nārāyaṇa and others [established] the four divine abodes among the dwellings of the God of gods other than Veṅkaṭādri.
Regarding the three jewels, they venerate the three tantras;
because they consist of root texts and commentaries, they are mutually dependent.
The wise one should know these three tantras as a single scripture:
the Sāttvata at Yaduśailendra, and likewise the Pauṣkara at Śrīraṅga.
And on Hastiśaila, he presides over the empire known as Jaya;
the Pādma-tantra is on Hastiśaila, and the Pārameśvara is at Śrīraṅga.
(9) And on Mount Yādava, Īśvara is proclaimed as the performer of all actions;
among Śrīraṅga and Mount Yādava, Hastiśaila is distinguished as superior. || 14 ||
Just as diamond possesses greater qualities than rubies and lapis lazuli,
so it was in the former Kṛta age when Brahmā, having directly beheld the Lord of Ramā, [attained this knowledge].
Having personally performed that supreme sequence of worship, he then, out of compassion, instructed it to his venerable disciples. (16)
"At that very time, the Lotus-born One causes them to perform worship.
Having heard this from Nārada, I spoke once again: || 17 ||
O Blessed One, beloved of Kamalā, when and how was You directly perceived?
O Lord, tell me this, as well as the glory of Hastīndra. (18)
Thus questioned by me, the venerable sage Nārada said:
"I have been well questioned, my child; in my opinion, you are worthy of praise. (19)
Today I shall describe to you the majesty of Karīśaila;
formerly, when I had approached him, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, [spoke].
The creator of the world, the lord of the gods, the four-faced one, being questioned,
[spoke] of the majesty of Hastiśaila, the bestower of boons, which is the essence of compassion.
I shall describe to you in brief, yet with essential substance, the majesty of that sacred field of Satyavrata.
Listen with care and affection, for this is a secret essence:
from the lotus at the navel of the Blessed One was born the Creator, who is born from the lotus (Abjasaṃbhava).
Having created the universe of moving and non-moving beings, he attained supreme pride;
namely, the threefold intoxication consisting of noble birth, virtuous conduct, and learning. (24)
He overcomes all [others]; how much more so when standing in the supreme station?
Thereupon, his mind being intoxicated with pride, he [addressed] the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā.
Desiring to effect [this] directly through yoga, he applied supreme effort,
which was opposed to the direct perception of the nature and other attributes of the God of gods.
He was warded off by immeasurable and great misdeeds,
even though a very great effort was exerted again and again.
He did not attain success and was frustrated in his concentration; then, dejected and intent on thought, he reflected again and again. (28)
(10) In vain has this great hardship been undergone by me, dull-witted as I am, through the play known as ascending and descending to the abode of the gods. (29)
Alas, not even a single moment was spent for the sake of liberation;
then, summoning his fortitude, the wise one returned to the world of mortals.
In the middle of the Gaṅgā, he began to perform a great and terrible penance,
standing on the tip of his big toe with his breath and all physical movement restrained.
With his arms raised and abstaining from food, he performed most severe penance;
yet his mind, fickle like a monkey, did not attain composure.
Consequently, he was unable to meditate upon the Lord of Śrī for even a single moment.
Then, while the Creator was thus distressed and emaciated, an incorporeal voice arose from the sky: ||| 33 ||
A meritorious voice manifested, awakening the Lotus-born One:
"Your mind is entirely filled with the essence of the great bliss of authority. (34)
Without purification, one does not attain purity even through a thousand horse-sacrifices;
how can mental composure be achieved for an impure mind in this world? (35)
If the mind is unwell, how can meditation be successfully accomplished?
If you fear delay due to the weight of duties or the passage of time, [then meditation is impossible]. (36)
I shall describe an easy means; listen attentively as it truly is:
two hundred yojanas to the south of the Gaṅgā. (37)
It was five yojanas wide and five yojanas long,
reaching to the shore of the eastern ocean, and honored by all for its many excellent qualities.
This field of accomplishment is of great merit, highly esteemed by the Lord of Śrī;
it is renowned as Satyavrata, illuminating its name according to its true meaning. (39)
A single act of dharma performed there indeed increases a thousandfold;
therefore, if you were to worship Hari with even a single horse-sacrifice there, [the merit would be immense].
"You will certainly obtain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
There, in the Śarvatara Kalpa, [you shall see] the imperishable Viṣṇu and the elephants of the quarters. (41)
On the peak of a certain excellent mountain, they performed worship;
then the Lord, the ocean of compassion, appeared before them.
From that time forth, the lord of mountains, whose beloved form was like Kamalā’s lover (Viṣṇu) and whose eyes were like lotuses, attained the fame of being the Elephant Mountain (Karigiri). 43.
Having made that very [place] the sacrificial altar, perform that horse sacrifice;
through the power of the glance of compassion from the Beloved of Lakṣmī, you shall become great. (44)
"You shall become blessed, successful in your purpose, and pure; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words, Viriñca was delighted in his heart. (45)
He quickly approached the meritorious field of Satyavrata,
which Tvaṣṭṛ had made beautiful by carving the peak of Hastigiri with chisels.
This sacrificer prepared a sacrificial altar worthy of the sacrifice, and according to the scriptures, he [worshipped] Lakṣmīśa, the cause of all causes. (47)
He, Aja, performed the horse sacrifice (Vājimedha), the most excellent of all sacrifices;
therein, in all the mantras, he used the names of the respective deities.
While these were being recited, this Dhātṛ, meditating within his heart upon the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā, offered all the oblation to Him.
By offering even this much with devotion,
the lotus-eyed Lord Hari alone is sufficient to consume all sacrificial offerings.
Taking them up himself and tasting them with devotion,
he would [provide for] those who did not receive their respective allotted portions at the proper times.
The minds of the gods, who were looking upward and had been deceived, became agitated;
then they all approached Brahmā and questioned him.
"What is this that is happening? Are we deluded, or has our intellect been shaken?
To them, Brahmā, smiling, spoke with words of consolation.
"O gods, you were created by me in the past; I am your creator and your father. How is it that a father should wait upon his sons out of humility? (54)
Indeed, you must be propitiated by those who are well-versed in the paths of saṃsāra and who desire their respective fruits, for you possess the authority to grant them. (55)
Hari, the inner self of all, the Lord of all, and even my own father—
the god who is the beloved of Kamalā— is the one for whom this oblation is offered.
In this sacrifice of oblations, everything is merely names contained within the mantras;
however, for you, their respective referents are the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Kamalā.
This is the flow of the essence of the sacrifice of wine, its very pith and sweetness;
know that this alone is [the path] even for men who are supremely devoted to the One. 58.
(12) Thus addressed, the gods, freed from agitation and satisfied by their comprehension of the essential meaning, honored Prajāpati, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (59).
It is said that for every hundred auspicious undertakings there are a hundred obstacles;
likewise, a hundred impediments arose during that great sacrifice.
The God of gods, the Lord of Ramā, with supreme compassion and joy,
pacified all the obstacles that had arisen.
Then, at that time which possessed many virtues and was suitable for the offering of the omentum,
auspicious omens appeared everywhere, captivating the mind.
In the month of Meṣa, during the bright fortnight, on the fourteenth lunar day,
under the auspicious asterism of Hasta, conjoined with Sunday.
When the offering of the omentum (vapā) belonging to the morning libation was completed,
Hari appeared from the fire, seizing that very omentum in his lower jaw.
In a celestial chariot called Puṇyakoṭi, which resembles ten million suns and blazes like refined gold, the Lord is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi.
Facing westward, he shone with a blazing crown and diadem;
his forehead was adorned with a vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and he possessed lotus-like eyes.
He was endowed with the beauty of sesame blossoms and a nose like a wish-fulfilling creeper,
and possessed lower lips capable of eclipsing the splendor of a piece of coral.
He possesses the grace of the Kaustubha jewel hanging within his conch-like, deep throat;
the Śrīvatsa mark adorns his chest, and his broad chest is beautified by the splendor of his necklaces.
He is enchanting with his four arms resplendent with five weapons,
and with one hand holding a lotus, he prominently displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā).
Adorning himself with a mace and a bow in his left hand,
he held the divine and supreme sword Nandaka at his waist.
He is the one who, agitated by the brilliance of the deep navel-sunkenness of his shimmering yellow garment,
is as radiant as the thighs that steal the playful charm of the plantain tree belonging to the garden of Kāma.
He is wondrous with the expanse of beauty from the soles of his feet, which have the form of mirrors;
he is beautiful with a pair of shanks that rival the luster of his calves. || 72 ||
His feet were enchanting, stealing away the very essence of the lotus’s beauty;
with his two eyes filled with the essence of compassion, he gazed upon the four-faced one.
(13) Showing favor out of respect, with the corner of his lower lip quivering in a smile, he thus [spoke] himself, exalted and beautiful in form and youth. (74)
Having served the Lord, the beloved of Ramā and the Master of the Universe, who had manifested in embodied form,
they were all filled with joy, their eyes uplifted as having achieved their purpose.
"O, what fortune! O, what fortune! thus he proclaimed loudly;
even the four-faced Brahmā gazed upon the infallible Lord with all eight of his eyes.
He personally performed various acts of service with joyful intensity, attending upon the Lord who removes the suffering of those who bow before him and grants boons.
Gradually, his agitation subsided, and the Lord, impelled by Nābhi, said:
"O Lotus-born one, behold the majesty of the field of Satyavrata."
By means of a single horse sacrifice, you have desired the fruit of a thousand; therefore, there is purity of mind and clarity of consciousness.
Through that [steadfastness], the perfection of meditation is achieved; this is what you desired, for indeed, the fruit you awaited at the end was said to come through the sequence of stages.
"O Prajāpati, you have reached the first stage with ease;
O observer of noble vows, I am pleased with this horse sacrifice of yours. (81)
This sweet essence of the Vapāra flower is dear to my heart and has captivated my mind;
it is enchanting like the nectar of the essential fragrance of supreme, exclusive devotion.
"Among all edible things, she shall always be my favorite.
Therefore, choose a boon for yourself as you desire. (83)
"Everything shall be accomplished for men once I have come within the range of their vision"—thus was he instructed by the Lord, and the knower of the supreme truth rejoiced. (84)
Having bowed many times and offered praise, Brahmā entreated the Lord:
"Just as it was in Vaikuṇṭha, in the world, and likewise in the Ocean of Milk," (85)
Thus, may your residence be here in this field of Satyavrata, upon the peak of Hastiśaila, which is saluted by all the worlds. (86)
"May men always behold you in this celestial palace of ten million merits"—thus entreated, the Lord, the Blessed One who is affectionate toward his devotees, [granted his wish]. (87)
"For the welfare of all the worlds, let it be so," Brahmā thus assented to Adhokṣaja, the God of gods, during that Kṛta Yuga.
Then, in the Tretā age, Mahāśāntagajendra worshipped Acyuta, propitiating Hari in that very same form himself. (89)
Then, tormented by a crocodile, he offered lotuses plucked from the tips of his own hands;
having sought refuge, he was liberated by the Giver of Boons.
Hari led him to his own abode by means of his vehicle, Garuḍa.
Then, in the age known as Dvāpara, the preceptor of the gods himself [appeared].
Having propitiated the boon-granting God, they attained their desired perfection.
Then, at the beginning of the Kali Yuga, the boon-granter spoke to Brahmā: || 92 ||
Reflecting upon the entire world with a deeply joyful inner soul, he thought:
"This Kali age has arrived; all people are now intent only on their own self-interest. (93)
Due to the upheaval of time, not a single true devotee will be seen, whether in ten thousand years or even in a parārdha; unless perhaps someone such as this [should exist].
The world will not approve of one who is distinguished by excellence;
out of envy, someone may attribute faults to his very head. (95)
Everyone else will proclaim that very same thing in every way;
in the end, through his own despair, there will surely be a fall from his mental state.
Likewise, this powerful Kali age will come to pass;
therefore, my child, it does not please me [to stay] on the summit of Hastiśaila.
"In this divine form, I have vowed to dwell here for the duration of the Kali age, and my stay in this very place shall continue until the end of the kalpa."
Therefore, let it be done in this manner here, so that I may grant you my favor;
for I am the giver of boons, O Creator, the compassionate one toward those who are devoted.
Therefore, let this meritorious spot be called the Pavilion of Renunciation (Tyāgamaṇṭapa);
as for the name Pavilion of Yoga (Yogamaṇṭapa), it was given to Śrīraṅga by me.
Let the Veṅkaṭādri mountain shine forth with the name Puṣpamaṇṭapa;
let whatever other place on the mountain exists be called Vidyāmaṇṭapa. 101.
This is the most excellent merit, a field and a beautiful place;
it is divine, pleasing to me, and the best among the fields of liberation. 102.
There is no field or sacred ford whatsoever equal to this;
therefore, O Brahmin, by my command, let a residence be established here.
Because he is the essential nature of all mantras, he is superior to all on earth; such is the ultimate nature of this abode of the [divine] form. (104)
No one else would be able to understand it, except for a person who has been gazed upon by my glance, once I have mentally adopted the style appropriate for Kālikā. (105)
The Tantra called Pāñcarātra has been duly brought down; according to the method taught therein, [the rites] based on the fundamental acts and festivals [are to be performed]. (106)
Having established the three forms, perform the worship; and let the offering of oblations be respectfully prepared according to the prescribed rule. (107)
Among the three jewels, the tantra known as the Jayākhyam is said to be the most excellent; let the consecration and other rites be performed according to the procedure prescribed therein. 108.
The two descendants of Upagu and Kauśika were students of the Kāṇva recension;
both were experts in the scripture of surrender and firmly established in their own spiritual steadfastness.
Having initiated them according to the path of the Jayākhyatantra upon the lotus mandala,
and having consecrated them in the office of the preceptor (ācārya), perform worship for those two.
Let those born of that very lineage worship me until the end of the aeon,
together with the tantra known as Jayākhyam and the Pādma-tantra.
May [the Lord] always honor me with both the root text and its commentary;
for there is no fault of mixing tantras here between these two tantras. 112.
O Lotus-born One, whether in the role of preceptor, officiating priest, or in worship, these two are considered by me to be the primary kinsmen who bring me joy. (113)
Having determined with their minds which of them are fit for those various services,
let them be initiated and appointed there according to the prescribed rule.
In this section, regarding those two alone who are of noble lineage,
there are the sages Śāṇḍilya, Bharadvāja, and likewise Mauñjāyana.
And these five principal members belonging to the [five] lineages have resorted to the Kāṇva school; they are all engaged in this my ritual work according to the illustrious Prāñcarātra Tantra. (116)
"O child, I have been gratified for a long time here by those two through the power of their asceticism; therefore, this boon was granted by me out of affection when requested by them. (117)
Together with the Vedic mantras specified in the Kāṭhaka Sūtra, they were interspersed with divine mantras perfected in the teachings of the Blessed One. || 118 ||

p. 16) All the sacraments beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), as well as the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and the occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as the ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), must be performed by them without sloth. (119)
O Lotus-seated One, by this very conduct alone— just as with milk mixed with sugar— my mind becomes filled with joy.
O sinless one, coming here every year in the month of Caitra on the full moon day, you shall worship me, the all-pervading Lord, in my own form.
Every day at night, however, Śeṣa, the best of the serpent-bearers,
will worship me in a non-material form.
Thus instructed by the King, Vidhi, though his mind was dependent on another's will,
personally carried out those very tasks with affection and respect.
At the time of his descent as a god, a celestial chariot of incomparable radiance,
divine and composed of all the gods, emerged from the midst of the fire.
In that very manner, by the command of the God of gods, the giver of boons,
the consecration was duly performed upon the earth according to the rite for the site (vāstu-vidhi).
At the command of the gods, Viriñca clearly instructed Viśvakarman on the manner of constructing the divine abode. (126)
Carrying his command upon his head, he constructed a divine abode by the very path prescribed by him, under his direct supervision.
Because the God of gods consists of the three root mantras,
that triple seat was first placed in his presence together with the syllable Om.
For the purpose of recollecting the six-syllabled mantra of the Lord of Ramā,
he constructed six steps on the southern half-portion of the maṇḍapa.
Consisting of the twenty-four principles and numbering twenty-four,
it subsequently appeared as a flight of stairs equal in measure to the Gāyatrī.
Then, recollecting the supreme King of Mantras known as the "Duality," he whose inner self was free from possessiveness fashioned two radiant staircases.
Manifesting the ten syllables as those which remove the suffering of the prostrate and which please the Divine through the divine mantra, he then performed the ten [rites]. || 132 ||
What is the use of saying more here? This great abode of the God of gods attained the status of being characterized by the defining marks described in the scriptures of the Lord. 133.
(17) Karīśa, the beloved of Kamalā, at the proper time, having given instructions to the lotus-born Brahmā according to his own will, caused his own abode to be constructed by him.
Then, when the time had been indicated by the Lord, the Lotus-born One prescribed the ritual for consecration according to the path of the Jayākhyatantra.
He had Viśvakarman fashion the primary image (mūlabera) out of wood, the ritual image (karmārcā) out of silver, and the festival image (autsavam) out of copper.
And then, according to the prescribed rite, Vidhi likewise caused the offering of oblations (bali) to be performed for the teacher Aupagāyana and the ascetic Kauśika.
And having duly initiated his two highly fortunate sons at a time when the solar disc was like a lotus, each resembling a son of a god, [he established them]. 138.
Through them, he caused all the work, beginning with the plowing, to be performed up to the consecration;
and previously, in the month of Vaiśākha under the asterism of Śravaṇa, he made the formal vow for the final purificatory bath.
On the ninth day, Vidhi caused the hoisting of the banner according to the prescribed rite;
on the first day, he had the Lord of Gods [installed] within a brilliantly shining pavilion.
Out of compassion for his devotees, he caused the processions to move in the morning;
at night, he celebrated the festival of the Lord with the lion as his vehicle.
On the morning of the second day, he performed the ritual of riding upon the swan-vehicle;
at night, he celebrated a great festival with the solar disc.
On the third day, at dawn, he performed the festival of Garuḍa;
for in ancient times, this was the first festival held after the descent of the Lord.
The Lord, the husband of Ramā, seated upon the divine Vainateya,
first revealed his own transcendent form.
Then, in the center of the principal gopura, specifically in the middle of the front of the gopura where Garuḍa is the vehicle,
service to the deity is especially distinguished.
This meritorious [rite], which removes all sins and is proclaimed as the path to liberation,
was performed by Hanumān at night for the sake of the God of Gods.
On the morning of the fourth day, Hari revealed his own form upon the surface of the remaining throne to his devotees, as if he were in the supreme realm.
At night, there was a festival for him as he occupied the orb of the moon;
in the morning, having assumed the form of Mohinī, he mounted a palanquin.
On the fifth day, the Lord of Gods gladdened all his devotees;
at night, however, he celebrated the festival of the God with the carrying of the child. (149)
On the sixth day, at dawn, there was a festival of flute-singing at the Kalpataru tree;
having mounted the lordly elephant during the night, he displayed a divine form. || 150 ||
On the seventh day, having placed the divine chariot [in the water], he celebrated a festival;
on the eighth day, however, Hari immersed himself in a wooden trough filled with water during the daytime.
At night, mounting his horse, he delivered all the worlds from suffering;
on the ninth day, the Lord of Ramā arranged for a palanquin procession.
Having displayed a playful display of lover’s anger toward the two lotus-eyed ones,
he performed the ceremonial bath (avabhṛtha) in the preeminent lake of Ananta.
At night, the Lord, stationed in the celestial chariot named Puṇyakoṭi,
wandered throughout the entire city and purified all the worlds.
On the tenth day at midday, there was a festival of flower offerings;
at night, a city procession was arranged with a great celestial chariot.
Having duly planted a victory banner topped with a bird-king (garuḍa), which leads one beyond all obscurations,
the worshipper is highly honored.
Thus, with great enthusiasm, he caused a grand festival to be held;
in this very manner, the procedure for the great festival was established to be performed every year. (157)
Festivals occurred in succession for the fortnights, months, solstices, years, and so forth;
those two great sages, the descendants of Upagāyana and Kauśika, were both initiated. (158)
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods here with devotion in this very manner, this abode of great majesty has attained the renown of Hastiśaila. 159.
Where the God who removes the suffering of those who prostrate and grants boons is worshipped, his worshippers—high-souled and radiant with virtues—become subject to his power. (160)
He is superior even to all the foremost followers of the Pāñcarātra on earth;
thus has the majesty of Hastiśaila been fully described. 161.
This is indeed the compendium of the *Tantrasāra*, the manual for the worshiper of the Lord, just as it was previously heard by me from the mouth of the sage Nārada. (162)
In this very manner, everything has been explained with affection as it arose in the course of discussion;
now, I shall commence the primary tantra itself. (163)
"Listen with attention and with great faith and devotion.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Purpose of Commencing the Scripture," in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Creation of Brahmā.
The sages said:
"O great sage, you are our refuge for us who are submerged in the mire of ignorance."
Just as was previously stated by the Lord to the sage, the son of Brahmā.
You ought to relate all of that today in detail and according to the truth, [O Nārada, son of Brahmā, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of existence]. (2)
Śāṇḍilya said:
Having placed his own self before him for the benefit of true devotees,
and having remembered the lotus feet of Hari and bowed his head in salutation— (3)
With palms joined in reverence, composed in mind, and with face and eyes wide open in joy,
he bowed down out of affection for the sake of pacifying the afflictions of dualistic suffering.
Having approached, he recited this hymn at his feet.
[The Praise of the Blessed One composed by Nārada] Nārada said:
Salutations be to the Supreme Lord, the ultimate cause and the transcendent.
To you who possess a thousand heads and a thousand feet, who have a thousand eyes and ears, and whose marvelous valor is a thousandfold! 6.
Salutations to the one whose body possesses the splendor of a thousand suns, who has the radiance of a thousand moons,
the supreme swan, and that which is higher than the highest.
Homage to the one whose form is sattva, to the peaceful one, and to the refuge of the universe;
to Bhava, to the remover of worldly existence, and to the source of creation.
Salutations to the one whose womb is gold, salutations to the sustainer of all bodies;
salutations to you, the Supreme Self, who consists of the three Vedas and the three qualities from the beginning.
Salutations indeed to You, who dwell in the cave of the heart-lotus, who reside within the limit of the supreme ether, and who are truly graspable by those practicing the yoga of devotion. 10.
You are the fish with closed eyes, you are the tortoise, and you are the upholder of the mountain;
having assumed that foremost form, the circle of the earth was supported by you.
Fear and fearlessness were both held by you within the single body of Narasiṃha;
as Vāmana, you concealed your form, and as Trivikrama, you expanded it. (12)
O Lord, by means of your delightful form as Rāma, and likewise by the three forms of Rāma,
you have conquered the Daityas and the Rākṣasas who were disguised in secret forms.
You are Kṛṣṇa, the pervasive Lord Dāmodara Hari in the form of a child;
you are the universal form, and for the gods you are the Lord Kapila of the Sāṅkhya tradition.
You are indeed the goal of yogis, the soul of Śeṣa, and the upholder of the earth;
you are Saṅkarṣaṇa for the wise, and the flower-armed god of love for those possessed by desire. || 15 ||
And as Aniruddha, you are the life-force of all, O Acyuta;
by you, O Janārdana, this entire world was created through your nature as Brahmā.
O Keśava, having yourself become Viṣṇu, you protect that which is established;
O Govinda, in the form of Rudra, you destroy the world in an instant.

O Lord of the entire universe, you carry the sacrificial oblation (havya) to the gods through the form of the sacrifice and by means of the mouth of the fire, and you carry the ancestral offering (kavya) to the ancestors. 18.
With devotion, I propitiate you, the Lord who bestows liberation from worldly existence, the God who grants the happiness of the gods, and the giver of nectar to the deities. (19)
Within your belly abide the worlds and the continents together with the oceans,
along with the gods, the dānavas, and the sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
All that exists—humans, demons, rivers, and mountains—is situated within you; you abide as the inner essence of everything.
You are the primordial one of this world; by remembering you, we become eternally awakened and happy wherever we may abide.
You are the Praṇava with its three measures, and you alone are Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ;
you are indeed the creator of the ego, the triad that delivers the worlds.

[The prayer offered by Nārada, desiring to behold the form of the Blessed One and wishing to know the manner of the creation of the world: "Therefore, O Lord, instruct me quickly so that I may cross over [this ocean of existence]."
Having presided over supreme intelligence, may I attain further spiritual welfare. || 24 ||
O Lord of Gods, reveal your own true form to me, your devotee, who desires supreme knowledge and is terrified by the fear of worldly existence.
Tell me how all this was created by you, from the abode of Brahmā down to the end, and likewise how the sky became so difficult to traverse through your supreme illusion. (26)
[The Blessed One’s manifestation of his two forms, consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest] Śāṇḍilya:
Thus urged by supreme devotion, the Supreme Lord—
By the divine seer Nārada, who possesses perfectly pure intellect.
At that very moment, Hari revealed to him who had been spoken of— the entire Self, which is both manifest and profound, and yet essentially partless.
Then the sage, the son of Brahmā, having attained supreme satisfaction, spoke again with great affection and full of humility. (29)
Through your grace, that which is difficult even for the gods to attain has been known by me;
now I desire to hear of your manifestation and your dissolution.
Regarding the times of the creation and dissolution of the world,
the Blessed One said:
"O Brahman, this world which you see here has been fashioned by Māyā."
It is divided by many distinctions such as time and so forth, possessing various essential natures. || 31 ||
For my day is indeed the period of manifestation, and its dissolution occurs at the arrival of night;
know that a thousand divine yugas constitute my single day.
When such a dissolution has occurred, the night should be known to be of equal duration;
however, when the day begins, it is characterized by the period called creation.

O bull among sages, without having first mastered his own causal nature, for the sake of the effect, he created the four-faced Brahmā from the lotus at his navel by the power of his knowledge and yoga— a being composed of water and enveloped in majesty. (34)
Impelled by me through the aperture of the navel, my heart-lotus—which exists within my internal organ and consists of the nature of mere representation—[is sent forth]. (35)
Resembling a thousand suns, with a thousand moons as its filaments,
containing a thousand fires within it, with a golden stalk and great radiance.

In the midst of that, I created the four-faced Manu, who is Brahmā. Through his union with the specific power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), he became the eternal source of the worlds, possessing a body of knowledge (vidyā-deha). || 37 ||

(22) He was perfected in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), was endowed with the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*, and was possessed of the powers of creative emanation. || 38 ||
[The manifold creation brought about by the predominance of the quality of rajas:
When I was not known by him and he had become arrogant, having acquired the notion "I am," he was defiled by rajas. (39)
Then he performed his own manifold creation in due succession,
consisting of those elements which had previously been latent, both gross and subtle.
Those called sentient and non-sentient are manifested in succession:
gods with their many divisions, as well as humans and animals. (41)
Having seen all things whatsoever that exist within this world, down to the stationary beings, as his own abodes, the Grandfather [Brahmā] beheld them all within himself.
Due to the predominance of passion and the consequent subjugation of his sattva-nature, this four-faced one lacks the capacity to properly sustain his own world.
In this world, however, there is nothing done or left undone without the arising of a sentient being.
[The Blessed One’s recourse to yogic sleep for the support of the earth:
Having thus assumed his own great form accompanied by a lotus, he placed it within the waters for the purpose of supporting the earth. (44)
O best of the twice-born, having resorted to yogic sleep, I remained there.
Indeed, as Brahmā was being born, two drops of sweat appeared; from these were born Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were radiant with power. They achieved victory over all the worlds.
Taking refuge in the lotus stalk, they remained within the interior of the belly;
then there arose two invincible beings known by the names Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Consisting of desire and anger, and exceedingly filled with darkness (tamas),
they remained established, having been made to increase by the pride born of darkness.
What is this? While speculating about that lotus among themselves, they remained intent on their curiosity, having taken refuge in the depths of Pātāla.
Furthermore, from that Pātāla down as far as Kālavaiśvānara,
having then produced a fiery illusion, those two went beneath the fire.
(23) There was no end to the lotus-stalk, which was enveloped in flames of splendor;
O twice-born one, when they had fallen into some delusion out of pride, then— [50]
Then, having resolved to go upward, I reached that higher place; meanwhile, that lotus had vanished, and we both were filled with wonder.
But when those two most terrible ones stood still, they wondered, "Where has that lotus gone?
And rising up from the midst of the water, they beheld this earth.
They set their minds upon traveling through the worlds of the foremost sages;
and having seen all that splendor, such was the thought that arose in them both at that time.
Regarding the complete appropriation of all worlds, beginning with the earth,
they then conquered all the worlds as well as the intermediate realms between them.
The entire world of moving and non-moving beings was pervaded by an exceedingly painful darkness.
[Due to the theft of the Vedas committed by those two, the four-faced Brahmā suffered a loss of knowledge; through the increase of unrighteousness, the world fell into a state of wretchedness.]
Brahmā was deprived of the Vedas, and at that very moment, another one came into being.
O Brahmin, since he formerly resorted to the Veda as his eye even without the Vedas, he established the instability of the world and brought about a great foundation of unrighteousness. (56)
Then those two wicked ones, characterized by darkness (tāmasa), returned once more to the midst of the waters.
At that time, Brahmā was awakened by the gods together with the sages. (57) [The Awakening of the Four-faced One Performed by the Sages]
Remember the Primordial God, for you were born from the lotus;
he alone is the bestower of our welfare, provided that the Veda is true. (58)
"Out of pride, you did not recognize the Supreme Cause, by which this painful misfortune has been established in this world. (59)
That Blessed One is your cause, and he is our cause;
remember Viṣṇu, the unconquerable, O Lotus-born one, who is the supreme cause. (60)
[The Blessed One’s Praise Composed by the Four-Faced One as Awakened by the Sages:
Thereupon, Brahmā, his passion stilled and his mind focused solely on pure being, became intent on offering praise together with all the deities and sages. (61)
"My Vedic dharma has perished; O Acyuta, I have no refuge!
Save me, save me!"—thus he spoke repeatedly when he was overcome with extreme distress. (62)
(p. 24) [The granting of fearlessness by the Blessed One:
At that time, when my sense of "mine-ness" had reached a state of exhaustion, I descended as a Brahmin.
When the Vedas had been lost and Brahman had fallen into a state of non-Brahmanhood, || 63 ||
"Fearlessness has been granted by me to them, and this world has been brought to rest;
moreover, a twofold form consisting of knowledge and illusion has been created by me. (64)
[The extraction of the Vedas from Pātāla, performed by the Blessed One after assuming a form consisting of knowledge:
By means of a form consisting of knowledge and consisting of the Śabdabrahman.
The Vedas situated within the netherworld were indeed retrieved by means of the syllable Om.
[The four-faced one's mastery of the Vedas through the entry of the Lord whose form consists of knowledge:
Then, having entered this body born from the lotus, I—
Then, having regained consciousness, he caused the Vedas to be recited once again.
Then all the lords of the worlds remained exceedingly joyful;
freed from the fear of darkness and delusion, they returned to their own abodes.
Assuming an illusory form, I stood before them both in my second body to engage the Blessed One in combat with them.
But those two wicked ones, intoxicated with pride, are desirous of fighting with me. || 68 ||
Then, with a body composed entirely of illusion and possessing many arms,
those two were made to fight me for many thousands of years.
[The slaying of the two after perceiving their invincibility by assuming a form consisting of mantra:
O twice-born one, having realized that those two were invincible, I became invisible;
then, having assumed a great form composed of mantra and consisting of power (śakti). (70)
And by those two [arms], he was indeed difficult to overcome and likewise difficult to behold like the sun;
yet I, seizing him effortlessly by the neck with my pair of hands, [held him].
Massaged by his two thighs, the gods departed free from all thorns;
[the etymology of the word *medinī*:
the Earth (*vasundharā*) was filled with the fat (*medas*) produced therefrom. (72)
From that time forward, she has been called Medinī;
thus, O sage, this creation of Brahmā has been described by me to you. (73)
Indeed, many other creations of manifold forms have passed away—
such as these in their manifestation and grossness, the number of which is not known.
The first twice-born among these was a follower of Pradhāna; his foremost disciple was a supreme Vaiṣṇava.
What else shall I tell you? Speak, for whatever doubt remains. (75)
"O tiger among sages, even now I shall declare that to you.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Creation of Brahmā," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Primary Creation.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the worlds, Master of the universe!"
Tell me of the primary creation, which is indeed that which is beyond this gross [creation]. || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
(The definition of Pradhāna) O twice-born one, it is beginningless, unborn, unmanifest, and composed of the three qualities.
Know that which has the characteristic of a single essence to be distinct [from the body], standing in the place of a lamp. || 2 ||
(From the Pradhāna, the production of the principles beginning with Mahat occurs in sequence);

and that which has arisen is differentiated in sequence as sattva, rajas, and tamas; for indeed, from the aggregate of the three guṇas arises [the intellect] characterized by dharma, jñāna, and so forth.

O best of the intelligent, the intellect (buddhi) and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which consists of three aspects—the luminous aspect (prakāśātmā), the transformative aspect (vikṛtyātmā), and the third, the elemental aspect (bhūtātmā). || 4 ||
From the taijasa [element] and from samāna alone, the five organs of perception are born:
namely, the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose, in their respective order.
And by means of his own transformation, he created the pentad of organs;
these are traditionally known as speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals.
Know that he is indeed always the elemental self and the creator of the sources of the elements;
likewise, [he is] sound and touch, as well as those which designate form, taste, and smell.
From the [subtle] elements, the gross elements were born: ether, air, fire, water, and earth; these five possess an increasing number of qualities by one at each stage.
This is the creation of Pradhāna, which is insentient by nature.
Nārada said:
"Pradhāna is insentient, and its manifestation is of that same nature. (9)
And tell me, O Lord, what kind of relationship of producer and produced can there be between things that are mutually insentient? For in this matter, my doubt is great. (10)
(The logical justification for the relationship of cause and effect among insentient things) The Blessed One said:
"O twice-born one, just as a seed is insentient, so too is a grain of rice."
That which is seen as the producer in other things is likewise the reality in that very reality.

For there is indeed a single continuum belonging to that which is of the nature of the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), that which is the locus of passion and so forth, and that which is both conscious and unconscious. (12)
Nārada said:
O Lord, how can this insentient reality become sentient again—this principle which is the locus of these qualities, yet which is one, though existing in manifold ways? (13)
(An Exposition on the Possibility of Consciousness Being Joined to the Insentient) The Blessed Lord said:
That reality of the Self, whose nature is consciousness, exists as non-different from Brahman.
Therefore, O twice-born one, this shines forth as if variegated by the non-sentient and the sentient.
Just as iron is seen to be moved when presided over by a magnet, even so has this been declared by me. (15)
Nārada said:
"O Lord of Gods, the cause for the connection between this conscious [Self] and this insentient [body] is being stated;
I understand this to be as contradictory as shade and sunlight. (16)
(The cause of bondage in the conjunction of consciousness and the unconscious, and of liberation in their separation,) the Blessed Lord said:
"This individual soul (jīva), whose nature is indeed consciousness, is joined with beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā)."
Or rather, O twice-born one, it is for the purpose of removing the latent impressions (vāsanā) from the supreme Brahman.
That [power], possessing those attributes, arises subtle and of a single form;
it is both pure and impure in nature, yet pure, consisting of supreme bliss.
Having arrived through the sequence of the pure creation, he abides within the inner self in the form of an ocean of compassion, capable of bestowing liberation upon living beings.
For he indeed resolved: "Let there be liberation for this performer of ritual action.
Then that power of the Universal Self, conforming to his will, [acted].
(27) Relying upon the inner consciousness, it remains for that moment, invisible like the power of a mantra; awakened by that, O twice-born one, (21).

And when the aggregate of karma has reached its destruction, the inner self, whose nature is consciousness and whose own form was previously overwhelmed by [the light of] radiance, attains oneness with Brahman. (22)
Therefore, indeed, there is no destruction of karmas that have not been experienced;
nor can their manifestation occur without a substratum. Thus it is. (23)
Residing therein, that portion of Brahman indeed applies itself to the support consisting of Māyā—the support of the qualities (guṇas), which is extended and insentient—O twice-born ones. (24)
For when the self is joined with its power (śakti), it perceives its own latent impressions (vāsanās),
which consist of both auspicious and inauspicious natures and reside eternally within the substratum of Māyā.
When one whose discernment is indeed unimpaired enjoys the fruit of latent impressions without attachment, he is swiftly liberated from bonds and proceeds gradually toward the Supreme.
Then, lacking discernment, he may become attached to the enjoyment of illusion which consists of the qualities;
possessed of latent impressions, he is bound by those very impressions, even though he remains unchanging in essence. (27)
Thus, having come to rest, he repeatedly experiences both dissolution and emergence;
this is the purpose of the connection between the conscious and the unconscious. (28)
"O Nārada, I have spoken; what shall I say to you now?
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Primary Creation," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Reality of the Pure Creation.
Nārada said:
"O Lord, I desire to know the pure creation according to its true nature."
And that which exists as the supreme state beyond these two creations. || 1 ||
(The manifestation of Acyuta and others, who are non-different from Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman):
The Blessed Lord said:
"That which is the all-pervading God, the supreme, eternal Brahman..."
In this world, the universal consciousness is characterized by supreme bliss.

But that which is non-different from Vāsudeva and the others, possessing the splendor of a hundred fires, suns, and moons—that is the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord whose nature is that [splendor]. (3)
Having agitated that which was self-illuminated by means of his energy, which is like lightning and like a hawk, the Lord Acyuta, whose form is light, emitted him, O twice-born one. (4)
That Acyuta, possessing unchanging splendor, expands his own form by taking refuge in Vāsudeva, just as a cloud [spreads] over the sun's orb. || 5 ||
Having agitated his own self, he then brought forth a true, radiant form, just as the ocean produces a bubble.
He, known as the light of pure consciousness, produced by himself from his own self the great expansion of light called Puruṣa, which is infinite.
[The inner controller-ship of Vāsudeva, who has manifested as the Self of the Person, over all the gods:
And he indeed is the supreme lord, the refuge of all the gods;
he is their inner controller, just as the sky is for the stars. (8)
O twice-born one, just as fire, though itself inactive, impels a multitude of sparks,
so too does this Supreme Lord impel [beings], even though they have no desire [to act].
For those living beings bound by prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), in order to bring about the cessation of bondage, [one should contemplate] one's own body... and furthermore, both of these.
[The Incarnations as Parts of Him]:

Know that those who are the primordial incarnations, entrusted with the office of protecting the world—all of them are parts of Him; likewise, all beings born of the quality of goodness (sattva) are His parts. 11.
[The abiding of the Puruṣas, who are real and immutable, within the supreme form of Vāsudeva as non-different from each successive essential nature:
And He (Vāsudeva) is indeed non-different from the Real; therefore, the Real is likewise [non-different from Him].
That which has a single nature through both [means] is indeed non-different from the Imperishable.

The Person (puruṣa), who is always non-different from those two, is indeed supported by and situated within them; he is both real (satya) and immutable (acyuta). That triad, moreover, is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa). 13.

And he abides in Vāsudeva, whose nature is peaceful consciousness. [This is the demonstration of the non-difference, with illustrative examples, between Vāsudeva whose form is consciousness and the three forms— Acyuta and the others— that have manifested from him.]
He is the inner controller, whose nature is light, whose form is consciousness, and he is firmly established. || 14 ||
In that triad, whatever arises in such a manner always without desire, all of these, being of the nature of non-conceptualization, flow forth into one another. (15)
O tiger among sages, like a lamp, they indeed bestow light upon both themselves and others; likewise, though existing in a state of mutual distinction, they remain so without any deliberate volition.
O twice-born one, because of their extreme purity, they take on the state of reflections within one another, like a mirror [reflecting] mirrors. 17.
O best of Brahmins, just as no distinction arises between the sky and a crystal,
so too there is non-difference among those two aspects of light.
This supreme secret has been fully revealed by me to you: the beginningless and endless creation of the infinite Great Self. 19.
Nārada said: O Lord of All, by your grace all this has been understood by me—
how indeed you, though unmanifest and formless, have assumed a manifest form.
O Blessed One, I desire to know your true nature as it really is—your gross, subtle, and supreme forms, both within the self and externally. (21)
How can this triad be manifested for those situated in the objects of the senses without the power of your grace? Grant me your favor and tell me.
[The description of the form of the Blessed Lord existing in three ways as gross, subtle, and supreme.
Śrī Bhagavān:
O Nārada, by means of my own yogic power, I am indeed the creator, the protector, and once again the destroyer, appearing in a gross form.
In a subtle form, I dwell within the hearts of all beings;
I also bestow grace upon my devotees whose minds are purified.
O Brahmin, I pervade everything with my supreme form of bliss, which is all-encompassing and stainless, just as sap permeates the finest of trees.
When the root is watered, it becomes endowed with crest, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit.
Nārada said:
"O Lord, the world was created by you and is sustained by you. (26)
In the end, you alone are remembered as the one who effects destruction in the form of Time;
and those worlds beginning with Pātāla have arisen from your navel. (27)
Furthermore, the re-establishment of the Dharma was indeed accomplished by you once again;
the Daityas were destroyed by you—this has been heard and understood by me. (28)
In what manner and by what means you yourself perform this, I truly desire to learn that from you in great detail. (29)

[The demonstration that the form of the mantra, which is divided twofold as having both a differentiated (sakala) and undifferentiated (niṣkala) nature, serves as the cause for both bondage and its opposite.
The Blessed Lord said:
O best of Brahmins, through the power of yoga, she who is ancient and consists of mantra—
both partless and with parts— is auspicious, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

And by me, with a most tranquil mind, has been composed this auspicious work which provides perfect illumination for the worlds, established precisely according to the sequence of the origin of mantras.
Indeed, for the destruction of those two embodied defects consisting of darkness (tamas),
she herself remains in the world as Prakṛti, the protectress of the universe.
She who performs such deeds as these within this womb of existence quickly liberates her devotees by effecting the complete destruction of their bonds. (33)
Nārada said:
"O Creator of the Universe, if you have favor toward me, then instruct me completely regarding that yoga, its mantra, and its very power. (34)
[On the statement that the thorough knowledge of mantras, their potency, and so forth, is rooted in the knowledge of Brahman:
The Blessed Lord said:
"All this, concerning which you have questioned me, is preceded by Brahman. (35)
"O Lord of the Lords of Yoga, what is that Brahman by means of which those [states] you have described do not arise?
Nārada said:
"What should I understand that Brahman to be, O Lord of the Lords of Yoga, by means of which [those states do not arise]? (36)

O All-pervading One, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, for those who are devoted, the manifestation [of your power], the mantra preceded by [your presence], and likewise the ritual implements of the mantra, quickly come forth. (37)

The Blessed One said: "O Nārada, through knowledge that is non-different from That and which has been fully realized, union with Brahman arises; therefore, one should practice knowledge thoroughly. (38)
Nārada said:
O Lord, tell me that knowledge which bestows the perfection of Brahman and its characteristics, by knowing which there shall be no more birth, death, or bondage to worldly existence. (39)
The Blessed Lord said:

Know that knowledge is twofold—namely, that which is called "being" (sattā) and that which consists of "action" (kriyā). The accomplishment of that which is called "being" occurs through that which is termed "action."
Through the repeated practice of that which is called "existence" by means of that which is called "activity," steadfastness shall arise. || 40 ||
Nārada said:
O Lord, first tell me what kind of knowledge consists of action, by the practice of which I may come to know that which is called "Being," which grants the perfection of Brahman. (41)
[The twofold nature of action through the divisions of *yama* and *niyama*]: The Blessed One said:
"Action and knowledge are twofold; first, that characterized by *niyama*."
That which is called Yama is indeed supreme, and it is remembered as being innate (svābhāvika). || 42 ||
Having accomplished that which is called restraint (*niyama*) and that which is joined with self-control (*yama*), which bestows perfection—Nārada said:
"Tell me the characteristics of these two, upon which the supreme state depends. (43)
"O Lord of the World, [please explain] in detail for me, who have fallen into the ocean of existence, the exposition of the restraints and observances.
The Blessed One said:
Purity, sacrifice, austerity, and likewise the study of one's own Vedic texts preceded by hearing [the scriptures]. || 44 ||
Absence of cruelty, lack of harshness, and unfailing patience; truthfulness, the welfare of living beings, and non-injury even toward others. (45)
Non-violence toward the property of others, great self-restraint of the mind, and lack of longing even for the enjoyments that serve as food for the senses. (46)
Whether on a seat, in bed, on the road, or even while eating,
one should not abandon the meditation residing in the heart, which yields the fruit of bliss.
Giving according to one's own power, truthful speech that is not harsh, and always maintaining an even mind toward both enemies and friends. (48)
Uprightness, freedom from crookedness, and compassion toward all living beings—he who is endowed with these limbs is Yama, the restrainer of self-restraint. (49)
[From the accomplishment known as action, there arises knowledge non-different from Brahman; by that, there is the attainment of Brahman.
Thus, a human being attains the knowledge known as existence from that which is called action.
From that knowledge called "existence," which is non-different from Brahman, further knowledge arises. (50)
From that knowledge which is non-different from Brahman, one is united with the Supreme Brahman;
[this attainment of Brahman is liberation characterized by the absence of rebirth].
That which is called the *jīva* is endowed with beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 51 ||
His attainment of Brahman is that which consists in non-rebirth;
it is the state of being a perfect knower of Brahman, characterized by even a slight degree of non-difference from Brahman. (52)
A slight attainment of Brahman is indeed considered non-different from it.
However, due to the association with ignorance (avidyā), the distinction of the Self as gods and so forth arises;
yet, through various forms of knowledge, that very Self attains its true nature.
Regarding the reality consisting of the qualities (guṇamaya) and that which consists of perfect knowledge (samyagvidyāmaya), Nārada said:
"What indeed is called the 'qualities' (guṇa), and what is ignorance (avidyā), wherein the Lord is composed of knowledge? (54)
"O All-pervading Lord, that which was spoken by you attains reality through various kinds of distinctions"— [this is the definition of the nature of ignorance]. The Blessed One said:
The equilibrium of the three qualities (guṇas) is that which is ignorance (avidyā), possessing manifold forms. || 55 ||
And [he described] the very source of the arising of defects such as passion and the rest.
Nārada said:
"That which was previously declared as the correct means for attaining Brahman... (56)
And tell me, what are the characteristics of that which you have called the Self?
[The Definition of the Individual Soul and the Self] The Blessed Lord said:
That which is the abiding nature of consciousness, which has not emerged from self-awareness and so forth; || 57 ||
"O twice-born one, that Self which is colored by the passion for qualities has been described.
Nārada said:
Knowledge is the true nature of the Self, while Māyā is indeed its colorer. (58)
"Tell me, O Blessed One, that Brahman which was previously urged by me;
for I do not fully understand that for whose sake ritual action is performed. (59)
(33) That which, once attained, no further rebirth in this world is experienced by the wise— [this is the description of the Supreme Brahman]. The Blessed Lord said:
Brahman is characterized by bliss and is devoid of everything that is to be abandoned.
Self-cognizable and incomparable, it is the supreme pinnacle, the supreme goal;
liberated from all activity, it is the Lord, the refuge of all. (61)
Just as everything material and attached is situated within the wish-fulfilling gem,
so too does everything exist everywhere within that which is all-pervading.
It is without beginning and without end; it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
Its hands, feet, and faces are everywhere, and its eyes, heads, and mouths are on all sides.
Know that which possesses ears everywhere; it stands pervading everything, illuminated by all the senses along with their qualities, yet indeed devoid of them.
For that is unattached everywhere, and indeed it is present everywhere;
it is devoid of qualities yet the enjoyer of qualities, situated both within and without all things.
Know that [the Supreme Self] is both moving and unmoving; because of its subtlety, it is not perceived.
Thus the Supreme Lord, the Paramātman, dwells within the heart even while remaining at a distance.
Though undivided from the elements, it is perceived as divided; it is the sustainer of beings and their states, and it both creates and withdraws.
That light which illumines all luminaries stands beyond ignorance;
it is itself knowledge and the object of knowledge, and it is attained through meditation upon it. 68.
Devoid of all [ordinary] colors and tastes, yet endowed with all fragrances and flavors;
he is the omniscient, the all-seeing, the all, the Lord of all, and the Sovereign.
The Supreme Lord is composed of all powers, independent,
beginningless, endless, and entirely free from all suffering.
Having thus known the Supreme Brahman through supreme knowledge, when that person is not born again in this saṃsāra, then he [is liberated]. || 71 ||
Nārada said:
"That which has been described by you through characteristics such as having hands and feet everywhere—that cannot be established as one; explain how that is possible."
(34) O Nārada, this greatness of the Lord of the World, who is omniscient, exists because of his infinity and his sovereignty. (73)
Just as I have not yet declared his state of surpassing all others,
so too does this majesty of his exist in Acyuta.
Because it is beginningless and prior to everything, it is neither existent nor non-existent;
O best of the twice-born, it is non-existent [as a perceptible object] because it is not an object of the senses. (75)
Know that it is self-cognizable, just as the fragrance of flowers and the like;
for in this way, everything is indeed withdrawn by the Supreme Self.
Therefore, indeed, the omnipresence of that which is all-pervading is inferred;
for it is not limited by space, nor is it separated by time. (77)
Therefore, because he is all-pervading, the Lord is remembered as one who protects from every side;
just as the sun illuminates with its upward, downward, and horizontal rays, so does he shine forth.
Likewise, because it is of the nature of light, the Unborn (Aja) is therefore the eye of all;
just as among all limbs, the head is proclaimed to be the foremost.
O best of men, for ordinary beings in this world, it is not so;
however, because of his equanimity and purity, the Lord Siddhaśiras is [different]. (80)
Since all the subsequent flavors are indeed always present within him who is of a peaceful nature everywhere, he is therefore remembered as "all-faced" (sarvamukha). || 81 ||
Know that the aggregate of sounds is indeed the Supreme Lord;
therefore, he possesses ears everywhere, just as the serpent has eyes and ears on its body.
Just as fire exists within a mass of iron, appearing distinct yet as if non-distinct, so too does the Lord abide, pervading all this while remaining separate from it. (83)
Just as some object appears upon a stainless mirror, yet that object does not belong to the mirror, while the reflection belongs to it, O twice-born one; (84)
Thus, though endowed with and yet free from the qualities associated with the senses, the Lord, the Sovereign of all, is all-pervading within this world composed of māyā. (85)
Know that he is always unattached, like water on a lotus leaf;
because he sustains all things, because of his universal form, and because of his infallibility, he is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Therefore, remaining like one indifferent, he is the enjoyer of the qualities of the *guṇas*;
just as water remains within a jar that is always situated inside it. (87)
Likewise, it is situated both outside and inside the entire world;
just as the space contained within a jar is perceived when the jar is being carried away. || 88 ||
Just as space does not go anywhere, yet the movement or stillness of a jar is perceived through the eye,
so too is the movement or stillness of the All-pervading Lord inferred.
Piercing through many lotus petals one after another,
it is not perceived at all times because of its extreme subtlety, like time itself.
Due to ignorance, that which is situated extremely far away is conceived as being within the heart through knowledge;
when that occurs, the self consisting of consciousness is realized by one's own direct experience as being close at hand.
And that which is the wind of space—since there is no difference between those two, there is likewise a unity of case-inflection between the elements and the Supreme. 92.
All beings, whether conscious or unconscious, moving or stationary,
are filled by the Supreme Lord, just as medicinal herbs are filled with sap.
O twice-born one, by the single, undifferentiated cause of being the sustainer of beings, light and darkness are indeed dependent upon the sun. (94)
In the same way, the independent Light brings about creation along with its withdrawal;
it is the illumination of the luminaries, and of the senses such as hearing, just as the mind is for them.
Even though sound and the other objects are not perceived [as they truly are], one nevertheless hears them otherwise;
just as light is distinct from darkness, so too is that [true perception] distinct from ignorance.
That very knowledge is also the object of knowledge, just like the flame of a fire;
for it is devoid of all colors, such as white and the rest, because it is formless.
