Just as [the color white] is devoid of conceptual construction through sweet and other tastes, so too that [reality], though devoid of all conceptualization, is metaphorically described by all colors, like the neck of a peacock. (98)
Due to the influence of the aesthetic flavors (rasas), He is likewise the essence of all flavors;
yet, being devoid of all [material] colors and flavors, He is therefore remembered as Acyuta (the Unfailing).
He is omniscient because he knows all things; he is all-seeing because he perceives everywhere;
and he is the Lord of All because of his equality with respect to omniscience and other such qualities. || 100 ||
It is logical that [the Self] is endowed with all powers within, possessed of the majesty of the six qualities, self-dependent due to its autonomy, and beginningless because it is ancient. (101)
For there is no end to this, it is therefore infinite; because of its satisfaction, it is free from suffering.
Indeed, the Lord of All, who is formless, is perceived through practice.
Just as fire [is not perceived] apart from wood, or just as ghee [is not perceived] apart from milk, so too it is not possible to speak [of it] without one's own direct experience. (103)
Just as sweetness residing in sugarcane is perceived even though it is formless,
so too is the Lord, the imperishable Supreme Self, present within one's own body.
Free from rejection and acceptance, its form is the bliss of pure whiteness;
it cannot be delimited by means of valid cognition, for it is the great essence of consciousness. 105.
He who shines in the space of the heart, free from illusion—this is the Lord Nārāyaṇa, devoid of all limiting adjuncts. || 106 ||
Take refuge in that supreme Lord who is indefinable and perceived by the highest knowledge, for he is self-cognized and exists even without a further object to be characterized. 107.
That which is devoid of analogies and beyond the reach of the intellect and the senses in worldly transactions—that cause is incomparable; those who know it are indeed fearless.
The Supreme Brahman, which transcends all phenomenal existence and resembles the purity of a crystal, is liberation;
those who are liberated go to it, and their abiding place is in that supreme state.
Indeed, though existing as a single entity, he dwells within all things through their various distinctions;
for that Great Soul has neither measure nor form.
By way of fire, wind, and water, and by means of ten thousand times ten thousand lotus-fibers,
he remains within extremely subtle atoms measured by a single sixteenth part of a grain.
Furthermore, among those [elements], in the gross forms, the pervasive Supreme Self, Adhokṣaja, is established according to the measure of the gross light previously described. || 112 ||
In the form of wind, he remains as the source of all beings who exist in crooked ways, and as the creation of all earthly things that are shaken from their forms without exception. 113.
Abiding in the form of the six tastes within all medicinal herbs, he is omnipresent;
they worship that imperishable one by means of many different names.
O best of Brahmins, he is indeed the Lord by virtue of his nature as Puruṣa, and likewise as the essence of Śiva-Sūrya and as Soma. || 115 ||
Furthermore, O Nārada, it exists as the nature of Agni and Soma, as sound, as the nature of the knowledge of light, and as time. (116)
Thus, by virtue of being the self of the field of living beings and likewise by virtue of being the self of the elements,
the one supreme God assumes the form of various powers and selves.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, the ultimate goal for those who know Brahman;
[this is the description of the attainment of Brahman by practitioners along with illustrative examples], just as people enter the interior of a great city. 118.
In the same way, the worshippers of Viṣṇu manifest many emanations in all directions;
for those who meditate are indeed always absorbed in the objects of meditation which have become the Lord.
O twice-born one, just as the digits of the moon enter the sun when its essence is exhausted, so too do yogis whose delusion has been destroyed enter Viṣṇu.
Just as water that has fallen separately upon the earth from a cloud attains oneness through the mass of falling streams,
so too do all yogis attain oneness within the Blessed One.
Just as various fuels and other substances, having entered into a fire,
are consumed without being individually perceived, so too are those who worship within Brahman.
Just as the waters of a multitude of rivers, having entered the great ocean,
have their distinctions unperceivable in that water, so it is for yogins in the Supreme.
O Sage, take refuge eternally in Him whom the knowers of the Self worship, from whom the sun shines forth; we are born from but a ten-millionth part of His essence.
Likewise, he who has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
the Lord who is filled with a thousand arms and who sustains a thousand selves.
O best of Brahmins, Śrīnivāsa is expanded by thousands of radiances, wears a crown,
has the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, and is adorned with the Kaustubha gem and other ornaments.
The moon and sun are located in the region of the eyes; Sarasvatī is in the assembly of the tongue;
and his breath is the wind, which rises upward until the end of time.

He whose ears are the cardinal directions and whose arms are the intermediate directions; he whose soles are to be known as existing from the netherworld (pātāla) downwards in the expanse of his feet. 128.
The fire of universal destruction is his radiance, and the clouds are the mass of his hair;
the gods and sages dwell within the pores of his body as his body hairs.
Fire is in the mouth, water is in the sweat; indeed, the planets, the stars, and so forth, are his impurity.
This impurity exists only by way of conventional designation, but not so in the ultimate sense. (130)
O Brahmin, I have thus explained to you the reality of Brahman according to its true nature;
having known which, you shall never again enter into this tumultuous cycle of existence.
O Brahmin, although this knowledge is all-pervading and resides within this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, it is nevertheless very difficult to attain.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Pure Creation and the Principle of Brahman," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Arising of the Knowledge of Brahman. Nārada said:
O All-pervading Lord, I desire to hear in its true essence the knowledge that is non-different from Brahman.
By which that which is to be known, residing within the internal organ, is fully attained. || 1 ||
[The fact that knowledge is obtainable solely through the practice of yoga:
The Blessed Lord [declared that] knowledge, which is entirely stainless and free from all limiting adjuncts, [is obtained only through the practice of yoga].
For that indeed arises for the disciplined one through the gradual practice of yoga. || 2 ||
By that means it is attained, O Brahmin; otherwise it would be difficult to obtain.
O Lord of the World, how could such knowledge as this arise in Nārada?
Please explain in detail that equality of the object of knowledge which would thus arise;
[through the power and efficacy of the Blessed One’s grace, there arises a desire to know the true nature of one's own self by attaining equilibrium of the qualities].
O Nārada, [I shall describe] the fruits situated upon the tree of worldly existence, O Blessed One.
And for those whose karmic juices have ripened and who are wandering in the ocean of existence,
through the power and efficacy of the Lord’s energy, the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya) may occur in an instant.
From that equanimity, an immediate equality of action arises;
from that equality, however, inquiry proceeds, which bestows the attainment of the Self.
Who am I, and of what nature am I? And what is this cage of suffering, wherein I have always remained without any peace?

Having thought thus, he then goes to the house of the perfected Guru. [This refers to the disciple who has approached with the desire to know (vividiṣā), being fit for application to the means according to his qualification.
And knowing his state of suffering, the omniscient one, manifesting in the form of the Guru— || 8 ||
Having understood that which shines as active, one should employ it accordingly;
but when that [activity] has been perceived within the seedless state, [the mind] reaches the supreme plane by its own power.

But in Nirvana—which is free from fear, full of bliss, and consisting of pure consciousness—or indeed in the Mantra [tradition], which is capable of bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one is authorized. || 10 ||
[The manner in which knowledge arises for one engaged in the propitiation of the mantra according to their own capacity:

But the great person who is intent on the propitiation of the mantra, who is not covetous of its supernatural powers (siddhis), who is devoted to it, established in meditation upon it, and supremely dedicated to its ritual practice; 11.
Then, desiring to face that [truth] and established in the vow of celibacy, he correctly contemplates existence as something great that bestows suffering and sorrow. (12)
It is impermanent, unstable, and miserable, crowded with old age and death; it is overcome by the fear of the union of dualities, insatiable, and transient. (13)
By constantly reflecting on this, as well as through the grace of mantras and the like, and also by means of bodily discipline, one shall attain supreme dispassion. || 14 ||
And from that dispassion, O Brahmin, the mind which has been turbidified by sense-objects attains clarity, just as water does in the autumn season. (15)
It attains a state of serene stability like a waveless ocean;
it is as motionless as a lamp in a windless place, facing directly toward awakening.
When a person characterized by consciousness enters that which is like the mind (or thought), and attains full awakening, that is remembered as the supreme knowledge. || 17 ||
That very consciousness indeed arises sequentially like the sun within the space of the heart;
by that, the object of knowledge is attained, just as the world is perceived through the rising of the sun.
Enlightenment is the culmination of the knowable; it arrives gradually, step by step.
For then, indeed, there is a state of equal flavor between that [knowledge] and him [the knower].
O Nārada, this knowledge which brings about the cognition of the knowable, which is endowed with sequential order, bestows liberation, and is unadulterated, has been fully revealed to you. (20)
Although that which appears as if possessed of difference is logically non-different from it, know this to be so by its very nature; indeed, there is nothing beyond this.
"O tiger among Brahmins, does [Brahman] exist there, or what proceeds therein? O sage, just as this self-luminous realm has been revealed to you by me, so it is. (22)
What has been experienced by you cannot indeed be spoken of by me again;
for where does speech exist regarding that which is inexpressible, being devoid of conceptual cognition? (23)
Just as the sweetness of the six flavors is not experienced by ordinary sense organs,
so too [the Self] would not manifest externally.
For that direct perception is indeed made manifest only by means of analogy; this is for the sake of engaging those who are dull-witted, but certainly not for those who are not dull-witted. (25)
O best of Brahmins, being devoted to inquiry, you should experience this through the state of equal flavor (samarasatva); therefore, you yourself must stabilize that which has been experienced.
By completely relinquishing all possessions, you shall attain absorption here in that incomparable, innate bliss which is the very nature of the bliss of being. (27)
Whatever has been reported by me to you must never indeed be spoken; and whatever was experienced by you at that time, consider it as having been done for my sake.
Devoid of all analogies, beyond the reach of speech, and self-cognized, the supreme reality exists—unsupported and transcending the senses. (29)
For one who is established in bliss within the Self, [that bliss] is manifested even without the instruments;
for all instruments are composed of primordial matter (prakṛti), and especially so those born of the mind.
[The ease of means for mantra and meditative absorption:
Here, the multitudes of mantras together with their ritual formulas are the means, and they bestow accomplishment;
therefore, there are meditative absorptions arising from mudrās and other such instruments, as well as those born of the true nature of reality. (31)
Likewise, all mantras endowed with ritual action are accomplishers of the true reality;
they overcome ten billion obstacles accompanied by the incitement of adversaries. (32)
And they strike that [body] incessantly, facing it from all sides;
for whatever is coarse, by comparison with Brahman, is preceded by mantra. (33)
It is known to destroy all nets of obstacles and to annihilate one's vigor, just as the burning power of fire is extinguished by water. (34)
The flood of obstacles, which consists of illusory forms, is destroyed by means of mantras and other such methods;
just as those standing near a king accomplish the goals of others. (35)
O Brahmin, having understood that mantras and the like thus swiftly bring about supreme success associated with royalty, he who always remains thus, devoted to that alone; || 46 ||
"He shall indeed accomplish it without delay by means of the desired path.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Arising of the Knowledge of Brahman," in the glorious *Pañcarātra-jayākhyasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the sixth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Principal Mantra. Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, the supreme consciousness has been attained by me."
And because of the fickleness of the mind, it does not indeed attain stability for me. || 1 ||
Therefore, tell me all the previously mentioned means (upāyas) in their proper sequence— those which bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation in their entirety.
[The commencement of the investigation into mantras:
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, Nārada! You have questioned me regarding this which is the very essence."
For indeed, everything that has been questioned by you is preceded by mantra.
Therefore, I shall proclaim the auspicious mantra that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
which grants the fruits of various supernatural powers (siddhis) in its gross and subtle forms.
Endowed with the Śakti, the limbs, and the enclosures, and displaying many wonders—[this is the method for the conceptualization of the Mātṛkā-pīṭha]:
on a level and pure plot of ground, well-smeared with clay and cow dung. (5)
Sprinkled with the five products of the cow, smeared with sandalwood paste and other substances, sheltered from the wind, well-covered, and perfumed with incense; || 6 ||
First, one should indeed worship [the deity] with soft white water-lily flowers or with auspicious flowers alone, using its own name preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, having recited [the mantra] many times and having spread out earth upon the ground,
[one should fashion] a square or a well-rounded [altar] measuring two cubits or one cubit.
Having made the seat of the *mātṛkās* perfectly level and having spread it out as well, [one should contemplate the various modes of the Blessed One’s presence within the syllables]:
she is both one and yet divided into groups, and even at the end of the groups there are unequal syllables. (9)
O best of the twice-born, the first [mantra] consists of sixteen syllables beginning with the letter 'a';
the Lord, whose nature is Agni and Soma, resides therein, ending with the visarga.
The Supreme Lord is eternally well-established as the essence of the principles (tattvas) within the five groups of five syllables, beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma'.
O best of Brahmins, he indeed abides here in the form of the states [of consciousness] through the sequence beginning with waking,
within this most excellent group of four letters starting with 'ya' and ending with 'va'.
Abiding in the form of the Self beyond the fourth state (turyātīta) within the letters from Śa to Kṣa,
[it manifests as] illumination, sharpness, pervasion, grasping, casting forth, and movement.
For cooking (pāka) and attainment (prāpti)—these eight are established within the solar portion, following the sequence among these short vowels beginning with 'a'. (14)
Fluidity, coldness, satisfaction, luster, clarity, tastiness, exhilaration, and bliss—these eight are considered the lunar qualities. (15)
Established in the long vowels beginning with *ā* as the essence of the Mātṛkā,
they are indeed always mutually inseparable from one another.
Furthermore, for each of the eight [elements], there are eight [lotuses] situated both externally and internally;
the collection of principles (tattvas), beginning with earth and ending with the Puruṣa, is arranged in sequence.
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state (turya) exist here above;
established there is the supreme, eternally risen, and transcendent sound of ultimate light.

Supreme bliss, equanimity, and freedom from the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower—this is declared to be the essential nature of the all-pervading Self that transcends the fourth state (turyātīta). || 19 ||

"Thus, having contemplated the state of the Blessed One, the letters being delineated possess the nature of the body of the Blessed One’s Mātṛkā; such is the power of the phonemes, which is pervasive and accessible through direct experience."
And having understood it, one should cause it to be written down in the form of letters by anyone at all.
O Brahmin, even though it is perceivable by people, the supreme, divine Puruṣa whom you previously experienced is not like the scripts of the alphabet.
This body of Mātṛkā is established in four ways. (p. 43) [The sequence of the placement of Mātṛkā upon one's own form:
Just as jewels are strung together by a single thread, O Nārada, so too is she. (22)
"In the same way, the letters [are produced] by me, whose nature is the imperishable thread";
having held this in his mind, he who extracts the mantras [attains success]. (23)
The attainment of both visible and invisible fruits arises for him from that mantra.
Thus, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā-mantra alone upon one's own body, || 24 ||
When each of the principles (tattvas) has been filled with its respective substance and manifested, one should bathe, wear white garments, and be adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste. (25)
[The Procedure for Extracting the Mantra-Mātṛkā] The mantra-practitioner should spread out that very [mātṛkā], arranged in eight distinct groups,
within the great eight-spoked wheel, which is beautifully adorned in its center. (26)
Having written the syllables from 'pra' to 'kṣa' in the order of the vowel groups starting with 'a',
and having inscribed the Praṇava (Om) in the center, one should draw the supreme Lord as the Wheel of Syllables (varṇacakra).
One should write each syllable of the group, according to its own name, upon the spokes of the wheel;
this continues until the entire group is completed, situated within its respective intervals between the spokes.
One should first worship the Mātṛkā, joined with vowels and consonants,
with water for the feet, the arghya offering, flowers, incense, lamps, and unguents. [The Method of Worshipping the Mātṛkā] || 29 ||
Having worshipped with offerings of fruits, roots, and the like, using the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Mātṛke," one should then, with devotion, worship the Person whose form is the Mātṛkā.
With one's own name as previously mentioned, with prostration, and with the *praṇava*,
one should then worship each syllable individually in sequence by means of its own designations.

And having meditated upon him as shimmering with the form of the midday sun, [there is a distinction of names for the forms of the Blessed One, which are the syllables, in the sequence beginning with 'a']: the letter 'A' is remembered as the first, immeasurable, and all-pervading. (32)
Likewise, the letter *A* is known as the Primordial God (*Ādideva*), Bliss (*Ānanda*), and the Protector (*Gopana*).
The letter *I*, designated as Rāma, is proclaimed as the Desired (*Iṣṭa*) and the Inflamed (*Iddha*). (33)
The letter *ī* is indeed the five dots (*pañcabindu*), the illusion (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu, O lord of the twice-born;
the letter *u* is called Bhuvana, as well as Uddāma and Udaya. (34)
The letter *ū* is the Lord of the World in the realm of vigor (*ūrj*), and likewise the support of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The letter *ṛ* is Truth (*satya*) and the abode of cosmic order (*ṛta*); it is indeed the goad (*aṅkuśa*). (35)
Know that the syllable *ṛ* is the seat (*viṣṭara*), and its expansion is indeed the flame.
The Lord is declared to be the essence of the *liṅga*, and the syllable *ḷ* is remembered as the savior (*tāraka*).
The letter *ḷ* is Dīrghaghoṇa, while Devadatta is Virāṭ;
the letter *e*, known as Tryaśra, is the formless source of the universe.
Ai is known as Aiśvarya and Yogadhātṛ; Samairāvaṇa is remembered as Ai; Okāra is Otadeha, and Odana is Vikramī.

Then there is Aurva, the one called Bhūdhara, the one remembered as Aus, whose nature is medicinal herbs (auṣadha), the one who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds, the all-pervading Vyomeśa, and indeed Aṅkāra. (39)
The Visarga is known as the creator of emanation, while the letter 'A' is the Supreme Lord;
the letter 'Ka' is both Kamala and Karāla, the supreme Prakṛti.
The letter Kha is he whose body is firm, the soul of the Vedas, and the creator of the universe;
the letter Ga is the destroyer of disease, Govinda, the wielder of the mace. || 41 ||
The letter *gha* is indeed remembered as Dharmāṃśu, radiant and luminous;
the letter *ṅa* is Ekadaṃṣṭra, the self of all beings, who brings all things into existence.
The letter *ca* is the fickle one, the wielder of the discus, and he is called the moon-rayed one;
the letter *cha* is the destroyer of deceit, and he is remembered as the meter and the Lord of meters. (43)
Ajita is the destroyer of birth and the eternal nature of the letter Ja;
Jhaṣa is said to be the letter Jha, the equal self who recites the Sāman hymns.
The supreme one is called Īśvara; the letter Jña is the sustainer of the principles (tattvas).
The letter Ṭa, belonging to the Moon, is known as Āhlāda, which brings nourishment to the universe. || 45 ||
The letter Ṭha is said to be Kaustubha, and likewise Nemi is Dhārādhara;
the letter Ḍa is Daṇḍadhāra, and Mausala is Akhaṇḍavikrama.
The letter Ḍha is Viśvarūpa, Vṛṣakarmā, and Pratardana;
the letter Ṇa is proclaimed as Abhayada, Śāstṛ, and Vaikuṇṭha. || 47 ||
The letter *ta* is known as Tālalakṣman and Vairāja, while *tha* is remembered as Sragdhara, Dhanvin, Bhuvanāpāla, and Sarvarodhaka. (48)
The letter *da*, which grants opportunity, is known as Damana, the bestower of peace;
the letter *dha* is proclaimed as Mādhava, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow and the sustainer. (49)
The letter *na* is declared to be Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and the Path; the letter *pa* is Padmanābha, the Purifier, and the Western Face. (50)
The letter *pha* is Phullanayana, Lāṅgalin, and known as Śveta;
the letter *ba* is Vāmana, Hrasva, and he is also sung of as Pūrṇāṅga.
The syllable *bha* is to be known as the wielder of the *bhallā* weapon, the bestower of success, and the eternal;
the syllable *ma* is recited as the crusher, time, and the primary principle. (52)
The letter *ya* is the fourfold state of existence; it is subtle and is called the conch (*śaṅkha*).
The letter *ra* is the support of all worlds, the fire, the fire of time. (53)
The letter *la* is called Vibudha, the Lord of the Earth, and the Lord of Puruṣas;
the letter *va* is known as Varāha, the Support of Nectar, and Varuṇa.
The letter Śa is proclaimed as Śaṅkara, the peaceful Puṇḍarīka;
likewise, the letter Ṣa is Nṛsiṃha, Agnirūpa, and Bhāskara.
The letter *sa* is nectar and satisfaction, while the moon (*soma*) is recited as such;
the sun is the letter *ha*, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is proclaimed to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (56)
Ananteśa is the letter *kṣa*, the end of the groups; he is remembered as Garuḍa.
These are proclaimed to be the names for all the letters without exception. (57)
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, that which is the correct enumeration and designation of each letter following and preceding the others is what is known as the "commonality."

[The status of these syllables, which are portions of the Blessed One, as the cause for the arising of mantra when they are mutually unconnected through the relationship of primary and subordinate members:
These words, which are portions of the Blessed One, possess radiant forms.
They are the cause of all mantras, empowered by the power of the Blessed One.
Through their mutual relationship as constituent parts, they proceed to the arising of mantras;
in this world of the moving and the unmoving, there is nothing that is not permeated by them.
Having thus performed the pervasive visualization of the phonemes within one's own state of being, the rite of worship [and the sequence for extracting the mantra] proceeds:
then, one should extract the mantras from the wheel of one's own heart situated upon the ground.
The first seed-syllable (bīja), which is the last letter of its respective class, is differentiated by the seven classes;
it is joined with five dots (bindus) at its head and conjoined with the Lord of Space (Vyomeśa). (62)
This is the divine, excellent seed-syllable that bestows the fruit of all desires;
it is the third from Ananteśa, joined with the final letter of the vowel class.
The second seed-syllable of that [mantra] removes the fear of old age and death;
it consists of the fifth vowel joined with the twenty-fifth [consonant]. (64)

Of these two, one should write the first seed-syllable, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is auspicious, endowed with the word of salutation, and is the Lord who is the refuge of all powers. (65)
O twice-born Nārada, this body consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) is my gross manifestation; yet, in comparison to the elemental body, it is somewhat subtle.
Through another supreme form, he indeed shines forth in a gross body;
endowed with most excellent qualities, he is invisible to anyone whatsoever.
Moreover, even when alone it bestows the accomplishment of all goals;
how much more so when joined with the twelve-syllable mūrti-mantra! || 68 ||
Then one should offer a portion to Nārāyaṇa, the Soul of the Universe;
this is known as the Mūrti-mantra, conjoined with the syllable Hrīṃ and the utterance Svāhā. || 69 ||
[Description of the Greatness of the Mantra] It consists of both conceptualization and its transcendence; it is the first of the three-syllabled mantra that has been proclaimed.
It is the support for qualities such as *aṇimā* and bestows the siddhi of rising from the netherworld (*pātāla*).

He grants liberation to one who desires liberation; he grants enjoyment to one who desires enjoyment; he grants a kingdom to one who desires a kingdom; and he grants prosperity to one who desires wealth. || 71 ||
Whatever desires one prays for, he grants them all to the practitioner simply by the utterance [of the mantra], provided that practitioner’s self is properly cultivated in that [mantra].
[The Meditation on the Deity]:
O Brahmin, one should meditate upon the Lord, the God who is without beginning or end, the creator of the world, who possesses four arms and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace. (73)
Four-faced, with beautiful eyes, lovely, with lotuses in his hands;
Vaikuṇṭha, with the face of Narasiṃha, Vārāha, and the face of Kapila.
White-complexioned, mounted upon the lord of birds (Garuḍa), adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with all auspicious marks, wearing garlands and garments, the omnipresent Lord.
Wearing a crown and the Kaustubha gem, his body smeared with camphor, possessing the splendor of ten thousand times ten thousand suns, and saluted by all the gods. (76)
[The eternal presence of Lakṣmī and others in the form of the Blessed One:
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are the goddesses who always reside in him;
endowed with their own collection of powers, they are indeed formless and partless. (77)
Just as the rays belong to the sun and the waves to the ocean,
so too does Kamalā belong to the Lord of Śrī by virtue of His sovereign power.
O Lord, Kīrti likewise, surrounded by millions of various distinguished marks, took on a physical form through such a divine ordinance. || 79 ||
There is indeed nothing that is not pervaded by her, whose body is universal;
for whatever fame arises for anyone at any time, it is produced through her own power. (80)
O Brahmin, all those [energies] are traditionally known by their specific modes of manifestation;
thus Jayā exists as the pervasive state of the Lord of Victory himself.
Whatever illusion exists in this world among the gods and others,
O Blessed One, know that it has arisen from Your supreme illusion alone.
O best of sages, apart from that supreme, partless form of his which is the ultimate reality, what else exists within this ocean of principles in its fourfold aspect?
Through the powers of the Blessed One, by means of the correct division of yoga,
and through the capacity of the knowledge of their own light, they have attained the state of possessing form.
[The Method of Meditating on Lakṣmī and Others] These should be meditated upon by the foremost of practitioners for their own spiritual accomplishment;
they have one face, two eyes, and two arms, and are adorned with beautiful earrings. (85)
Resembling the interior of a lotus, lovely, adorned with girdles and strings of beads,
wearing white garlands and garments, and decorated with necklaces and armlets.
They were endowed with all the auspicious marks, possessed full and elevated breasts, had large eyes like blossoming blue lotuses, and faces adorned with smiles. (87)
They were adorned with locks of hair resembling swarms of moving bees,
and were further embellished with various wonderful tilakas upon their foreheads.
Their lips were reddish-pink, their teeth were like bamboo seeds or pearls,
their foreheads were marked with crescent moons, and their hair was smooth and curled.
O Nārada, the goddesses, holding nooses and goads, who accomplish all desires and goals, are situated on the filaments and petals in the divisions of the directions starting from the east. (90)

Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and facing the God of gods, I shall now proclaim their various mantras for the purpose of worship. [The commencement of the exposition of the mantras of Lakṣmī and others. 91.
By those who have constantly propitiated them, they accomplish their desired aims;
that which is the second [mantra] from the root mantra is the seed-syllable leader alone. (92)
This is indeed proclaimed as the common heart-mantra for all of them;
now hear separately, in due order, their four form-mantras.
[The Lakṣmī-mantra:
One should first utter the Praṇava (Oṃ), and immediately thereafter the heart-seed syllable (Hrīṃ).
Then, having placed the two-syllabled word "Lakṣmyai" at the beginning, one should append the limbs (aṅgas) at the end. 94.

Then, at the end of that, one should place the word "puruṣeśvara," which consists of the final letter of the consonant groups (kṣ) joined with the vowel 'a' (kṣa), for the purpose of the "vasthitā" mantra.

Furthermore, O Brahmin, that heart-mantra is the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*, followed by the two seed-syllables *hrīṃ*, then accompanied by *svāhā* and preceded by the *praṇava*; this is the king of mantras. (96)
The twelve-syllable mantra known as Lakṣmī, together with the Mūrti-mantra, is as follows:
the heart-seed preceded by the Praṇava, followed by the word for fame (kīrttyai), and then "namaḥ. [This is the Kīrtti-mantra. || 97 ||
The king of mantras for fame consists of the previously mentioned number [of syllables], joined with *hrīṃ klīṃ svāhā*, and follows the word "vigrahāyai" after the word "sadoditānandapadam. (98)
[The mantra for Jayā:

The seed-syllable of the heart (Hrīṃ) joined with the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by the three syllables of "Jayāyai" and "Namaḥ"; then the first vowel (A), the word "Jita," and then the two syllables "Dhāma. (99)
Having established the foot for her who is thus situated, one should again place that seed-syllable of her heart;
and the third [syllable] is situated as the support of all worlds.
Vyomeśa and Pañcabindu, followed by Svāhā—O Nārada, this is the supreme mantra known as Jaya, consisting of twenty syllables. (101)
[The Māyā-mantra:
First the seed-syllable preceded by the Praṇava (oṃ), then "to Māyā" (māyāyai), and then "namas" (namaḥ).
Thereafter, one should join the word "beyond delusion" (mohātīta-pada) ending with the letter *n* (i.e., *mohanī*). (102)
Immediately after that, there is the letter *da* joined with the second vowel;
then follows the three-syllable word *śṛtāyai*, and thereafter comes the *māyā*-seed syllable (*hrīṃ*). (103)

One should extract the *pradhāna* (the letter *p*) mounted upon fire (*r*), adorned with the fourth vowel (*ī*), joined with the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds (*e*), and ending with *svāhā*. (104)
The *māyā-mantra* of the predecessors is recorded as having a number of syllables equal to that [of the root mantra].
[Description of the Heart and Other Limb Mantras:
I shall now explain, according to reality, the limbs (*aṅga*) of the God of gods. (105)
Equipped with those [mantras], the practitioner becomes invincible even to the gods of the thirty;
he shall accomplish all tasks that grant long life and happiness. (106)

If a devotee whose self is permeated by that [deity] is intent upon the practice of mantra, he should extract the seed-syllable preceded by "Ananta" (A) and adorned with a bindu (the nasal drop). [This is the Heart Mantra. 107.
Know that the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra), preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ," is partless (niṣkala).
I shall now tell you, exactly as it is, the form-mantra (mūrtimantra) belonging to this very [deity]. || 108 ||
The Praṇava, conjoined with the Bindu, is Sūrya; the Moon holds the Visarga.
Thereafter, one should utter the word "Śuci" and then extract the form of Agni.
Thereafter, one should offer salutation to the letter *da*, adorned with the *praṇava* (OM); this is the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) conjoined with the form. || 110 ||
O Brahmin, this seventeen-syllable mantra bestows all accomplishments; it is the Śiromantra.
One should place that very mantra, joined with the second vowel, upon the head. (111)
Having thus extracted it from there, one should first place the Praṇava (Oṃ) and the prostration (Namaḥ) at the end; know that this is the partless Head-mantra (Mūrdhāna).
Now I shall declare the mantra of the Form (Mūrti), which is the attendant of this very [deity];
one should extract the one called Padmanābha, and likewise the solitary [mantra] following it.
O best of the twice-born, its fruit is the support of all worlds without exception, which culminates at the end; it indeed rests within the fire of time and is the end of all things. (114)
Then one should extract the mantra known as Prāṇa, with Madana situated above it;
next comes the word "śiras," followed by "pada," and finally the word "svāhā" at its end.
Know, O Nārada, that the Śiromantra consists of thirteen syllables.
[The Śikhāmantra:
One should first utter the Praṇava, and immediately after that, the name of Sūrya. (116)
Adorned by Viṣṇu upon his head, who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds;
indeed, "namaḥ" is at its end, and this is the partless (niṣkala) Śikhā-mantra.
Now I shall state its form-mantra, which bestows the accomplishment of all aims:
the syllable "pa" [of Padmanābha], mounted upon the syllable "ca," followed by the letter "da," with the conch-syllable "śaṅkha" positioned above.
O Nārada, one should carefully fashion that [image] with its body pierced through;
then, from that [base], a man [should be made] endowed with Rāma, characterized solely by the mark of the tāla.
Ending with "vauṣaṭ" for the crest (śikhā), this is remembered as the crest-mantra;
it consists of thirteen and a half syllables and bestows the fruits of various supernatural powers (siddhis). || 120 ||
[The Armor Mantra]:
One should prescribe the syllable of the armor as being between the *natipraṇava* (namo namah) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), adorned by space (*vyoma*) and joined with the fifth vowel. 121.
In the mantra of Kṛṣṇa’s form, which bestows the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should extract the syllable known as Śaṅkāra, adorned with bliss (Ānanda). 122.
Then, one should meditate upon that very same Vairāja situated upon a boar,
as well as the solitary Puṇḍarīka and the solitary Kālapāvaka.
Then one should uplift Vaikuṇṭha, which has ascended into the four states of existence; one should form the word for the armor (kavaca), adorned with the syllable *huṃ*. (124)

This fifteen-syllable mantra is said to possess a dual nature; it begins with the *praṇava*, ends with *namaḥ*, consists of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and is adorned by space (*vyoman*). (125) [The Eye Mantra]
The Netra-mantra, conjoined with the vowel *au*, is indeed partless (*niṣkala*).
It is pure, mounted upon fire, a lotus marked by concealment.

p. 51) Then, one should extract from that [mantra] the syllable *rā* mounted upon *śaṅkara* at the end, followed by the western face (*paścimānana*), and then *ajita*, which is the support of nectar (*amṛtādhāra*). 127.
One should give the word "Dhareśa" alone as the eye, followed by the three-syllabled word;
at the end of that, one should utter "vauṣaṭ"—this is remembered as the mantra of the eye.
O twice-born one, the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) consists of fifteen syllables and a half-syllable; it bestows success.
It begins with "Namaḥ," followed immediately by the Supreme Self situated within the *praṇava* (OM). 129.
That very [seed-syllable], accompanied by the *visarga*, is the weapon (*astra*) endowed with form and mantra;
it is indeed known as "Dattāvakāśa" (granting space), its body adorned with *māyā*.
One should place the *pavitra* mounted upon the *sragdharā* meter, and above that, the *codana*;
likewise, the *madana* situated in the *satya*, and the *pavitra* bearing the mark of the *tāla*.
Then one should extract that which is situated in fire, as well as the absolute and the eternal;
at the end of that, one should extract the immeasurable one called Soma.
O best of the twice-born, he is situated in Vairāja, and he too is established in Anala;
one should indeed mark him with concealment (gopana), for this is the four-syllabled Piṇḍa-mantra.

And from that, [one should extract] the subtle *kevala* [mantra], adorned with the word *phaṭ*, consisting of the fourteenth vowel, serving as the weapon (*astra*), and joined with the half-syllable. || 134 ||

[I shall now state] the mantras for the three faces of the Lord previously described as having four faces, beginning with the Nṛsiṃha face; they reside within those starting with Nṛsiṃha, and I shall explain them concisely. (135)

Together with their bodies, in their respective locations, along with their limbs and their retinues, they should be meditated upon and worshipped with diligence by means of the mouth alone of the deity. (136)
O Sage, one should first extract the Praṇava, which is joined with the Viśvāpyāya;
then the Ajita [syllable] situated in the fire (Ra), combined with Odana (Sa). || 137 ||
Having placed the letter *ca* above the moon (*i*), and having spread it (*pa*) over that, one should extract the "slayer of birth" (*ja*); below that, the reciter of the *sāman* (*ha*). (138)
One should place the letter *ra* situated in fire (*analastha*), and below that again the letter *rj*.
Above that is the pervasive (*vyāpin*), and likewise at the beginning is the supporter of the earth (*bhūdhara*); thus it should be done in sequence. (139)
O Brahmin, this is the seed-syllable (piṇḍākṣara) of the second [mantra], ending with "namaḥ";
and for the sake of radiance, there is the three-syllabled word "jvalanāyutaśabda. (140)
One should then join the word "nṛsiṃhāya" followed by "svāhā.
This nineteen-syllable mantra belongs to Nṛkesarī, who is both with and without form. (141)

O twice-born one, when it is worshipped, remembered, meditated upon, and recited, it destroys the faults arising from the *samayas*, as well as the afflictions caused by spirits and planetary grahas. (142)

One should first extract the Praṇava, and immediately after that, the one called Sūrya; then that very same [syllable] situated in the Lord of the World (Lokeśa), and above that, Vyoma and the lunar [syllable]. (143)

Then, having taken the seed-syllable *ra*, one should place *Dharmāṃśu* (the Sun of Dharma) beneath it; and beneath that, again, one should place *Anala* (Fire), situated upon the support of *Prajñā* (Wisdom). 144.
Above that, its nature is medicinal, and then it becomes the pervasive lunar [nature] in due order;
at the end of these two groups, one should employ the word of salutation (namaskāra).
Then, for Kapila, there should be the word "anantabhāsāya";
one should make this seventeen-syllable mantra accompanied by "svāhā. (146)
The extremely formidable one named Kapila, who grants peace from all dualities and is the cause of accomplishment, should be constantly recited during the performance of expiatory rites. 147.
Likewise, O Nārada, for the sake of attaining liberation without delay,
one should first take up the syllable Om and then utter the name Govinda.
Then, above that, is the body of Otā, which is the Lord of Men (Puruṣeśvara) situated in the upper region;
it is endowed with the power of sovereignty over the three worlds, and the letter Ṭa is above that.
O twice-born one, the syllable *mū* situated on the boar is called Amṛta;
above that is the syllable ending in *o*, which bestows sovereignty over the three worlds. (150)
At the end of this, one should place "namaḥ" joined with "viśvāpyāyasam";
then one should give the two syllables "kṛṣṇa" and the word "piṅgalāya. (151)
"Varāhāya padaṃ svāhā" is the mantra consisting of seventeen syllables;
it is remembered as bringing about peace, prosperity, nourishment, and health. || 152 ||
The Vārāha mantra, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, must be protected and recited.
[Now, the mantras beginning with Kaustubha:
Listen now to all the mantras, beginning with Kaustubha and ending with Aṅkuśa, in their proper order. (153)

O twice-born one, from the perpetual propitiation of those for whom there arises infinite prosperity comes the Kaustubha mantra; therefore, the Kaustubha, which is permeated by space, is the Supreme Self. (154)
O Nārada, one should then cause it to be permeated by fire from above and below;
that indeed should be marked with the syllable *A* and caused to be empowered by the *ūrja*.
Then, accompanied by Vyoman, one should offer salutation;
immediately thereafter, one should offer a seat to Prabhātman, and then a seat to Kaustubha.
Accompanied by "svāhā" and the Praṇava, this sixteen-syllable great mantra of the Kaustubha is proclaimed; there is nothing that it cannot accomplish.
One should extract the *mālā-mantra*; at the end of the *praṇava*, one should place the Lord of the Earth (*dhareśa*),
and below that, having established Varuṇa, who is known as Tṛpti.

The *piṇḍa* joined with *māyā* and *vyoman*, and accompanied by the word of salutation (*namaskāra*), should be followed by two syllables of the land (*sthala*) and then the word arising from water (*jalodbhūta*). (159)
Then the word *bhūṣite vanamāle svāhā* follows;
this mantra of the garland is said to consist of nineteen syllables. || 160 ||
O Brahmin, this bestows the fulfillment of all desires upon the one who constantly worships it.
[This is the Padma-mantra.
One should append the mantra known as Vāmana at the conclusion of the Praṇava. (161)
That which is called Soma should be joined below it, situated above Uddāma;
endowed with the power of sovereignty over the three worlds, it is the Piṇḍa accompanied by Nati. || 162 ||
Immediately after that, one should give the station of Śrīnivāsa to Padma;
the mantra of Padma, accompanied by Svāhā, consists of thirteen syllables. (163)
O twice-born one, it bestows incomparable and imperishable prosperity upon devotees.
[The mantra of the conch:
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should invoke the Supreme Self. (164)
One should perform the separation up to the end of the world with that which bestows sovereignty over the three worlds;
one should perform the salutation and the sequence, for this very syllable is threefold.
And "Mahāśaṅkhāya svāhā"—this mantra named Śaṅkha consists of thirty-three syllables;
it is declared to be an exceedingly auspicious yantra that bestows intelligence and knowledge. || 166 ||
[The Cakramantra:
The eternal *praṇava* at the end, joined with the *siddhikṛt* mounted upon *rā*;
likewise, the lotus with blossoming eyes thereafter. (167)
At its end, however, there should be a solitary *hlāda* (the letter *ha*) devoid of vowel;
having extracted the *paramātman* (the letter *sa*), it is joined with the goad (*aṅkuśa*) and so forth. 168.
One should mark the head with the word *aurva*, and at its end join the word *namaḥ*.
After that, one should utter the three *phaṭ* syllables, followed by the phrase *viṣṇucakrāya*. (169)
With the two syllables "svāhā" at the end, this seventeen-syllable mantra,
joined with four half-syllables, is this entire universe.
[The Mantra of the Mace] One should extract the Praṇava at the beginning, and at its end, Gadādhara;
with Pradhāna situated above it, and Puruṣeśvara below it. (171)
One should place Vyomeśa, joined with Jagadyoni, upon the head;
then, taking the letter Ja, one should place it situated upon the seat (viṣṭara).
Combined with the visarga and so forth, adorned with the word of salutation (*namas*), followed by *sahasrāśri-gade svāhā*, this is the eighteen-syllable mantra known as the Gada-mantra. (173)
This great mantra, which grants all desires and destroys the web of obstacles, is the Garuḍa-mantra:
having first taken the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should then follow it with Ananteśa. (174)
One should place that [mantra] consisting of Satya and the others, which is undivided from above and below, beneath it;
for it bestows sovereignty over the three worlds through the giving of sovereignty over the three worlds. (175)
One should adorn the head and then extract the essence of the Veda;
that too, like Ananteśa, should be fashioned adorned with vowels and consonants.

Furthermore, one should add the *kūṭa* mantra together with the creator [of the world], ending with *namaḥ*; and at the end, for the one who has reached the infinite, there is the word for Garuḍa ending with *svāhā*.
The seventeen-syllable mantra of Garuḍa has been proclaimed;
by the perfect recollection of which, all suffering goes to its dissolution. (178)
[The Pāśa-mantra:
First, having taken Vaikuṇṭha, one should place *raṃ* mounted upon it;
then, together with Vyomānanda, the words *kaḍ ḍha kaḍ ḍha*. (179)
Accompanied by two clouds (dhārādhara), the word *varapāśāya* indeed constitutes the foot;
one should place *svāhā* at its end, making it seventeen syllables. (180)
This mantra known as the noose (pāśa) is indeed a savior that brings swift accomplishment.
[The Hook-mantra (aṅkuśamantra):
One should place the syllable Om at the end, and above that, the one designated as Virāṭ. (181)
Immediately after that, one should place a lotus joined with the sky (vyoman), the brahmin (vipra), and fire (anala);
and above that, one should place the sky situated upon Ṛtadhāman.
The word *pada* [is placed] for the sharp-trunked one, and then the word *aṅkuśāya*;
followed by *svāhā*, this king of mantras of the goad consists of fifteen syllables. (183)
He is said to be one who performs actions swiftly and is characterized by constant desire for peace.
[Beginning the exposition of the five secondary limbs (upāṅgas):
Now, the five secondary limbs are indeed the designators of Truth and the other [virtues]. 184.
O divine sage, listen well as I speak to you the stainless nature of Brahman, which is all-pervading and the bestower of all perfections, along with its secret teachings. 185.
By the arrangement of which the practitioner attains success anywhere whatsoever, that mantra-form becomes the bestower of fruit for one who has quickly become identical with it. (186)

Through the placement (nyāsa) and the contemplation of pervasion (vyāpti-bhāvanā) of that mantra—which has been offered in sacrifice and enveloped by the powers (śakti) and limbs (aṅga)—the practitioner may become equal to the Lord of the Gods. || 187 ||
Indeed, for the sake of achieving perfect cessation, one should always apply [the mantra] when the self has been consecrated and when the five ancillary limbs have been consecrated. (188)
There should be constant restraint of the distracted fluctuations of the mind;
[this is the seed-mantra of the five ancillary limbs beginning with Truth]. That group known as the Self beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is adorned with five syllables, || 189 ||
Having established and joined the first [deity] beginning with Suparṇa in reverse order,
one should install the first with the one called Bhūdhara and the other with the one named Ūrja.
The third was by Lokeśa, while the fourth was by Viṣṇu himself;
the fifth was by Ādideva, who pervades everywhere at the summit. (191)
In the case of the *dvija-aṅkāra*, one should insert each [syllable] from the whole into the middle;
this is remembered as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of that which is designated as "five. || 192 ||
But they arise from this [source] as its manifestation in the form of the supreme;
indeed, O Nārada, by way of subtlety, pervasiveness, and the quality of being the sustainer.
In each [of these], these five are established as a group;
their forms are like extinguished fires, arisen together with the supreme mantras. (194)
The first king of mantras is traditionally taught as belonging to the primordial god Viṣṇu, the Great-Souled One known as Satya, who is designated by the name Mahāvibhava. || 195 ||
And the second is proclaimed as belonging to the all-pervading Vāsudeva;
thereafter, the third seed-syllable is said to belong to Saṅkarṣaṇa. (196)
O tiger among brahmins, know that the fourth [Upāṅga] belongs to the high-souled Pradyumna, and the fifth Upāṅga belongs to the all-pervading Lord Aniruddha. (197)
He who knows this fivefold mantra, which begins with Satya and ends with Aniruddha, which is pure and designated as the "subsidiary limbs" (upāṅga), truly knows the Truth; it is not otherwise.
Thus [is described] the first [part] of the pure, all-pervading, three-syllabled, and two-seed-mantra-like supreme mantra of the Lord, whose nature is subtle. (199)
Beginning with the form-mantra (mūrtimantra), that which is designated as mantra is proclaimed in due order; it correctly bestows the desired [attainment] upon those devotees of purified soul. 200.
O Sage, be free from fear; sacrifice to this and worship it according to the procedure seen in the scriptures, for it bestows whatever is desired. (201)
"O Supreme Lord, this supreme mantra has been understood by me through its gross and subtle divisions according to its essential nature, yet it has not been fully realized. 202.
Previously, you indicated that his supreme form is the mantra-form;
if you are gracious toward me, please explain it to me in brief. (203)
[The Definition of the Supreme Nature of Mantra] The Blessed Lord said: O Brahmin, that mantra which was previously described is not a mantra without its embodied form.
(57) Beginning with *prabhu* and ending with *visarga*, he is the embodiment of a mass of nectar. || 204 ||
He consists of all the gods, is pure, the self of all paths, and the supreme Lord;
he has a body composed of all powers, is of the nature of light, and assumes a subtle form. || 205 ||
Having assumed a gross form by its own will for the sake of those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, it is presided over by the all-pervading Supreme Lord, whose nature is light.
Know that the power of mantra is indeed supreme—subtler than the subtle, formless, and eternally consisting of the essence of light; it is finer even than an atom.
Free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi), pure, and bestowing the fruit of proximity to Me—that is indeed My supreme mantra, the body of Myself, which grants the highest fruit. || 208 ||
[The description of the manifestation of the existing mantras in their subtle, intermediate, and gross forms from that which is all-pervading and transcendent, consisting of pure consciousness:
And the supreme body, free from modification, is known as the sacrifice (yāga).
Beyond this fourth state, there is my supreme state known as the Knowable.

Those whose inner selves are purified behold that [reality], which is free from the distinction between the grasped and the grasper and is characterized by the bliss of pure consciousness, as being identical with it.
From which the supreme king of mantras, known as light and sound, originates;
wherein the seven categories of existence, once understood, attain manifestation. (211)
In that indeed all worlds are established by way of color and form;
that which exists beyond the two [principles] as the cause of the primary causes (pradhāna). || 212 ||
Listen now to how it is situated according to the very sequence of the arising of mantras;
O Nārada, having joined them in due order by way of emanation.
He is the one who has manifested the distribution of the seven castes,
and he is the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, whose form is that of the sun, moon, and fire.
This aggregate of phonemes, which is the support of all worlds without exception and the bestower of sovereignty over the three realms,
is my supreme embodiment as mantra.
O Sage, this king of mantras— which is graspable through meditative cultivation, incomparable, and unmanifest— has today been revealed by me to you, for it is indeed the very life-force itself.
For that which generates the power of the entire wheel of mantras,
by means of that mantra and according to the prescribed rite, through the arrangement of being woven warp and woof— || 217 ||
Just as a seed, even when empowered, is like a stainless crystal, so too is it perceived through the stainless ether, which is both visible and invisible. (218)
Other mantras are likewise pervaded and thus fully contemplated by that;
the Nārada mantra has been correctly proclaimed by you according to the very sequence of creation.
Instruct me in that by which I may today become one who has accomplished his purpose—
that which is changeless, supremely pure, and abides beyond all perception.
How did that all-pervading Brahman come to assume the form of mantra? [An Analysis of the Sequence of Emanation through Mantra]— The Blessed Lord said:
Know that his one supreme power is she who practices his dharma.
O Brahmin, by that [power] the Supreme Lord, the creator of the universe, is served;
he is celebrated as the "Great" (Bṛhat) because of his greatness, and likewise as eternally arisen bliss.
This [condition] is not possible for Him who is eternally pure at all times;
for the Blessed Lord consists of power and is augmented by all powers. (223)
Indeed, it faints simultaneously with my [consciousness] which has Agni and Soma as its essence;
for light is the Sun, while joy is called the Moon. 224.
Consciousness is contained within these two, and both their rising and setting are likewise so;
that very person, O twice-born one, is of the nature of fire and moon, having consciousness as his form.
That form of fire which consists of the three qualities (guṇas) is indeed composed of knowledge;
the conscious self (cidātman) remains presiding over it, just as a moth [presides over] a flame. || 226 ||
Then the Lord, remaining there, should cause [the soul] to reach the stage of Pradhāna;
once the element of earth (kṣmātattva) has been mastered, he attains the state of being the Lord of Puruṣas.
Pierced by the latent impression of "mine," one should fill it with splendor;
then the entire multitude of principles shall attain sovereignty over the three worlds.
But from that fiery ego-sense, he then turns away;
he attains his own state, which is the state of the supreme condition. || 229 ||
One should cause [the deity] to assume either a gross form or a subtle one enveloped by power;
by resorting to these two, one becomes a benefactor of the worlds. (230)
He bestows both liberation and enjoyment, such as sovereignty and the like;
therefore, He who consists of both the gross and the subtle is indeed to be worshipped.
The three-syllabled mantra is supreme; by means of it, one should initiate the devotees who have fallen into the ocean of existence in due order, but never by any other [means]. (232)
The initiated one is indeed liberated from bonds, having renounced all possessions;
he either desires the falling of the body or has his mind focused solely on Yoga. || 233 ||
Every supreme devotee should be united with [the Self] and shall partake of Nirvana;
established in that, one attains the supreme state through both the gross and the subtle.
O Brahmin, for those living beings whose selves are purified, it soon attains manifestation upon the realization that they are indeed united with Viṣṇu. (235)
But he who, while reciting the mantra, meditates on that which has emerged from the five locations according to the order of emanation, his heart's desire is swiftly accomplished. (236)
Or else, having arisen from the *vigraha* and being endowed with the existence of pervasion (*vyāpti-sattā*),
one should again step outside after having ascended that state from which [the deity] descended.
Abandoning conceptual elaboration, it proceeds; when recollected, it attains liberation.
This occurs gradually through the visible path of the wind's movement and its functional activity. (238)
Having withdrawn everything from the heart, as well as from the upper locations,
through constant practice permeated by the nectar of that service, O Nārada, (239)
There may be stability of the body, as well as the power for enjoyment and liberation;
therefore, his worship should always consist of meditation and recitation. (240)
O Sage, no external ritual involving flowers, incense, and the like should be performed, because the worship of the entire body has been ordained.
For that which is called the partless, there is no such thing as cultivation when it is free from duality;
rather, its unmodified nature is presided over by this [consciousness]. (242)

Because he is indeed his progenitor through the yoga of the emergence of the state to be cultivated, one should likewise meditate upon another [deity] as being exactly like this one, such as a lion and so forth. (243)
Whether in a separate sacrifice or one performed collectively, for the sake of accomplishing the fruit without obstacles;
likewise, upon the attainment of Brahman, in enjoyment, or in the collection of rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth. || 244 ||
For this indeed is the power of the three-syllabled mantra:
its essence should be understood as being threefold, consisting likewise of the three qualities (guṇas).
O Brahmin, he who is always the soul of the three worlds is said to be the soul of the three Vedas;
one should know him to be the three sacrificial fires, and he is action consisting of speech and mind.

The mind, the intellect, and the ego—possessing the senses of cognition and action as well as the elements—exist in three ways through the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire; they too are the three imperishables. (247)
Nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), and that third one, the Lord (īśvara)—He is the three channels within the body, endowed with the three locations. (248)
In this very way, O Nārada, he who knows the manifold nature and the all-pervasiveness of this mantra knows the truth, and not otherwise. (249)
Thus, this entire collection of mantras, which is preeminent and brings peace to all calamities, has been revealed exactly as it truly is; it must not be told to just anyone.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Principal Mantra," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Mantras for the Ritual Implements.
The Blessed Lord said: "Now listen to the characteristics of the mantras known as the Support and the Seat."
O Brahmin, without these, the worship of the Lord of Mantras does not take place. || 1 ||
[The Mantra of the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti):
O best of Brahmins, one should install the support of all worlds as being like the container and its contents;
O lord of sages, it is considered that the power called Māyā resides above the Supreme Self.
The seed-syllable (bīja), preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "namas," is born from the Support-Power (ādhāra-śakti);
its form is likewise endowed with a capacity equal to that which is supported.
[The Kūrma-mantra:
Having extracted the Praṇava first, one should place the preceding [syllable] of Ananteśa;
the twice-born should then split it with the fire of that very time for both [mantras]. (4)
O twice-born one, likewise, with that power which bestows sovereignty over the three worlds,
the seed-syllable expressive of the Tortoise and the Fire of Time is joined with a salutation.
Above the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) is the stainless one of radiant form,
surrounded by hundreds of flames, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
[The Anantamantra]: That which belongs to Ananteśa, previously endowed with secrecy, joined with Vyoma, and known as Ananta, has been proclaimed for the Nāga king. (7)

One should meditate upon this auspicious and excellent seed-syllable, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ," [visualizing the deity] whose face is like the full moon and who is adorned with a thousand hoods.
And [one should meditate on] the one who holds a discus and a plough in his hands, bowing down to the Supreme beyond the supreme;
[this is] the mantra of the Earth (Dharā).
And that seed-syllable named Ananta, which is situated above Pradhāna. || 9 ||
That too, when ascended by the Lord of the Earth, is proclaimed as the earth [element], marked by the two infinite expanses of space and, as before, confined at its beginning and end. (10)
One should remember her, resembling saffron-water, adorned with gold and jewels, with palms joined in reverence at the level of her head, meditating upon the Lord.
[The Mantra of the Ocean of Milk:
"The nectar situated within Varuṇa, joined with the Primordial God—this is the king of mantras for the Ocean of Milk, O best of the twice-born, when conjoined with Vyoman. (12)
One should place the *praṇava* at its beginning and the word of salutation (*namaskāra*) at its end;
it is white like a pure jasmine flower or the moon, and enveloped by rays of light.
One should meditate upon the profound form, which possesses the splendor of the full moon scattered [with light].
[The Lotus Mantra:
Now I shall proclaim the mantra of the lotus, which causes its presence. (14)
The Praṇava at the beginning and at the end of the Praṇava, followed by the Pavitra; then the Bhuvana conjoined with Vyoma, and thereafter the word Ādhāra. || 15 ||
And at the end, "namo padmāya" [is added], and the word of the preceding phrase [is repeated];
it has the form of a tranquil fire and resembles the rising sun. (16)
One should indeed meditate upon him who has two arms, who is short, who hangs down from his belly and other parts,
who is radiant with white teeth, and who is surrounded by divine bees.
One should meditate upon the triad beginning with the lotus as being manifest (vyakta), unmanifest (avyakta), and supreme (para);
and that triad situated below it which is capable [of being so conceived] should likewise be understood in this very same way.
This path of mantra for the six supports has been proclaimed.
Now hear from me the six mantras known as the seats, beginning with the seat of Dharma and the others, which are situated above this. (19)
O Nārada, one should join each name with the others— Dhartṛ, Ajita, and Amṛtādhāra— along with those called Vibudha, according to both the reverse and the direct order.
Then, O twice-born one, the deity Devadatta, whose self is the Liṅga and who is a perfect flame, should place Vāmana, Soma, and Uddāma above the Praṇava. (21)

It bestows sovereignty over the three worlds; for all beings, there shall be the fourfold aims beginning with Dharma, corresponding respectively to the Vedas and the Yugas, as well as their opposites.
The cool, the nectar, the lotus, and then the triad of the sun, moon, and fire—O twice-born one, the syllable *praṇava* (Om) is the designation for these, as well as the word of salutation. (23)

O Brahmin, hereafter [the teacher] should bestow the auspicious seat of consciousness (bhāvāsana), which is inlaid with the light of awareness (cidbhāsā) and is beyond both the gross and the subtle, belonging to the Lord.
By means of the immeasurable Sun, by that which is called Space, and by Nectar,
conjoined with the Supreme Lord— or else by the Self as declared in the *Tritāraka*— (25).
Thus, O best of the twice-born, this collection of mantras for the purpose of worshipping the sacred seats (pīṭha) has been declared; this is a secret. Now listen to another.

[The Kṣatrapāla Mantra: One should divide the collection of mantras beginning with Kṣetreśa—which is capable of crushing obstacles—along with the one called Ananta, by means of Time and the Fire. (27)
Then, this mantra of Kṣetrapāla, which bestows sovereignty over the three worlds, is divided by the seed-syllable *sādi* (sa) and adorned with the syllable *oṃ* at the end. (28)
[The Meditation on the Field Protector (Kṣetrapāla):

One should visualize the Field Protector at the boundary of the sacrificial field as having a massive body, resembling a dark blue cloud, with a staff in his hand and his left hand forming a fist. (29)
[The mantras for the [deities] beginning with Śrī and ending with Padmanidhi:
Puṇḍarīka, then Cakrī, Pavitra, and then Śāśvata; Varāha, Gadādhvaṃsī, Sūkṣma, Śānta, and Pavitraka. (30)
O tiger among sages, one should gradually write this collection of letters,
which is the support of all worlds, resting and adorned by space.
Having placed *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) above the first [syllable], the valiant one [then places it] over the four;
from that, five dots (*pañcabindu*) for two, and *lokeśa* (the syllable *haṃ*) for the other two. (32)
Adorned with the syllable Om as their designation and with acts of salutation, all these excellent mantras indeed bestow the fruits of their own inherent power. (33)
O Brahmin, [this is the case] in the presence of Śrī together with Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, of Jaya and Vijaya, and of the conch and lotus situated near the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. (34)
[The meditation on Śrī and the others, ending with Padmanidhi]: One should visualize Lakṣmī holding a lotus and a jar, seated upon a lotus.
All [deities] from Caṇḍa to Vijaya are to be known as having four arms. (35)
Bearing maces and discs, with conchs in their hands, these beings of great strength were indeed threatening the non-devotees, intent on the destruction of all faults. (36)
Those two rivers, possessing the beauty of women in the bloom of youth, carried a water-filled jar as their reservoir of water. (37)
And Śaṅkha and Padma, the two guardians of the treasures, stand upon treasure-vessels;
they have large tusks, tawny eyes, two arms, and are identical with the Blessed One.
[The Mantras from Gaṇeśa to the Ancestors] Now listen to the collection of mantras beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with the ancestors.
[The Mantra of Gaṇeśa]
Having raised up Gadādhara, one should pierce him with the support of wisdom.

One should place the syllable *aṃ* upon the head [of the mantra], followed by the word "to the Lord of the Gaṇas" (*gaṇādhipataye*), preceded by the word of salutation (*namaskāra*), and one should also join the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) at the beginning of it. (40)
This nine-syllabled mantra is indeed the designator of Vighneśa;
it destroys all ailments and should be applied in six ways, or otherwise differentiated.

One should oneself sequentially place the six [syllables] beginning with Ādideva, along with the long vowels and excluding Virāṭ and Jvālā, as the pervasive [seed-syllable] upon the head of each of the five, according to their respective classes.
Namas, svāhā, then vauṣaṭ, huṃ vauṣaṭ, and phaṭ—these are declared to be the six classes [of mantras] for the heart and the other [limbs], in their respective order. (43)

[The Meditation on Gaṇeśa] O twice-born one, one should meditate upon him who has the luster of the campaka flower, seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) upon the pericarp of a three-petaled red lotus with six auspicious filaments. (44)
With his right hands granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a rosary, one should meditate upon him as resting; his fourth left hand rests upon an axe.
One should visualize two fish-seals (matsyamudrā) with the hands in the gestures of granting boons (varada) and fearlessness (abhaya);
that which arises effortlessly from the clashing of the index finger and thumb. (46)
One should place the six limbs—[the deity] with a massive body, a single tusk, a protruding snout, and an elephant face—upon the filaments, and [the remaining] three limbs upon the three petals. (47)
[The Mantra of Vāgīśvarī:
Having first taken the Praṇava (Oṃ), immediately thereafter Suparṇa;
then at the end of that, again that same initial syllable, and after that Soma in two parts. 48.
O Nārada, one should join the fire of time (kālapāvaka) both below and above the first seed-syllable; then, one should apply that same [fire] alone to the second.
One should place the third and fourth syllables in the shape of a conch;
with a garland and a conch, one should arrange them joined above and below that.
Again, in the very same initial sequence, having joined Māyā with two [syllables],
and that Ādideva with two [syllables], they are all above Vyoman.

At the end of that, having joined the Mother-letters (mātṛkā) preceded by the [initial] syllable and ending with *kṣāṃ*, followed by "vāgīśvaryai namaḥ," there is an auspicious mantra of sixty-one syllables. || 52 ||
I have declared this mantra which bestows mastery over speech;
it consists of Soma situated in Anala, combined with the vowels arising from the limbs of Gaṇeśa. (53)
Her six limbs should be divided, beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
[The meditation on Vāgīśvarī:
One should visualize a lotus situated between the solar and lunar mandalas. (54)
In the midst of that, one should contemplate the Goddess, resplendent with the brilliance of a fire-chamber, liberated from all limiting adjuncts (upādhis), yet endowed with all forms. || 55 ||
Such is her manifold form; now hear also of her meditation:
she is as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, with a conch and a lotus raised in her hands. (56)
With her hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a book;
she has two eyes and one face, and is adorned with golden earrings. (57)
For this Blessed Lady is indeed the meditating subject, the power of the All-pervading Lord whose essence is sound;
when thoroughly practiced, she swiftly grants the desired object to practitioners. (58)
The mantras for the gurus are as follows:
two *praṇavas*, the pervasive syllable (*vyāpin*), and the letter *ga* arising below that;
followed by "obeisance to the guru" at the end—this is the mantra for the worship of the guru. (59)
At the end of the three *praṇavas*, [the syllable] with the void (*savyomā*) faces west;
after that comes the word "Supreme" (*parama*), followed by "Salutation to the Guru" (*gurave namaḥ*).
This mantra belongs to the Guru of Gurus; learn it from that Guru.
Beyond this, there is the fourfold mantra beginning with "Mantra" and following "Padmanābha. (61)
One should place [the mantra] filled with bliss above the void for Parameṣṭhin;
then one should give the word "salutations" (namaḥ) along with the head-word (sanamastaka) to the ancestors—now listen to me regarding this.
[The Mantras of the Ancestors:
One should place the five *tāras* and *āhlāda* above the ether (*vyoman*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
however, *kālānala* and [the others] are below that, above the Lord of All Worlds (*sarvalokeśvara*).
Having formed a *piṇḍa* (syllabic cluster) from the phonemes uttered in their proper sequence, one then forms the word:
"Svadhā to the ancestors, obeisance to the assembly of ancestors. This is the king of mantras.
O tiger among the twice-born, the mantra of the *pūrvasiddha* has been declared; now, regarding those who are *pūrvasiddha*, it is said:
at the end of the *praṇava* and *ṣaṭka*, there is bliss adorned by space. (65)
One should offer salutations on the word *tathā* and so forth to those who have attained perfection;
having first worshipped this collection of mantras, one should thereafter perform the worship.
Those mantras of Lokeśa, preceded by the primary mantra, which are used in whatever rite;
now hear the characteristics of the scriptures of Lokeśa’s mantras. (67)

Then, O Nārada, according to the principle of emanation, one should unify this syllable consisting of the bliss of space (vyomānanda) and the vital breath (prāṇa) situated above the Lord of the Earth (dhareśa).
The mantra of Indra has been fully described; now learn from me that of the others.
O twice-born one, having extracted the two vital breaths (praṇas) in sequence, ending with fire (ra) and time (ma): 69.
The second vowel conjoined with the ornamented head of space (the letter *ha*)—
these two are proclaimed to be the seed-syllables of Śikhin and Antaka respectively.
The pervasive man, whose nature is the *liṅga*, should be joined as before like a *piṇḍa*;
[this applies] by means of the seed-syllable of Īśa, but understand it otherwise for the others.
Having extracted the Supreme Self, one should then place it twofold with two [syllables];
then, above those, one should place the two known as Varāha and Sūkṣma, namely Vyoma and Ānanda.
In due order, one should know the two seeds born of Varuṇa and Vāyu;
having placed above the portion of Dharma the syllable known as Vārāha.
As before, the seed-syllable of the Lord of the Stars (the Moon) is remembered as being endowed with two vowels;
it stands above the Sun and *ūrjā*, and is likewise marked by the pervasive [syllable]. (74)

One should place the seed-syllable known as Īśāna, endowed with the power that nourishes the universe and joined with the Primordial Deity (Ādideva), into the ether (vyoma) above the one called Prāṇa.
One should place Vaikuṇṭha below that, and the seed-syllable of Nāgeśvara;
then, as before, one should assign the Self consisting of the Vedas upon the Sun conjoined with the vowels.
The seed-syllable of Brahmā has been declared, as well as that of Paravyomeśvara;
for all [deities], the Praṇava comes first, followed by their own respective names joined with "namaḥ. (77)
[The Mantras of the Vajra and Other Weapons:
Now, listen to the auspicious mantras of the weapons in their proper sequence, as they abide, concisely stated according to their respective applications. (78)
Having extracted Ajita twice and placed it above the Pradhāna,
one should place these two— the support of all worlds— above and below.
The first [seed-syllable] is that which rises above Lokeśa, and the second is joined with the five dots;
these two seed-syllables, conjoined with the visarga, are born from the Vajra and Śakti.

These two, Akhaṇḍavikrama and Āndrī, are situated in the Mardana [position]; they should be known as being enriched by the emission (visarga) of Lokeśvara in the case of the staff (daṇḍa) and the sword (khaḍga). 81.
The two known as Āhlāda and Ajita are situated in Śata and Varuṇa;
they should be understood as being joined with Visarga and Ānanda, and are designated as Pāśa and Dhvaja.
Having extracted the Supreme Self (Paramātman), one should thereafter extract the one called Anala;
above those two, one should place Anala and Śāśvata in sequence.
Then, one should join each [letter] with the *soddāma* *visarga*.
The two, the mallet (*mudgara*) and the trident (*śūla*), are proclaimed by Someśa as being the two brahmin weapons (*dvijāyudha*). (84)
One should place that which is known as the *paraprakṛti* upon the fire, together with the *odana* and the *visarga*; thereafter, one should join [the *odana*] to that very [fire]. 85.
Now this seed-syllable known as Sīra is described for the deity Vārija: having extracted the letter *va* (Varuṇa) and placed it upon the letter known as Nara (na), [it becomes *nva*]. (86)
The Pādma [mantra] is said here to be joined with the Visarga, the Primordial God;
the Lord of Bījas called Prāṇa is likewise pervaded by Fire alone. [This is the Viṣvaksena-mantra. (87)
p. 67) That [form], endowed with the sovereignty over the three worlds, then ascended above the *ūrja*;
thereafter, having assumed the form of a boar (*vārāha*), it was adorned by the mountains and the sky. 88.
Thereafter, one should place the word "namaḥ" after "Viṣvaksenāya";
for this mantra of Viṣvaksena is proclaimed to begin with the Praṇava (Om). || 89 ||
Indeed, his original seed-syllable (pūrvabīja), when deprived of the vowel *ū*, becomes the group of limbs (aṅgagaṇa) when differentiated by the six long vowels, just like that of Gaṇeśa. || 90 ||
Accompanied by the *praṇava*, one's own name, and the six classes (*jāti*),
the pentad of ritual service mantras (*aupacārika-mantra*) is now being described. (91)
O Mahāmati, that which is common to all, such as the root mantra and the rest, by the mere knowledge of which—without recitation, meditation, and so forth—[the goal is attained]. (92)
Because it is performed at the proper time, the worship becomes complete.
[The mantra to be employed for the invocation is:
the supreme three-syllabled word accompanied by two *praṇavas*. (93)
Then one should extract the second [mantra] consisting of five syllables situated in the abode;
thereafter, that which consists of eight syllables, the supreme state, which desires to bestow grace.
O twice-born one, one should join the letter *da* situated within the letter *ya* at the end;
thereafter, one should extract that which is endowed with the primordial deity and marked by the *tāla*.
Then [he meditated on] the one named Varuṇa, who wears only a garland;
then the support of all worlds, joined with the source of the universe. || 96 ||
And at the end, one should bestow the Supreme Self accompanied by Gopana, joined with Rāma, along with Dhruva, and then Kāla alone.
Then one should give the Vairāja mantra alone, which is a three-syllabled word that bestows success;
thereafter, one should give the two-syllabled mantra "Mantre" and then the single syllable "Śaṅkara."
