Then one should place [the syllable] which is the support of all worlds without exception and is joined with Māyā;
thereafter, one should extract the Fire (Ra) conjoined with Vikrama (Sa) and Vyoman (Ha). || 99 ||
O Brahmin, the supreme mantra consists of thirty-eight syllables, beginning with the word "namo namaḥ" followed by the syllable "praṇava" (om), which is endowed with great splendor. 100.
O Brahmin, listen further to the mantra to be employed for invocation;
[the mantra] to be applied during the services beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) is known as the "Aupacārika-hṛd," by which the worship is performed. (101)
At the end of the *praṇava*, one should join the breath (*prāṇa*) adorned by the void (*vyoman*) three times; thereafter, one should utter the six-syllabled phrase: "This, this, this. (102)
And then take [the water] with the fifteen-syllable mantra "gṛhāṇa ca tataḥ svāhā," which is indeed always suitable for all ritual services, beginning with the water for washing the feet.
To avoid deficiency or excess, the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī should be employed:
one should then place the Praṇava, followed by "vidmahe viśvarūpāya," and immediately thereafter "dhīmahe viśvātītāya. (104)
Thereafter, at the end of the two words [namas te], one should add "tanno viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt.
One should employ this at the end of all ritual acts for the sake of completion. || 105 ||
For the purpose of remedying deficiencies or excesses, there is the supreme Gāyatrī of Viṣṇu;
it consists of twenty-four syllables and is joined with the word "namaḥ" and the Praṇava (Oṃ). || 106 ||
[The mantra to be employed for propitiation:
One should first extract the Praṇava (Oṃ), then Viṣṇu conjoined with Vyoma (Ha), then give the syllable Hrīṃ, and again Viṣṇu in the same manner. 107.
Then one should give the syllable for Prāṇa accompanied by Vyoman (Ha), followed by Soma alone (Sa),
then the two supreme letters (Au and Au), and thereafter the station of Parameśa (Ma).
"Be gracious! Oṃ, ending with 'namas', this mantra indeed consists of eighteen syllables;
it should be employed for the propitiation of the mantra, concluding with the binding of the mudrā. (109)
[The mantra to be employed for dismissal:
Oṃ, O Blessed One, embodiment of the mantra! One should give the eight-syllable word;
and at its end, having joined that which is mounted upon Varuṇa and called "Nectar" (Amṛta). 110.
Then one should bestow the six-syllabled mantra, "Attain the state, attain the state";
then again the three-syllabled mantra, "Forgive me," ending with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), and one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*). || 111 ||
One should employ the king of mantras consisting of twenty-six syllables, beginning with the word *namo namaḥ*,
at all times for the purpose of dismissal (*visarjana*) of the entire collection of mantras.
But the syllable known as *jñapti*, which is situated upon a boar, is Vyomeśa joined with Viṣṇu, placed between the *namaḥ* and the *praṇava*. (113)
(69) O twice-born one, this mantra belongs to Saurabhi and is joined with its own name;
it is for the purpose of completion and for the sake of nourishing them at the end of their enjoyment. (114)
Thus, O Brahmin, this treasury of mantras has been declared exactly as it exists;
it causes the destruction of all sins and brings about the pacification of all sufferings. (115)
For this must be kept secret from those who lack devotion, and especially from the deceitful, the atheists, the wicked, the rogues, and those who act with hypocrisy. 116.
And for those who are devoted, though they may be atheists, who practice faith and self-restraint, who delight in their gurus and the scriptures, and who follow the path of right conduct. || 117 ||
This should be spoken to those who have realized the truth, who rely on firm faith, and who are absorbed in that [truth];
for others, it would be otherwise.
And it is said: "He who, out of delusion, greed, injustice, or lust, speaks regarding these [images] which are devoid of devotion and faith, that lowest of men goes to hell. (119)
O tiger among brahmins, this applies even to one who has attained perfection; what then need be said of one who has not?
Therefore, having first observed the principles of justice according to their true nature, [one should act].

One who has approached [for instruction] should speak according to the rule, provided that he listens according to the rule; for he who speaks without justice and he who listens without justice [are both at fault]. || 121 ||
Both of them go to a terrible hell for an inexhaustible time;
knowing this, O tiger among sages, [understand] this supreme secret. (122)
The means of attainment (sādhana) must be explained in terms of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, not for one who has not been examined.
Whatever exists in this world, all that is perishable. (123)
Wealth and such things grant pleasure for only a moment, like a dream;
whereas the performance of ritual conduct according to the scriptures, as well as mantra and gnosis, are imperishable.
It bestows infinite, eternal happiness and increases from moment to moment.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Auxiliary Mantras," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now, in the Jayākhyasaṃhitā, the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Binding of Mudrās," the Blessed Lord said:
I shall now explain, in due order and according to sequence, the treasury of mudrās for this very collection of mantras, by means of which [the deities] are always present.
And it should be [employed] by the foremost of practitioners for the accomplishment of enjoyment and liberation;
first for the root mantra, and after that for the others. (2)
The mantra-practitioner should indeed bind the mudrā at the time of bathing within the water,
at the time of performing the self-assignment (nyāsa), and at the conclusion of the worship upon the ground of the maṇḍala.
In the images, in the arrangement of mantras, in the vessel for the arghya offering, in the water vessel, at the conclusion of the full oblation, and when the mantra resides within the fire; (4)
For the destruction of those who cause harm, for the pacification of all obstacles, and for the accomplishment of the purpose of all undertakings, this treasury of mudrās is proclaimed here. (5)
O Sage, one should take hold of the middle finger of the downward-facing left hand with the [middle finger of the] right;
the other three fingers of the right hand remain like a fist. (6)
Having joined both thumbs together, this mudrā is known as Jayā;
one should visualize Garuḍa beneath her, in her left hand.
One should meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu on the back of the right hand;
this mudrā is named Jayā, which accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
One should employ the Śakti-mudrā for the God of Gods together with Tārkṣya:
having extended the left hand upward, the fingers remain spread apart. (9)
The fingers should be slightly contracted at their tips;
the thumb should form a bridge-like structure, meeting them face-to-face in the middle among the other fingers.
One should bind the Śakti-mudrā, which bestows happiness, facing the heart;
indeed, this mudrā brings about the presence [of the deity] in the body endowed with Śakti.
Then, know that with the index finger [one performs this] in the worship of Lakṣmī and in the Śaktis;
with the right hand, one should form a fist [this is the Hṛdayamudrā]. 12.
O twice-born one, having placed the thumb in the middle of the hand, it should be joined at the heart;
this shall be the mudrā called Hṛdaya, which is effective for all mantras. (13)
[The Head Seal (śiromudrā):
One should extend all the fingers and touch them with the thumb. This is renowned as the Head Seal (śiromudrā), which brings about the presence of the mantra. (14)
Having formed a fist at the location of the crest-lock with the index finger positioned pointing upwards,
this is renowned as the *śikhāmudrā*, which brings about the destruction of all malevolent beings. (15)
For this [mudrā] is indeed proclaimed as always being for the destruction of faults and obstacles;
therefore, one should first bind it with effort in the sacrificial hall.
When joined with the mantra, it effects the destruction of all obstacles.
[The Armor Mudrā]:
O twice-born one, the branches of both hands are grasped at their tips. 17.
The space between the two [hands] should indeed remain unjoined, supported by the binding of the wrists;
this is the Vārmaṇī mudrā, by which one should touch both shoulders. (18)
It is impenetrable for wicked assemblies, for bhūtas, vetālas, and yogins;
and at the time of performing the rite, one should diligently bind it together with the mantra. (19)
[The Eye Mudrā]:
With the fingers of both hands interlaced and closed, the backs of the hands are joined;
the two index fingers are joined at their tips, forming a hollow between them. (20)
With the two thumbs joined at their bases and crossed with one another, this is the mudrā called Locanā; one should display it near the eyes.
[The Weapon Mudrā]:
One should snap the index finger with the thumb in the ten directions;
then, with both hands moving swiftly, one should gaze intently with the eyes.
Known as the "Weapon-Seal" (Astramudrā), it strikes terror even among the gods;
how much more so for those of wicked birth when it is employed in conjunction with speech, mind, and body? (23)
[The Siṃhamudrā:
With the right hand turned upward, having bent the three fingers of the left hand, one should extend the thumb and the index finger sideways. (24)
With the gaze slightly raised and directed downward, joined with a steady look, it causes the destruction of bondage by the noose and the eradication of all calamities. (25)
This is the Lion Seal (siṃhamudrā), known as "Astonishment," which possesses great splendor.
[The Kapila Seal: One should press the middle finger between the index finger and the thumb. (26)
One should extend the ring finger and then the little finger of that [hand];
when these two are positioned far apart from each other, this mudrā is known as Kapilī. || 27 ||

For this is the accomplisher of all siddhis, effective for the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest; it is the *kroḍamudrā*, when the middle and ring fingers are joined in the left hand which is turned downward. (28)
When the thumb is joined with the little finger and the two index fingers are extended, this mudrā is known as the Kroḍātmikā. || 29 ||
She who crushes all mechanical devices and wards off all the wicked,
she who resides within the mouths of the mudrās, should be appointed to her respective place.
[The Kaustubha-mudrā:
O Brahmin, with the middle and ring fingers shortened and held in the center of the palms like two fists, those two fists are then placed at the back of both hands. (31)
One should join the two index fingers through the gap between them and extend them;
then, one should join their tips together and place them upon the tips of the thumbs.
With the two index fingers in the middle, joined with one another in sequence—this is said to be the Kaustubha mudrā; now hear the description of the garland mudrā (mālāmudrā).
The *mālāmudrā* consists of grasping eight branches with both hands, not too far from their tips; they should be held smoothly and allowed to hang down, whether one is seated or standing. (34)
O Brahmin, one should properly extend both arms so that they hang down between the thighs, reaching as far as the wrists;
this is proclaimed as the Mālā-mudrā.
[The Lotus Mudrā]: With the two thumbs joined together and the fingers remaining spread apart, this is indeed the Lotus Mudrā, which bestows nourishment and good fortune. || 36 ||
One should grasp the left thumb with the fist of the right hand;
then, one should place the fingers of the left hand over those of the right. [This is the śaṅkhamudrā. 37.
One should join the tips of the left index finger and the tip of the right thumb together, facing each other and firmly pressed against one another. (38)
This would be the mudrā of Śaṅkha when it is held with the palms facing upwards;
as for the Cakramudrā, both hands are clearly extended and joined together. (39)
From its rotation, it is proclaimed as the Cakravartin-mudrā;
it is the destroyer of all sufferings, the supreme among mudrās that pierces through [all bonds]. (40)

Having formed the mudrā of the mace by making a fist with the right hand and placing it upon the head of the left thumb, one should display it in this manner; this is the most beautiful mudrā of Kaumodakī.
Known as the Gadā-mudrā (Mace Seal), it crushes the army of defects.
O twice-born one, having first extended both hands and then brought them together, this is the Pakṣirāja-mudrā (King of Birds Seal). 42.
One should place the tips of both thumbs at the base of the ring fingers;
facing downwards and resting upon the wrists.
Having joined them closely together at the tips, one should place those two fingers—the pair consisting of the left index and middle fingers—from both hands. 44.
One should make [the fingers] raised and sparse, and also curved toward each other;
clearly raised and joined like a tail, with the pair of little fingers [so positioned]. (45)
This is the mudrā of the Great-Souled King of Birds alone; [it is the noose-mudrā (pāśamudrā)].
Then, having extended the right hand, [the thumb and the little finger are drawn out]. (46)
From the tip of the forefinger, by forming it like a bridge, the three fingers beginning with the index finger are bent like a hood and joined together like a triple creeper. (47)
This is the noose mudrā; now learn from me that which is called the hook.
[The Hook Mudrā]: The little finger and the middle finger of the left hand should be placed in the middle;
the thumb should be positioned behind them as if on their back. (49)
O twice-born one, the index finger should be placed in front and curved like a goad;
this is the Aṅkuśa mudrā. Now hear [the mudrās] for Satya and the others.
[The Five Mudrās beginning with Satya] (p. 74): One should cause the five fingers of the right hand to touch one another; they should be raised and directed toward the face. (51)
This is the mudrā of Satya, occurring prior to the emergence of the Upāṅgas;
it is proclaimed as the second [mudrā] through the joining of the thumb and the index finger.
The third is proclaimed through the union of the thumb and the middle finger;
but the fourth, O Nārada, is through the union of the thumb and the ring finger.
From the joining of the little finger and the thumb of the fifth [finger], the Mahājayā mudrā is produced.
Having placed the left hand upon the heart, it should be turned upward and extended.
But on the back, one should perform the binding of the fist with the right hand.
With the thumb positioned above the fist and gazed upon by the two eyes—
this, O observer of good vows, shall be the divine mudrā of the King of Mantras.
She is renowned as Mahājaya, the accomplisher of all yogas;
she eternally bestows all siddhis and fulfills all mudrās. || 56 ||
By this [seal] the entire universe, from Brahmā down to the limit of conceptualization, is sealed;
it belongs to the one who is endowed with the power of all limbs and is the abode of all mantras. 57.
O Brahmin, thus have I described this collection of mudrās for the seed-mantras (garbha-mantras) of the partless, immutable, and seven-syllabled [Brahman]. || 58 ||
Listen to the characteristics of the mantras and mudrās of the supporting seats.
O twice-born one, the *ādhāraśakti-mudrā* and the *kūrma-mudrā* consist of two fingers thrown inward between the two fists. (59)
The right fist of the left [hand] should be behind [it], devoid of contact;
this is upon the Ādhāra-śakti, above which are the Tortoise and Fire.
[The Anantāsana-mudrā: Having bent both the ring finger and the index finger of the downward-facing left hand so that they touch the back [of the hand], they are placed upon the middle finger. (61)
Below those two, O Sage, one should form the middle finger straight and facing downwards;
the little finger, together with the thumb, should be made well-extended.
O twice-born one, by this [mudrā] the Anantāsana-mudrā is described;
for she exists having embraced this entire world within her lap. (63)
She is established as the preeminent among all the *ādhāramudrās*.
Having first uttered her mantra, which is protracted (*pluta*) and contains many vowels (*bahumātṛka*). (64)
Arising from the differentiation of the powers of sound, it is graspable as a positive entity and unstruck (*anāhata*);
then, in its emission, it is designated by the name "the seat of Ananta. (65)
O Brahmin, one should perform the visualization of the bound [state], conjoined with meditation on true being, during the sacrifice of constant authority for mantras of diverse forms. (66)
For the sake of swiftly accomplishing ritual actions, one should diligently apply the *pṛthivīmudrā*:
first, one should bind two fists with both hands joined together. 67.
With the three fingers [excluding the thumb], one should join the two index fingers to the tip of the thumb; then, having done so, one should again bring them together at their base.
This, however, is the Pārthivī mudrā; now hear of the Sāmudrī [the Ocean Mudrā]:
the two hands are joined together with the tips of the nails touching at the joints of the fingers. (69)
The ritual acts should be performed with the fingers interlaced, facing one another; one should move that which is held between them at the tips of the thumbs, which are without support.
One should form the middle with both hands, making it deep like a hollow;
this is the previously mentioned mudrā of the Milk Ocean, as well as that of the Lotus.
From the yoga of mantra as well as from meditation, a state of otherness indeed arises.
[The fourfold mudrās beginning with Dharma:
Having placed the two hands so that they do not touch, one should then join them. (72)
Placing face to face with the two index fingers, one should then release it;
having formed that same kind of bond, one should release it from the two ring fingers. (73)
Having withdrawn that as well, one should employ the two little fingers;
with each finger bound, one should place the pair of thumbs joined together. (74)
Know that the group of mudrās for this tetrad beginning with Dharma follows in sequence.

For the lotus situated above that, as previously described through the application of mantra, there is the mudrā of the three abodes characterized by the sun, moon, and fire; specifically, it consists of the joining of the index finger and the thumb of the right hand. (76)
Having performed that binding, one should then gradually expand it and again make the collection of branches stand upright and separate. (77)
This is the mudrā of the three abodes; now learn from me the one called Haṃsa.
[Haṃsamudrā] One should make the two hands clearly extended in the form of an añjali.
This is the perfectly pure mudrā of the ultimate reality for the meditation seat;
this binding of mudrās for the mantras of the seats has been declared by me. (79)
O best of sages, the ten mudrās of the seeds beginning with Kṣetreśa and ending with Padmanidhyadhipa are now described in order.
Having grasped the fingers as counted with both hands, one should press them firmly and raise the two thumbs; this is the Kṣetreśa-mudrā. (81)
This is the mudrā of Kṣetrapāla; now hear from me that of Śrī and the others.
[The Śrīmudrā:
Having placed the two hands palm-upward and close together, O Nārada, (82)
Then, having made all the fingers curved and positioned at the middle, one should gradually bring the two thumbs to a state of clarity by letting them fall [down]. (83)
This first mudrā of the seed-syllable Śrī has been described to you;
it is the Caṇḍamudrā, born from the seed-syllable Caṇḍa, formed by raising the index finger from the left hand. (84)
Know that very same [mudrā] from the right hand as belonging to the one named Pracaṇḍa;
it is indeed the Jaya-mudrā.
Having indeed raised [the hand] from the middle of the left hand of Jaya. || 85 ||
The Vijayamudrā is proclaimed as belonging to the seed-syllable known as Vijaya from the right side. || 86 ||
[Gāṅgamudrā] Having positioned the left ring finger as before, know that to be the Gāṅga mudrā.
(p. 77) [Yāmunamudrā]
O Nārada, the mudrās of the seed-syllable of Āmuṇa have been described, beginning with the southern one.
[The Conch Mudrā:
For the Lord of Treasures (Nidhīśvara), the little finger is extended from the left hand of the Conch. [The Lotus-Treasure Mudrā]
When that same [mudrā] is raised upward from the left hand of the one called Padma, [it is the next]. || 88 ||
[The Gaṇeśa-mudrā:
With the right hand, using a fist formed with the thumb, one should press down upon the index finger and the ring finger of the left hand. (89)
And for conchs blown with effort, the middle finger should be applied to the back [of the hand] so that it appears hanging down like a hand. 90.
One should visualize the little finger of the left hand not too close to the fist, positioned outside the thumb of the right hand, like a fang.
O twice-born one, the left thumb and the other [right thumb] should be slightly bent and turned sideways,
so that they both appear like the ears of an elephant.
This is the mudrā of Gaṇeśvara, which causes the destruction of all obstacles.
[The Vāgīśvarī Mudrā:
Having first joined the wrists of both hands firmly together... (93)
Having joined the two index fingers at their tips so that they are elevated and meet at the middle,
one should likewise do the same with the pair of ring fingers.
Having doubled it firmly, one should bend it face downwards;
O twice-born one, one should gradually touch each of one's own palms with it.
O twice-born one, one should make the two thumbs clearly separated and likewise the pair of little fingers, with the remaining fingers held together.

This is the mudrā for one who desires the hearing of the Word; whoever binds it day after day while reciting [the mantra], he will become that very state, and his intellect will descend [into that realization]. 97.
Having brought the two hands together face-to-face and fully extended them,
they should be applied above the forehead while the head is bowed. (98)

This is indeed the mudrā of the Guru, the most venerable Guru, and of the Father, the most venerable Father—the mudrās of the assembly of Fathers. Having placed the right hand face upwards, one should then [arrange] the group of fingers. (99)
One should slightly bend the joined thumb and then extend it; then, by means of the fingers becoming somewhat transverse, one should gradually turn it slightly downward.
This mudrā is known to bring eternal satisfaction to the host of ancestors;
therefore, it should be displayed with great effort at the time of worship. || 101 ||
Whatever satisfaction indeed arises from a Śrāddha performed on a specific occasion,
that is increased a hundredfold for the ancestors through the worship [of the deity] by means of the binding of the Mudrās.
[The Siddha-mudrā]: One should place both hands palms upward at the region of the navel;
with the left hand on the back of the right, this is the mudrā of the lineage of the Siddhas. (103)
With the *varābhaya-mudrās*, one should clearly form the right hand facing outward from oneself,
and likewise fashion the left hand hanging down and facing away. (104)
O twice-born one, these two mudrās known as Varā and Abhayā should be understood, in brief, as belonging respectively to Indra and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas). || 105 ||
One should display the weapon (astra) named [the goddess] previously described, joined with power (śakti), sequentially with each mantra beginning with Vajra. || 106 ||

Regarding the worship of the weapons of the World-Protectors in their proper sequence, the Viṣvaksena-mudrā is formed as follows: the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger of the left hand are positioned in the center of the palm. (107)
Of those [fingers], the thumb should be on the back and the index finger raised;
it should be positioned at the region of the bridge of the nose, and then with the right hand... (108)
Having likewise formed a fist with the three fingers as before,
one should double the index fingers and press them against the tips of the thumbs.
With his staff-like arms raised like those extended for hurling a discus—
this is the mudrā of Viṣvaksena, which cuts down all the works of the Creator.
[The Invitation Mudrā]: One should slightly bend the right hand toward the heart;
with the thumb clearly separated from the fingers, this is known as the mudrā for invitation. (111)
[The Mudrā of Dismissal]:
Both hands, with fingers slightly spread, should have the shape of the edge of a sword; having placed the two thumbs straight like a staff, one should gradually form the fist-closure. 112.
One should perform this mudrā with the little fingers and so forth during the dismissal;
it is the Surabhi-mudrā.
Having joined both hands together, they should be well-pressed and turned downwards. (113)
Then, having joined the two little fingers together with their thumbs in close contact,
the pair of middle fingers should be placed on the backs of the opposite hands;
likewise, the pair of ring fingers and the pair of index fingers should be extended.
This mudrā, known as Kāmadhenu, fulfills all desires;
one should always practice the application of mudrās in two ways. (115)
But that which consists of consciousness is the internal form, a radiant casket;
O Brahmin, that which arises from action, speech, and mind is threefold, both external and internal. (116)
Whoever, knowing the ritual procedure, binds the mudrā according to this method, by him this entire universe is sealed, granting the accomplishment of non-rebirth. (117)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Binding of Mudrās," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*, the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing," [spoken by] the Blessed Lord.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing one's qualification, I shall first describe the ritual bath (snāna),
by which a devotee, once consecrated, becomes fit for the fire-sacrifice (homa) and the worship (yāga).
[The two-fold nature of bathing:
One should perform the two types of bathing for the purification of the accumulation of impurities;
having bathed according to the general procedure, one should then bathe according to the specific procedure. (2)
Bathing is twofold: the common worldly bath and the distinguished bath consecrated by mantras.
This too must be preceded by the rules of purification; therefore, I shall first explain that to you. (3)
Three applications of clay should be made to the penis with intervals between each;
five should be applied to the left hand, and three to both hands for the sake of purification. (4)
This is the purification for the voiding of urine; it is the same immediately after the voiding of feces.
There should be five applications of clay to the anus, and likewise an equal number of intermediate applications of clay.
Ten [applications] should be given to the left hand, seven to both hands;
purification of the feet is by three, and purification of the shanks is by five.
Then, O Brahmin, one should apply seven applications of clay to the waist to remove the defect of bodily sweat and to pacify external impurities.
Thus has it been prescribed for devotees and those learned in the Vedas during the rainy season;
because of this statement regarding the monsoon, there is the removal of even a single speck of dust from that [place].
Those devoted to ritual practice should always perform [the bath] during autumn, summer, and spring;
even from among these, however, one should omit the clay application one by one.
O Brahmin, during the winter and the cool season, those learned in the Vedas who abide in self-restraint should perform purification on the path in accordance with the place and time.
Having thus removed the coating of odor, one becomes pure through the purification of the mind.
Having performed the cleansing in this manner for the purpose of bathing, one should first sip water (ācamana) and then dig [for the earth].
Having taken earth from a pure place with a ritual stake consecrated by the Astra-mantra, and having gathered it while reciting the Astra-mantra, he should proceed to a body of water.
[The Ritual of Bathing] Therein, first, one should wash the water's edge with the water of the *astra* mantra;
then, having divided the clay into two parts, one should set them aside, and subsequently take one portion. (13)
Having placed cow dung, darbha grass, and consecrated sesame seeds,
one should perform the bath with the worldly portion enriched by cow dung.

Then, having first performed that bath, one should perform the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*). [The sequence for the ritual bath: In the ritual bath, however, one should divide the portion of earth into two parts again. (15)
The feet and so forth should be washed by one person according to the sequence as before;
having performed the washing of the hands, one should immerse oneself within the water.
p. 81) [The Mantra-Placement and Seal-Binding as Limbs of the Bath]:
Having arisen, one should place the six-limbed mantra upon one’s own body;
then one should perform the placement of the mantra and execute the binding of the mudrās. || 17 ||
O twice-born one, when water flowing in a stream comes into contact with impurities such as insects, its purification occurs in this manner:
it is purified by flowing, and likewise even when drawn out. (18)
O Brahmin, even if the water of Varuṇa were stainless when heated by the rays of the sun and moon,
it would not be so in the ritual procedure of the mantra.
[The Wearing of the Purifier:
Two purifiers made of darbha grass, consisting of three, five, or seven strands, joined with firm knots, and consecrated with the Astra-mantra; 20.
Having placed it in both hands below the ring fingers,

[one should consecrate the clay— which has been divided into three parts on the left hand according to the distinction of the locations starting from the base— with the three mantras beginning with the Astra-mantra in sequence].
Having set aside the remaining clay with a portion left over, he took it up while uttering a weapon-mantra.
One should divide that [line] on the left hand into root, middle, and tip;
then one should recite with the weapon-mantra and the root-mantra, along with the limbs, in due order.
[Regarding the application of the earth consecrated with the weapon-mantra:

Having taken earth over which the weapon-mantra has been recited, one should scatter it in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, below, and above, while employing that mantra together with the binding of the mudrā. (23)
By that [sound], the obstacles that seize one's bath, stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
flee in a state of agitation before it has even fully gathered.
[The application of the earth consecrated by the root mantra:
Taking that portion of earth which was previously consecrated with the root mantra and remains [there], one should recite it while taking it and casting it into the midst of the water. || 25 ||
Therefore, O tiger among the twice-born, at that very moment it becomes completely filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā and the waters of the Yamunā.
Prayāga, Cakratīrtha, Prabhāsa, and the Puṣkara lakes become present through the power of this mantra. (27)
Then, at the end of the mantra, one should utter the word "pada" for Viṣṇutīrtha;
with that salutation, there shall be proximity to Viṣṇutīrtha. (28)

[The application of only the root mantra at other sacred sites: Whenever one performs a bath at another sacred site, one should employ there only the root mantra, excluding the term "Viṣṇu-tīrtha. (29)
A wise person does not utter this name at other sacred sites;
for if one should remember another name while in the presence of a sacred site, [the merit is lost]. (30)
In the case of ordinary bathing rites at a lake or similar body of water containing non-aging waters, the *snātaka* should depart after cursing that sacred site for a moment.
Having properly proclaimed the rivers such as the Gaṅgā and the sacred fords (tīrthas),
one should duly recite the mantra for the Viṣṇu-tīrtha during the sequence of the ritual bath.
[The application of the portion of earth consecrated with the limb-mantras:
Then, having mixed with water the portion situated in the palm of the hand which has been recited over with the limb-mantras, one should make it smooth and heat it with the rays of the sun. (33)
While [the disciple] is covered by a cloud, he should visualize his own mantra situated in the sky like the sun;
having shown it to him with his hand, he should touch all the limbs of the disciple with both hands.
[The method for the consecration of the sacred site:
Then, by means of the two types of concentration (dhāraṇā), one should perform the consecration of the sacred site and the water according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
Starting from the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) up to the object of one's resolve,
one should fill everything with fire, which is enveloped by garlands of flames.
Having rendered the world free from impurity, one should remember the Tīrtha as having a peaceful form;
and having again dissolved it into Viṣṇu, who is peaceful and consists of pure consciousness.
Formerly, having remembered that [the stream] which was like a drop of dew and limited in extent, it emerged from the source of Brahmā through the power of Śakti.
Swelling with torrents and waves as it falls with great velocity,
it shall fill everything up to the abode of Brahmā, resembling the moon in luster.
One should constantly contemplate that collision through the verses of observation;
within the entire primordial nature (svarūpa), there is the seat of the Lord.
O Brahmin, having offered that, one should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa above it—pure like ten million moons and surrounded by streams of pure nectar. (41)
When this is done, it shall become a sacred ford (tīrtha) whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, rich with a multitude of powers and vomiting forth the essence of nectar.
Then one should perform the immersion accompanied by emergence from the water, using fragrant, pleasing, pure, and various auspicious *āmalaka* fruits. (43)
The mantra-practitioner, free from sloth, should bathe with the ritual honors due to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
[Now follows the procedure for the subsidiary rites following the bath:
Then, remaining within the water, he should recite the mantra according to his capacity. (44)
He, whose form is radiant and luminous, rises within the heart;
from the heart, he extends forward and beyond, reaching as far as the distant limit of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta).
O Nārada, having seen the Supreme Person standing before him in person,
he rose from the water and beheld that very same one situated in the sky.
Then, having reached the water and seated himself at ease,
he should place the heart-mantra, white in form, upon the tip of the goad-mudrā.
One should exhale [the breath] from the center of the *tīrtha* joined with one's own internal wind (*anila*),
and then draw it back in again by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) accompanied by the appropriate *mudrā*.

Having thus approached the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in the prescribed manner, O Nārada, one should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the Praṇava and the Heart-mantra known as Upacāra.

O twice-born one, with water that is very clear and reaching up to the knees, using one hand and reciting the *pādya* mantra along with the *hṛdaya* mantra accompanied by the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), [one should perform the rite]. 50.
Having visualized the deity stationed there, together with his limbs and retinue, one should perform the ritual attendance while reciting this mantra. || 51 ||
Then, with the syllable Om (praṇava), one should satisfy all the ancestors and gods according to the rule;
thereafter, one should discard the bathing cloth while it is mixed with sesame seeds.
Then, having put on a pair of well-washed garments that do not cause fatigue—
or else a lower garment together with a yogapaṭṭaka beneath it— 53.
For one must never be clad in only a single garment;
rather, when another place has been purified by the Astra-mantra, one should remain seated upon the seat of Ananta.
Having meditated upon the support, the seat of Acyuta in the midst of the water, and having summoned him together with the entire collection of mantras, one should establish him there. (55)
One should satisfy [the deities] with water alone, ending with Viṣvaksena,
using their respective mantras, with both hands in front of oneself in due order.

Having gratified the deities, sages, nāgas, and those who move through the planets, spirits, and the sky, as well as all things down to the stationary beings, he should then gratify his own lineage in due order.
Then, one should remember the Lord Sāsana departing from the midst of the water;
for the purification of the sacred site (tīrtha), that mantra was previously placed in all directions.
O twice-born one, impelling the breath through the tip of the nose as before toward the gods,
having unified that [breath] with it, one should cast forth the water like semen.
Having filled [the vessel], one should place it upon the heart with the *sopasaṃhāra* mudrā.
Thus has the water-bath (*audaka-snāna*) been described; now learn from me the mantra-bath (*māntra*). 60.
[The Mantra-bath: In the absence of water, or during difficult times and cold weather,
or when traveling, for swift success, or for independence in important tasks— 61.
Or, O best of Brahmins, having observed that [the time] has arrived during either the night or the day,
one should wash one's feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water drawn from a vessel.
Having purified the ten directions as before, one should then sit down;
having applied the Astra-mantra to the palms of the hands, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body in due order.
One should perform that [rite] with the root mantra and so forth, together with the entire collection of mantras;
for [the purification resulting from] a mere bath of water, devoid of ritual consecration, [is insufficient].

O Nārada, the fruit that belongs to one who has performed ritual ablutions at sacred fords such as Prabhāsa and others should be known to be a hundredfold greater from [the merit of] this collection of mantras.
[The Bath of Meditation]:
Now I shall describe the bath of meditation, which is superior even to the two preceding ones.
One should contemplate the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who abides in the sky, whose form is the mantra. (66)
One should contemplate the stream born from the water of His feet falling upon one's own head, entering one's own body through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*). 67.
By means of that [water], one should wash away all impurity residing within the body;
at that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion (viraja) and arises like a crystal. (68)
This bath is remembered as being a hundred times superior to the bath performed with mantras;
therefore, one who is devoted with faith should perform at least one of these baths.
Since all ritual acts preceded by bathing yield their full fruit, therefore one who desires his own welfare should perform the bath first. (70)
O best of the twice-born, a living being becomes pure by the mere act of bathing; how much more so one who is devoted to ritual action, yet whose soul is devoid of discernment? 71.
Endowed with the sequence of duties pertaining to one's social class and established upon the path of the virtuous—
thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*. 9.
Now begins the tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Samādhi," [concerning the journey to a secluded place for the purpose of meditation]. The Blessed One said:
O Nārada, having offered a blade of dūrvā grass, a flower, a leaf, or sesame seeds along with water upon his own head and at the site of the topknot, one should [proceed].
Then, taking a vessel filled with water in his hand,
he should go to a secluded, solitary place that is pleasing and free from defects.
Meditating on the mantra situated in the center of the heart, which has the form of a fully awakened fire,
he should remain silent, not looking toward the various directions, with his breath restrained.
[The portion to be performed at the time of reaching the site:
Having reached the site, one should expel one's own mantra through the tip of the nose;
having placed the *astra* outside, one should strike the earth with the foot. 4.
Preceded by the mantra, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu as possessing all attributes and seated upon Garuḍa.
[Regarding the options for seats such as darbha grass:
Having reached a solitary place, one should arrange a beautiful seat.
On *darbha* grass, a hide, a cloth, or a sacrificial wooden board,
having saluted Hari with devotion and the lineage of one's teachers in the mind, one should carry out the mental practice preceded by the remembrance of the Guru. (6)
Having received their mental command with his head bowed,
O Brahmin, he should carry out every mental rite exactly as it is prescribed.
[The Purification of the Seat] Having sprinkled the seat with water consecrated by the recitation of the root mantra,
one should again apply a snap of the fingers joined with the mantra for its purification. (8)
[The Purification of the Hands] O Nārada, listen now to how one should perform the purification of the hands:
both palms, both backs of the hands, as well as all the fingers. (9)
Having purified [the hands] with the weapon-mantra through the practice of visualization and recitation,
and having thus performed the purification of the hands, one should carry out the purification of the place.
[The Purification of the Place:
Having meditated upon the deity in a blazing form, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns, surrounded by millions of flames, and vomiting fire from his mouth. (11)
With that, one should fill everything up to the end of the world of Brahmā;
one should contemplate the mass of directions as blazing with the splendor of the mantra.
O best of the twice-born, remembering this entire circle of the earth as being ripened by the fire born of the mantra, like an earthen vessel [consumed by heat]. (13)
Thus, the purification of the locus occurs through the sprinkling of waves of nectar.
O Sage, now hear the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) exactly as it is, in its proper sequence.

[The Section on the Purification of the Elements] Know that the body, composed of the five elements— earth, water, fire, air, and ether— is like a magician’s illusion, devoid of qualities such as knowledge and the rest. 15.
As long as it has not been thoroughly purified by continuous meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), this body remains impure, dependent, born from semen and blood, and subject to decay. (16)
For that long, this would be unsuitable for matters such as mantra-installation (nyāsa) and the like;
[the seed-syllables of the elements beginning with earth are:
Śaṅkara, Agni, Soma, and the Sun who is their end. (17)
One should indeed apply these five colors in their proper sequence:
with Dhareśa, Varāha, Anala, and then Kambu.
Then, O best of the twice-born, one should join all [the mantras] with the Pradhāna,
and place the Ādideva, endowed with the sovereignty of the three worlds, upon the head.
(87) O Nārada, these seed-syllables of Earth, Fire, Wind, and Space, endowed with the names of Earth and the rest respectively, terminate in *huṃ phaṭ*. (20)
In the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should recite these [syllables] joined with the syllable Oṃ three times;
they are established in sequence as the five supreme lords of the elements.
The deities of the primary elements, earth and the rest—
Aniruddha and the other four, preceded by Satya— as previously mentioned,
exist as their powers (śakti); one should address those elements with them in due order.

Having caused Hari to emerge from the southern door of the *suṣumṇā* [to the outside], [one performs] the methods of entering the great elements such as earth into his own body, pervading them, and dissolving them therein.
Resembling a thousand suns, it was situated in the center of a circular mandala.
Having meditated upon him as the essence of mantra, seated in the supreme state, possessing the luster of molten gold, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths above.
Below that, however, is the circle of light (prabhācakra), joined with the presiding deity of the principle;
having meditated upon it as the partless mantra-body, one should [proceed] below that in sequence.
[First, the abode of the earth element:
One should contemplate the earth as four-cornered, yellow in luster, marked with vajras, endowed with the five [objects] beginning with sound, and filled with mountains and trees. (26)
One should meditate on her entering from the outside into one's own body by means of inhalation (pūraka), as she is adorned with cities, ramparts, excellent rivers, islands, and oceans.
While reciting that mantra, one should then contemplate it as resting;
by means of that [light], the space from the knees down to the soles of the feet is gradually pervaded.
Then, O best of the twice-born, by means of retention (kumbhaka), the king of mantras gradually attains dissolution into one's own mantra-form and into the power of fragrance (gandha-śakti).
[The abode of the water-principle:
One should then expel that power of fragrance externally by means of exhalation (*recaka*);
and into the great receptacle called Water, one should likewise [expel] the water and its majestic manifestation (*vaibhava*).
The oceans, rivers, and their currents; the six flavors along with the medicinal herbs; and whatever beings exist within the world that have water as their element—[all these he created]. (31)
Having meditated upon the external manifestation of Varuṇa, which is shaped like a half-moon and adorned with a lotus-banner, one should then [meditate] upon the body by means of that.
Having filled [the body] very slowly by means of the practice called *pūraka*, [one should contemplate] one's own mandala within the body, from the root of the thighs to the knees. (33)
O twice-born one, one should remember that everything is completely pervaded by that *kumbhaka*;
and having contemplated within it the Varuṇa mantra known as *dhāraṇā*.
All that maternal wealth has dissolved into its midst;
from there it enters the power of taste (rasa-śakti), and that power [dissolves] into the circle of fire (vahni-maṇḍala).
Having cast the abode of the fire-principle (*tejastattva*) by means of exhalation (*recaka*), one should then [place] the majestic fire,
which has the form of a triangular world and is adorned with radiant [flames]. (36)
By means of lightning, the moon, the sun, the stars, and the jewels of precious minerals;
by those with bodies that are self-luminous, and by those bodiless beings who move through the sky.
Having thus pervaded that great majesty with blazing svastikas,
one should then meditate upon that tiger among sages as consisting of pure light and composed of the subtle elements alone.
Uttering that very [mantra] while it resides within that maṇḍala,
one should meditate upon it as having entered [the body] in the same manner as before, by means of that very instrument.
Having pervaded and fixed one's attention from the navel down to the anus,
O Brahmin, one should contemplate that entire manifestation as being composed of fire.
The mantra, exhausted within the body of its own mantra-form and consisting of the nature of fire, undergoes dissolution into the power of form; and that power consists of pure consciousness.
[The Abode of the Wind-principle:
By that [power], her own mantra-body is dissolved by her own power;
she should cast the power produced by the exhalation (recaka) outside into the support of the wind. (42)
Then, one should indeed visualize the power of Vāyu on the outside;
it is circular, resembling a royal sapphire, and endowed with fiery reflections.
One should meditate upon that [lotus] as being filled with various kinds of fragrances and their many qualities,
and as being pervaded by its own mantra known as *dhāraṇā*.
Likewise, having meditated upon its own form and mantra and having uttered it, one should collect [the substance] very slowly with the tip of the nose, using the aforementioned method. (45)
One should meditate upon that [wind] as pervading from the neck down to the region of the navel;
then, by the very same procedure previously mentioned, one should contemplate the manifestation of the wind element.
O Great Sage, remembering that [the universe] has dissolved into the presiding deity,
one should remember that imperishable power within the great power known as Sparśā.
[The abode of the principle of space:
One should dissolve that which is all-pervading, eternal, invisible, and endowed with the power of its own manifestation, into the sphere of the sky within the great support called Sound. 48.
Then, having meditated upon the entire manifestation outside of the body as being called "space"—
filled with various sounds, formless, and having the luster of collyrium— 49.
O twice-born one, one should meditate upon that space, which is filled with countless Siddhas who are bodiless and consist of sound, by means of the mantra known as Vyoma through concentration.
He always maintains his own self by his own power,
as sound, mantra, and form, pervasive even within all manifestations.
Having thoroughly enveloped [the deity] with the intellect and having placed it within the body,
one should meditate upon it as being pervaded by that very means previously described.
The yogi should sustain [the breath] through the power of expansion from the ear up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) by means of the kumbhaka [retention], for as long as possible.
O Sage, one should subsequently meditate upon that [light] as transformed within one's own mantra;
then, the mantra of concentration known as Vyoma (the Sky) has entered into dissolution within the power of sound.
[The contemplation of the entry into the partless state of the power of sound, which has successively become the locus for the dissolution of the powers of smell and the rest:
One should contemplate that power as it proceeds through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
She is joined with the fourfold power and is imperishable through the [offerings] beginning with fragrance. || 55 ||
One should take refuge in the partless mantra, which transcends space and is stainless;
it is that which is even beyond those powers, such as Satī and the others.
Know that group of six to be partless (niṣkala), and its pervasion has been described previously.
One should thus lead the elemental manifestation, along with its mantras, to its dissolution in due order.
[The attainment of the state of liberation for the individual soul by means of leading it from one stage to another, starting from the gross body, through its arrival at a specific circle of light:
That consciousness which has become the individual soul (jīva), shimmering like a star, [is led forth].
But that which is to be cultivated is rested and emerged from the cage of the elements. || 58 ||

In this supreme mantra, which is free from conceptual proliferation and whose form is known as the five powers, one should, by means of this sequential yoga, [unite] the individual soul with the Self through the Self. (59)
One should behold that supreme, all-pervading Lord within the space of the heart—immovable, possessing the brilliance of the sun, and filled with shimmering radiance. (60)
Then one should practice the supreme samādhi abiding within the body of mantra;
that which is the supreme body of mantra is manifest within the sequence of syllables.
When one has understood that everything from the sun up to the sky is transcended by the causes that are powers,
and that this [world] is thus to be abandoned, then one is nourished by that state.
Unsatiated and with his purpose yet unfulfilled, he [proceeds] by resorting to the lotus-heart through the mantra, and having grasped the reality of the Self with the rope of knowledge. (63)
One should meditate upon oneself as emerging from the upper part of the hollow of the heart by means of one's own self;
for that crest-lock is indeed the flame of the mantra-fire through the channel of the light-form.
Suṣumnā, resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk, ascends upwards;
O Nārada, having remembered that [path] which reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one proceeds by that excellent way.
Gradually exhaling one's own self by means of the wind of discernment (vijñāna),
one should thus place the sixfold causal mantra-essence as non-pervasive.
And from that supreme form of the Lord above,
O tiger among the twice-born, there arises an incomparable mass of splendor.

O Nārada, it is situated at the hub of that wheel of light, delighted by the bliss of its own inherent joy; such is the nature of the Self-principle (ātmatattva) for one who abides in state after state.
That great bliss which arises for the pure conscious self, who is liberated from the body and exists as absolute consciousness—that indeed is the supreme Vaiṣṇavī power. 69.
Having made that individual soul (jīva), which performs unceasing actions, one with oneself,
it arises in a certain place and remains established in that very same place once again.
And know that, O Nārada, it is free from conceptual construction and inexpressible.
[This refers to the meditation on the incineration and reduction to ashes of this material body, once it has been contemplated as having been abandoned.]
Thus, having reached his own abode and cast off his material body, [he remains].

Established therein, one should burn the body-mass, which is devoid of the powers (śakti) and their subtle elements (tanmātra), consisting of the six sheaths (ṣāṭkośika), essence-less, and resembling burnt grass.
By means of the fire produced from the mantra, which arises from the churning of desire,
[one consumes] the support of all worlds, together with the four states of existence.

One should place [the syllable] situated above Lokeśa in the sky, and above that, one should place the self-designation of the fire of desire (icchāgni), beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*. (74)
O twice-born one, starting from that region of the foot, one should meditate upon that glowing mass as resembling a heap of ashes, with the fire extinguished. (75)
Then, having meditated upon the falling of that ash with joy, subtle, pervasive, preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, he was thus endowed [with it]. (76)

Then, having flooded the ashes scattered in all directions with water produced by meditation— water which, when sprinkled with one's own mantra, takes the form of milk— one should perform the visualization of the complete immersion for that which has been meditated upon as reduced to ashes, thereby [liberating it] from its downfall.
[Now, the sequence of meditation on the creation of the body consisting of unprecedented splendor:
Having encapsulated this "Lamp" mantra with the two [mantras] as before— one being Varāha mounted upon Amṛta and endowed with the bestowal of sovereignty over the three worlds— 78.
From that ocean-like form of milk, one should meditate upon the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings;
and as it is poured down from above, a multitude of streams of the nectar of the twice-born [falls]. (79)
Having emerged from the station of Turya, one should meditate upon it again and again;
there, having indeed placed the Vaiṣṇavī power consisting of the support (ādhāra) in the center.
One should meditate upon that which has become the seed of all, and the lotus arising from it—
consisting of the principles (tattva) of the six paths, white, full of splendor, and auspicious.
One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is mantra, situated in the center of that [space], pervaded by three mandalas and radiant with shimmering rays of light. 82.

O twice-born one, one should meditate upon Him as partless, absolute, pure, and the embodiment of the five excellent mantras; furthermore, one should contemplate Him as being intensified by the powers of those mantras.

One should meditate upon the mantra consisting of the five elements beginning with space as the pentad of Īśvaras, and then one should recollect their pervasive manifestation (vibhava) as it emanates from them, beginning with space. (84)
One should meditate upon the mass produced by conjunction as being free from the cage of worldly existence,
resembling a thousand suns and possessing the radiance of a hundred moons.
Having thus produced this supreme aggregate, which resembles stainless crystal and is free from old age and death, one attains both enjoyment and liberation. 86.

O tiger among sages, that which is the innate means of accomplishment for all embodied beings—having attained that through this very sequence characterized by the desire to create (sisṛkṣā)—[one proceeds]. (87)

Having brought about the emergence of power from his own waveless feet, he then takes recourse in his own bliss from the Great Bliss and in his own infinity. [This is the sequence of the entry of the individual soul (jīva) into the created body. 88.
From that [state], the Mārīca-nābhasa-cakra arises, as well as one's own form,
which possesses the radiance of ten million suns and quivers with its own luster.
O twice-born one, having thus brought the Self from its own abode by means of the self— shaped like a kadamba bud and as pure as a drop of dew at night— 90.
One should cause one's own mantra-body to enter through the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) as before,
by way of the channel of moonlight (*jyotsnā-nāḍī*), into the interior of the lotus of the city of eight (*puryaṣṭaka*).
Indeed, meditating upon his own designator by means of the partless sound (*niṣkala-dhvani*),
[one should meditate on] the Self-mantra,
which is the support of all worlds and which causes the nourishment of the universe. (92)
One should mark it with the name "Amṛta," and at its end, "namas ātmane.
This mantra, which denotes the Self, should be known as the "Tāraka" (the Savior). || 93 ||
Then, the mantra becomes partless, as does the sun;
having reached the fivefold egoity, it assumes the form of light.
One should sprinkle one’s own body with a stream of nectar from one’s own mantra;
then, having drawn that independent image forth, one should place it within the heart.
The supreme power is waveless and consists of great bliss;
from her own bliss arises the circle of light, which is her own radiant form.
Such is the path of the *sauṣumna*, as well as the *piṇḍa-mantra* and the partless (*niṣkala*) mantra;
then there is the collection of mantras beginning with Śakti, and the pentad of the Lords of the Dhāraṇās. (97)
One should remember that which is the collection of their wealth—the aggregate—as a mass, entirely set ablaze, both as a single whole and as existing separately. (98)
O Nārada, this purification of the elements is correctly declared to be threefold, by means of the instrument (karaṇa) known as gross, subtle, and supreme. || 99 ||
"You are a devotee, one whose self is purified, steady-minded, and unwearied;
because you are dear to me in this way, [the teaching] along with its secret has been proclaimed to you. (100)
O best of Brahmins, as you have toward me, so should you act toward whoever shall be like you;
you should reveal this to him, and not to anyone else who is inferior.
He who practices exclusively that supreme merit which removes rebirth, bestows meditative absorption, and grants the purification of the elements, goes to the eternal Brahman.
O Brahmin, how much more so for one whose mind is united with the physical form—such a person, having praised [the deity], should worship the God with a purified self and a serene intellect. (103)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Samādhi," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the eleventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Placement of Mantras" (Mantranyāsavidhi).
The practitioner of mantra, whose body has been thoroughly purified, should perform the placement of mantras;
by the mere act of placing them, he becomes equal to the God of gods. (1)
Through this, one gains the qualification for all rites beginning with worship,
and by means of it, the manifestation of all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) shall indeed occur.
Having performed which, one may remain fearless even in a region crowded with the wicked;
and by that which has been prescribed, there shall be victory over untimely deaths.
[The Preparation of the Seat] One should place upon the ground that which was previously described as a wooden plank;
and upon that, one should place an ocean together with a lotus.
Then, with effort, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of Tārkṣya using each of their respective mantras accompanied by meditation; having meditated upon him, one should then sit down.
[The visualization of the enclosure wall outside the seat:
Having repeatedly cleared the directions with the Astra-mantra, one should again and again visualize an enclosure wall outside the seat, resembling a dense mass of arrows. (6)
One should envelop the entire form, including its walls, with armor in the form of a blazing tunic;
[this is the purpose of the ritual placement].
Just as with the Siddhas and others, O twice-born one.
While those situated in the sky are invisible, one should perform the self-assignment (nyāsa);
for they carry away the power of a mantra that is not protected.
Therefore, by this method, one should first perform the protection;
having first performed the placement on the hands, one should then perform the placement on the body.
[The ritual placement on the hands (hastanyāsa):
One should place the root mantra, conjoined with the form-mantra, upon the thumb; in this very same sequence, one should place the deities upon the index finger and the others. 10.
Having indeed assigned all the limbs to the fingers ending with the little finger,
one should then apply the heart and the other [limbs] in sequence to those beginning with the little finger.
One should place the Astra-mantra on the thumbs up to the tips of the fingers, and the Locana-mantra on the fingertips; one should place Nṛsiṃha on the right hand and Kapila on the left.
One should place the left hand and so forth on both [sides], as well as the boar on the fingers;
the Kaustubha gem on the right palm, and likewise the forest garland on the other.
One should place a lotus in the middle of the right [hand] and a conch on the surface of the left;
and in that very place, one should place the wheel, the weapon of great radiance, along with Ananta.
And [he placed] a mace, blazing with its own splendor, in his right hand;
first from the base of the right thumb, extending to the left [thumb].
One should place the Gāruḍa mantra on the ten fingers in sequence;
likewise, one should place the noose on the palm of the left hand and the goad on the right.
One should gradually place [the mantras] beginning with the heart upon both hands—
the five seed-syllables of the limbs, starting from Satya and ending with Aniruddha.
Then, one should place the seven-syllable mantra, which stands above all mantras, upon both hands from the nails to the wrists.
By this procedure, one should first perform the placement on the hands.
(The reason for the precedence of hand-placement over body-placement:
The supreme Vaibhavī Śakti resides within the hollow of the heart-cakra. (19)
Assuming a wind-like form, they are established in ten ways;
by their own will and through their own flow, they have issued forth via the path of the hands.
Depending upon the ten channels, those very [channels] are considered to be the fingers;
for this very reason, O best of the twice-born, in the form of the Lord known as Śakti, || 21 ||
Having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of the collection of mantras, one should then perform the placement upon that which consists of the elements.
[This is the placement on the body.
Listen now to the correct procedure for the placement of the assembly of mantras upon the physical form. 22.
Having first performed the placement of the root mantra over the body from the head down to the feet by way of pervasion, one should then perform it again from the feet up to the head.
Then, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of all the limbs using the Mūrti-mantra,
sequentially upon the head, the mouth, the pair of eyes, the right and left [shoulders], and the heart.
On the back, the navel, the waist, the knees, and then the feet—
in this sequence ending with the *hāva*, there is the twelve-syllable *nāda*.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the form-mantra, one should then place the deity;
likewise, one should place Lakṣmī on the left shoulder and Kīrti on the right.
One should place Jayā on the right hand and Māyā likewise on the left;
immediately thereafter, one should assign the limbs, beginning with the heart.
Then, one should place the heart-mantra between the breasts, the head-mantra on the crown of the head,
the crest-mantra at the site of the topknot, and the armor-mantra on the two shoulders.
O twice-born one, one should place the Netra-mantra on the two eyes and the Astra-mantra on the palms of the hands;
one should place Nṛsiṃha on the right ear and Kapila on the left ear.
Having placed the Vārāha, the leader of mantras, at the limit of the left ear,
one should place the Kaustubha gem in the middle of the chest and the forest garland (vanamālā) on the neck.
Then, O twice-born one, as before, one should place the lotus and other [symbols] between the thighs;
thereafter, one should assign the great mantra known as Garuḍa, along with its subsidiary limbs and the host of attendants.
Or else, O best of the twice-born, one should do so gradually without interruption, first at the two feet, then the abdomen, the head, the navel, the heart, and ending at the top of the crest-lock.

p. 96) One should further install that group of five in the same sequence beginning with the Truths (satya), specifically within the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), in the center of the heart, and in the lotus of the navel. || 33 ||

One should then join [the breath] in the body through the sequence of the navel, the region between the genitals, and the two feet, and finally from the top of the head down to the soles of the feet, like a suit of armor.
The seven-syllabled great mantra is the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa;
all other mantras reside within him, and he is the innermost core of them all. (35)
He is the supreme instrument of this very assembly of mantras;
since he stands at the head of all, one should place him above everything else. (36)
O best of sages, the wheel of powers (śakticakra) is indeed manifold, extending from the heart to the navel;
by merely placing it [there], union is achieved.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner upon the hands and the body,
one should then display the respective mudrās for the entire collection of mantras, beginning with the root mantra, that have been placed.
One should display one's respective mudrās accompanied by the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa). [The method of meditation to be performed by the practitioner:
Thereafter, one should meditate upon oneself as having a form, in the likeness of Viṣṇu. || 39 ||
By means of the previously described yoga of meditation, one's own form— or the universal form, or whatever form is desired— is enveloped in the majesty of the six qualities.
I am that Blessed One Viṣṇu; I am Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
indeed, I am Vāsudeva, the all-pervading, the abode of beings, the stainless one.
O Sage, having attained such a firmly established ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the best of practitioners becomes absorbed in that very state before long. (42)

"Through placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), as well as through contemplation (bhāva) and yoga born of the middle way—thus has the ritual of placement (nyāsakarma) been briefly explained by me to you. (43)
"Practice according to the rule and protect [the mantra] with diligence.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Deposition of Mantras," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*. 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Mental Sacrifice.
The Blessed Lord, having thus become identical with Viṣṇu, was formerly the practitioner by his own self.
Then, one should worship Viṣṇu by means of a mental sacrifice.

[The method of conceptualizing the six [lotuses], beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Padma, according to their distinct locations through the division of parts at the commencement of the mental sacrifice:
One should meditate on Śakti, whose form is the Ādhāra, between the navel and the genitals.
And above that is Kālāgni, and above him is Ananta.
Above that, one should meditate upon the goddess Vasudhā, filled with four [elements],
by means of the four steps divided from the root (kanda) down to the end of the navel.
Having meditated on the Ocean of Milk at the navel, therefrom arises a lotus extending to a thousand petals and enveloped by a thousand rays.
[The conception of the seat upon the lotus: One should place a seat resembling a thousand rays of light upon its back.
[The manner of conceiving the sixteen legs of that seat, beginning with Dharma:]
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty as the fourth.
Having brought it down with one's own mantra, one should place this tetrad in the four directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya), extending as far as the northeast (īśāna).
Upon the four legs of the pedestal are these white lion-faced beings,
possessing human bodies and endowed with supreme courage.
One should assign Adharma, as well as Ignorance (Ajñāna), Non-detachment (Avairāgya), and Non-mastery (Anaiśvarya) to the eastern quarter and so forth, up to the northern region.
These figures in human form, radiant as the bandhūka flower,
are located in the northeast direction and in the southeast direction.
Between Yātudhāna and Varuṇa, and between Vāyu and Varuṇa,
one should place the four beginning with the Ṛgveda, colored yellow and having the forms of a horse and a man.
Between the directions of Īśāna and Soma, between the directions of Antaka and Agni, between the directions of Yama and Rākṣasa, and between the directions of Saumya and Sāmīraṇa. || 11 ||
The collection of ages beginning with Kṛta, and Kṛṣṇa in the form of a bull-man—
all these have four arms, and they hold [the others] with two of them.
p. 98) With their palms joined together, they bow down to the Lord of the World with two verses.

[Upon the throne of Dharma and the others, according to the division of its parts and by way of distinct locations, there are five successive seats ending with the white lotus, the sun, the moon, fire, and the king of birds.]
Having placed these three, beginning with a white lotus, upon them, [one should perform] the manner of conceptualization.
O Nārada, with the mantras previously mentioned by me,
one should place the King of Birds (Garuḍa) and the Boar (Varāha) one above the other upon that [foundation].
Having divided [the body] into five equal parts from the navel to the end of the heart,
one should meditate upon the pervasion of this mantra-throne.

[The pervasion of the principles (tattvas), beginning with the five elements and ending with Īśvara, occurs sequentially across the eleven stages from the Power of the Foundation (ādhāraśakti) up to the Sovereign of Birds (pakṣirāja):
Starting from the Power of the Foundation up to the supreme stage of Mantra.
But when the power of support for the elements fails, the subtle elements [dissolve] into the fire of time.

Likewise, O twice-born one, speech and the other organs, as well as the infinite sense-faculties, remain pervading [the elements]; the ear and the others reside in the earth, and the mind resides in the Ocean of Milk.
The ego (ahaṅkāra) is supported within the lotus of infinite petals;
and the intellect (dhī), having presided over the eighteen [faculties] beginning with dharma, is situated there.
Above that lotus is Prakṛti, the undivided equilibrium of the guṇas;
there Kāla, which rests upon the three abodes, is situated within the Puruṣa known as Bhāva.
And Garuḍa is presided over by Īśvara himself through his lordship;
thus, in the case of Janārdana, who is the embodiment of the mantra, there are eleven positions.

[The commencement of the meditation on Viṣṇu: He beheld Viṣṇu, the god who is the soul of the universe, whose form is the support of the Lord, seated within the body, undivided yet appearing as if divided. (21)
One should meditate on him returning from his own abode by means of the initial flow;
[first, the meditation on the nature that is beyond the mantra:
one should meditate on the state beyond the mantra, extending as far as the circle of rays. (22)

Then, by means of the subtlest division, one should contemplate [the contemplation of the essential nature of the mantra which exists as both the supreme and the subtle] through the self of the mantra;
[it is] the supreme form consisting of light, characterized by exhilaration and bliss. (23)
The subtle *liṅgamātra* alone, characterized by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and possessing luminosity, is [to be meditated upon];
then, the gross form is to be meditated upon through its various distinct manifestations. (24) [This is the recollection of the gross nature.]
[The Sovereignty of Viṣṇu, whose mantra-form abides as the supreme subtle self:
The Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa is even a hundredth part of the tip of a hair;
he is the enjoyer of the guṇas, the substratum of the guṇas, possessed of guṇas, and likewise devoid of guṇas. (25)
The Lord of the body is renowned as the sovereign consisting of all the gods;
that Puruṣa, the size of a thumb, dwells within all bodies. || 26 ||

Just as a gem, when distinguished by various qualities such as blue, yellow, and so forth, undergoes a change in its appearance, so too does the All-pervading Lord undergo a change in form through the distinction of meditative absorption.
This Brahmā, as well as Rudra, the Moon, the Sun, and Prajāpati, were born from the mantra originating from the Supreme Self; they are therefore of that same nature.
That which is indeed the intellect (*buddhi*), the agent of discernment, is the possessor of that [pure nature] in the supreme state;
or rather, it is the knower of that, as previously distinguished, like the radiance of the moon. (29)
She indeed abides in four ways as the power of the Teacher of the World, consisting of the nature of knowledge and action, and having the essence of sovereignty and grace. (30)
O Nārada, those five alone, preceded by intellect (buddhi), exist as modifications within the previously mentioned powers (śaktis). And of these [powers] as well—
Without intellect (buddhi), even the fourfold transformation is perishable;
those deities beginning with Lakṣmī who are established in four ways are they. (32)
Together with them, He who possesses all limbs (the Lord) is always to be worshipped within the hollow of the heart-lotus;

for Lakṣmī and the others, who constitute the powers (śakti) of the Supreme Self, are the primordial material cause (mūlaprakṛti) of the eightfold modifications such as virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), and so forth.
For their transformations indeed govern the path to the highest good. || 33 ||
Those who are devoted to the people who have always sought refuge in me,
and who remain established in this world, are indeed those who possess knowledge of dharma and other such virtues.

O best of the twice-born, this quartet beginning with unrighteousness (adharma) exists as a transformation of these [qualities], leading one onto the path of what is not conducive to the highest good.
Toward those beings who revile the guru, fire, mantras, and scriptures, everything else is composed of illusion; know that illusion to be mine. (36)
(p. 100) Separateness as well as unity— these have been previously explained by me through these two [as the specific power of Viṣṇu,
the supreme light of consciousness whose nature is mantra, established within the center of the heart-lotus].
Thus has been proclaimed the Saṅgha, the supreme mantra-circle. || 37 ||
Situated in the center of the heart-lotus is the imperishable light of consciousness,
shaped like a cluster of kadamba flowers, possessing a universal form and the luster of a gem.
Resembling a great jewel-lamp, with an unbroken radiance, rays issued forth from his ear-holes and other apertures. (39)
O twice-born one, just as a mass of light goes out from a jar that is full yet has a hole when it is joined with a great lamp,
even so does [the soul] depart from the body.
The mantra, which is indeed a collection of rays, spreads outward through the channels (nāḍīs).

O twice-born one, this mantra-essence is also always imperceptible to the senses; furthermore, qualities such as stability belonging to the elements like earth, as well as all things, have the Supreme Self as their sole substratum.
Nevertheless, by this same principle, direct perception is characterized as that which consists of the five qualities of the elements—earth and the rest—which reside externally. (42)
Therefore, that [state] is to be perceived by him through direct perception as something beyond the senses;
its earthly quality is stability, for it is by means of that quality that she (the earth) is stable.
One should rely upon that which arises through mutual influence;
for even that pleasure belonging to it is perceived when there is water. (44)
O Sage, how could there be such a quality in that water otherwise?
For by the mere recollection of the mantra, a great mental joy arises. (45)
That attribute of fire known as form, which belongs to the Supreme Lord and has been transformed into the nature of form, resides within the fire that is identical with the mantra-self.
Since meditative absorption (dhyāna) is never found anywhere without fire, for that which is the nature of touch belongs to wind, O Mahāmati. (47)
The subtle quality belonging to air, which resides within the body of the mantra, arises when that [quality] has been withdrawn into the internal organ. || 48 ||
Since space possesses emptiness, its emergence occurs from that;
for that quality, O Great-minded One, is indeed contained within the nature of mantra. (49)
"And because it is ungraspable by ordinary instruments without meditative cultivation (bhāvanā)—having thus previously understood the power of mantra according to its true nature... (50)
The invocation, preceded by mudrā and mantra, is that by which the presence [of the deity] occurs when the time for worship has arrived;
it is the mantra accompanied by mudrā known as "invocation. (51)
O best of the twice-born, one should mentally utter [the mantra] with *pūraka* (inhalation),
and thereafter, having summoned [the deity], one should do so mentally with the *mūrti-mantra*.
