One should visualize his form as described in the section on meditation, situated in the center of the heart-lotus;
one should meditate upon the root mantra, presided over by the Supreme, blazing with light. (53)
[The manifestation of the invoked deity:

One should effect the manifestation of that deity, who is the essence of the mantra and whose nature is Brahman, by means of the mantras beginning with the *ātma-mantra* and all the other mantras, as before. (54)
Without performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs, one should mentally recollect that placement within the body;
likewise, one should offer flowers, the arghya oblation, incense, a lamp, garlands, and ointments.
With a mind full of reverence and with devotion, he first offered water for the feet, then performed the eight-limbed prostration, and mentally uttered cries of "Victory! (jaya).
Having formed the Brahma-mudrā for the Blessed One, one should indeed display it, saying:
"Welcome to you, O Lord of Gods; O Acyuta, may you accept my presence."
"Accept this mental worship, which has been cultivated according to its true meaning; for you have recognized that the Lord is well-pleased and inclined toward showing grace. (58)
[Now, the commencement of the mental sacrifice in detail:
O best of the twice-born, one should commence the mental sacrifice in detail with pure, imperishable, and auspicious substances produced by mere resolve (saṅkalpa). 59.
One should worship the God who grants all desires and who bears the form of the mantra;
first, there should be anointing and rubbing with unguents, then bathing, and then the application of ointments.
Having offered garments, garlands, and fragrant perfumes,
one should meditate upon [the deity] adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and crowns.
One should adorn [the deity] with a variegated waist-string made of gold and gems,
and with pure pearl necklaces set with rubies.
One should offer to Viṣṇu a parasol resembling the full moon and provided with a golden handle, as well as an auspicious peacock-feather fan. (63)
Having offered to the Blessed One incense that is fragrant, sweet, and abundant, mixed with camphor powder, as well as a garland of lamps with ghee; (64)
Then, having offered the madhuparka soaked in honey and clarified butter, as well as various sacrificial animals in embodied form and likewise the purifying bird; || 65 ||
First, one should offer these four kinds of food: medicinal herbs, śāli rice, dūrvā grass, and a tree laden with excellent fruit, all personified. 66.
Various pure offerings for the deity, consisting of many kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten,
as well as heart-pleasing fruits and roots produced in all six seasons.
And having offered various drinks containing the six flavors, O twice-born one, all those things to be enjoyed by oneself [should be offered] through the power of devotion and faith. (68)
One should also offer to the deity various stringed instruments, provided they are not discordant, accompanied by dance and song, even if they belong to the eastern directions. 69.
And one should contemplate all the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, and the like, as well as the recitations of hymns of praise belonging to the three worlds, dedicated to the God of gods.
Fanning with a yak-tail whisk adorned with a network of small bells, and [offering] canopies, banners, and various kinds of flags; 71.
Having offered with devotion to the Lord, with a serene inner self, elephants, horses, cows, and vehicles, all adorned with fine garments; 72.
Then, while he is offering those [substances] and causing them to be accepted, one should remember oneself,
along with one's sons and wife, as being joined with salutation to him.
Having offered [the oblation], he bowed with his head, filled with tears of joy, mentally forming the *kāmadhenu* mudrā accompanied by the mantra. (74)
Having performed the binding, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu’s [mudrā] which fulfills all desires;
having worshipped the Lord, the Teacher of the World, situated at the tip of the lotus in the space of the heart.
The entire mantra-body is indeed both with parts (sakala) and of the nature of being partless (niṣkala).

[Therein is the worship of the limbs beginning with Lakṣmī, the distinction of the dissolution-sacrifice (layayāga) and so forth, the six powers, the six limbs, and the emblems such as the lotus. || 76 ||
The ornaments, such as the Kaustubha gem and others, as well as the three faces, and the forms beginning with Satya were likewise manifested within the body of the Lord. (77)
Having pervaded [all things] as suchness, they are of that very nature in their respective places;
all of them, residing within that body, are to be worshipped in due order.
O Brahmin, this Layayāga is proclaimed for Lakṣmī and the others, performed with their respective mantras, flowers, and ointments, without the retinue. (79)
Therefore, one should always worship the retinue residing within the body of the root mantra, whether in the support of the heart-lotus, in the [divine] form, or wherever else.
This sacrifice, known as Layayāga, is concise and bestows all accomplishments.
The King of Mantras is in the center of the pericarp, while Lakṣmī and the others are in the filaments and so forth. (81)
O Nārada, in that [state] all [the deities] are indeed with form and complete, yet they are designated as "enjoyment" (bhoga) through the sacrifice alone, which exists as something distinct.
Now, however, the worship of the lotuses and so forth is prescribed for those holding office, as well as for the purpose of the sacrificial enjoyment (bhogayāga) of all mantras. (83)
Now, understand the placement by division within the heart-lotus:
one should place Lakṣmī, belonging to the All-pervading Lord, situated upon the filaments in the eastern part.
One should place Kīrti to his right, Jayā behind Hari,
and Māyā, who dwells upon the filaments, on his northern side.
O twice-born one, having performed the placement of the limbs (vidyāṅga-vinyāsa) upon the filaments, and having installed the heart-mantra of Viṣṇu in the space between the east and the south; 86.
One should place the head in the northeast and the crest-lock (śikhā) in the southwest;
one should then assign the armor (kavaca) of the Lord in the northwest.
In front, in the region of the filaments, is the eye, and in the directions, the weapon;
on the right petal of the lotus of the Lord of Mantras is Nṛkesarī.
Kapila is on the western petal and Varāha on the northern petal;
the Kaustubha gem and the forest garland are in the space between the eastern petals of the Lord.
Having placed the two lotuses and conchs near those two petals with the mantras of Nṛsiṃha and Kroḍa, one should likewise place the mace and the discus.
Nearby is the jewel-garland, and Garuḍa is not far from it;
the noose is near that, and the goad is close to the mace.

One should place the secondary limbs (upāṅgas), beginning with Aniruddha, upon the tips of the petals; [specifically] on the north, west, south, and east, for that which is situated in the pericarp. (92)
Beginning from the leaf of that lord, having placed the Satya-mantra upon all four leaf-tips, extending as far as the leaf of Vāyu; 93.
O Nārada, when the root-mantra has emerged from the aperture of Brahmā,
it flows within the stalk of light, which is without support and possesses spreading rays as its tendrils.
One should place the seven-syllable mantra, which is partless and absolute, upon the pericarp called Mahānanda, which is strewn with the filaments of Ānanda.
Indeed, that state of being permeated by that [divine nature] is its worship, performed through enjoyments produced by mental resolve that follow the path of conceptualization. (96)
How should there be worship of him, since he stands beyond them?
Having thus deposited the assembly of mantras, one should worship them in sequence as before. (97)
Having meditated upon each one with its own mantra, attend to that meditation;
and one should always employ it in the place of enjoyment for the mantras. (98)
Then one should meditate upon that previously described form of the mantras as being partless (niṣkala), yet subsequently permeated by the manifest (sakala) aspect situated externally.
Just as a stainless crystal, through some coloring, does not admit any distinction between itself and that coloring; || 100 ||
But through non-attachment, it may enter into another crystal;
in this way, one should meditate upon the entire form together with the partless. (101)
O best of sages, know that for a mantra situated in the station of enjoyment and established in its office, it possesses both natures.
One should meditate on that entire [form] situated within the lotus of his heart;
however, one should meditate on that form as being partless (niṣkala) when it abides without support.
Then, having first formed this thought in his mind—"These two, though distinct in nature, abide as one"—the twice-born man should thereafter worship them. 104.
Just as a tree stands at a great distance from the qualities of the earth, so too does the earth remain far removed from the qualities belonging to the tree. 105.
Such is the inseparable connection between the Sakala and Akala mantras;
for the attainment of the supreme state does not arise from meditation on the Sakala alone. (106)
(105) Since mantras are by nature devoid of parts, accomplishments (siddhis) are likewise far away;
therefore, they are attained through meditating upon them in sequence, worshipping them, and pleasing them. (107)
[The Special Worship] O Brahmin, one should perform the special worship of Acyuta by extending the joined palms filled with golden flowers. 108.
Having recited the root mantra with effort through the inhalation (*pūraka*) and other breath-control techniques,
[one should continue] until its manifestation, sounding like the prolonged ring of a bell.

Having meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is filled with a mass of shimmering rays and possesses the splendor of hundreds of fires, suns, and moons, one should restrain [the breath] within the two corners of the mouth.
One should place that añjali upon one's head toward that very embodiment of mantra;
then one should again offer arghya, and once more a beautiful añjali of flowers.

Having displayed the mudrā known as the root [mudrā], one should begin the mental recitation (japa), without a fixed number and according to one's capacity, by means of the instrument known as the bell. 112.
And for Lakṣmī and the others who reside in the abodes of enjoyment, one should sequentially display the mudrā with the mind and perform the recitation once for each.
Having praised [the deity] with the ear-entrancing mantras and purificatory hymns, one should properly propitiate [him].
O best of Brahmins, having thus performed the mental sacrifice (mānasa-yāga) in this sequence, || 114 ||
[Now, the method for the mental fire-sacrifice (mānasahoma):
O Sage, one should perform such an auspicious fire-sacrifice that bestows the glory of liberation; one should meditate upon the abode of fire situated within the navel-center. 115.
The triangle is completely surrounded by the unmanifest, which consists of the three qualities;
then, having churned the fire-drill of meditation, one brings down the fire of consciousness.
O twice-born one, it is perfectly pure, refined, radiant, and always with its flame directed upwards;
because it has Vāsudeva as its essence, it dwells within the inner selves.
One should recite the root mantra as far as the range of sound extends;
from that place, one should draw forth the divine, supreme nectar of blissful clarified butter.

Having taken up that which has flowed from the ocean of Brahman’s clarified butter and reached the state of being waveless, one should enter through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the path of nectar.

One should meditate on the mantra as it flashes forth from the heart through the central path (madhyamārga), which is composed of consciousness and endowed with light, augmented by the power of Brahman.
(106) That which stands like upward fuel in the fire of its own cause located at the navel, [is situated] in the naturally blazing fire of Brahman, with the belly glowing all around. (121)
Having recollected the mantra, one should imagine that nectar—just as the ghee previously brought by the twice-born—is falling upon his head from the garment of the twice-born. (122)
Having fully gratified the fire of consciousness (cidagni), which is of the nature of mantra, located at the navel,
one should again contemplate it as situated within the flame-tip in the lotus of the heart.
And while pronouncing the Lord of Mantras with a protracted vowel (*pluta*), endowed with meditative concentration,
one should thus maintain a single-pointed focus upon that which resides in the two locations.
Afterwards, one should dissolve everything— including whatever has been performed with mantras— into Viṣṇu, who is both the essential nature of mantra and the embodiment of manifold mantras.
One should visualize the right hand as being filled with water, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
in its center, one should recollect the partless mantra (niṣkala-mantra) as being filled with rays of light.
Having contemplated the attainment of the fruit arising from the sacrifice as being of the nature of Lakṣmī,
one should utter the root mantra and likewise visualize [the deity] in the center of the palm.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon the partless mantra above that;
having placed his knees on the ground with his head bowed, he should offer it to Viṣṇu.
Then, O best of the twice-born, with a mind inclined toward faith and being thoroughly satisfied, he respectfully made that his own and it should be meditated upon with reverence. 129.
O twice-born one, this mental sacrifice removes the fear of old age and disease, pacifies the flood of sins, and brings about the cessation of worldly existence.
Through the yoga of constant practice, one may be liberated from the fall of the body;
yet that man who performs this even once with supreme devotion [attains the same]. (131)
O Sage, I am pleased with him who follows the prescribed rite in due order;
moreover, he stands as the foremost among all officiating priests. (132)
He shall deliver his ancestors who have passed away, as well as those yet to come, and even those in the present;
how much more so one who is constantly disciplined and whose mind is absorbed in that state? (133)
For one who stands upon the path of mantra-adoration and is endowed with faith and devotion, there is no return to this world; he goes to the supreme state. (134)
Having understood this, one should always perform the mental sacrifice with diligent effort.
This supreme secret has been told to you today by me, O Nārada. (135)
(107) This should never be spoken to those who are not disciples, nor to those who lack devotion;
rather, it is for those devoted ones whose minds are purified and who are utterly terrified of worldly existence. || 136 ||
This secret should be spoken only after having correctly examined the disciple's disposition.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Mental Sacrifice," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Outer Sacrifice.
Formerly, the Blessed Lord, having performed the mental sacrifice according to this procedure, [proceeded as follows].
Then, one should worship the deity situated within the mandala through ritual action joined with devotion.

One should meditate right here upon that desired collection of mantras which was previously [visualized] in the center of the heart-lotus, as it vibrates and moves along with the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
One should not dismiss him until the external rites have been performed;
for, O best of the twice-born, he must be placed within the vessel of honor (arghyapātra).
In the mandala, in the rosary, and in the fire situated within the sacrificial pit—
[this is the determination of the necessity of the external sacrifice by way of questions and answers]—
[Nārada].
O Blessed One, by your grace, that which destroys ignorance has indeed been known.
The heart-āgama, accompanied by both primordial wisdom (jñāna) and discerning consciousness (vijñāna), bestows all accomplishments;
for what purpose, then, should worship be performed externally within a mandala? || 5 ||

"O Blessed One, explain this to me, for I have a great doubt regarding it. The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, the latent impressions (vāsanā) arising from external objects are firm, having been accumulated over many lifetimes."
For by her, whose nature is impure, the self has been made liquefied, though it is pure;
she is the pure ritual action pertaining to the mantra, which bestows a tranquil state of being.
She is proclaimed for the purpose of its origination and destruction;
one should become absorbed in her through both external and internal activities. (8)
And for those whose latent impressions (vāsanās) have been firmly uprooted, there will be a gradual attenuation;
O Brahmin, the practitioner who consists of that [Reality] shall presently become embodied.
"That one becomes absorbed in that [reality] upon the fall of the body—this has been declared by me.
Nārada said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, tell me how the sacrifice is performed within the maṇḍala."
p. 108) If you are inclined to show favor toward me, [please explain] the essential nature of the mandala as well.
The Blessed One [on the arrangement of the mandala]:
Listen to the arrangement of the mandala of Viṣṇu, who possesses wondrous splendor.
I shall explain in brief that by which you will indeed attain the highest good:
having examined the earth in its various forms, endowed with fragrance and color. (12)
Having previously purified it with great effort using ploughs and other tools,
she was freed from wicked thorns, made firm, and capable of bearing the weight of elephants.
Behind that, one should construct an auspicious pavilion whitened with lime,
well-adorned with canopies, banners, and cloths.
There, at the outset, one should diligently identify the site of Brahmā with the intellect;
one should construct an elevated altar made of wood, which is suitable for the sacrifice and the officiating twice-born.
Having empowered the five products of the cow with the Astra-mantra by means of its splendor,
and having smeared the thread in front, one should then empower the altar.
O Nārada, one should lay down the initial and final lines there, as well as the middle line;
then one should construct a square measuring eight cubits or half of that.
From the position of the Brahma-point, using a thread half the length of the diameter,
one should mark the central line equally from two directions.
O Nārada, having first drawn a thread through the marks and the intervening spaces,
one should then repeatedly cross over them, making marks on the north and the south.
In the same way, one should likewise make two other marks in those two directions using that very same thread, proceeding from mark to mark.
O twice-born one, having stretched the thread upwards and positioned it between the two fish-junctions,
let it extend toward the south and north, and be situated from east to west.
Then, one should mark the four directions with a measuring line half the length of the mandala; having placed that same measuring line upon those marks at the back, [one should proceed].
Having marked the corner points with marks equal to those on the east side, one should then [draw] four lines using a thread positioned at the diagonal.
O Nārada, for the sake of the perfection of the field, one should indeed give [the portions] from corner to corner;
having then divided that field into sixteen equal squares with level lines. (24)
In the center, with four steps, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus;
likewise, one should fashion a group of eight lotuses in the eight directions.
In the cardinal directions, there is a set of four lotuses for the worship of the goddesses;
in the intermediate directions, there are another four, upon which those ending with Satya are situated.
Among them, O Sage, the ninth is honored where Keśava resides;
one should cause the central lotus-field to revolve fourfold.
O twice-born one, having excluded one-eighth part of the sky, the remaining half outside becomes the pericarp by means of an internal circular rotation.
One should fashion the filaments with the second [turn], the joints of the petals with the third,
and the tips of the petals above the circumambulation with the fourth.
One should cast two threads from corner to corner upon that lotus;
furthermore, one should likewise cast eight threads within the intervals between those threads.

By means of the thread situated at the lotus-junction, one should rotate the eight petals according to the sequence of the directions; by joining them with the circle, other [petals] are likewise situated on the outside.
The lotuses should be fashioned with care, well-proportioned to one another;
and having divided the portion of the filaments fourfold, it should be distributed upon each petal.
There should be three filaments in the center according to each [petal];
in the nine-petaled lotus that is joined together, the paths are half the size of the pericarp.
Having laid out the extensions of the lines, one should draw a square outside the cluster of lotuses using either a sixth or a fifth part of that measurement.

One should divide that into three parts in the cardinal directions; the pedestal (pīṭha) shall consist of one part. One should construct a lotus in each of the four directions and a door all around them.
O best of the twice-born, one should make the *karṇa* with exactly two parts;
the *upakarṇa* with four, and from that, there shall be a corner (*koṇa*) at each corner.
Having unified and purified the full twenty-two squares,
one should make the western door distinct and devoid of lines.
One should make the pericarp yellow in color, the filaments yellowish-red, and the eight petals white; the intervening space should be like the sky.
The corners of the pedestal and other parts should be yellow, while the limbs are reddish; the four doors are white, and one should adorn the corners with red. (39)
On the exterior, one should draw three lines, the last of which is red, yellow, and black;
and within, by means of the sixteen vowels situated in the Śakti.

[The Varieties of Mandalas and Their Different Results] Alternatively, one should always draw a twelve-spoked [mandala] permeated by the twelve vowels, or an eight-spoked one, provided with a hub and a rim. (41)
The straight and beautiful spokes are pervaded by the eight groups of letters;
one should draw a lotus at the hub of the wheel, characterized by the previously mentioned features.
Alternatively, a very beautiful lotus should be drawn inside a conch,
or on the Kaumodakī mace, or in front of it, or upon an image resembling the Kaustubha gem.
O Sage, whether in the form of a flower garland or in the form of his own insignia, when offered in a sacrifice for the attainment of one's desires, the wise know that it grants what is wished for.
In the nine-naveled [mandala], one obtains supreme accomplishment pertaining to both this world and the next;
when the sacrifice is performed in the interior of the lotus, prosperity always increases. (45)
Within the center of the discus (cakra) there shall be sovereignty that causes the destruction of the enemy faction;
indeed, in the conch (śaṅkha) during rites of pacification (śāntika), one becomes fortunate in the mace (gadā).
Through the Kaustubha there is the attainment of sovereignty, while nourishment is indeed found in the Puṣpamaṇḍala.
This sacrifice known as Padmodara is prescribed as being situated in the center of the lotus and other such designs.
[The prescription that the jar, the flower-mandala, the sacrificial ground, the image, and so forth, are also locations for the external sacrifice:
Listen now to another [instruction], joined with various colors, regarding the interior of the jar.
A firm jar made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. || 48 ||
One should fill it with milk, or else with curd or fragrant water, ensuring it is free from the "root of time" (kālamūla) and devoid of living beings that cause fear. (49)

It should be densely packed with all kinds of gems and medicinal herbs, its interior filled with *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and fruits; it should be provided with white mustard seeds and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and infused with saffron water.
It was adorned with excellent, tender tree branches,
marked with conch shells, svastikas, and lotuses, and anointed with sandalwood paste.
It is adorned with white garments, silk cloths, garlands, and so forth;
in its center is a lotus seat, and in the center of that is Janārdana.
With Vainateya (Garuḍa) standing above, Lakṣmī and the others are situated as before;
however, for the sake of a concise worship, the sacrifice is prescribed to be performed in a single water-pot (kumbha).
Having smeared the ground with cow dung or with clay and water, one should draw a circle there, or alternatively,
a square.
Or else, O best of sages, one should worship the God there with pure flowers blooming in their season for the sake of liberation from the cycle of existence. 55.
Having placed a new, white cloth, scented with incense and perfumes, upon a clean spot behind him, he should worship Hari thereon.
Or one should have an image made of clay, stone, or wood;
one should then prepare a beautiful pedestal, either with a lotus or alone.
Whether in pure water, or in a blazing fire devoid of smoke,
or situated in a temple, one should contemplate the Supreme Lord in his embodied form.
[One should worship] Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch and the discus, who is honored by gods and siddhas, and who has been installed by sages or men endowed with devotion. (59)
And one should worship that image with its own mantra,
omitting the invocation (āvāhana), O Brahmin, when it is situated on the ground, immovable, made of stone, and marked with the discus.
Or, O Brahmin, when [the ground] has been moved or marked with the mudrās called Śaṅkha and Padma,
one should worship the Lord there above just as before.
Having diligently accomplished one [of these] from among these sacrifices,
one should worship with ritual action joined with devotion that which grants all desires.
O Sage, according to one's ability, with offerings or according to one's wealth—
[now follows the method for the outer sacrifice within the mandala]—
one should take up the arghya vessel made of gold, silver, or other materials. (63)
Whether it be made of stone, clay, or wood, or fashioned from the leaves of the *palāśa* or lotus,
one should wash it with water consecrated by mantras and smear it with saffron and other unguents.
And there, one should offer the *arghya* consisting of many ingredients, consecrated with the *astra-mantra*.
(p. 112) [The *arghya* substances:
White mustard seeds, sesame, *dūrvā* grass, barley, and white rice grains. (65)
This arghya is declared to be provided with water, milk, and fruit;
having consecrated it with the root mantra, which is the embodiment of a mass of nectar.
[The Application of the Arghya: O Sage, having divided that which is situated in two vessels into two portions,
one portion is established in the support of the partless (niṣkalādhāra) as being of the nature of the partless.
One should project that mantra-wheel, vibrating through one's own vital energy (*vīrya*),
and having established it before the mandala, first worship it with flowers and other offerings.
One should properly perform the second consecration by means of the two types of *dhāraṇā* consisting of Agni and Soma; listen attentively to how this is done. (69)
First, one should burn [the object] with the masses of the sun’s fierce rays;
then, having visualized it as reduced to ashes, one should [reconstruct it] with the rays of the full moon.
O Nārada, one should further contemplate that which was indeed burnt by the sun as being filled once more by the falling stream of waves of nectar.
Having consecrated it with the primary mantras, such as the root mantra and others, and having formed the wish-fulfilling mudrā which flows [with nectar] while joined with the mantra; || 72 ||
Having assumed the form of a cow, resembling the snowy mountain and standing upon a path without support,
he should smear his two hands with the fragrant substance taken from the vessel of the *arghya* offering.
Having sprinkled the mandala and the pavilion, one should burn all the sacrificial materials without exception using the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
and then flood them with the root-mantra (mūlamantra).
When the assembly of materials is pure, it then becomes fit for sacrifice;
having then paid homage to Viṣṇu, one should recite the root mantra. (75)
[Door Worship]: Established in one's own form, one should worship with flowers held in the hollowed palms (añjali).
Taking up the vessel for the respectful offering (arghya), along with flowers, incense, and unguents... (76)
One should then worship the outer door, up to the lamps and the food offerings. [The Worship of the Door Deities:
At the base of the udumbara tree, in the middle of the outer door. (77)
Immediately after that, one should worship the Kṣetrapāla stationed on the ground, Lakṣmī situated above the door, and [the deity] located above the threshold (udumbara). (78)
At the base, on the southern and northern branches, are Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa;
likewise, Jaya and Vijaya are at the exterior and interior of the door.
Then, between the two branches, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā on the left and right respectively. 80.
By that same sequential method, one should worship the two lords of treasures named Śaṅkha and Padma, who reside inside the door, with offerings of water for honor, flowers, and so forth.
[The Procedure for Entering the Sacrificial Temple] Having performed the sacrifice at the door, one should then take a flower with the thumb and the three fingers directed toward the front. 82.
Having consecrated it with that weapon-mantra, one should visualize the discus above it—
possessing sharp spokes, blazing in form, and raining down fire and thunderbolts.
O Brahmin, one who destroys the multitude of obstacles should cast [the offering] within the sacrificial hall;
then, he should raise his right index finger with its tip facing upward.
Having remembered her, who is joined with the *śikhā* mantra and possesses a radiance flashing like lightning, he should enter the sacrificial hall while whirling that [garland] around.
[The sprinkling of the seat and so forth, which is a remnant of the act of seating:

Then, having sprinkled one's own seat with water from the *arghya* vessel, and having struck it with a flower while reciting the weapon-mantra (*sāstra*), O twice-born one, [one should place it] upon that [seat] in due order. (86)

One should first worship the assembly of mantras preceded by the foundational power (ādhāraśakti); thereafter, having sat down, one should perform the specific rites of inspection and sprinkling which constitute parts of the worship.
And that supreme [reality] resides in the heart. || 87 ||
One should place that splendor called Nārāyaṇa in the middle of the eye,
and one should likewise take recourse in that previously mentioned [splendor] named Vāsudeva.
Having gazed thoroughly at the entire mandala with a pair of steady eyes,
one should again sprinkle the arghya vessel with water from kusha grass.
[The sequence for the conceptualization and worship of the seats, beginning with Ādhāraśakti:
Thereafter, one should commence the worship in due order with water-offerings (arghya) and flowers, starting from Ādhāraśakti and preceded by meditative reflection (anusandhāna). (90) p. 114)
Having first established the gross seat of the mantra (mantrāsana) at the end of the yugas,
one should then place [the deity] there, in the upper middle region, according to the previously described procedure.
Having placed twice eight [deities] beginning with Dharma— possessing splendor and bearing supreme forms—
upon each of the eight directions, one should again and again assign that group of sixteen.

O Brahmin, one should then place [the deity] who bears a subtle form and was previously within the range of Īśa at each individual location, starting from the lotus and ending with the fire-chamber. 93.
Having contemplated that very [deity] situated within the womb, one should install it;
then, one should worship it with its respective mantras until the conclusion of the seat of contemplation (bhāvāsana). || 94 ||
Layer upon layer with yoga, using flowers, incense, and ointments,
one should fashion a square and elongated maṇḍala on the back of the pedestal near the ritual site at the end of the age. || 95 ||
Then,
one should fashion a square and elongated mandala for the God of gods, to the south, upon the [other] mandala.
Starting from the northwest corner and extending as far as the domain of the northeast,
the twice-born should first worship Gaṇeśa and the others with their respective mantras;
therein, he should first worship Gaṇeśa with his own mantra.
Then one should worship the goddess Vāgīśvarī, and at her side, Garuḍa;
thereafter, one should worship with devotion the Guru, who is designated as the Supreme (Parama). 98.
After that, Parameṣṭhin is to be worshipped; then one should sacrifice to the host of ancestors and the assembly of primordial Siddhas, who are entirely intent on meditation upon the Blessed One.
One should request permission from them in the proper sequence;
having received that with one's head bowed, one should then invoke the Lord from the heart-lotus according to the method of invocation and worship. 100.
O Sage, having invoked with devotion by means of the mantra accompanied by the mudrā, one should utter the root-mantra which resides in the heart and is all-pervading. (101)
Having brought it down gradually by means of the exhaling breath (recaka),
very slowly through the two channels at the point of their junction, which is formless and stainless.
Therefore, O Brahmin, with a mind free from conceptual construction and illuminated by the nature of consciousness, one should offer a handful of flowers as an oblation to the all-pervading Lord.
Having placed [the vessel] upon the head with both hands turned downwards, one should first perform worship according to the procedure prescribed for the *layayāga*. (104)

[The sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) preceded by meditation on Lakṣmī and the others] with flowers, water-offerings, ointments, and incenses, in due order, using the root-mantras and so forth; then, from the radiant form of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, through his splendor... 105.
One should meditate on Lakṣmī and the others as they issue forth like a mass of sparks;
then, one should place each one individually in the appropriate place for enjoyment.
[The sequence for the placement of mantras in the mandala:
Listen now to how the mantra is to be placed upon the mandala;
one should place it exactly as it is, within the center of the lotus above. (107)
O best of the twice-born, the root mantra should be [visualized] as before, endowed with its form;
and one should likewise visualize Lakṣmī within the pericarp of the lotus situated at its front.
One should place Kīrti in the southern part and Jayā at the back;
then one should place Māyā within the pericarp of the northern lotus.
The heart-mantra is in the southeast, the head-mantra in the central lotus of Īśāna,
the crest-mantra in the middle of the southwestern direction, and the armor-mantra in the region of the northwest.

Then, on the petal situated in the center of the lotus, directly in front of the deity, one should place the Netra-mantra; and on the petals at the intermediate directions, the King of Weapons (Astra-rāj).
In this very [mandala], there are three figures ending with Varāha, known as Nṛsiṃha and so forth, in sequence;
they occupy three petals of Viṣṇu in the cardinal directions—specifically in the south, the west, and the north. (112)
One should place the Kaustubha gem upon all the petals of the Lakṣmī-lotus yantra; likewise, having placed the forest garland upon the lotuses of the heart.
One should invoke the lotus and place it upon the petals of the *kīrti* lotus;
likewise, one should place the conch upon the petals of the *śikhā* lotus, and the discus upon the *jayā* lotus.
Then, O Brahmin, one should place the mace upon a petal within that lotus;
thereafter, O twice-born one, one should place the noose upon the petal of the illusory lotus.
Then, having invoked the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), one should place the goad upon the petals of the lotus located at the support of the head, specifically at the four gates.
One should place the *satya* [syllable] upon the pericarp;
then, above that, having taken recourse to the right side upon the Brahma-lotus. (117)
O Nārada, having placed the embodied form in dependence upon the embodied, it is deposited within the mantras;
likewise, one should place Vāsudeva upon the upper part of the head.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of Saṅkarṣaṇa upon the topknot;
then, one should place Pradyumna above the pericarp and over the armor (kavaca).
One should place Aniruddha above Lakṣmī and the others as the supported [deity],
and then one should place the seven-syllable mantra above the root mantra.
From the east up to the northeast, one should place the eight [deities] beginning with Indra on the outside;
then one should assign Nāgeśa below, and Śeṣa above.
One should likewise place Brahmā, the lord of the gods, and the lineage of the world-protectors;
thereafter, one should place the weapons outside of them.
Following the sequence starting from the east and extending as far as the domain of Īśāna,
one should place the weapon of Nāgeśvara below and the Brahmā-weapon above.
O best of the twice-born, one should meditate upon Viṣvaksena situated in the sky in the middle between the north and the direction of Tryambaka, as he approaches from the midst of the firmament.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras within the mandala in this manner,
one should then contemplate the meditation procedure for each mantra according to its specific placement as it exists. (125)
O Sage, I have previously taught you the root mantras of the deities; now listen with a one-pointed mind to that which has not been spoken regarding the heart-mantras and the others. 126.
[The method for meditating on the heart-mantra: Having the appearance of white and red colors, with one face and four arms, seated upon Garuḍa, and endowed with a lotus and a conch in his hands. 127.
One should meditate upon the right hand as being adorned with a mudrā, and the second left hand as joined in the abhaya (fear-dispelling) gesture. 128.
With white ornaments and garlands, and his body smeared with camphor,
one should always remember the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) facing the God of gods.
[The Method of Meditating on the Śiromaṇi-mantra] O twice-born one, one should meditate upon [the deity] as red like the bandhujīva flower, holding a lotus and a discus,
joined with his own mudrā, and with a hand in the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā). (130)
His limbs were smeared with saffron, he possessed a radiant red luster, and was captivating;
he was adorned with red ornaments and decorated with red flowers. || 131 ||
In the presence of the Lord of Mantras, one should likewise recollect the Head-mantra.
[The method of meditating on the Crest-mantra: One should visualize him as having the appearance of a swarm of moving bees, and bearing a lotus and a mace (kaumodakī). 132.
One should [worship] the bearer of his own seal, joined with the hand of protection (abhaya), likewise joined with musk, and with black flowers and other offerings. (133)
O Nārada, one should meditate upon the face with a gentle smile,
and likewise upon the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra) which has the hue of honey-tawny and holds the conch and the discus— such is the method of meditation for the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra). || 134 ||
One should meditate upon the Supreme One, joined by a pair of hands and occupied with his own mudrā,
anointed with mixed ointments and likewise adorned with mixed flowers and other offerings.
And while gazing [at the Lord], O twice-born one, one should meditate upon the armor of the All-pervading One;
[this is the method for the visualization of the mantra of the eye:
it has a reddish-yellow luster, and [the deities] hold a mace and a lotus in succession. (136)
He is endowed with his own mudrā by means of both the right and left hands,
and his limbs are smeared with saffron and white sandalwood paste.

One should meditate upon him whose body is adorned with yellow flowers, ornaments, and garments, who possesses beautiful eyes, and whose face is graced with a smile; one should likewise recite the mantra of his eye.

[The method for meditating on the weapon-mantras: One should visualize the great mace and discus, which eclipse the luster of sapphires and are raised aloft, joined with their respective hand-gestures (*mudrās*) that are auspicious and resemble gold. (139)
One should always meditate upon the weapon-mantra of the Lord, adorned with ornaments and the like, possessing the prowess of the fire of universal destruction, and facing one's own master.
All are remembered as having one face, and all have Garuḍa as their seat;
thus has been described this auspicious meditation on the limbs, which removes sin. (141)
(118) Comprehend the three mantras preceded by Nṛsiṃha: [The method of meditation on the Nṛsiṃha mantra] emitting fire with a roar like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution. (142)
The Supreme Lord, who holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus,
possesses the luster of molten gold and is adorned with various ornaments.
O twice-born one, one should meditate upon the omnipresent Lord Nṛsiṃha, whose limbs are adorned with various ointments, who wears abundant garlands, and who is clothed in red silk garments.

[The Method for Meditating on the Kapila Mantra] One should meditate upon him who resembles the rising sun, with tawny hair, beard, and eyes; four-armed, with noble limbs, and adorned with lotuses and other ornaments. (145)
One should meditate upon the leader of mantras, the son of Kapila, who wears a white upper garment, is adorned with ornaments of pearls, and bears white garlands. 146.
[The Method of Meditating on Vārāha:
O Nārada, one should meditate upon Him who has four arms, who possesses great luster, who is adorned with yellow ornaments, and whose complexion resembles a king among heaps of stones. 147.
As before, it is adorned by the assembly of insignia beginning with the lotus, and it features the Lord of Mantras in the form of Varāha, whose eyes are honey-tawny. 148.
One should meditate upon the fierce [deity] whose eyebrows are like flickering lightning, whose beard and mane are tongues of flame,
and who is endowed with two fangs resembling the tips of the crescent moon.
Seated in the lotus posture and contemplating their own cause, situated below the pericarp and facing forward—these, O Sage, should always be remembered. (150)
[The Method of Meditating on the Kaustubha and Others:
One should meditate upon the Kaustubha gem as having two arms and a radiance equal to a thousand suns; likewise, one should meditate upon the Goddess Vanamālā, who wears various colors. 151.
O twice-born one, [he saw] his beloved, lotus-petal-eyed and resembling a mature woman;
[he saw] a lotus with the luster of a white water-lily, and a conch shell resembling the kunda flower and the moon. (152)
One should meditate upon the discus with the luster of a sapphire and the mace with the brilliance of gold;
[one should also meditate upon] the maiden who is beautiful like a sixteen-year-old, yet possesses the freshness of youth. (153)
[The Method of Meditation on Garuḍa] With a red beak, great vital power, and eyes with terrifying frowns;
having the appearance of molten gold, adorned with a circle of wings. (154)
O Brahmin, one should meditate upon Garuḍa, who has the face of a vulture and a broad belly;
[this is the method of meditation for the noose and the goad:
one should meditate on the Lord of the Noose, who is dark like a fresh blade of dūrvā grass and has the face of a serpent. (155)
One should recollect Kṛṣṇa as holding a goad, with a long nose and a terrifying appearance;
all [the deities] are adorned with their own mudrās, two-armed, and possess beautiful earrings. 156.
They should be meditated upon as having human forms, resplendent with their own radiance;
O Sage, this meditation on the mantras of the emblems has been described by me. (157)
[The Methods of Meditating on the Fivefold Group Beginning with Truth] Now, understand in brief the meditation upon Truth and the others:
one should visualize Truth as two-armed, white, and having the appearance of a hundred moons. (158)
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, his eyes opened in meditation, wearing white silken garments and adorned with ornaments such as strings of pearls. 159.
One should visualize the Lord of Mantras standing upright, his limbs anointed with white sandalwood paste and adorned with white flowers, seated upon a leaf of Brahmā. 160.
O twice-born one, one should then meditate upon Vāsudeva, who has four arms, a serene countenance, and is seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana). Thus [should he be visualized]. 161.
The Lord holds a conch and a lotus, bestows boons and fearlessness, and has the form of a tranquil fire—neither white nor excessively red. || 162 ||
One should meditate upon the god Saṅkarṣaṇa, and thereafter one should remember Pradyumna,
who has the luster of the color of a yellow campaka flower and eyes as broad as a lotus.
Then one should meditate upon Aniruddha, who resembles the autumn sky;
all [the other forms] are equal to Vāsudeva in their arms, ornaments, and emblems. 164.
Likewise, these are seated within the lotuses of the *brahmarandhra*;
[the method of meditating on the seven-syllable mantra:
resembling pure crystal, formless yet possessing form. (165)
He indeed possesses all forms and is yet devoid of all forms;
his hands and feet are everywhere, and his eyes, heads, and faces are on every side. (166)
The Lord was illuminated on all sides by a network of serene rays, possessing a form as pure as crystal, which issued forth from his own body. (167)
O Sage, one should meditate upon the seven-syllable mantra situated in the place of enjoyment, wherein the wheel of mantras is reflected exactly as it exists. (168)
Having meditated thus and performed worship according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*),

one should offer oblations (*argha*), water for the feet (*pādya*), flowers, fragrances, and unguents. (169) [The method for the external sacrifice of the group of mantras follows immediately after meditation by means of the sequence of ritual placement.]
With numerous fragrant ghee lamps, adorned with hanging flowers, placed upon pedestals raised on bases filled with śāli rice; || 170 ||
With great delights that increase auspiciousness, uninterrupted, and combined with guggulu resin;
likewise with various kinds of foods—those to be chewed, those to be eaten, those to be licked, and those to be drunk.
And with offerings of honey-mixtures, various portions of fruits and roots, diverse divine milk-rices, sweetmeats, *kṛsara*, and so forth— (172)
With many well-prepared offerings, drenched in honey, clarified butter, and other substances,
one should first offer the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadughā) mudrā for each individual enjoyment.
One should meditate upon her together with the mantra as before and sprinkle her with the water of the *arghya* offering;
having offered flowers and the *arghya*, one should touch her with the hand of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, one should then announce [the offering] with the head bowed low;
whatever was previously declared by me to you regarding the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga), [that should be performed]. 175.
One should offer all that to the God of gods in his many forms;
for even an enjoyment that is not physically present follows the state of being an ancillary limb [of the ritual].
Having meditated upon each of those with the mind and with devotion, O Sage, one should offer them all to Viṣṇu according to the sequence of the entire group of mantras.
Having first performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped Keśava once again,
one should recite the root mantra and fill the hollowed palms with flowers. (178) [The manner of offering handfuls of flowers]
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the Supreme Self as the mantra with the luster of a ruby, merged within all mantras, through the yoga of extraction. || 179 ||

Through the divisions of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth, by means of sound whose nature is intensely expanded, that [unmanifested] is manifested in many ways, remaining until the cessation of sound. (180)

O Brahmin, [the Self manifests] first through the nature of the sound of the lute strings, then indeed through the nature of light, thereafter through the nature of exhilaration, and subsequently through the nature of the glory of bliss. (181)
Therefore, he transcends all states of being, pervading everywhere through his omnipresent nature,
as the inner self of peaceful consciousness, free from the waves of the density of existence and sentience.
Having thus gradually plunged into that which is free from the six waves and beyond the sphere of conceptual construction,
and then returning step by step, || 183 ||
Having meditated upon the mantra as the thousand-rayed sun, he should discharge the nectar born from its thousand rays onto the head of the God of gods by means of the *recaka* breath.
Then, holding the incense burner unbrokenly in the right hand—
[the ritual for the incense burner]—
it is divine, marked with lotuses and wheels, and has the form of a lotus as its base. (185)
One should fashion a single stalk, and the rest [should be] the all-pervading Lord with seven hoods;
he is always depicted with palms joined in reverence, meditating upon the supreme cause. 186.

The omnipresent Lord should be fashioned (or: one should fashion him) with a discus and a plow in his hands, seated upon a lotus throne, offering incense, and adorned with a network of tinkling bells. || 187 ||
They know that wheel to be the heart of the wheel and the lotus to be the hollow of the heart;
those which are the spokes in the wheel are known as the twelve channels.
O Brahmin, those which are known as the *kiṅkiṇīs* should be understood as the subtle channels (*sūkṣmanāḍī*),
within which the central power (*madhyamā śakti*) indeed resides, resembling the curve of a serpent.
Having the appearance of a smoke-grey color, she emerged after piercing the egg;
arisen from the heart of the fire of time (kālāgni), she dissolved at the end of the truth (satya).
For when the self is awakened by that [wisdom], the Lord, assuming the form of the mantra, becomes present; he then swiftly and uninterruptedly burns away [all obscurations]. || 191 ||
[The Ritual Procedure for the Incense Vessel Mantra] O brahmin seer, attend to that mantra by means of this [instruction]:
having first extracted the syllable *oṃ*, then again the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (192)
Then the word *vyomānandena* joined with *saṃyuktam*, followed by the word *anantāya*, then the word *kālāgnirūpāya*, and likewise the word *jagaddhūma*. (193)
One should offer a footstep to Sugandhin and to Sarvagandhavaha;
joined with "namaḥ" and "svāhā," this supreme mantra consists of thirty-one syllables. (194)
O twice-born Nārada, I have fully explained to you the mantra of the incense vessel,
which, when joined with the appropriate mudrā and meditation, is the supreme bestower of all accomplishments.
[One should worship] that which has been honored, fumigated, and anointed, its form infused by the placement of the mantra.
Having unified [them] by means of one's own word within the heart, through the inner self.
[The Procedure for Ringing the Bell] Thereafter, one should properly ring that bell, which bears the mark of a wheel,
which causes the three worlds to tremble, and which destroys all evil beings. (197)
For this is the messenger of mantras, the awakener of those who are asleep;
it is the warder-off of all obstacles and the one that brings grace to all mantras. (198)
At the end of the Praṇava, this resonance indeed merges into the power of sound (śabda-śakti).
Mantras are said to have the phonemes as their body, and the deities have the mantras as their body. (199)
Those [mantras] rooted in the resonance of the bell are awakened and grant the accomplishment of one's actions;
the power arising from the supreme sound takes the form of the resonance of the bell.
O best of sages, having attained the state of phonemes through those very sounds, the bodies of mantras are conceptualized in thousands of diverse forms. (201)
Indeed, by her own will, through this power, and by her own capacity, she herself [acts] here for the sake of bestowing grace upon those devotees whose minds are purified. (202)
O tiger among sages, because they provide protection through reflection (*manana*), and because they bestow their own state, they are therefore proclaimed as *mantras*. (203)
Those sounds are unmanifest and likewise formless;
yet, when a bell is struck, they emerge by the thousands.
For this very reason, O best of sages, she is proclaimed as the Mother of Mantras;
she is the power (śakti) named Ghaṇṭā, Vāgīśī, and Sarasvatī. (205)
All mantras are established in speech, and speech is established within the mantra;
therefore, the entire universe, both external and internal, consists of the very nature of the mantra.

Everything pertains to the sound of the bell; therefore, one should ring it first during the invocation, the offering of water (arghya), the incense, the lamp, and the enjoyment of the food offering (naivedya). || 207 ||
One should employ it constantly for the sake of successfully accomplishing the purpose of the mantra.
Except at the time of worship, there is no benefit in moving it elsewhere. (208)
Without this [knowledge], one who desires success in worship cannot accomplish their task;
therefore, listen to this supreme mantra belonging to her. (209)
[The Determination of the Bell Mantra] Having first taken the Praṇava, and after that Ananteśa,
that [seed-syllable] is conjoined with fire above and below, O best of sages. (210)
Then, one should mark it with five dots as the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds;
thereafter, at its conclusion, one should give the word "Jagaddhvani."
There is another step consisting of the mantra alone, joined with the syllable *svāhā*;
at its end is the Supreme Self, situated upon the support of wisdom.
O Sage, one should place upon the mountain [the syllable] joined with the head-sound (m),
situated within the nourisher of the universe (vi), which bestows sovereignty over the three worlds.
The thirteen-syllable mantra known as Ghaṇṭā bestows all accomplishments;
at the time of its placement, one should indeed pronounce it with a protracted vowel.
[The Method of Ghaṇṭā Meditation:
O best of the twice-born, attend to that meditation joined with concentration.
One should meditate upon the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as being face-downward and filled with the clamor of people. (215)
And above that, there is a lotus with its stalk, having eight petals, with scattered leaves, very white, possessing filaments, and a beautiful pericarp. || 216 ||
In the center of that, one should contemplate the Goddess endowed with eight arms;
in her four principal hands, there are emblems such as the lotus and others.
Then, in sequence, [he holds] a lotus, a conch, a noose, and a goad;
likewise, a crystal rosary and a book of wisdom. (218)
In her other two hands she displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
she is seated in the lotus posture, with eyes as broad as lotus petals.
Resembling the interior of a lotus, adorned with a garland of lotuses, covered with the ornaments of knowledge, and wrapped in yellow garments. || 220 ||
One should display the mudrā of the God of gods, whose nature is Nārāyaṇa;
then, O great sage, one should worship Lakṣmī and the others, as well as their mantras, with devotion. (221)
(124) One should worship again with the arghya, flowers, and incense, ending with the offering of incense.
[Now the hymn of praise:
Then, O Nārada, one should praise the Lord of Gods with this hymn. 222.
With the syllable *praṇava* (*om*) at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end, [the mantra] is indeed recited three times:
"Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one! Salutations to you, O creator of the universe! (223)
"Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa.
[The manner of offering the madhuparka and other items: While reciting this, he should offer a vessel completely filled with curd, mixed with honey and clarified butter. (224)
Placing the vessel in the palm of the hand, one should contemplate the Lord situated within it,
using the root mantra arising from His own essential nature.
O Nārada, having offered that with the excellent wave of the surging nectar of bliss,
one should again cast a handful of flowers with devotion.
Then one should offer to Viṣṇu golden bracelets and other ornaments;
immediately thereafter, betel-leaf for the sake of a favorable omen.
Having indeed washed both hands with fragrant water drawn from the arghya vessel, they should become completely stainless.
Having purified them with offerings of food, incense-bowls, and other vessels,
and having smeared those two [hands] with fragrant substances, they should honor one another with the *arghya* offering.
Having offered that to the Lord, he should thereafter, endowed with speech, action, and mind, [perform the sequence for completing the external sacrifice]:
"O Lotus-eyed One, Soul of the Universe, Janārdana, whose form is mantra! (230)
"O Lord of the World, accept this from me, a miserable one, forever.
Having spoken thus, he placed a flower with water in his right hand.
O Nārada, one should place [the vessel] before Viṣṇu with the root mantra,
and then one should properly contemplate it as a shimmering array of stars.

O tiger among the twice-born, she entered the mouth of the Blessed One, passed from the mouth into his heart, and then from the heart back out again by way of the sequence known as withdrawal (saṃhāra).
As before, one should unite [the self] with the Supreme through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
then, having bowed to the Blessed Lord with devotion by means of the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga). || 234 ||
Having risen from one's seat, one should cast those arghya-flowers into it;
for at that moment, one must not abandon the mantra so that it does not become void. || 235 ||
Whether through ignorance or even through knowledge, whatever has been deficient or excessive [in my service], O Eye of the World, it must be forgiven by me, a wretched servant. (236)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the External Sacrifice," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Japa.
Nārada said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, tell me of the majesty of Viṣṇu, who is the Self."
The definitive conclusion regarding the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) has not been understood; how, then, could that be?
The Blessed Lord said: Having thus gratified the Lord of Gods in a water-pot or within mandalas and the like,
one should thereafter gratify the God by means of the prescribed rite of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
Then he bestows all desired objects of the heart. [The threefold nature of recitation:
One should perform the recitation in a threefold manner, with the rosary held in the hand. (3)

One should perform vocal recitation for minor rites, whispered recitation for rites of accomplishment, and mental recitation for the sake of liberation; one should meditate upon the God in every respect.
A beautiful rosary should be made, invisible to other people.
[Regarding the procedure for the rosary, therein are the specific details concerning the size of the beads:
One should make the superior [rosary] with beads the size of a bone from the axle, well-rounded. (5)
The middle size is said to be the measure of the interior of a *ghātrī* fruit;
the smallest is declared to be the measure of a *badara* stone.
One should perform one hundred and eight repetitions, or half of that, or even a quarter;
and this should be done according to the prescribed rule for each specific rite.
One should have an excellent golden [image] made there for the sake of attaining wealth;
for the sake of nourishment and the acquisition of beauty, one should use silver in rites for the ancestors.
O tiger among sages, for the sake of attaining intelligence, vigor, and great splendor, the rosary should be made of copper of medium quality.
For the accomplishment of yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs, one made of tin is prescribed;
for the subjugation of rākṣasas and piśācas, however, it should indeed be made of lead. (10)
For the purpose of accomplishing the subterranean realm (pātāla), however, one made of iron is prescribed;
for the accomplishment of the serpents and nāgas, it should be made of bell-metal.
But at that time, one should make the smaller [sūtra] out of iron for minor tasks;
thus are the rules for sūtras made of the various metals remembered. || 12 ||
O best of sages, I shall describe the classification of those made of jewels;
indeed, everything made of jewels bestows longevity, health, and prosperity. (13)
Crystalline [beads] especially grant liberation and are used for rites of pacification;
these three types—excellent and so forth—are equal in all ritual actions.
Now I shall describe the supreme procedure for seeds produced from roots;
for the sake of good fortune, the first three should always be made of coral.
O son, for the sake of liberation and for the pacification of intense afflictions,
I shall describe the domain of those arisen from the waters, which bestows all perfections.
One who desires prosperity should begin the recitation with lotus seeds and conch shells;
for longevity, wisdom, fame, and peace, pearls grant all accomplishments.
That triad which has been proclaimed through the divisions of superior and so forth—one from among these, such as the middling, should be selected on an auspicious day. (18)
Immediately thereafter, one should wash the jewels with fragrant water mixed with wine.
[The specific rule for the thread:]
Having obtained a new, firm thread made either of hemp or cotton, || 19 ||
Having tripled it and then folded it four times so that it is very firm,
and having wrapped it well, O twice-born one, one should wash it as before.
[The method for joining the gems in the sūtra: The gems should be placed therein according to the sequence of the joining process;
all the gems must be perfectly equal, free from deficiency or excess. || 21 ||

O tiger among sages, for the purpose of recitation (*japa*), one should always use beads with unstrung threads (*maṇibhiḥ kramasūtraiḥ*) for the *niṣkala* mantras; however, for the *sakala-niṣkala*, one should use [beads] with strung threads (*sūtraiḥ*).
(127) But in the case of the entire [thread], according to one's desire, the beads are like the meaning of the thread;
O twice-born one, they are in pairs upon the thread, facing one another. (23)
One should join the back [of one image] to the back [of another] so that they are attached to each other;
having joined them, they should be very firmly fixed so that there is no gap between them.
[The formation of the rosary's circular shape: O best of sages, the beads,
strung together with that single, uninterrupted thread, form a circle.
From the junction of the two jewels, one should wrap the thread with the thread so that it takes the form of a bracelet—stiff, circular, and well-defined. (26)
[The conception of Meru on the rosary]:
O Brahmin, beyond the number of beads at the joints of the knots, one should conceive of Meru in the middle with a single small bead. (27)
[Attention to the purification of the rosary:
Having anointed it with sandalwood paste and other substances, one should place it in an auspicious vessel;
having worshipped it with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should then perform its purification. (28)
Having visualized [the disciple] as burnt by the weapon-mantra, one should drench him with the armor-mantra impelled by the Wind,
and then with the root-mantra which has the nature of supreme nectar.
Having thus purified the thread previously, one should then contemplate it as being like a body—
[the contemplation of the rosary as a divine body]—
as another stainless Nārāyaṇa with four arms. (30)
One should meditate on [the deity] with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding joined palms;
and one should contemplate that thread situated at the Brahma-door as being like a topknot.
O best of the twice-born, learn here the mantra for one's own [deity];
first utter the *praṇava* (oṃ), and at its end, one should place the *kaustubha*. [This is the mantra for the rosary. 32.
One should mark that [mantra] with the protection [syllable], endowed with the sovereignty of the three worlds;
at its end, one should place the five-syllabled word for the rosary (*akṣasūtra*).
The king of mantras for the rosary is said to be accompanied by the salutation (namaskāra).
One should indeed perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa for that rosary with this mantra during its consecration and worship according to its own specific mantra. (34)
(128) And one should worship it with one's own mantra, then gradually within that assembly. [The procedure for the sequence of visualization upon the rosary of the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti:
That supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti is non-different from the Supreme Self. || 35 ||
Having the luster of a moving full moon, yet enveloped in rays like the sun,
she was intensified by the fierce brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon.
O best of Brahmins, one should remember her as being situated in the center of the heart-lotus according to the sequence of emanation as before,
restrained by the retention (kumbhaka) following the inhalation (pūraka).

One should again meditate on her as she rises from the heart-lotus up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); then, O Brahmin, one should contemplate her gradually emerging from that aperture with slow and steady radiance.
As before, one should contemplate [the energy] reaching the end of the twelve via the path of the junction;
then, by means of the yoga called exhalation (recaka), one should visualize the thread with it. (39)
[The recollection of the sacrificial hall through its illumination by the light of the rosary]: Then, one should recollect the entire sacrificial hall as illuminated by the rosary,
like the sky by the full moon.
[The procedure for meditating on the unity of the mantra-soul, the Lord’s parasol, the thread, and the syllables of the mantra:
Thereupon, the King of Mantras is partless. (40)
One should contemplate that [the deity] is immersed therein, joined with the multitude of mantras;
for the power of the Lord is the essence of mantra, consisting indeed of the syllables of the Sūtra-mantra. (41)
One should meditate upon everything as unified, just as water is merged with milk;
there, having taken hold of the back of the flower-offering, one should contemplate this [presence of the mantra with parts and without parts] in the sequence of emanation upon the rosary. (42)
O twice-born one, as the mantra— both with parts and without parts— descends from behind the well-consecrated rosary, it returns according to the sequence of emanation.

[The taking up of the rosary with a prayer to the Lord and his permission: "O Acyuta, having thus informed the Lord of the Gods, I take this rosary made of beads, which has assumed a physical form resembling a mass of sparks. (44)
"Give [this] for the purpose of reciting the mantra"; he should remember that it has been given by him, and after receiving it upon his head, he should then utter the words, "Be gracious. (45)
[The Procedure for the Consecration of the Mantra upon the Rosary, Preceded by Worship:
Having obtained it, one should subsequently bathe it with water from the *arghya* vessel;
having worshipped it with flowers, incense, and other offerings, one should then install the mantra upon you [the rosary]. (46)
The common vessel and the means of accomplishment are completely surrounded by those preceded by the powers; O Lord of Gods, be present here; O Acyuta, be firmly established.
O Sage, having thus consecrated the mantra upon the thread known as the rosary within this net of jewels called the Sūtra, [it remains] as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. (48)
After it has been established, one should indeed display one's own mudrā;
[the akṣasūtra-mudrā] should be made attached and positioned transversely, bent from the right hand. (49)
O best of the twice-born, one should touch the four fingers with the tip of the thumb, following the sequence starting from the index finger and ending with the little finger.
One should bring the thumb upward, touching the tip of the little finger;
this is the mudrā of the rosary, which causes [the deity] to be eternally present.
Thereafter, one should begin the recitation while remaining invisible to other people.
Prior to the commencement of the recitation, a specific contemplation must be performed:
the instruments of speech and mind should be united with the mantra, which is the Supreme Self. (52)
One should first contemplate that which has been conceived by Viṣṇu in the form of Śakti;
whatever has ascended to the mind, that very thing, when joined with speech, becomes an object.
O Nārada, consciousness, joined with the object and with speech as the third,
gradually ascends to the state of action within the realm of transformation.
In this way, O Brahmin, the mantra evolves sequentially from the fourth state (turyā) down to the waking state (jāgrat); then, indeed, it returns again in the reverse order.
The instrument is the very nature of speech, and speech is of the nature of consciousness;
that which is the mind is the mantra, and that which is the mantra is the unborn Hari.
One should again dissolve everything from Brahmā down to the waking state right back into this very [reality];
that which is the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, as well as the Śakti who is Nārāyaṇī. (57)
For through that very transformation, it attains the state called the Fourth (turya);
the Fourth becomes the state of deep sleep (suṣupta), and deep sleep proceeds to the state of dreaming (svapna). || 58 ||
Just as one who is awake enters into a dream, so too from the waking state and the rest; (p.
130) [The Description of the Distinctions of Waking and the Rest] one should contemplate the unification and oneness [of these states] up to the power of the Lord. 59.
O Brahmin, that which is impermanent and appears as diverse, this external web of objects, is declared to be the waking state. (60)
The realization of impermanence that always exists above this [world] is fragile;
it is like a dream, yet for him, that dream becomes the cause of awakening.
Know deep sleep to be tranquility, which is indeed beyond the state of dreaming;
when that [state] reaches Viṣṇu in the form of Śakti, it attains the state of the Fourth (turyatva).
Equanimity with that [state] is called the "Beyond the Fourth" (turyātīta);
it is the supreme mantra beyond all mantras, as well as both the gross and the subtle.
O Brahmin, one should contemplate oneself as the fifth [element] in unity;
having performed this contemplation in this manner, one should likewise begin the recitation (japa).
[The meditation on the sequential emergence of the mantra from within the heart-lotus and so forth, outwardly along the thread of the senses:
Residing in the center of the heart-lotus is the Supreme Lord, whose form is light, resembling a stainless crystal, and vibrating with his own radiance. (65)
From that, a great power consisting of sound emerged like a flame;
it is pure, possessing the attributes of that [sound], and from it indeed arises the succession of phonemes.
The mother of mantras issued forth from her, and from the very tip of her [hand] issued the king of mantras,
O best of sages, just as a flower issues from the tip of a creeper.
In this very way, one should remember the sequence as it has been declared regarding the rosary;
one should cause that [sequence] to dissolve into the heart, and likewise cause the reality of the dissolution into the heart to dissolve in that same manner.
Regarding the single Lord of Mantras, both internal and external:
O Brahmin, when that one [repetition] occurs, it is designated as a hundred thousand repetitions (*lakṣasaṅkhyā*). (69)
Since recitation performed while established in this manner is counted by means of a rosary with effort, that indeed is remembered as the true count of recitation. (70)
By this sequential method, the performance [of the ritual] shall be like that of Viṣṇu;
relying upon the yoga of Viṣṇu, one should collect [the offerings] die by die.
Indeed, from the very moment the vital breath (prāṇa) arises until it reaches the point of culmination (niṣṭhākṣa), one must not cross over Meru;
thereafter, one should perform circumambulation of that which abides as the form of Meru. (72)
And of the partless mantra, which resides above that, which is in the form of a knot, all-pervading, stainless, and of great soul. || 73 ||
Since leaping with the back must be avoided, O Nārada,
one should proceed very slowly, leaving only the tips of the fingers remaining at the base of Meru.
One should perform a rotation with the thumb, which becomes a leaping over the *nameru* [mountain];
and between the base and middle of the thumb, it should be rotated like an umbrella. (75)
The mantra should be recited according to this procedure while endowed with meditative visualization;
[the rule for visualization is established according to the distinct forms of the mantra, based on the differences in purposes such as rites for pacification, enrichment, and so forth].
In rites for pacification, one should meditate on it as having the luster of crystal, and in rites for enrichment, as yellow.
For subjugation, it has the luster of a *kiṃśuka* flower; for attraction, like a king or a mountain; for killing, like collyrium; and for causing dissension, like the wing of a blue jay. (77)
In the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), one should always meditate upon and recite the mantra that has a smoky appearance.
[The twofold nature of recitation: Recitation is traditionally held to be of two kinds, according to its supreme (para) and non-supreme (apara) forms. || 78 ||

O twice-born one, for the purpose of entering another body, for the impelling of the principles (tattvas), and for the accomplishment of cruel rites, the light-filled recitation (japa) is prescribed. (79)
Therein, one should contemplate the stainless sound that is inwardly absorbed;
it brings about the destruction of defects and suffering for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (80)
For the sake of pacifying all undertakings and for the purpose of their effortless accomplishment,
as well as for the attainment of happiness and good fortune, one should likewise perform the rite of establishing the sacred fires (ādhāna).
The recitation (japa) consists of what is called sound; therein, one should inwardly contemplate Janārdana, whose nature is light resembling a drop of dew at night.
From the heart-lotus, one should contemplate the sound arising by means of one's own mantra;
it is eternally manifest, and by that very [sound], one is freed from effort.
When a mantra is recited while established in the state of inhalation and exhalation and infused with meditative cultivation, it indeed bestows the fruits of all desires. (84)
Then, O Nārada, having produced a sound generated by effort, he focused his attention solely on his own mantra as before. (85)
It has passed from the syllable to the non-syllable, free from the fault of death;
it is neither delayed nor too hurried, and is likewise devoid of indistinct words. (86)

Free from mental distraction and endowed with an exceedingly exalted intellect, [the time for recitation varies for qualified practitioners according to the distinction of their qualities such as *sattva*]: in the forenoon, at midday, or in the afternoon of the day. (87)
The three periods for those of sattvic temperament and the others have indeed been declared in succession.
Having performed it thus, O Brahmin, one should recite the mantra and offer it like a sacrifice.

O best of the twice-born, by worshipping month after month with offerings such as water for the hands and flowers, the Lord Viṣṇu, whose very self is mantra, shall quickly become the bestower of perfection.

[The Procedure for Rejuvenating the Rosary and Discarding the Previous Thread] Having performed the rejoining, O Nārada, one should discard the previous rosary with the mantra known as *visarjana*, accompanied by the appropriate mudrā. 90.
Having made the cord new and consecrated it as before, one should wrap it;
then one should again perform the joining of the gems according to their proper positions.
Having bathed it according to the rules, the mantra-practitioner should again place therein that which was previously brought forth out of fear of breaking the thread.
Having performed worship as well as a fire-oblation (homa) to remedy any defects in the ritual,
one should take the thread of the Purāṇa and divide that which is made of threads.
Having tied it with a piece of stone, one should cast it into deep water;
having thrown it while reciting the Viṣvaksena mantra and sipping water (ācamana), one should remember Hari.
O best of Brahmins, with a concentrated mind, one should [recite] the root mantra seven times.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Japa," in the glorious *Pañcarātra*, the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fire-Service. The Blessed Lord said:
Having performed the recitation according to one's capacity, one should worship the Lord at the conclusion of the recitation.
Then, with devotion, one should worship with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and flowers, followed by incense and unguents.
Afterwards, O Brahmin, one should gratify the Lord situated in the midst of the fire. (p.
133) [The commencement of the procedure for preparing the sacrificial pit:
One should construct a sacrificial pit endowed with the proper characteristics on the northern side of the deity. || 2 ||
Either in a temple or elsewhere on a well-characterized plot of ground,
one should prepare a level and auspicious pavilion provided with an exit for smoke.
There, one should first construct an altar that is square on all sides;
above that, one should fashion a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
A square, level, and excellent altar, or one that is circular and pleasing to the mind,
situated toward the two directions [of east and north], is beneficial for rites performed for specific desires.
