Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, [one should act] in the center and in all directions.
[The difference in results according to the distinction of directions for the sacrificial pits:
When Hari, whose essence is the mantra, is heated within a pit situated in the northeast direction... || 6 ||
It bestows worldly accomplishment upon that noble-souled one who desires such success;
one intent on traveling through the sky should offer oblations into a fire-pit situated in the eastern direction.
For the purpose of subduing enemies, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the southeast direction;
indeed, one who desires peace should always perform the oblation in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of the southern direction.
For the purpose of destroying others, in a pit situated in the direction of Nirṛti; and for one desiring victory over untimely death and for the pacification of all calamities. || 9 ||

When the mantra has been fully gratified by the oblation in the sacrificial pit of the western direction (the quarter of Varuṇa), [the wise one], having offered into the sacrificial pit of the western direction, should thoroughly gratify the mantra; when the mantra has been fully gratified in the sacrificial pit of the northwestern direction (the quarter of Vāyu), then [the rite is complete]. || 10 ||
This king of mantras bestows various treasures without delay; it grants health, prosperity, and nourishment. (11)
There is no need for deliberation regarding the satisfaction in the Saumya-direction pit;
[the dimensions of the pits vary according to the number of oblations]:
in a homa of fifty-fold number, the pit should be twelve finger-breadths in measure.
In the case of one hundred and eight oblations, the fist should be equal to the span of the forearm;
and in the case of one hundred and fifty oblations, the fist should include the thumb and the little finger.
For a thousand oblations, the pit is one cubit; for that called ten thousand, it is two cubits;
for a hundred thousand oblations, four cubits; and for ten million oblations, eight cubits.
[The measurement of the excavation]: The excavation is praised everywhere as being half the width [of the platform].
Taking the measurement of one's own front girdle, the length of the excavation in front is twice that. 15.
Having abandoned the binding of the girdle, one should then begin [the construction];
[regarding the different measures of the girdles according to the different measures of the sacrificial pit]:
the measurement of the girdles is twelve barley-corns. || 16 ||
O Great-minded One, for a sacrificial pit measuring twelve finger-breadths, the height of the girdles is proclaimed to be equal to its width.
By thus combining the three girdles into one,
the width and the height shall each be four and a half finger-breadths.
For a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (ratni), the girdles (mekhalā) are prescribed to be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) wide;
for a pit of one and a half cubits, they are two finger-breadths. (19)
For a pit measuring one cubit, the level [of the altar] is traditionally held to be three finger-breadths;
for a two-cubit pit, O best of the twice-born, the girdles are four finger-breadths [in height].
For a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) of four cubits, all [the measurements] should be six finger-breadths;
for one of eight cubits, they are declared to be eight finger-breadths.

[The characteristic of the navel: O best of the twice-born, one should then fashion the navel of the fire-pit in the middle of the directions, resembling an *aśvattha* leaf and situated upon the girdle (*mekhalā*). (22)
As for what was previously stated by me regarding the measurement of the girdles in sequence:
having combined all of that together, one should mark it from the center with a thread. (23)

There, one should gradually diminish [the measurement] from the outside like a half-moon, and with increasing intensity, until it reaches the interior starting from the mouth, according to this sequence.
O Brahmin, on both sides it should be shaped like the lip of an elephant; likewise, from the measurement of the waistband at the back, it should be made slightly elevated for the twice-born.
O Sage, from the measurement of a single girdle, one should gradually decrease it by one-third or by half; indeed, the height of the girdles should be reduced accordingly.
O twice-born one, that [pit] situated above the girdle should indeed be slightly elevated;
its measurement should be one-fourth of the single girdle within the interior of the sacrificial pit.
One should cause it to emerge from the other [channels] and indeed lead it downward;
having stepped upon the ground of the girdle, it should reach as far as the excavation. || 28 ||
Thus has been described the characteristic of the navel as it truly exists;
know that the construction of the square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is like that of the sacrifice.
Having indeed drawn a thread across the middle of the square, one should then rotate it;
thus, one should make a perfect square, devoid of all intermediate corners. || 30 ||
[The classification of sacrificial pits: For the daily and occasional *homa* offerings, the pit should be made either circular or square;
it must have three ridges and be provided with a lip and a navel. || 31 ||
O best of Brahmins, for the rite of throwing [the sacrificial ladle], the pit (kuṇḍa) should be either with two girdles, very smooth and beautiful,
or even with a single girdle.

[The Excellence of Offering in a Fire-pit] O Brahmin, one should perform the offering of oblations either in a movable or a fixed pit; indeed, there is no auspiciousness in the recitation of mantras without a fire-pit. Therefore, one should prepare a fire-pit. 33.
[The method of performing the oblation when a sacrificial pit is impossible due to defects in place or time:
If, by reason of the place and time, a sacrificial pit cannot be constructed, one who desires success must not allow the oblation to be interrupted on that account. (34)
For when the ground has been purified, smeared, and provided with fresh clay,
the oblation (homa) is properly prescribed for the mantra that has been consecrated.
The square pedestal (piṇḍikā) is recommended on all sides externally;
one should fashion a lotus in the center, a Śrī-padma situated within that lotus.
When the auspicious pit has been prepared in this manner, one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya),
either in the sacrificial hall or in another house, O great sage.
Having performed the preliminary rite of warding off obstacles as before, he should then enter;
or else, he may perform it right there after providing another auspicious seat.
There, having sat down according to the previously stated rule and being composed in mind, [the method for the consecration of the sacrificial pit]:
if, however, at the time of commencing the pit, the consecrations have not been performed; 39.
And once you have attained perfection, all of them shall become submissive to you in due order;
then, one should strike them with flowers using the right hand while reciting the weapon-mantra.
And having taken a clod of earth from one part within the center of the pit with the thumb and ring finger, he should extract it while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra. (41)
Having leveled it with the Astra-mantra alone so that there is no longer any unevenness,
one should sprinkle it with the Kavaca-mantra and then pound it.
One should smear it with fragrant water and purify it with the Astra-mantra;
one should diligently scrape it with a blade of Darbha grass using the King of Astras.
On the ground, within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should draw three equal lines starting from the southern direction and proceeding in order until reaching the northern direction.
Starting from the western part, one should lead that [line] facing east;
in its middle, there should be another triad of lines facing north.
Having thus delineated it according to the rule, one should sprinkle it with the *kavaca* mantra;
then, with *darbha* grass blades whose tips are unbroken and which have been consecrated with the *astra* mantra.
One should adorn the entire wall of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) once it has been raised;
having thus constructed the enclosure (akṣavāṭa), one performs the supreme consecration of the pit.

Having performed worship with the [nābhipūjana], one should then, in the center, worship the navel— which resembles the moon— with the *arghya* and other offerings using the *praṇava*, according to that very same procedure. (48)
[The Worship of the Girdle] In the worship of the three girdles, one should employ the heart-mantra.
[The Worship of the Three Principles in the Three Girdles]
Then, those three principles (tattvas) are to be worshipped above the triple girdle.
O twice-born one, having first worshipped the sacrificial pit with the threefold *praṇava* and with offerings of water, ointments, and incense, [to the deity] known as Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśa.
[The method of installing the power named Nārāyaṇī, preceded by the visualization of the seat beginning with Ādhāraśakti within the sacrificial pit at the crossroads:
Upon the darbha-grass mat with flowers placed in the pit at the crossroads...
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with the heart-mantra, one should then worship upon that.

Having worshipped the fire and taken it up, one should circumambulate the sanctuary three times; then, having deposited it through the path of the *yoni*, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*).
(137) And there is the Vaiṣṇava seat preceded by the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti);
therein, one should know the power called Nārāyaṇī, characterized by the brilliance of lightning. 53.
She had attained the state of being the very form of Lakṣmī, her body was enveloped in nectar,
she possessed a beauty surpassing all others, and she was endowed with every power.
Having brought down through the path of eternal emanation that [goddess] who abides within all other things by virtue of her delicacy and beauty, into the lotus of his heart; 55.

Formerly, by means of the sequence of meditation alone, [he was extracted] from the heart-lotus by means of the Heart-mantra, joined with his own name and preceded by the syllable Om and the word "namaḥ. (56)
Having cast [the deity] out with the *recaka* breath from the center of the heart-lotus of the *kuṇḍa*,
and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should display the lotus mudrā.
One should thus effect the presence [of the deity] conjoined with the wheel-mantra.
[The sequence for the production of fire:
First, for the sake of producing the fire of the Blessed One’s power— || 58 ||
Having taken fire produced from a fire-drill, or that arising from a sun-crystal, or from iron or stone, or even ordinary worldly fire that is not defective; || 59 ||
Then, in a vessel made of bell-metal, copper, or a new earthenware one,
one should strike it with the Astra-mantra and sprinkle it with the Śikhā-mantra; these are the five external purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the fire, beginning with striking and sprinkling.
One should worship with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and likewise envelop [the deity] with the armor-mantra;
then, O Nārada, one should drench [the deity] with nectar using the eye-mantra (netra-mantra).
[The contemplation on the fire having reached the navel, after first bringing it to rest within one's own self and descending from stage to stage according to the order of emanation:
Then, having approached by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should bring it to rest within one's own self.
Then, having extracted [the soul] in sequence into the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti) as before, one should join it [there]. || 62 ||
Then, having brought that [consciousness] back down step by step according to the order of emanation,
one should remember it as far as the limit of the locus of sound, and from there, until it has reached the navel.
[The sequence of the fire-oblation when the specific radiance has been meditated upon as residing in the navel-pool:

One should worship with the *praṇava* that which resides in the navel and consists of Agni and Soma, using three kinds of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and with offerings such as clarified butter (*ājya*), etc., with devotion. (64)
Then, O twice-born one, one should worship with the seed-syllable of the three [deities] differentiated;
by the offering of a single oblation, he who stands there becomes awakened. (65)
One should recite [the mantra] along that path while meditating on the nectar of clarified butter within the heart. Then,
by means of one's own mantra, the Fire is to be raised from the navel-pit of that [fire].
O Brahmin, having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should place the *ajita* at its end;
then, one should join the support of all worlds above it. (67)
Then, O high-minded one, one should place the power of the mountain (the letter *ra*) above and below that very [seed-syllable];
this bestows sovereignty over the three worlds upon the head of this seed-syllable.
Then, having joined them in sequence, one should apply this group of seven, beginning with Dhareśa and ending with the one named Suparṇa, to this [same] group of seven.
The stalk extends upward and downward; likewise, above it is the space of Māyā.
Having taken the station for Tejas, one then takes the station for Saptārcis.
The mantra of Agni, accompanied by *svāhā*, consists of eighteen syllables.
[It is the casting of the fire-essence, awakened from the navel-pit by its own mantra, into the fire contained within the vessel.]
The end of the body, characterized by the sound *dhū-dhū*, is awakened by the light of the sound *sat*.

O Brahmin, freed from the smoke of conceptual construction and possessing the sparks of true consciousness, one should cast [the mind] by means of the end of sound (nādānta) along the path of accomplishment as before.
Formerly, when the fire contained in the vessel has been taken away, for the sake of purifying the fire,
one should take it up with both hands, whirl it around, and cast it back into the sacrificial pit.
[The specific visualization of the fire cast into the center of the sacrificial pit:
Then, one should meditate on that fire, which has been smelled by the Śakti known as Nārāyaṇī residing in the middle of the pit, as it enters one's own heart through the tip of the nose. (74)
One should offer three, five, or seven fuel-sticks with the heart-mantra for the purpose of awakening the fire;
however, O Nārada, one should do so with the eye-mantra for the sake of awakening the fire.
[The Circumambulation with Fire]: One should perform the circumambulation with fire using the *hṛdaya* mantra with moistened hands.
[The Strewing of Grass].
Then, with the Astra-mantra, [he should cast] the star-diagram three times in each of the four directions.
In the east and other directions, however, it should be covered by their tips according to the root-text;
one should always complete the spreading toward the north of oneself.

Having established the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should set down whatever materials are required for the fire-ritual—the vessels for the *praṇītā* water, the *idhma* fuel, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and other necessary implements.
Specifically, there should be a pair of *praṇītā* vessels and likewise a pair of *idhma* fuel bundles. (78)

In this same manner, having sprinkled everything with the root mantra— including the pair of *srak* and *sruva* ladles as well as the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*)— one should then place them upon the sacrificial grass (*staras*).
Immediately thereafter, having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water,
one should meditate upon the excellent seat therein and install it with the root mantra of Viṣṇu.
Having thus established the mantra for the completion of the sacrifice (yajña-pati) in the northern direction,
O Brahmin, one should then offer the enclosing sticks (paridhi) with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
[He should place] sacrificial sticks produced from [suitable] wood, clearly defined, with their leaves attached, measured by the span of his hand,
and four barley-corns in circumference, within a hall measured by the span of his hand.
O best of the twice-born, for others, the circumference increases by two finger-breadths [per cubit] until the pit reaches eight cubits; beyond that, one should not construct it.
[The Worship of Brahmā and the World-Protectors] O Sage, one should then offer seats upon them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
upon those seats, one should constantly worship the world-protectors situated in their respective directions. (84)
One should worship Brahmā, Mahendra, Rudra, and the others with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
and one should perform the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with *kuśa* grass, beginning with the *upayāma* blades. (85)
O tiger among the twice-born, the *sruva* ladle should be purified twelve times with hot water using the *astra-mantra*; likewise, the *sruc* ladle should be purified in exactly the same two ways.

Having thus washed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the *śikhā-mantra*, they should then be heated by the fire situated within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). [This concludes the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva*.]
The definition of these two is now stated. || 87 ||
The knower of mantras should first fashion the wood for the sake of accomplishing the divine *sruk* according to the measure of his own forearm; it should be six finger-breadths in width. (88)
Then, by dividing the length into two parts, the staff is said to be octagonal;
having made it a measure of two and a half finger-breadths, one should subtract the remainder.
O best of sages, one should fashion an auspicious lotus-face at the base of the staff,
so that the staff appears as if situated within its pericarp.
Alternatively, having fashioned the handle as a triple-fold or a conch-shell, one should place it in the mouth and divide the front portion into two equal parts with effort. (91)
Then, the width of the portion at the front is two finger-breadths,
and for the portion situated as a staff, it is three finger-breadths all around, equal on every side.
Having given [the gift], one should then create a circular depression, a trench with the proper characteristics;
in its center, one should fashion a full-blown lotus with upward-pointing petals.
Know that the vessel of clarified butter (ājyakośa) is equal to seven or five palas;
and the pericarp, together with its filaments, is submerged in the center of the lotus.
Outside, there is a twelve-spoked wheel for the eight-petalled lotus;
outside the lotus, however, a conch shell should be made in each of the four corners.
Then, O Sage, having subtracted one finger-breadth from each of the two sides of the upper portion, that [portion] is then to be divided into three parts.
The ears [should be placed] with one part on each side, while the two shoulders are at the center;
the face is separated from the shoulders by one finger-breadth in the middle.
Having first excluded the width equal to the ear from that [total], one should then subtract the remainder, starting from the region of the ear. 98.
Just as the face of Varāha was [revealed] by the lineage-descended thread, so too [one should proceed] from the lotus leaf down to the very tip of the mouth. 99.
O Sage, one should fashion the channel for the clarified butter (ājyapraṇāla) so that it is level, or perhaps slightly less by one finger-breadth, and gradually tapering;
it should not be such that the clarified butter flows out too quickly. 100.
Then, O Brahmin, one should fashion a beautiful *sruva* ladle measuring one cubit;
its width should be two finger-breadths, and its thickness half of that.
From the measurement of its width, one should fashion a circle of two finger-breadths at its front;
it should be gradually hollowed out and sealed with a spherical mold.
In the center, it is adorned with a mark in the shape of a deer's footprint;
the neck, including the ears, measures three finger-breadths and is one-third of the width. (103)
At the base, on both sides, one should fashion a svastika two finger-breadths in length;
it may be endowed with various artistic designs, or the staff itself may be smooth.
The practitioner should fashion the *sruva* ladle in this manner for the rite of oblation;
thereafter, for the sake of consecrating the fire, he should perform the oblation with it.

[The twofold nature of the consecration of the fire: There are ten consecrations for the fire situated within the sacrificial pit, and five consecrations for that which is outside; thus, fifteen are traditionally taught. (106)
Sprinkling, striking on the outside, worship, veiling, and the rite of nectarization—these five [rites] for the fire were taught of old. (107)
[The consecratory rites beginning with the deposition of the embryo for the fire]:
O Brahmin, the purpose [of these rites] is indeed applied within the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), starting from the eastern Lakṣmī;
first the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa), then the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and thereafter the fashioning of the faces. 108.

The parting of the hair, the extraction of the mouth-fluid, the emergence [of the child], the birth-rite, the naming, the enjoyment, the first feeding, and all the other rites for the twice-born; 109.
And one should perform all the consecrations with the heart-mantra, O Nārada.
[Now, the preparations for the clarified butter:
In the rite involving clarified butter, one should indeed perform these ten [preparations] according to the prescribed rule. 110.
First, the placing upon the fire is performed with the *hṛdaya* mantra and the *kavaca* mantra;
likewise, the stirring and lifting out, as well as the secondary placing upon the fire.
The act of propitiation, as well as the act of purification, and then that which is called the lustration ceremony—these three, O Nārada, [are performed]. (112)
The ritual actions should be performed with the heart-mantra, and the veiling with the armor-mantra;
immediately thereafter, the acts of gazing and the nectarization should be performed with that same mantra.
Know that the prior touching of the clarified butter contained in the vessel with blazing *darbha* grass is the consecration known as *adhiśrayaṇa*.
Then, with both hands, having grasped a blade of kuśa grass that is bent at the middle and pressed between the ring fingers and thumbs, [he should place it] over the clarified butter. (115)
O Brahmin, one should lead this [fire] forward and lead that [fire] back; one should cast kuśa grass into the fire.
These two purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are proclaimed as the immersion and the emergence.
That which is called "relying on an adjunct" (upādhiśrayaṇa) is said to be its liquefaction;
it is the transferring [of the substance] into another vessel for the removal of defects. (117)
For this is the act of making [the deity] gracious; therefore, one should cast the pavitraka made of darbha grass into its midst, and that is the act of purification.
O Brahmin, taking a firebrand from the sacrificial pit that is blazing and free of smoke, one should perform a single circumambulation with it; that indeed is known as *nīrājana*.
After having cleansed [the deity], one should then meditate upon [the mantra] residing within the chest of the armor;
for this circling with the index finger is indeed the "concealment" (avakuṇṭhana).
O Brahmin, one should first perform the *avalokana* (glance) by means of the splendor residing in the heart that has reached the eyes; thereafter, one should meditate upon that which is above it.
Situated in the center of the lunar disc and accompanied by the dhenumudrā, one should indeed contemplate the mantra of the daughter of Surabhi, which shines like a hundred moons.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Mantras situated within that [lotus], resembling the Himālaya mountain,
being drenched by floods of nectar flowing from it— both that which originates from the moon and that which comes from the celestial cow.
One should meditate upon the clarified butter as being conjoined with all the ritual formulations (saṃskāra) and consecrated;
this which has been revealed to you is called "the rite of immortalization" (amṛtīkaraṇa). || 124 ||
Having gazed upon them and rendered them immortal, the two eyes should indeed be bestowed.
[The oblation of clarified butter is performed with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, respectively, on the right and left sides of the sacrificial pit.
Having filled the *sruva* with clarified butter, one should contemplate it with the seed-syllable of the Sun (*sūryabīja*). || 125 ||
And one should place the thousand-rayed [sun] in the middle of that, to the south of the sacrificial pit;
and having meditated upon the other [moon] in the *sruva* ladle by means of the syllable named Soma.
One should then place the full seed-syllable of the Moon (Śaśāṅka-bīja) to the north of that;
subsequently, within those two, in the middle portion of the sacrificial pit which consists of the nature of Agni and Soma, one should worship the deity whose essence is Agni and Soma.
For that which is the seed of the entire body along with its essential nature, wherein indeed the bodily constituents abide without division. (128)

Having meditated externally on [the object] as resembling a throat, situated within the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, it is indeed unified with the mantra consisting of those two stated seed-syllables. (129)
As before, one should personally offer that which has been held, accompanied by meditation and the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Then, all the oblation materials, such as sesame seeds and the rest, are to be consecrated with clarified butter (*ājya*). (130)
[The Analysis of the Purificatory Rites for the Fire] Now, for the sake of accomplishing all purificatory rites, the fire must be consecrated during the oblation (homa).
Having enclosed the fire with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should utter the name of the ritual action. 131.
"I accomplish [this], svāhā"—this is the sequence for all rites.
[Now, therein follows the analysis of the *garbhādhāna* sacrament:
That which is indeed the entry of the external [soul] into the hollow of the venerable womb. (132)
Know that, O Sage, the first sacrament is the *garbhādhāna* (conception);
and by the union of the sense of smell, the power of fire which resides within the womb of Śrī [is activated]. (133)

That which is of the nature of a flame, imperishable and subtle, is indeed the expansion of His consciousness; and through the gradual contact with the consciousness of the Lord’s power, [it becomes manifest]. (134)
One should offer clarified butter into the fire while recollecting that [deity] and using the mantra prescribed for it;
indeed, through the directing of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), this becomes the "impregnation" (*puṃsavana*) of the fire.

[Now, the conceptualization of the faces: From the face of that radiant one who has awakened, those [flames] emerge; they possess the power of illumination and burning for that which is currently formless. (136)
Know that the conception of her faces is merely for the sake of the ball-like form.
And hear, O Nārada, the names of those seven faces and their flames: [The names of the seven faces and flames]...
Hear the names of those faces and flames, O Nārada. (137)
Prabhā, Dīpti, Prakāśā, Marīci, Tapanī, Karālā, and Lelihā are situated pervading the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 138 ||

In the directions of Ishana, Agni, and the East, the triad beginning with Prabhā is prescribed; while in the directions of Rakshas, Varuna, and Vayu, that triad beginning with Marīci is located. (139)
From the center of the northern direction, situated toward the south, is one named Lelihā.
[The collection of seed-syllables of their facial flames:
The universal collection of seed-syllables for these [faces] ends with the seed-syllable of fire (RA). 140.
In the very sequence previously described, beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, [one should worship];
[now, regarding the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*)]:
the unmanifest and all its constituent parts, such as the head, hands, and so forth, reside therein. (141)
Those who, being awakened, resort to their own respective boundaries of action—for them, the conceptualization of division is called the *sīmanta*. 142.
[Now, the emergence from the mouths:
The faces, beginning with Narasiṃha, resemble shimmering stars;
they abide within the consciousness of Śakti, and that Śakti exists as their very self. 143.
O Brahmin, because they are perfectly transformed, they indeed emerge from there;
by their own power, each in its own place, it is called the exudation from the mouth.
[Now, the exit:
The breath does not emerge from the meditation within the womb of Śrī;
that exit occurs together with fire, and one should offer that as a consecrated oblation. 145.
[Now, the Jātaka:
That which occurs after one has emerged from the womb is declared to be the *jātaka*.
[The *prāśana*:]
O twice-born one, there should be bathing with gold, honey, and clarified butter, as well as the ritual consumption of them.
Thereafter, one should diligently perform the naming ceremony for the fire that has been born;
for the Vaiṣṇava fire, the name should end in the suffix "-kāra" followed by the syllable *praṇava*.
[Enjoyment:
O twice-born one, enjoyment begins with the first feeding of solid food and ends with marriage;
the single consecration of anointing the body should be offered as before. 148.
[Now, the consecration: Thereafter, the consecration known as *adhikāra* assumes many forms.
[The meditation on the fire, purified by the aforementioned consecrations, as being Nārāyaṇa.]
Thus, the fire, purified by the ritual refinements (saṃskāra) and having Nārāyaṇa as its essence— || 149 ||

Having meditated upon [the deity] situated in the middle of the sacrificial pit, possessing four arms and four faces, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, and radiant like the rising sun. (150)
[The Meditation on Entering the Heart via the Path of Flames]:

There, one should meditate on that [flame] produced from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which has arrived by way of the path of flames, possessing the radiance of supreme bliss, reaching as far as the nose and the twelve [finger-breadths]. 51.
Then, by means of the yoga of descent, one should visualize her entered into the heart.
[Now, the worship of the consecrated fire:
Having performed the worship of the consecrated fire with devotion, || 152 ||
O twice-born one, [one should worship] in due order with flowers, incense, curd, sesame seeds mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata), food accompanied by edible fruits, and clarified butter. 153.
Then, with a fully concentrated heart, one should satisfy the fire with one's own mantra, using sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other offerings, in sequence and according to one's capacity. (154)
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire with clarified butter, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*, one should then perform the worship of the deity in the midst of the fire:
"Then the worship of the deity must be performed in the middle of the fire. (155)

[In that regard, first is the manner of recollecting the Fire: One should first recollect that Fire, possessing form yet with stainless radiance, all-pervading and reaching every direction by the power and vigor of one's own yoga. (156)
With hands, feet, eyes, heads, and faces on every side, shaped like a *kadamba* flower, and resplendent with its own radiance. (157)
Filling the entire sacrificial pit from all sides with every form,
he is thus expansive, all-pervasive, formless, and intensely radiant.
Having meditated upon the fire as being all-pervasive like space, one should worship the Lord in its center with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
One should worship the Lord in the midst of that fire, having visualized the fire as being like space,
and likewise with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
[The Sacrifice to the Weapon and Other Deities] Thereafter, one should worship the Weapon (astra) and the Armor (kavaca). || 159 ||
On the path of the right arm, near Aniruddha,
one should place that which consists of Agni and Soma for the sake of self-protection.
p. 146) The deity is situated within the wheel;
[now, the procedure for the fire sacrifice (homa):
then one should commence the fire sacrifice.
With sesame seeds mixed with ghee, and with all materials prescribed for sacrifice; || 161 ||
Then, one should perform the rite according to the rules using oblations soaked in fragrant clarified butter.
One should offer oblations for Lakṣmī and the others at a quantity equal to one-fourth of that of the root mantra. (162)
O best of the twice-born, one should then offer half of that [portion] as a śakti-homa for the limbs, and with half of that again, one should perform the homa for the faces.
One should offer half of the oblations to the faces [of the syllables] beginning with Kaustubha;
half of that to those beginning with Satya; and half of that to the Supreme Imperishable (akṣara).
For those at the forefront, the number [of oblations] should be half, or joined with a half-portion, or even greater;
for one desiring success, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa) must be done in accordance with the recitation (japa), just as it is done at the time of recitation. || 165 ||
Having understood this, one should then perform from one hundred up to ten million fire-oblations (homas),
because a mantra that has not been satiated never bestows fruit.
With desires that yield inevitable fruits arising according to place and time— [this is the determination of the materials for the oblation]—
one should perform it with sesame seeds, ghee, milk, curd, or milk-rice. (167)
With prepared cooked foods, edibles, seeds, parched grain, and rice;
or with roots, fruits, and tender sprouts that are most highly praised. || 168 ||
O Brahmin, [one should worship] with fragrant flowers such as the *sthalapadma* and others, with white and other [colored] flowers,
with *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter, or with *śrīveṣṭaka* mixed with clarified butter.
Or with fresh dhātrī fruits and auspicious utpala lotuses, as well as very white and pale-red lotuses and beautiful bilva fruits. (170)

With blades of *dūrvā* grass whose tips are unbroken and as pure as the fine tusks of an elephant, with fuel-sticks produced from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, and likewise those made from milky trees; 171.
The *amṛtā* [leaves] combined with milk, along with *audumbara* [leaves] drenched in honey—[these branches] should have uncut tips, be unbroken, and be free from thorns. (172)
All [offerings] should be mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) or, alternatively, combined with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
(p. 147) [The difference in results according to the difference in oblation materials:
With sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, there is pacification (*śānti*) as well as all accomplishments (*siddhi*). || 173 ||
An oblation of ghee, milk, and curd bestows satisfaction;
however, with milk-rice, prepared foods, and edible delicacies, nourishment shall always be attained. (174)
When the king of mantras is gratified with seeds, grains, and rice,
the Supreme Lord, being pleased, always bestows what is auspicious.
An oblation performed with young shoots and fruits bestows satisfaction;
it wards off untimely death and brings diseases to a state of pacification. (176)
O Brahmin, when propitiated with land-lotuses and other flowers such as the white ones, he bestows incomparable good fortune without delay.
Through offerings of guggulu and other auspicious substances, as well as dhātrī fruits, he grants health to the twice-born;
and by means of lotus seeds smeared with clarified butter, he swiftly bestows prosperity.
One who desires subjugation or enjoyment should perform oblations with blue lotuses;
by performing oblations with dūrvā grass and amṛtā, one shall obtain an increase in lifespan. (179)
Through oblations of auspicious fuel-wood, the Lord bestows the pacification of defects.
Regarding the different measures for the oblation:
an oblation of sesame seeds is always recommended when performed with the *mṛgamudrā* gesture. (180)
An offering of clarified butter should consist of one karṣa, and that of milk especially;
an oblation of curd should be the measure of a śukti, and that of milk-rice (pāyasa) a handful (prasṛti). || 181 ||
One should perform the oblation with half a mouthful of cooked food and edible items according to their own measure,
and for all seeds, one should perform the oblation with a single handful.
One should offer five grains of *śāli* rice with the tips of the fingers, as well as fruits in their natural measure, and likewise sprouts. (183)
The third [offering] consists of pieces of root and flowers according to their own size;
pills the size of a jujube fruit should always be offered with guggulu resin.
Or, O best of Brahmins, if available, one should offer oblations of emblic myrobalan fruits the size of a *dhātrī* fruit,
or else stalks of *dūrvā* grass measuring four or eight finger-breadths in length.
The equal division [of the oblation] should be accompanied by the skin [of the sacrificial wood], measured by the extent of a fuel-stick.
[This is the determination of the specific occasions for the application of *svāhākāra*, *vaṣaṭkāra*, *vauṣaṭkāra*, and so forth:
One should always use *svāhākāra* in the fire-oblation (*homa*), and *vauṣaṭ* specifically in the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). (186)
One should always employ that very [syllable] *svāhā* in rites for peace (*śāntika*), or *vaṣaṭ* in rites of invocation (*āvāhana*).
One uses *svadhā* in rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkriyā*), and the syllable *phaṭ* in rites of destruction (*kṣayakarma*). (187)
For the purpose of achieving hatred, *huṃ*; for subjugation, *hīṃ*; and for the attainment of liberation, *namas*.
[The Method of the Full Oblation: At the conclusion of the ritual fire-offering (*karmahoma*), one should fill the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter.
But in the absence of abundant materials, one should fill [the vessel] with the substance for the oblation;
thereupon, one should place ghee upon it, and then offer arghya, flowers, and so forth. || 189 ||
Beginning from the base, the *sruk* ladle, together with the *sruva* spoon, should be worshipped;
that substance mixed with clarified butter is placed within the hollow of the *sruk*'s bowl.
Then, one should meditate on [the body] as resembling a flowing moon;
having extracted it full, one should remember it while restraining the handle of the sacrificial ladle at the root of the navel of the body.
One should extract the partless Lord of Mantras, who resembles the full moon,
from one's own body by means of the wind-power (marucchakti) starting from the base (āmūla).
Having established that great stream of nectar upon the support of Īśvara,
one should contemplate it falling into the lotus of the *sruk* via the path of the junction of the nostrils.
One should pour forth an immortal stream of clarified butter like a shower of wealth,
either into the center of the mantra or into the aperture of Brahmā.
One should correctly visualize [the deity] as having fully entered within the heart-lotus;
one should meditate upon the mantra, nourished by that [deity], through the stream of Brahman. 195.
Satisfied, joyful, nourished, and truly contented toward the practitioner, she is indeed endowed with the utterance of mantras and possessed of a physical form. (196)
O best of the twice-born, this [Purāṇa], endowed with meditation, has been fully expounded;
it eternally bestows all perfections and increases the fortune of liberation. (197)
[The necessity of knowing the fire through its distinctions of color and so forth for the accomplishment of ritual acts:
For the accomplishment of the rite, one should offer oblations into a fire with abundant dry fuel;
likewise, the colors, scents, sounds, and shapes of the fire [must be observed]. (198)
The modifications and the flames are to be perceived for the accomplishment of the rite;
that which possesses the luster of a ruby is the best, resembling lac or red dye. (199)
O twice-born one, for the sake of victory, a fire with the color of the rising sun is praised;
likewise, a fire that has the luster of the color of Indra’s anger or the hue of blood is auspicious. (200)
Resembling Indra’s bow, excellent, and likewise the color of saffron—the fire is desired here with the hue of red varieties of flowers. (201)
The scent of fragrant substances and the smell of ghee are auspicious;
the lotus-scent bestows long life, O observer of noble vows, as does a manifold fragrance. (202)
The fire prescribed for the rite of sorcery (abhicāra) always possesses a pungent odor, and its sound is like that of clouds, lutes, conchs, and drums. (203)
The sound of fire is the cause for its accomplishment; therefore, any other [sound] would be non-accomplishing.
A circular whirling [of smoke] is excellent, as are those in the form of a banner or a chowrie. (204)
Furthermore, it bestows success when it has the form of celestial chariots and canopies, palaces, bulls, or of swans and peacocks. (205)
When fire is observed to have a reddish hue according to its characteristics, and it resembles a broken ruby or has the luster of crystal, it is likewise auspicious. (206)
If the fire, having been described previously in its specific form, should attain circumambulation [of the practitioner] and mutual union, then that fire brings about accomplishment.
But if the fire performs an exchange with forbidden grass, such as that used for pigeons and the like, then, O Brahmin, it undergoes a reversal.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should indeed perform an additional hundred *homa*s for that purpose.
Furthermore, uneven flames of the fire, such as those with three peaks and so forth, are auspicious.
Flames that are short, short-and-tall, or long are said to bestow success;
likewise, one that is glossy, turning clockwise, and whose sound covers over the hearing [of other sounds]. (210)
He who always performs auspicious deeds, though lacking other qualities,
is praised for the fire-sacrifice when the fire is blazing, licking [the offerings], smokeless, and endowed with its proper qualities. || 211 ||

One desiring prosperity should offer oblations into a fire that is pleasing to the heart and bestows satisfaction; however, in the rite of homa, one should avoid a fire that has little luster, a poor form, and is filled with sparks. || 212 ||
A fire that is devoid of flames and smoke does not bestow success;
nor does one who offers oblations into a fire that is unawakened and smoky [achieve results]. (213)
There shall be a destruction of his karma, yet he experiences it for the sake of malevolent magic (ābhicāra);
that which is foul-smelling, licked, drunk, and black. (214)
He who repeatedly draws a circle (kuṇḍa) shall indeed suffer defeat.
[The variations of results according to the lunar days:
When the planets are auspicious, under a favorable asterism, during the bright fortnight, and on favorable lunar days... (215)
On the twelfth [lunar day], the omnipresent Lord, stationed in the fire, bestows dharma, kāma, and artha;
on the thirteenth, he grants good fortune, while on the eleventh, victory is certain.
On the fifth lunar day there is the attainment of wealth, and on the ninth, the Lord bestows fame;
these lunar days in the bright fortnight are declared for rites pertaining to good fortune.

However, for one seeking liberation, according to their desire, there is a difference in the fruit for a mantra that has been satiated— whether during either of the two fortnights— in the sevenfold radiance beginning with *prabhā*, when it is satiated in each one in succession, O Nārada, if the mantra has entered the form of the light (*prabhā*). || 218 ||
The Lord, established in radiance and bestowing the earth, swiftly grants knowledge;
situated above the light, he quickly scorches the enemies. || 219 ||
The pervasive Lord, when ascending in the Marīci [flame], swiftly bestows the destruction of enemies;
the mantra, when ascending in the Tapantī [flame], grants the pacification of all afflictions.
The omnipresent Lord, stationed at Karālā, shall effect the eradication of opposing forces,
O Sage, if the mantra is situated in the state of Lelihāna and has been properly satiated.
And at the end of the body, he shall grant whatever is desired as well as the supreme state.
O Brahmin, this ritual of the fire-oblation has been described by me in brief. (222)
[The prescription for the subsidiary rite to be performed at the conclusion of the fire-oblation:
At the end of the oblation, one should again worship the mantra together with the fire using flowers and other offerings;
one should display all the mudrās in sequence, beginning with the root mantra. (223)
Then, one should display the mudrā of fire accompanied by the mantra.
[The Fire Mudrā:
Having formed the hands in the shape of a lotus, with the thumbs and the little fingers [joined]. (224)
O twice-born one, having closed [the eyes] from the tip [of the nose], like a pericarp,
the remaining three fingers beginning with the index finger should be raised upward from both hands.
That which is cast without being attached is proclaimed as the *mudrā* of fire;
[this is the manner of offering a handful of flowers upon the head of the Blessed One, who is in the form of the mantra placed within the maṇḍala].
Then, having offered the oblation to Viṣṇu, one should proceed to the center of the mandala.
Having filled both hands with flowers placed upon them, one should contemplate the partless mantra (niṣkala-mantra) augmented by nectar. (227)
One should place that which is suffused with abundant light upon the head of the mantra.
[Now, the prayer:
"O you who abide in the midst of the fire, you have been gratified by this oblation through devotion to the Lord. (228)
Take into yourself whatever potency exists in the sacrificial substances;
contemplate them as having been received with a serene inner self. 229.
[Now, the method for the dismissal of those situated within the mandala:
Then one should perform the dismissal after offering arghya together with incense.
[Now, the placing of the prasāda upon the head.]
And the offering of water for grace, together with flowers, has fallen from above the pericarp.
Then, O Sage, having taken the powder from the mandala and placed it upon one's own head, one should apply the tilaka with that dust.
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead with yellow-red [pigment] from the mandala.
[The contemplation of the pervasion of one's own body by the mantra placed in the *arghya* vessel through inhalation]:

"O twice-born Nārada, that mantra which was previously deposited in two ways by means of the two *arghya* vessels— by means of the inhalation (*pūraka*) accompanied by the mantra and the mudrā," (232)
One should contemplate the body as being spoken [by the mantra], from the feet up to the head;
this is the contemplation that the mantras residing in the locus of enjoyment have entered the body of the principal mantra.
The mantras situated in the place of enjoyment, when worshipped according to their sequence, [grant success]. || 233 ||
One should visualize them as having entered the body of the principal mantra, just as flames merge into other flames or as rivers flow into the ocean. (234)
[The contemplation of that gross mantra-body, the locus of all mantras,
having entered into the supreme form through the sequence of its own causes, beginning with the subtle: O twice-born one, contemplate that gross mantra-form, the locus of all mantras.
One should meditate upon that which has entered into the subtle sense-organ of the intellect, which indeed possesses a dual nature.
But when the other [state] is of the previously described form, one should contemplate that subtle [reality], which possesses both natures, as having entered into one's own heart;
that supreme [reality], whose nature is radiant, rests upon the supportless state. (236)

One should meditate upon [the mantra] having entered the heart-lotus of the seeker of accomplishment. (p. 152) [This refers to the meditation on the pervasion of one's own body from head to foot by the radiance of the supreme form that has entered one's own heart.]
But by means of inhalation accompanied by mantra and mudrā, O Nārada, (237)
O twice-born one, one should contemplate the body as being spoken [of] by that mantra which has entered from the feet up to the head, even without deliberate effort. (238)
The mantra of that practitioner whose body trembles becomes propitious.
[The offering of *naivedya* to the initiated after the dismissal:
Having thus dismissed the Lord of Mantras, excluding the world-protectors and their weapons, || 239 ||
O twice-born one, one should offer the food offering (naivedya) to initiated brahmins who practice faith and self-restraint, as well as to disciples whose inner selves are purified.
[The gathering of flowers and other offerings employed in the worship of the root mantra:
One should gather the flowers, the weapon-mantra (astra), and the food offering (naivedya) employed for the root mantra at the same time as the mantra is being recited. 241.
[The worship of Viṣvaksena with that collected substance:
Even with that [substance] remaining in the vessel, one should summon Viṣvaksena from within the sky and worship him with devotion, having visualized him within the mandala. 242.
The omnipresent Lord has four arms and noble limbs, bearing a mace and a conch;
he resembles the fresh leaf of a mango tree, with tawny beard and eyes. || 243 ||
Having worshipped him who wears yellow garments, has four tusks, and is endowed with his two own mudrās,
one should then duly display his mudrā along with his limbs (aṅgas).
[Then, the worship of the mantra placed in the fire-pit with flowers:
Having gone near the fire-pit and worshipped the mantra with flowers;
[the application of the sectarian mark with ashes:]
One should apply an auspicious mark (tilaka) on the forehead with ashes consecrated by the Astra-mantra. || 245 ||
[The withdrawal of the mantra residing in the *kuṇḍa*]: Having performed [the ritual] like that of the *maṇḍala*, and subsequently having withdrawn it into oneself;
[then follows the sequence for the satiation of Viṣvaksena in the *kuṇḍa*].
Then Viṣvaksena should be propitiated with devotion using sesame seeds and unbroken grains of rice.
O twice-born one, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ";
then, having worshipped [the deity] within the mandala, one should perform its dismissal (visarjana).
p. 153) [The dismissal of Viṣvaksena:
O best of the twice-born, with his own mantra and the words "forgive me," accompanied by the appropriate mudrā, one should then visualize him ascending into the sky. 248.
Then, O Nārada, with a full water-pot consecrated by the recitation of the *astra* mantra, filled with milk, water, honey, and clarified butter, one should cause [the deity] to enter that maṇḍala.
Then, having raised Viṣvaksena from the sacrificial pit as before,
one should worship the world-protectors with flowers and other offerings, and thereafter satisfy them with libations. (250)

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with one's own mantra— either by offering a single oblation or, according to one's capacity, many more— one should then perform the ritual dismissal.

Having returned to their respective places in due order, along with their weapons and retinues, the Kṣetrapālas and others then proceed in sequence to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with clarified butter and other offerings. (252) [Now follows the sequence for the libation of the Kṣetrapālas and others with ghee and so forth.]
Beginning with Ādhāraśakti, all the seat-mantras (pīṭhamantra) and the Siddhāntas beginning with Gaṇeśa should be offered libations with ghee and other substances.
Then, one should repeatedly or according to one's own capacity pour the full [liquid] into all [the vessels],
whether it be that contained in the cups or that contained in the pitcher, having been brought down by means of mantra and tantra.
Having gradually withdrawn [the elements] as before by means of the tip of the nose,
the twice-born should then satisfy the Fire with his own mantra according to his ability. (255)
One should pour the full vessel, which makes [the rite] flawless, using the *pūrṇā* mantra;
having offered a handful of flowers into the fire-pit while recollecting the fire-mantra. (256)
Having smelled [the substances], one should indeed place them in the squares according to the sequence of descent.
[Now, the sprinkling around the fire:
Having filled the vessel with water, one should circumambulate the pit externally in a clockwise direction. (257)
One should indeed perform [the rite] starting from the northeast corner with an unbroken stream of water.
[The procedure for discarding the food offerings, etc., into the water:
Having withdrawn the food offering (naivedya), excluding the garments and ornaments, || 258 ||
One should cast [the substances] into the midst of unfathomable water as it flows;
having properly performed the wiping and the smearing, one should then scatter the white mustard seeds and other items. (259)

[The withdrawal of the armor and weapon mantras installed for protection: "Having previously employed the armor and weapon mantras for the sake of protection, one should now withdraw them after offering white mustard seeds and the like, parched grain, sesame, flowers, and unbroken rice. (260)
[The withdrawal of the ritual placement performed upon one's own body:
Having applied a tilaka from the place of sacrifice and having withdrawn the ritual placement from his own body, the wise man should indeed perform his meal and other such activities. (261)
O twice-born one, this procedure for the satiation of the mantra has been stated in brief. It must never be spoken to those who are uninitiated, nor to those who lack devotion. (262)

It should not be spoken to those established in other philosophical systems, nor to those whose souls delight in derision; rather, it should be spoken to a worthy recipient who knows the true nature of reality, or to a spiritual son who knows the secret commitments.

But toward a practitioner, or even toward one who is devoted to the guru, affectionate, free from envy, dedicated to truth and dharma, virtuous in conduct, and established in the observances (samaya), [one may bestow it]. || 264 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fire-Rite," in the glorious *Pañcarātra* *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*. || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear the supreme characteristics of initiation."
[This applies] to the initiate (samayin), the spiritual son (putraka), as well as to the practitioner (sādhaka) and the master (ācārya). || 1 ||
Tell me in detail about those who are lifelong celibates, as well as women and children whose souls are purified, if you are inclined to show me favor.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen; I shall explain the initiation for disciples of purified soul, so that they may possess the qualification for the worship of the deity, the fire, and the guru. (3)
For the sake of both spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti), I shall explain that initiation in three ways according to the distinction between the wealthy and the poor; indeed,
for those who possess great wealth, one should perform it through the sacrifice of the Great Mandala (mahāmaṇḍalayāga).
For an embodied being who is liberated from the attachment to wealth, who possesses but little wealth, who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, and who is truly a devotee of Viṣṇu; (5)
In the fire, the Guru should perform the rite with seeds accompanied by clarified butter, as well as with sesame seeds alone;
for one who lacks the ritual materials, the Guru should indeed grant favor through speech alone.
[The Necessity of Initiating One Who Has Approached:
He who is equal toward all beings, free from passion, devoid of envy, with senses conquered, pure, skillful, and endowed with all limbs complete; (7)
Always granting fearlessness to those who are afraid through his actions, mind, and speech,
he has attained the state of perfect awakening and is even there permeated by the Blessed One.
One who delights in the Pañcakāla, likewise one who knows the meaning of the Pañcarātra, having fully understood the reality of Viṣṇu as both one and manifold in its divisions; (9)
He consecrates the entire earth, how much more so those who have approached him;
[this is the instruction on the single Acyuta existing in manifold forms:
he is without support, without volition, unswerving from his own nature, and steadfast. (10)
Free from the phenomena of grasped and grasper, it is immovable and eternal;
I shall describe this very [reality] as the fruit, which abides in many ways. 11.

O best of sages, just as it truly is, the existence of Acyuta consists of a threefold pervasion within the principles (tattvas) which abide in a threefold manner— as the supreme, the subtle, and the gross— distinguished by the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader.
Pervading the other three principles—the gross, the subtle, and the supreme—it remains established.
That which is called Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśa, as well as another beginning with the ear— Acyuta, having pervaded these, stands manifest in three ways, ending with the intellect (buddhi).
Having known the triple Viṣṇu-tattva as one, though it appears manifold,
he should bestow grace upon all through each of its individual manifestations.

O twice-born one, according to their respective order among the Samaya-jñānas and so forth, the Blessed One—the embodiment of the mantra—exists in three ways: the Blessed One is first the single Piṇḍātman (the aggregate-self), and he is secondly twofold, enriched by the Upāṅgas (subsidiary limbs). 15.
Within the threefold collection of mantras, it is established in three ways;
[the threefold nature of the mantra-collection consists of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme].
The first part of the mantra-collection is said to consist of the mantras for attraction, ending with the *maṇi* (jewel) mantra. (16)

The first [category] begins with Lakṣmī and ends with Bhūdhara; the second is designated as "subtle" (sūkṣma); the third is known as "supreme" (para), beginning with the seven "hairs" (ūrṇā) and ending with the mūrti-mantras. || 17 ||
Having gathered the collection of *tattvas* (or mantras), he abides in the abbreviated ritual. [The mass of mantras,
which exists in a threefold manner as gross, subtle, and supreme, abides within each individual group— gross and so forth— as a triad consisting of the gross and the rest.]
Having himself divided the threefold [reality] into three groups of three, according to its form in the three states.
Lord Viṣṇu, who bestows grace upon the worlds, resides within the zodiac signs;
this triad, beginning with the goad and ending with Vainateya, is the grossest of the gross.
O Nārada, from the mantra of the mace (gadā) up to the conch (śaṅkha), the middle part is thick;
and from the lotus (paṅkaja) up to the kaustubha gem, the three [parts] at the end are thick.
From the Varāha mantra up to the end of the Siṃha mantra, the triad is known as subtle and gross; from the Astra mantra up to the Hṛdaya, the Lord becomes subtle and middling.
The subtle form, however, extends up to Lakṣmī within the power of Māyā;
that which is the root-mantra of the form, including its root, consists of seventeen syllables in its entirety. || 22 ||
Know this seventh [state] to be grosser than the others, bestowing all perfections; everything from Aniruddha up to Satya is that supreme-middling state.
Know that the ninth mantra-word, which is higher than the highest, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is the seven-syllable *piṇḍa*, the leader of the entire collection of mantras. (24)
And indeed, for all of them, there exists a progressive succession in order, by means of capacity, vigor, and various kinds of knowledge. (25)
And regarding the severance of existence (*bhavaccheda*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), and the various supernatural attainments (*siddhi*),
[the procedure] conforms to the threefold nature of initiation— concise, intermediate, and extensive— within the assembly of mantras and the assembly of principles (*tattva*).
O twice-born one, [I shall now describe] the determination of its threefold state, proceeding in order from the subtle element of smell up to the principle of Pradhāna.
The assembly of mantras, assuming a certain contracted form as the supreme [principle], exists in nine ways—gross, subtle, and so forth—in the midst of the activity of expansion. (27)
O Sage, through the application of sequential order, that one essence of mantra, though divided into many forms, exists in twenty-five ways. (28)
(p. 157) [An exposition on the twenty-fivefold state of each of the three divisions—namely, the objective, the divine, and the personal]:
According to the systematic arrangement of the personal (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaivata*), and the objective (*adhibhūta*).
But he remains from the principle of Īśvara down to the principle named Earth.

Then there are the Lord (Īśvara), primordial matter (pradhāna), intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti), mind (manas), the five sense organs beginning with hearing, and likewise the five organs of action beginning with speech. (30)
The five beginning with sound, and the other five elements beginning with space—this is the group of objective entities (adhibhūta); now hear the group of presiding deities (adhidaiva).
The seed-syllables beginning with 'ma' and ending with 'ka' are indeed declared, in their respective order,
to have the deities beginning with Īśvara as their presiding divinities within the [twenty-six] principles (tattvas).
And hear now, O Nārada, those mantras which are of the nature of the inner self (adhyātma) in their proper sequence:
the supreme mantra consists of seven syllables, for it is remembered as the divine inner self. (33)
Know that the pentad beginning with Truth (satya) is the supreme, immutable nature (prakṛti);
together with the Root-form (mūlamūrti), it is called the "internal" (adhyātma) aspect of the intellect (buddhi). || 34 ||
The mantra of Lakṣmī is in the ego; that known as Kīrti is in the mind;
the one called Jayā is in the sense of hearing, and the one called Māyā is in the sense of touch.
Know that the heart-eye is in the sense organ of sight; the head is traditionally taught to be at the tip of the tongue.
Know that the crest-lock is in the olfactory organ; armor is traditionally taught to be in the principle of speech.
The Netra-weapon mantra belongs to the principle (tattva) of the hands,
and the Siṃha-mantra is traditionally taught as supreme for the principle known as the feet and the one called the anus.
Know that the Kāpila [mantra] belongs to the organ of generation; in the case of sound, the Vārāha is said to be [the mantra];
while for touch, the mantra known as Kaustubha has the nature of the inner self (adhyātma). || 38 ||
Know, O Nārada, that for the element called form (rūpa) there is the lotus called Mālā, and for taste (rasa) it is Śaṅkha;
but for smell (gandha), it is the Cakra in the sky.

The mantra of the wind is remembered as the mace (gadā), that of fire is said to be the garuḍa; that of the water-element is called the noose (pāśa), and that of earth is designated as the goad (aṅkuśa).
The mantras have been declared in their full extent according to the true principles within the extensive sequence,
as well as in the concise, the intermediate, and the extensive initiation rites.
As long as this triad is not known, initiation does not arise;
thus is this Lord of the World, the Supreme Lord, whose essence is mantra. (42)
O Mahāmati, he indeed abides as the presiding authority and as the supreme principle within the twenty-five principles (tattvas) and the seed-syllables of those principles. (43)
O Brahmin, above stands the seven-syllabled state of Nārāyaṇī;
for that which was previously described as threefold is indeed that very same [state], and not otherwise.
[The determination of the presence of the Supreme Lord, who is of the nature of mantra, in that state, specifically within the three-syllabled mantra:
Having withdrawn all states of existence, He is established in a particular manner.
It is always united with the supreme subtle [reality] in the form of the gross, within the three syllables. || 45 ||
For the mantra will serve for the purpose of bestowing grace upon those who have cultivated their selves;
[this is the specific application of the three-syllabled mantra for the purification of the self, as it constitutes a limb of the initiation to be described].
Or, O Nārada, one should perform the initiation by reciting it three times.

When the purification is performed through the conjunction of Īśa and the subtle elements (tanmātra), one should perform it by uttering [the mantra] twice, due to the union of Īśa and Prakṛti. || 47 ||
Prakṛti is to be purified by means of two syllables, and likewise Īśvara by means of the *praṇava*.
[The method for purifying the principle of Īśvara (*īśvaratattva*) by means of the seven-syllable mantra, along with its rationale:
Alternatively, one should purify Īśvara by means of the seven-syllable mantra, or else by a single utterance. (48)
Since all mantras and the principles (tattvas) reside within that Piṇḍa in the Lord, thus the Viṣṇu-principle stands as all-pervasive. (49)
Having understood this correctly, one should then perform initiation with all the mantras along with the twice-born,
because all mantras are presided over by the Supreme Lord.
[The eligibility of disciples for initiation following an examination of their characteristics:

Having examined them, those who are disciplined, established in celibacy, pure, skillful, masters of their senses, steadfast, and devoted to the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire—these should be initiated. 51.
[He accepted] disciples endowed with the qualities of their respective castes and stages of life, humble, possessed of faith, devoted to the Lord, and distressed by the fire of worldly existence.
The master of mantras should initiate [the disciple] according to the rule, beginning with the initiation of mantra in its proper sequence;
listen as I describe how it exists through its many various divisions. (53)
[The threefold nature of the general initiation:
For all [initiates], the general initiation characterized by mantra consists solely of mantras;
likewise, it consists of the principles (tattvas), seed-syllables (bījas), mantras, meditation (dhyāna), and fire-oblation (havana). 54.
Furthermore, there is another threefold general [classification] for all those who have cultivated their selves:
it is concise, intermediate, and thirdly, very extensive. (55)
[The distinction between the fruits of the three types, beginning with the concise:
The concise [meditation] yields enjoyment for a short time and is restricted;
the middling [meditation] likewise bestows middling enjoyment and middling time. (56)
Through the power of burnt offerings and worship, it shall yield the fruit of infinite enjoyments for those who desire such enjoyments, extending extensively for imperishable time.
But in liberation, there is equality among the three types of initiation.
And that initiation which is called "special" (viśeṣa) is established as being fivefold. [The fivefold nature of the special initiation]. 58.
[The determination of the specific eligibility for each of the five types of special initiation:
The first is for those who know the rules (samaya), for the *balas*, for those whose minds are fixed on Viṣṇu, for devotees, and for virgins; the second is for the *putrakas*. 59.
The third is always for the practitioners established on the path to liberation;
O tiger among sages, the fourth bestows the state of union with Brahman.
For the teachers, however, it should be performed on the first lunar day, while for the women, it is on the fifth;

[this refers to the difference in the methods of joining the principles (tattva-saṃyojana) respectively within the general initiations (sāmānyadīkṣā) that are divided into the categories of concise, intermediate, and extensive].
I shall now explain in due order their equality, which is the compendium of reality.
By the mere knowledge of which the initiation proceeds correctly,
along with the three masses of mantras through the application of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).

That which was previously mentioned should be applied to the triad conjoined with the seed-syllable, for the sake of purification in the subtle elements (tanmātra), in primordial matter (pradhāna), and in that which is called Īśvara. || 63 ||
The division of the three groups which was previously described as ninefold [extends] from Aṅkuśa up to the end of the seven syllables, and also within the five subtle elements (tanmātras).

In the same way, through that method of withdrawal, [the elements] proceed in sequence from the mere smell onwards into the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), the intellect (buddhi), primordial nature (prakṛti), and indeed the Lord (īśvara).

Whatever was taught in the extensive third [chapter] regarding the internal [self] and so forth, that very sequence is to be understood here through the application of emanation and reabsorption. (66)
This is the definition of initiation (dīkṣā) and yoga for the three general types.
[Now, regarding the distinction between the five types of specific initiation, follows the distinction in the methods of uniting with the principles (tattva-saṃyojana) by means of mantras for each.]
Now, O Nārada, understand the specific nature of the group of five.
The three-syllable [mantra], distinguished by its divisions of words and endowed with the form-mantras, should be applied in sequence within the concise web of reality. (68)
One should place "hrīṃ svāhā" once for each of the five subtle elements (tanmātras). The second word, which is "viśvātmane," should be placed upon the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
One should apply the third [syllable] to Nārāyaṇa while recollecting him in the intellect;
then, one should offer "namaḥ" to the principle of Pradhāna and the three-syllabled [mantra] to Īśvara.
This first [mantra] of the fivefold special [set] has been proclaimed;
now hear the second, O best of Brahmins, which indeed bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). (71)
One should purify the elements beginning with the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) by means of the heart and the other centers in their proper sequence;
one should purify the ego (ahaṅkāra) by means of the eyes, and the intellect (buddhi) by means of the individual soul (jīva).
One should perform the union of Pradhāna with the heart-mantra of the Goddess in the middle, and the union of Īśvara with the Praṇava at that very place.
O Nārada, the initiation of the *putrakas* is prescribed by this rule;
now I shall describe in due order the initiation of the *sādhakas* for the purification of the principles (*tattva*).

Having purified the subtle element of smell with the three mantras of the mouth, [he purifies] that which is called taste with the six limbs, and the subtle element of form with the powers (śaktis). || 75 ||
One should purify that which is designated as touch by means of the entire root mantra;
having purified the subtle element of sound by means of Aniruddha, O Nārada.
One should worship the ego with Pradyumna, the intellect with Saṅkarṣaṇa,
primordial matter (pradhāna) with Vāsudeva, and then the Lord (Īśvara) with Satya.
In this manner, one should purify the reality (tattva) for the sake of the practitioner and the true Vaiṣṇava;
now hear the mantras of the guru for the purpose of initiation and the purification of reality. 78.
One should collect the subtle element of smell with the ten mantras of the weapons;
the subtle element called taste with those beginning with Lokeśa; and the subtle element called form with those beginning with Kaustubha. (79)

One should purify that which is designated as touch by means of the three faces beginning with the heart; that which is designated as sound by means of Lakṣmī and the others; and one should purify the ego and the intellect by means of the root mantra.
Then, having purified the Pradhāna with the five [mantras] beginning with Satya,
one should thereafter purify Īśvara with the seven-syllable mantra.
This sequence has indeed been proclaimed by the teachers for initiation; now hear from me the sequence of initiation for women, intended for the attainment of enjoyment. 82.
One should join the Puruṣa to the first principle, known as smell; then to the second, known as the subtle element of taste, and likewise to Sattva. (83)
Acyuta is in the third, and Vāsudeva in the fourth;
this tetrad at the beginning exists in its complete form.
And for the purification of those four subtle elements (tanmātras), the mantras should be applied;
furthermore, Aniruddha is to be joined in the fifth [element], and the Lord (Prabhu) again in the sixth.
Pradyumna is the large-eyed one, followed by Saṅkarṣaṇa;
the Niṣkala is to be joined as the seventh, and likewise the goddesses are to be joined as the eighth.
In the ninth, however, one should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world who possesses the three deities, by means of the three-syllabled mantra. || 87 ||
Having first understood the collection of mantras as abiding within the aggregate of reality (tattva),
the Guru should then commence the initiation on an auspicious day.

[The lunar days recommended for initiation: "O Brahmin, although I have previously mentioned the lunar days for worship, nevertheless, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is the most excellent for both initiation and the worship of Hari. (89)
Having gathered all the sacrificial implements on the tenth day,
[and having entered the sacrificial hall preceded by the observances of bathing and so forth],
he should bathe as before, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), remember Hari.
Holding flowers and water for the *arghya* offering in his hands, he should enter the sacrificial hall; [therein,
white mustard seeds consecrated with the *Nṛsiṃha-mantra* and other mantras are to be scattered all around the sacrificial chamber].
And having consecrated it with the Nṛsiṃha mantra, the Astra mantra, and the discus; || 91 ||
Thereafter, one should scatter white mustard seeds above, below, and in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
[with one's own mantra, the mace is established], having a body in the shape of a rampart and surrounded by various flames. 92.
One should place the mace, which is the embodiment of Śakti, there with its own mantra.
[The sprinkling of all materials is performed with the five products of the cow consecrated by the mantras beginning with Satya and with the three-syllable mantra.]
And one should prepare it in a new vessel with mixed water. || 93 ||
Then, one should consecrate the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the pentad beginning with *satya*;
having sprinkled everything with that very [liquid] using the three-syllabled root mantra.
p. 162) Meditating indeed upon that very [deity], with a pure silken cloth;
[this is the ritual for the jar.
Then, having taken one that is firm, bright, uniform, and without blemishes... (95)
A beautiful water-pot made of clay, or else of gold or silver, joined with gems, gold, excellent fragrances, fruits, and all medicinal herbs. (96)
Abounding in branches of auspicious trees, with its neck adorned by silk garlands, filled with filtered water, and accompanied by streams of water, it is auspicious. (97)
Smeared with sandalwood paste and the like, and sprinkled all around with water for respectful offering (arghya),
O Brahmin, one should worship the mantra together with its limbs and its retinue upon the seat of the mantra (mantrapīṭha) according to the prescribed rule. (98)
One should worship the mantra according to the previously stated procedure and in accordance with the rules; [the consecration of the *vardhanī*:
then, one should consecrate the *vardhanī* with the *sāstra* and the *cakra* mantra. (99)
There, one should worship the weapon (astra) situated upon the wheel as being of the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
[the procedure for rotating the jar is preceded by sprinkling the wall with a stream of water from the vardhanī vessel].
With that unbroken stream, she drenched the entire group of walls.
O twice-born one, in this manner, following the clockwise sequence starting from the northeast corner,
the water-pot should be carried behind [the image], either simultaneously or separately for an equal duration of time.
[Now, the procedure for installing the rotated jar:
The jar, together with the *vardhanī* vessel, should be placed upon rice and other grains;
then, facing the northeast direction, one should worship it again with flowers and other offerings. (102)
[The worship of the installed jar:
Having consecrated a pair of unwashed garments with the Astra-mantra, having perfumed them with incense and other substances, and having wrapped both [the jar and the image] in them; || 103 ||

Having performed worship with flowers and other offerings upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should then worship Hari in the sacrificial mound according to the ritual procedure for the sacrifice of Hari.
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship in the center of the fire.
p. 163) Having gratified [the deities] according to the previous rite, one should then prepare the *caru* (sacrificial porridge).
[Now, the method for preparing the *caru*:
Having first washed it with the *astra-mantra*, one should smear it inside with fragrant substances. 105.
O Nārada, having filled the sacrificial vessel with milk while reciting the heart-mantra,
and having observed that the milk has boiled, one should then add the rice grains.
One should move [the fire] with the four power-mantras (śaktimantra) by means of the lion-form;
one should lift the perfected [fire] out of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the mantra belonging to Kapila.
Then, having washed and smeared [the vessel], one should cover it with the root mantra of the form of the breast (kroḍamūrti) [of the deity];
[this is the procedure for the distribution of the prepared sacrificial food (caru) into four parts once it has been consecrated].
Having divided that into four parts. || 108 ||
Having first offered one portion to the deity propitiated on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
and having prepared the second portion saturated with honey and clarified butter, [one should place it] in the water-pot (kalaśa).
Taking one-third of that [portion], one should offer it into the fire;
one should present the *bali* offering to the retinue, from the site-lord (*sthaleśa*) up to the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
[The further worship of the deity at the three locations, such as the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), etc.
Having formed the mudrā and then recited the mantra, one should worship again with flowers and other offerings.
