Having summoned the disciples who are adorned, one should worship the deity situated in the three locations in due order. || 111 ||
[The sprinkling of the disciples:
O twice-born one, having placed the disciples—who have bathed well, who wear washed garments, and whose bodies have been purified—outside in the inner courtyard near the entrance. 112.
O Nārada, one should sprinkle [the deity] from the arghya vessel toward the east with the Astra-mantra.
[Now, the touching of all limbs:
One should perform the anointing of all limbs in sequence with the words [of the mantra] recited over the branch. 113.
[The casting of the consecrated arghya flower upon the head:
Having placed the arghya flower, consecrated with the Śiromantra, upon the head;
[the bringing about of the state of the disciples having bodies composed of mantra.]
One should perform the production of the fire according to the sequence as before. || 114 ||

p. 164) Then, according to the prescribed ritual for them, one should fashion a body consisting of mantra—[meaning that the teacher must perform a specific visualization within the disciple]—just as [he previously did] in himself, in the deity, in the fire, and in the water-pot. (115)

O Nārada, one should likewise meditate upon the disciple as being both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), and even beyond that, by means of the supreme [mantra] consisting solely of three syllables.
The manifest form (sakala) is declared to be the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace;
the unmanifest (niṣkala), however, is of the nature of Śakti, while the intermediate one is the leader of mantras. || 117 ||
But the Self (Ātman), which culminates in the supreme power (paraśakti), is established as the one who bows;
Prakṛti, presided over by the Sakala [deity], is manifest and possesses a distinct form. || 118 ||
The unmanifest consciousness of the Puruṣa is to be known as presided over by the Partless One (Niṣkala),
by means of the Lord in the form of mantra, whose nature consists of the manifestation of both the existent and the non-existent.
Everything— both the manifest and the unmanifest— is essentially consciousness when presided over by another.
[This is a statement regarding how the Guru alone is the liberator from saṃsāra for his own disciple, who contemplates their oneness in the manner described.]
In this way, [one should contemplate] the Lord, one's own self, and the disciple as being of the nature of Puruṣa. || 120 ||

O Brahmin, he who perceives the oneness of the Supreme at the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa), during initiation, and during the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), is the liberator from saṃsāra.
[The Petition in the Presence of the Lord in His Iconic Form]:
Then the Blessed One, whose form is the mantra, should be petitioned while standing upon the sacrificial ground:
"Those bound by the fetters of worldly objects—bodiless and helpless like birds and beasts—" 122.
"O Teacher of the World, by the power of your grace I shall liberate [them]; O Lord, having thus informed the Master and offered the sacrificial animals, [I shall do so]. (123)

O Supreme Lord, sons, disciples, and likewise servants—[the binding of the disciple’s eyes is performed with an unblemished cloth]; indeed, with a cloth that is unblemished, pure, and well-white. 124.

One should bind the eyes of the disciple with [a cloth] consecrated by the recitation of the Netra-mantra. Then, while the disciple’s eyes are thus bound, one should have him cast a handful of flowers onto the ground before Viṣṇu without reciting a mantra. (125)
[The Naming of the Disciple according to the Falling of the Handful of Flowers] O Brahmin, wherever that handful of flowers falls upon the lotus mentally visualized by the intellect,
one should divide that [lotus] into nine parts as before and mark it with the name of that [disciple]. (126)

Then, one should worship the water-pot (kalaśa) and the Vardhanī vessel along with the Astra-mantra, without reciting mantras, using [the names] endowed with the word "Viṣṇu" and joined with the designation "pati. 127.
[The Description of the Method for Preparing the Magical Thread] Taking a very white thread and treating it with lac-dye,
[the measurement of that thread therein is as follows:]
And [he should initiate] a disciple who has risen up in his presence, with both feet and head held high. || 128 ||
O best of the twice-born, having begun from the tips of both thumbs,
one should measure the length of the thread up to the end of the crest-lock.
Regarding that thread, one should perform any one of the methods such as being single-fold, double-fold, and so forth:
"One should indeed make it single-fold, or double-fold, or triple-fold;
or else multiplied by three times three, or even twenty-five-fold. (130)
[The contemplation of that thread as the unmanifest, which is the primordial nature of all transformations:

But the thread of the unmanifest sign (avyaktaliṅgasūtra) consists previously of the nature of ignorance and limited agency (avidyā-kalā); it is eternal, insentient, and pervasive, and upon it the entire universe is established. || 131 ||
Therein it becomes absorbed once more; from that, indeed, it proceeds forth.
One should contemplate everything situated therein as non-different, increasing the reality (tattva). 132.
O Brahmin, those which arise therein consist of the bonds of fetters; they are firm, variegated by passion, and inflamed by ignorance. (133)
Furthermore, they are divided by time, fixed, and likewise pervasive;
[the composition of that *sūtra* may be arranged at will according to any one of the modes— such as single, dual, triple, and so forth— in accordance with the sequence of the number of *tattvas*.]
One should string them together according to the sequence of the number of principles (tattvas), or according to the will of that twice-born one.
O Sage, one may compose it in a single way, or in two ways, or in three ways, or in nine ways; or else, one may arrange it in five groups of five, both concisely and in detail.
For the sake of uprooting the intermediate [impurities] of a disciple who seeks both worldly enjoyment and liberation,

there is the performance of a fire sacrifice (*homa*) upon the thread (*sūtra*)— which has been meditated upon as being the very body of the disciple— preceded by the meditation on its parts from the crest-lock (*śikhā*) down to the feet, according to the sequence of the emanation of the principles (*tattva*).
The prescription for what must be performed follows the very sequence of the emanation of reality, from the tip of the crest-lock down to the feet;
this pertains to one whose body will bear future fruits, once his ritual action has been completed. (136)
Having performed the visualization, one should offer oblations with mantras until the root cause is destroyed, so that they no longer obstruct one who is intent upon enjoyment and liberation. 137.
O best of sages, sometimes actions are forcibly impelled toward a living being who does not desire them, by means of the body, feet, and so forth. (138)
For he is the locus of karma only while possessing a material body governed by a Lord;
however, due to the absence of such a substratum, his karmas come to rest.
Just as the flames and other qualities of fire arise spontaneously without fuel, so it is for a living being who was formerly attached to enjoyments but later desires liberation at the end. (140)
One should perform this arrangement, but not for one who has already resorted to *nirvāṇa*.
[Having brought the thread near the *kuṇḍa*, within that body consisting of the thread, one should perform the previously mentioned single [rite] for the *tattvas* both in brief and in detail.]

The manner of recollection corresponds to the various ways of binding two, three, or more [verses] together: having placed the thread upon a leaf-cup made of auspicious leaves, or else upon a small bowl (mallaka). || 141 ||
The Guru, together with his disciple, should indeed proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit;
having then placed the Sautrāmaṇī mantras within the body of the disciple near the pit.
One should clearly visualize the assembly of principles (tattvasaṅgha) as distinct, according to the order of emanation;
or indeed, one may visualize the Lord alone, or him accompanied by Pradhāna.
Those two, the group consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and that which consists of many natures—namely, Īśvara, Prakṛti, Medhā, and the group beginning with Ahaṅkāra. (144)
Or, O best of sages, one should contemplate it in its ninefold expansion,
from Īśvara down to the earth, or according to the sequential order.
O Nārada, from the forehead down to the feet, according to the distinction of locations,
the reality pervades all and has dissolved into them all.
[The unity of the collection of realities is characterized by non-separation, like that of a lamp and its light:
Just as in a house there may be many lamps situated in different places, yet the light arising from them is not perceived as distinct [from the lamps]. (147)

O Sage, one should contemplate this collection of principles as being both distinct and non-distinct; though it is pervasive and thus essentially one, it should be understood as both separate and blended.
But having purified [the mind] through the intellect with the vision of knowledge as it truly is, one should apply [it];
in this very way, know that for him there is no distinction regarding the oneness of that [reality]. 149.
(167) For one established in initiation, that which is indeed oneness is simply the state of being blended;
[in that case], according to the view of binding them into a single unit, one should contemplate the Lord everywhere by means of a single utterance. (150)

[In the case of the two-fold method of recitation: One should meditate upon Īśvara by means of the practice of double pronunciation; in the Manifested state, however, one should meditate upon the Pradhāna-tattva, which is all-pervasive and assumes the form of the body. (151)
[In the case of the threefold binding:
By reciting [the mantra] three times, one should meditate on the all-pervading Lord from the crown of the head down to the heart;
from the heart down to the navel, one should contemplate the Pradhāna. || 152 ||
One should contemplate that group of elements from the navel down to the feet;
O tiger among sages, in the case of the ninefold knotting, listen to this very sequence in its ninefold manner. (153)
One should contemplate Īśvara at the head, Pradhāna within the chest,
Buddhi at the navel, and Ahaṅkāra situated at the root of the kanda.
From the two thighs arises the subtle element of sound, known as touch, born from the region of the joints;
from the two shanks arises the subtle element of form, and from the two ankles arises that which is designated as taste. (155)
One should meditate upon the seed-syllable associated with fragrance, conjoined with dhyāna, at the two feet; and upon the thread with nine knots within the body of the child.
When the time for initiation has arrived, the meditator should meditate upon the earth or up to the end of the elements;
then, on the forehead, he should visualize the Lord himself, whose form is consciousness and who faces in all directions. (157) [Now follows the fire-oblation of the principles.]
O Great-minded One, having visualized [the disciple] as complete with all sovereign powers by means of his own seed-syllable,
one should likewise perform the fire-oblation for the disciple immediately thereafter.
Having understood that the power of the unmanifest is indeed one hundred and eight times its own seed-syllable, or half of that, or a third, or a quarter, or even half of a quarter; || 159 ||

Having offered oblations and filled the ladle with the sacrificial offering, one should pour it over the child's head—filling it like a full vessel—and cast it into the pit, ending with the word "svāhā. || 160 ||
Then, one should likewise meditate upon that reality situated above the cluster of Sūtras;
thus, having briefly performed the oblation for the descent of Īśvara. (161)
One should meditate upon the Pradhāna in the middle of the two eyebrows with its own mantra;
indeed, one should offer it as an oblation in that very same manner, resembling a mass of vermilion.
One should contemplate the intellect (dhi) in the middle of the palate as having the luster of the color of the moon’s rays;
it resembles the juice of safflower and moves through the sky like a firefly. 163.

Then, at the root of the palate, one should contemplate the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); thereafter, between the palate and the ears, [one should meditate on] the Mūrti, which has the luster of a sapphire and resembles a kadamba flower.
And one should perform mental recitation after satiating [the deity] as before;
one should contemplate [the mantra] equally upon five points from the ear up to the heart-lotus. (165)

Then, having meditated upon the five [senses] beginning with hearing— blazing with throbbing stars— and having satiated them as before with their respective previously mentioned seed-syllables (bīja), || 166 ||
[One should meditate on] those situated in that place—[the rest of the verse is omitted]—and from the location of the *spanda* (*padma*) down to the navel, at a distance of five steps as before;
one should indeed remember the five [deities], Speech and the others, stationed there with their own respective seed-syllables as previously described. || 167 ||
And having uttered each one in sequence,
he should offer oblations and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) within five perfectly level footprints, extending from the navel to the top of the bladder.
Beginning with the subtle element of sound and ending with the subtle element of smell,
these [gross elements] are endowed with their respective qualities and possess the radiance of shining light.
Likewise, at the base of the thigh, in the middle, in the region of the intellect (?), and then below that;
[one should proceed] in sequence through the staff, the end of the vital points (?), and throughout the entire foot.
One should contemplate the five elements ending with air, fire, water, and earth;
then one should recollect the sphere of space, which is formless and the color of collyrium.
The [mantra] of Vāyu is blue and yellow; that of Tejas is honey-piṅgala (tawny); that of Āpa is like a pearl; and that of Pṛthivī is yellow like a gem.
The observer of the meditation should then utter the syllable *oṃ* as the seed-mantra, followed by *namaḥ*;
at that very time, for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*), the seed-mantra preceded by the *praṇava* [should be recited]. (173)
Then, with the respective name-mantras followed by *svāhā*, such is the procedure for the *saṃpāta* [offering].
The Guru, established in the state of the plane beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), should bestow grace. (174)
By a single utterance, one does not even abandon the ritual action of the disciple;
by a double utterance, one abides in the fourth state (turya); and by three, one reaches the state of deep sleep (suṣupti). (175)
Established in the waking state, one should offer oblations with all [the mantras] while situated on the nine dream-planes;
or [offer them] as one, as two, as three, as five, or as twenty-five.
Having offered oblations for the sake of the *saṃpāta* oblation and for the pacification of all dualities,
one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* at the end of the *homa*, accompanied by the continuous recitation of the seed-syllable (*bīja*).

O Great Sage, having recollected the mantra together with its root syllable ending in *vauṣaṭ*, these are the planes of enjoyment for that person who is designated as the individual soul (*jīva*). (178)
One should perform this coming and going without rest between the upper and lower [centers] until one is properly established by the Guru within the form of the mantra. 179.
Established therein and purified by the rays of the Lord’s power,
one who is stainless shall not again tread the path of the steps of impurity.
O Sage, having thus first performed the *saṃpāta* oblation and having prepared the *tattvasūtra* with another vessel, || 181 ||
Having wound it with a white thread and then gone to announce [the commencement],
one should perform the preparatory rites such as placing the materials— the colored powders, the water-pot, the scissors, and so forth—
either in front of the jar or in the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa), along with the water-pot. (182)
A pair of scissors filled with rice, a thread known as "the ray," and a probe made of gold, silver, or copper. (183)
O Nārada, having worshipped all the offerings, such as incense and lamps, with the root mantra, one should then touch them, gaze upon them, and cover them with a cloth.

[The Offering of the Bali] Then, accompanied by his disciples, the Guru should go outside the door; having driven away the spirits from afar with the Astra-mantra, he should cast the bali offering. 185.

[The drawing of the moat: One should draw a moat all around with a wooden peg consecrated by the recitation of a weapon-mantra, using water mixed with rice, sesame seeds, white mustard, and curd. (186)
Having sipped water and sat down, facing either east or north,
he should then administer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) to the disciples in due order, according to their caste and social standing. 187.
p. 170) One should then offer the five products of the cow for the purification of those who have eaten improperly.
[Consuming the Remnants of the Caru] Having sipped water, one should eat the remnants of the *caru* together with the disciples. || 188 ||
[Now, the procedure for chewing the tooth-stick and its disposal:
Having eaten [the meal], one should then chew the tooth-stick after consecrating it with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*).
[The variation in the size of the tooth-stick according to the difference in the qualified practitioners:]
For those beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, [the measurements] are nine, eight, seven, six, and five finger-breadths respectively. || 189 ||

One should give [the staff] to the Guru measuring twelve finger-breadths, down to [the size for] women and children; from this, it should be reduced by one [finger-breadth] at a time until reaching the limit for those who know the *samaya*.
Having eaten and disposed of those two, and having washed them with care,
he should then clearly rinse his mouth and observe the first morsel that has fallen.
[The thorough knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious:
O best of Brahmins, if it falls toward the west, the north, or facing the east, it is auspicious;
in the remaining directions, one should declare it inauspicious. (192)
These defects are considered to exist when the *pāta* is inauspicious, and to be free from defects when it is auspicious.
[Regarding the fire-oblation for the pacification of the inauspicious:
there, for the sake of pacifying the inauspicious, the Guru should perform the *homa* at dawn. (193)

O twice-born one, one should offer a hundred, a thousand, or eighty thousand oblations according to one's capacity, consisting of sesame seeds mixed with honey, clarified butter, and milk, along with fruits. (194)
With the name itself encased by the weapon-mantra (astra) and joined with "svāhā," one should utter the words "destroy the defect, destroy! at the end of the name.

[Now, the procedure for retiring to bed: Having sipped water and washed his hands and feet together with the child, he should circumambulate everything three times according to the sequence of the three locations. || 196 ||
Then the Guru should prepare a bed with the head pointing either east or south;
there, he should scatter darbha grass and white mustard seeds while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Remembering there the Blessed One, the unborn and all-pervading Nārāyaṇa,
she should observe a fast for one night and remain established in her religious observances.
One should recite the mantra a hundred times, or half, or a quarter, according to one's ability.
[The mantra of the Lord of Dreams:
The syllable *Oṃ* comes first; then *Prāṇa* (Ha), situated above *Lokeśa* (Va). (199)
Above that is the pervasive lunar [syllable], and immediately after that is the syllable *hrīṃ*.
Then one should give the six-syllable word: "to the Lord of Dreams. (200)
Then, for Viṣṇu, the Lord of Night, there is the three-syllabled sound;
when joined with "svāhā," it becomes the twenty-syllabled king of dreams-mantras.
[The specific procedure to be performed by the Guru after rising from bed at midnight:

Then, having risen from his bed at the time of midnight, the Guru, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), should perform the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa). || 202 ||
Having incensed the fire situated on the ground and raised it, one should contemplate it as unified;
then, in the case of the mantra-form residing in the jar, one should likewise construct the mandala as before.
And likewise, O Brahmin, one should beautify it and offer eight arrows outside in the various directions, consecrated with mantras and adorned with flowers and fruits. (204)
The five-colored thread, which rests upon the arrow and has been cut into three parts, should be covered with cloths so that no one else may see it. 205.
O Sage, because neither when already performed nor while being performed has it been honored by anyone desiring accomplishment, the falling of dust is to be avoided. 206.
[The Awakening of Disciples at Dawn]: At dawn, one should awaken the disciples and inquire about their dreams, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious.
[The Determination of the Distinctions between Auspicious and Inauspicious Dreams].
The preceptor, the gods, the twice-born, maidens, cows, elephants, horses, and lions; || 207 ||
A mirror, a conch, and kettledrums, as well as stringed instruments that resound;
likewise, the chewing of betel-leaf and the salutation of curd. (208)
Prepared food, raw meat, liquor, women, wine, and spirits;
an umbrella, a vehicle, white clothing, as well as other things such as white sandalwood—(209)
A garland is a necklace of pearls; the moon has risen full once more;
the sun stands in the sky with fierce rays; and the river has become the great ocean. (210)
A tree in full bloom, saffron, yellow pigment (rocanā), honey, parched grain (lāja), white mustard seeds, seed-grain, a new vessel, and milk-rice (pāyasa). (211)
Thus the preceptor was performing austerities, and the beautiful woman was singing;
others who were pleasing to the mind found praise in the world. (212)
Know that all dreams are auspicious, bestowing the fruits of accomplishment and liberation; those others which are contrary and cause distress to the mind are not so.
Those dreams which are censured, loathed by the world, and bringer of inauspiciousness—
O Sage, for the sake of averting the defects of such inauspicious dreams, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed for the tooth-stick after first inquiring about them.
Or else, for the sake of pacification, [the rite may be performed] with clarified butter alone while reciting the Siṃha-mantra.
[This is the prescription for the oblation intended as an expiation for deficiencies or excesses.
Then the Guru, together with his disciples, having bathed and entered [the hall] as before, || 215 ||
O Sage, for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) with all the mantras;
thereafter, one should worship the mandala according to the previously mentioned method and procedure.
Having completed everything at the conclusion of the fire offering (*homa*), one should cause the disciples to enter.
[Regarding the throwing of a handful of flowers from the hands of the disciples with their eyes blindfolded:
Having formed a handful of flowers in sequence and with their eyes blindfolded as before, [they should enter]. (217)
And he should cast [the vessel] rich in gold and endowed with gems and pearls;
afterwards, having opened their eyes, he should show everything to the disciples, who must perform prostrations to the Guru and other such rites. || 218 ||
Having prostrated before the feet of the Guru with devotion using the eight limbs of the body,
one should perform two circumambulations around the maṇḍala with the head bowed low.

Then the Guru, having approached the vicinity of the fire and sat down, should install the supreme circle of mantras within the abode of the fire. (220) [Now follows the specific injunction for the fire-oblation to be performed by the Guru; therein is the oblation for the satisfaction of the mantra.]

One should again offer oblations with mantras ending in *svāhā*, preceded by the prescribed ritual rules—namely the goddesses, the limbs (*aṅga*), and the true weapon (*satyāstra*)—using sesame seeds and clarified butter according to one's capacity. (221)

O best of sages, having performed the satiation of all the mantras according to the ten-part division for the purpose of the occasion of commencing the initiation— this is the fire-offering pertaining to the authority of the mantras. (222)
p. 173) For the purpose of the section on mantra-worship, one should perform another fire-oblation (homa).
One should offer oblations for each individual mantra in the sequence of five oblations each. || 223 ||
In this way, one gains the right to perform recitation, fire-sacrifice, study, and worship.
[Now, the fire-sacrifice for the purification of impurities:
For the sake of purifying impurities during initiation, one should indeed perform one hundred recitations of the root mantra.
One may offer eight additional oblations with ghee or sesame seeds as desired;
for the goddesses, twenty-five oblations are prescribed, and for the limbs, ten.
O Sage, for the lion and others, it was prescribed by means of eight [mantras] and seven;
for the Kaustubha and others, it was declared by means of six in the context of Satya and the rest.
For the seven-syllable mantra, having performed five oblations with ghee, one should indeed offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) while reciting the root mantra.
Then initiation becomes eternally mantric and characterized by its general nature;
through this, even without knowledge of one's own true nature, the Guru may cause [the disciple] to cross over.
O twice-born one, one should enclose [the name] with mantras, yet the name of the child [should be used];
this is the summary for the initiation by mantra alone. || 229 ||
[Now, the specific rules for what must be known regarding initiation:
The characteristics for the fire-oblation have been declared; now hear them as they relate to the reality (tattva).
At the time of initiation, the sequence of the principles (tattvapaddhati) must be understood by the Guru. (230)
However, so that it may become easy through the practice of what is to be known, and by the power of the purification of the mantra, the Guru indeed becomes pure. || 231 ||
And through the power of the purification of the Guru, the collection of mantras becomes stable;
this also occurs through the performance of fire-offerings (havana) and the restoration of the bond (sandhana) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
In the ritual of initiation (*dīkṣā*), whether it be extensive or medium, maintain this focus:

through the purification of the nine principles (*tattva*), all principles become pure by means of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—beginning with the subtle element of smell—purified in their proper sequence. (233)
These elements—earth and the others, with space as the fifth—are indeed pure;
within them, two groups consisting of the sense organs are to be known. (234)
First that which consists of the organs of action, and then that which consists of the organs of perception;
thus, through the purification of the subtle elements (tanmātras), the twenty principles are indeed purified.
By the purification of the ego (ahaṅkāra), the purification of the mind (manas) is said to occur here;
by the purification of the intellect (buddhi), however, the cognitive states (pratyaya), along with their errors (viparyaya), become purified. (236)
By means of the pure Pradhāna, the manifest and unmanifest are purified;
by means of the pure Īśvara, the conscious Puruṣa becomes pure. (237)
One should effect dissolution in that very nature of the Supreme Brahman, which is the supreme reality beyond purification, wherein one attains absolute oneness. 238.
Immediately following the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) by means of the sequence of the initiation of knowledge (jñāna-dīkṣā),
the best among those who know the Vedas [Śukra] previously understood this in brief.
[The Specific Regulation for Purifying the Principles for Disciples Seeking Liberation] One should purify the path of disciples seeking liberation in due order.
Listen attentively to me as I explain that process in detail. 240.
[The method of withdrawing the principles of the disciple into the fire, which has been meditated upon as having the nature of a form consisting of mantra:
Having meditated upon the fire as being like space, the collection of mantras that has indeed been deposited therein—
In the form of the all-pervading, [he perceives] the sequence of principles within that.
Having meditated upon each reality (tattva) in sequence, one should unite them in their entirety.
[The purification of the disciple’s body, characterized by inspection, sprinkling, and so forth:
Having seated the disciple in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) near oneself... 242.

Having gazed as before and having sprinkled [the object], one should touch it with the mantra-hand. [Now, the contemplation on the emanation of the principles (tattvas): Previously, indeed, from Īśvara down to Earth, one should contemplate the prior [emanation] in three ways. (243)
One should perform the creation established in its own nature and withdraw it in that same manner;
thereafter, one should clearly contemplate the complete creation within the body of the disciple in due order.
By means of which [initiation], when the time for initiation has arrived, one swiftly brings about the awakening of the insentient principles residing within the body of the disciple. (245)
[Then, the leading of the cord of the noose to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit after first obtaining permission:
Then, having gone to the mantra residing in the water-pot and having prayed to it with the mind, and having obtained permission, he takes up the cord of the noose contained within its fold. (246)
One should indeed go near the sacrificial pit, open it, and place [the vessel] there;
then, with the root mantra, one should satisfy [the deity] with a thousand or a hundred oblations. || 247 ||
O best of sages, at the conclusion of the initiation, the full [offering] (pūrṇāhuti) should be given with the root mantra to the Blessed One, the supreme cause of creation. (248)
However, for each individual ritual action among the single or multiple applications,

one should bring the disciple’s form into meditative absorption through samādhi, establishing a state of single-pointed concentration, [characterized by striking, which effects the purification of the disciple's body]. 249.
Now, having recited the root mantra many times, which has arisen from the recitation of the mantra, one should then offer flowers with that same root mantra.
One should strike his heart with [the mantra] ending in *huṃ* and *phaṭ*;
thus, one should quickly bring about awakening for him who resides within the center of the *piṇḍa*.
[The method of purifying the principles (tattvas):
First, within the earth-principle (kṣmātattva), there is the birth of consciousness and its manifestation as light;
then, the contemplation of its pervasive presence within each respective [principle] as it abides in itself. (252)

Furthermore, through the power of awakening by means of mantra, one should contemplate the state of sovereignty therein; and from that sovereignty, one should then contemplate the enjoyment thereof and its resulting satisfaction. (253)
One should effect the completion of the living being's enjoyments, their separation at the end of those enjoyments,
and then the extraction (uddhāra), proceeding sequentially from one principle (tattva) to the next.
In this manner, one should contemplate the various types of karma with respect to each principle (tattva). Having offered a hundred oblations for each principle, O Nārada, [one should proceed]. 255.
One should offer all principles (tattvas) into the fire by means of the seed-syllable conjoined with the mantra;
having uttered the internal mantra, one should utter the supreme two-syllable mantra "asya. (256)
At the end of that, one should utter the name of the disciple followed by the seed-syllable of the principle (tattva);
at the end of the seed-syllable, the name of the principle, and then the word "purify" (śodhaya). || 257 ||
Thereafter, one should indeed utter "svāhā," followed by the word "śamam" and the word "naya";
this mantra, joined with the salutation (namas), is for the rite of fire-offering (homa). || 258 ||
Having recollected the disciple as being of the nature of the earth-element, one should contemplate that jewel of reality;
and by means of the act of awakening consciousness, [the disciple] is placed before the tip of the sacrificial ladle.

Having meditated upon that very [reality] as the subtle self of the manifestation of emanation, and having severed the knot of the earth-element, one should fashion the tip of the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) from the thread. (260)
O Nārada, having joined [the breath] with the full [vowel] and by means of the goad (aṅkuśa) in the fire,
one should thus effect the withdrawal into the Supreme Cause of Mantras through this method of dissolution.
O best of Brahmins, one should bring the element known as earth (kṣmā) to rest within the blazing fire-pit;
by this same sequence, it is likewise applied to the water-element (aptattva).
Having withdrawn that [power] from him in the same manner, one should indeed bind his splendor with a noose,
just as Garuḍa did to Māruta with his mace.
Then, O Nārada, for the purpose of purifying the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra), one should cast the full vessel into the space [of the sky] by means of the discus, using the conch mantra.
One should indeed offer the full oblation with the Padma mantra for the purification of the subtle element of taste,
and one should cast [the oblation] with the Mālā mantra for the purpose of purifying the subtle element of form.
O best of Brahmins, one should join the principle known as touch with the one named Kaustubha;
for the principle of the subtle element of sound, one should perform the union with Vārāha.
One should apply the *upastha* [mantra] to those established in speech (*vāṅniṣṭha*), along with the five [limbs]:
Kāpila, Siṃha, Astra-netra, and Varman. (267)
O best of Brahmins, hear now the procedure for the senses that must always be performed:
with the *śikhā*, with the head (*śiras*), with the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), and then with *māyā*. (268)

By means of the *jayā* mantra, starting from the sense called hearing up to the end of the senses through the sequence of dissolution, one should constantly [perform] the rite of fulfillment, including that designated as the sense of smell. (269)

One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for the mind with the Kīrtimantra, for the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) with the mantra named Lakṣmī, and for the intellect (buddhi) with the complete root-mantra.
By means of the fivefold [discipline] beginning with truth, one should lead primordial nature (prakṛti) to dissolution;
and one always leads the person (puruṣa) to tranquility in the state of the Lord (īśvara). || 271 ||
The Guru, his mind serene, [performs] the final oblation with the seven-syllable mantra;
indeed, there is no reality higher than Īśvara within the entire collection of principles.
The person, having descended step by step from the principle of Īśvara,
is that by which the very nature of Īśvara indeed shines forth perpetually.
Therefore, by means of the sequence of initiation alone, one should extract [the soul] from there and cast it back again;
at that time, for the sake of the disciple's enjoyment, dissolution (laya) must be performed right there.

[The specific meditation to be performed by the Guru: Then, the one who possesses his own self, having been initiated and purified, known as the support of the Lord, should meditate upon that which is formless and beyond syllables—the Universal One who is the soul of all. (275)

Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end and whose form is imperishable within the imperishable, one should thereafter recite the root mantra in reverse order. (276) [This is the description of the method for the full oblation intended for the sake of enjoyment.]
It is the form agitated by the supreme nectar, the unfailing nectar itself,
which emits that which is incomparable, inconceivable, and beyond the reach of the senses.
O Nārada, resembling the moon and the sun, bearing the bond through emission, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered with the word "vauṣaṭ" at its end.
Having thus offered the *pūrṇāhuti* for the sake of enjoyment, one should immediately offer another *pūrṇāhuti*, characterized by its complete perfection, for the sake of liberation. (279)
But he who possesses all perfectly purified principles, situated above Īśvara,
is like Acyuta, having three deities, by means of the syllable-mantra.
Having meditated upon the disciple as being with parts (sakala) and likewise oneself as being without parts (niṣkala),
one should meditate upon the clarified butter (ājya), which is intent on the fulfillment [of the rite], as both with and without parts.
Likewise, having previously separated the disciple’s body from [its] karma through meditative cultivation (bhāvanā),
one should then join the two ladles (srucau) before the fire by means of unification.

Having established his own consciousness—abiding in the nature of the Teacher—within the disciple's head by means of his partless essential form, just as before, [the Guru] should do so gradually. (283)
Until one indeed reaches the state of one's own bliss, which is the bliss of perfect fullness;
thereafter, in that state of repose in one's own bliss, the incomparable abode of great bliss.

The divine, imperishable majesty of one's own power, which transcends the six waves and the [six] qualities, and is free from the sequence of mantra and mudrā, is to be realized through the grace of the Guru. (285)
Then, O twice-born one, having visualized the radiant form extending from consciousness to sound and ending with the self, and having recited the seven-syllable mantra, [one should proceed]. 286.
(p. 178) He should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with that [mantra] ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
[The Method for the Oblation of Attaining Union with Brahman:
Thereafter, the Guru should perform the oblation for the sake of abiding in union with Brahman. || 287 ||
With these ten great words beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*,
[one worships Him who is] inconceivable, indefinable, incomparable, and free from all affliction.
[The soul] becomes subtle, all-pervading, eternal, firm, immutable, and sovereign through ten oblations of the *daśā*; likewise, one should again perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Having likewise meditated upon the disciple, oneself, and the Supreme,
one should again cast the third great full oblation ending with *vauṣaṭ*, as before.
O Brahmin, just as one might contemplate milk and water as one in a single place,
so too should one contemplate the disciple, oneself, and the all-pervading, sovereign Lord Viṣṇu as one.
O best of sages, when it has become one and attained equanimity in the waveless state,
then the Vaiṣṇava initiation becomes the giver of liberation, the giver of emancipation, and the giver of the ultimate goal.

O Sage, by means of the yoga of the withdrawal of the principles (*tattvasaṃhāra*), the Guru— having ascended to the peak of the mountain of Brahman, which consists of unimpaired bliss and consciousness— [performs the conjunction of the principles, which were previously established through the process of emanation, into the body of the disciple], so that there is no further rebirth. (293)
One should cause [the disciple] to descend by way of emanation into the divine city composed of mantra;
this disciple has previously performed the fire-oblation (homa) consisting of Viṣṇu.
One should meditate on [the breath] as it emerges, drawn out by the wind of consciousness, slowly,
and as it returns step by step from the midst of the ocean of Vāsudeva.
Just as one directs the flow of water along the path of its discharge,
so too [one directs the breath] into the supreme mantra, the subtle, and the ultimate.

When the first part of the word is pure, which is the locus for the emergence of the principles (tattvas), then one should unite [the practitioner] with the Self as it proceeds from principle to principle. || 297 ||
Having purified the consciousness of the disciple, he should take [the essence] for the portion of Brahman;
for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees, he should unite it with the body of the disciple. || 298 ||
Having thus completed the initiation that bestows union with Viṣṇu,
one should then worship the Lord Viṣṇu, who is all-pervasive and situated within the fire, as the Mantra-form residing in the midst of the sacrificial flame. (299)
Having meditated upon the supreme form of the mantra, one should again recollect it with its formal attributes;
having worshipped it with water for the guest, flowers, and other offerings, the Guru should cause [the disciple] to hear the pledges (samayas). || 300 ||
[Now, the instruction on the pledges: One's own mantra should not be taught nor spoken in public;
one's own scripture should be kept secret and protected like one's own body. (301)
In whatever manner and wherever it may be, one should not utter [the name] alone;
however, with self-restraint, one should never utter the name of the Guru without devotion. (302)
Having first uttered the word "Viṣṇu" strung together with the syllable Om, and then the word "Pāda," he should bow his head with palms joined in reverence. || 303 ||
One should not command him out of delusion, nor should one step over his shadow;
furthermore, one must not tread upon his seat, bed, or vehicle.
Unwavering devotion toward the guru, the sacred fire, the mantras, and the scriptures;
the recitation of mantras at dawn, and the constant worship of the All-pervading Lord. (305)
At the time when the day is nearly spent, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity;
on the twelfth lunar day, whether of the bright or dark fortnight, one should perform the ritual of complete exhaustion.
Out of inability [to act otherwise], he remains at night preceded by gifts and worship;
there is supreme devotion toward the Vaiṣṇavas, and especially toward the teachers.
One should perform worship according to one's ability and protect those who have fallen into distress;
one must carefully guard one's mudrās and rosary, and not disclose one's mantra. || 308 ||
One should prostrate from afar at the feet of the guru and perform the salutation of his feet;
one must never sit upon a high seat in the presence of Hari.
O Nārada, one should not sit upon a seat marked with the signs of the conch, lotus, or discus;
nor should anything whatsoever be eaten without first offering it to Hari or likewise to the Guru.

One who is self-restrained should carry upon his head the water for ritual offering (arghya) that has been enjoyed by the mantra, as well as whatever has been consecrated by the mantra and obtained from the abode of Viṣṇu. || 311 ||
If, after casting it into water, it should indeed fall upon the ground,
one should perform a special worship every fortnight, month, or year.

On the twelfth day, one should perform an auspicious vigil right there together with the Vaiṣṇavas; likewise, a pilgrimage to the temple should be undertaken, and gifts should be given according to one's capacity.
One should perform recitation and listening, and carry out the study of the scriptures, remaining constantly vigilant, except for the two twelfth days (the Dvādaśīs). (314)

On the new moon and full moon days, on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, and during eclipses or the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign—except for these occasions—one should not enter one's home [if it has been previously abandoned]. 315.
In the presence of a guru, a guru’s brother, a community of ascetics, or Vaiṣṇavas;
or on a carriage road, a crossroads, or a path—even if an uninitiated person is nearby—[one should not recite]. (316)
Nevertheless, O Sage, one who desires welfare must neither perform nor listen to the exposition of the scriptures for a fool who is not a devotee of Viṣṇu and who lacks devotion. (317)
At the commencement of that [rite], there is worship of the Guru; in the middle, especially so;
and at the end, the special sacrifice, play, and the great festival.
Fruit, root, as well as flower, fragrance, food, and whatever is new—one should first offer each of these to the Guru and the mantra before using them oneself. || 319 ||
One should never employ one's own mantra for the sake of protecting others when it has already been established as common; nor should one practice it even in times of calamity.
O Nārada, for the sake of the world, one should perform the rites of the Garuḍa-mantra against malevolent spirits even in an assembly, out of supreme compassion for those who are helpless. (321)
One should meditate upon Lord Viṣṇu, who resides between the sun and the moon, situated within the fire of the cow and the aśvattha tree, and who dwells within the bodies of the guru and the brahmin.
Viṣṇu is to be known as the mother and the father; Viṣṇu is to be known as the beloved guest;
Viṣṇu is to be known as one who takes refuge in Viṣṇu; and the self (ātman) is to be known as being like Viṣṇu.
Wherever the censure of the teacher due to his envy is heard, one should not dwell there; one should depart and remember Hari.
O Nārada, one should never dwell nor ever speak with those who have reviled their guru or the Lord’s scripture. (325)
One should not harm the wives of others through action, mind, or speech,
especially when performing circumambulation, setting out on a journey, or making a gift.
At dawn and while traveling, one should repeatedly recollect one's own mantra;
whether in a dream or before one's very eyes, it may manifest as a wonder that bestows great joy.
Even if it should arise spontaneously, it must not be told except to one's guru;
know, O twice-born one, that this is the common stream of commitments (samaya). 328.
And among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—namely those who are Samayins, Putrakas, Sādhakas, and Gurus—it is from among these that [the teacher] bestows happiness. (329)
O Nārada, one should likewise give to women and children those that are non-contradictory and non-afflictive;
specifically, one should give to women those endowed with devotion to their husbands.
To a woman who is widowed, one should provide anointing and cleaning at the temple of Hari, as well as self-restraint and moderation in eating.
And from the observance of the commitments (samayas), accomplishment arises without delay; for one who knows the commitments, the mantra always becomes manifest.
"For one who knows the *samaya*, the accomplishments (*siddhi*), ending with liberation, shall be attained.
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, he offered the collection of *samayas* into the fire before him. (333)
[The instruction of the disciple in the mantra, heart-visualization, worship, and so forth, preceded by the bestowing of Viṣṇu’s hand:
Having applied a tilaka with ashes, the Guru should proceed to the front of the maṇḍala;
there, O Sage, he should duly worship the Lord of Mantras as before.
Then one should apply the Viṣṇu-hand upon the head, the back, and within the heart;
one should touch everything from the head down to the soles of the feet with the mudrā. || 335 ||
The preceptor should cause the disciple to recite the mantra preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the heart-sacrifice (*hṛdyāga*).
[This is the worship of the deity residing in the jar:
with the mantra and various offerings as they have been described according to the occasion. (336)
One should worship the deity residing in the jar with devotion, as if it were the Lord himself, through the power of the mantra.
[Now, the worship of the Guru:
Thereafter, one should worship the Guru by prostrating with the eight limbs. 337.
Placing his head at the soles of the feet and filled with tears of joy, he should say:
"O Lord, together with my sons, wife, and wealth, I am your servant. (338)
O twice-born one, filled with devotion, he should offer himself to the guru, or a village, or a heap of jewels, or gold, both wrought and unwrought. (339)
Together with herds of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and male and female servants—whatever object was appropriate for each, or whatever would please the Guru. (340)
Even if everything is given, there can be no freedom from debt toward the Guru,
who has been honored with pure devotion by means of the water used for washing his feet.
O best of Brahmins, by means of sincerity, one becomes free from debt to the Guru.
At the conclusion of the initiation, one should satisfy the Vaiṣṇavas with food and other offerings; thereafter, the preceptor should gratify the Pāñcarātrika Vaiṣṇavas. (342)
Indeed, according to one's ability, without deceit, by means of food, wealth, songs,
auspicious instrumental music, hymns, and discourses on the scriptures, [one should observe special rules for passing the night]. (343)
Then, having passed that night, for three nights, five, or seven [days],

the initiated one, endowed with faith, should perform worship through recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and the dismissal of the Blessed One residing in the three places, as well as the worship of Viṣvaksena. (344)
Having sequentially dismissed Hari, who resides in the three locations, according to the very procedure previously mentioned,
one should thereafter worship Viṣvaksena as before.
[The Description of the Method for the Avabhṛtha Soma-drinking: One should prepare two auspicious jars according to the previously mentioned rite;
filled with honey, clarified butter, and milk, one should sprinkle with one of them during the sacrifice.
Having consecrated it with the second root mantra situated within the moon and having established it for the purpose of drinking the soma from the very beginning; 347.
O best of the twice-born, the preceptor, having mounted his vehicle, takes that water-pot with which the mandala was sprinkled and holds it in the palm of his left hand.
O Sage, one should place the king of weapons on its back while reciting the mantra;
surrounded by disciples preceded by auspicious rites, he should proceed.
Having offered worship with drums and the sound of conchs into the water,
and having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).

And having brought that [vessel] completely filled with water, O Nārada, he performed the sprinkling with the flowers, the arghya-offering, and other materials used in the sacrifice that had been cast therein. (351)
And [he should place] one standing amidst fruits and branches, wearing a garland of flowers around his neck, covered with a white cloth, and consecrated by all mantras. (352)
Having entered the sacrificial hall, the Guru should then sit in the center,
facing either east or north, by means of the application of the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa).
And for those who have been initiated in due order, one should sprinkle their heads with a continuous stream;
for those desiring accomplishment, this is done with the unbroken streams of the Wheel, the Weapon, and the Lion for the sake of success. (354)
At the conclusion of the initiation, everywhere, the preceptor should diligently bestow the auspicious *avabhṛtha* bath upon the disciples according to this rite, out of compassion. (355)
O Sage, just as the preceptor prepares a water-pot for the bathing of the practitioners themselves during an initiation, so too should he always prepare one for the concluding bath (avabhṛtha).
Having bathed with an auspicious water-pot that embodies all sacred fords (tīrthas), he should again worship his preceptor along with his retinue.
Being pleased and having been worshipped, he would then grant the drinking of Soma in due order from vessels consecrated with the Astra-mantra and joined with the lunar disc.
Then, each vessel should be filled with nectar using the mudrā and the nectar-mantra, which has the nature of a mass of ambrosia.
[Now, the Gurusacrifice:
Then, on another day, O Sage, the disciple of true prowess should perform the gurusacrifice with great magnificence. (360)
Having drawn a square and elongated mandala with auspicious powders,
one should then place a cotton-filled seat upon a wooden plank.
Then, following that very sequence of supports, the disciple should worship with flowers and other offerings;
having anointed, rubbed with unguents, established, touched, and covered with beautiful things.
With garments, bracelets, and armlets, he should request today of the Blessed One Janārdana, who is the very form of the Guru: "Please sit down behind me."
Once he is seated, one should worship him with flowers and other offerings while reciting this mantra:
"To the one whose form is the sun, moon, and fire, who illuminates the dense forest of ignorance. (364)
Salutation to the Guru for the sake of quelling the heat of the fire of the threefold suffering;
having placed before him various and abundant sacred offerings as a food-oblation (naivedya). 365.
Fanning [the deity], he should stand before him, intent on whatever service is required;
then, after the deity has eaten, been satisfied, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should worship him and then massage his feet.
O Brahmin, having obtained the permission of the teacher who is seated on his bed, one should then eat oneself, with a peaceful mind and head bowed low. (367)

(184) [The Fruit of the Procedure for Initiation of Teacher and Disciple] O Brahmin, that teacher who performs initiation according to this prescribed procedure, and he for whom it is performed, both attain liberation. 368.
Keep all of this secret at all times from those who are not devotees;
however, reveal it especially to your devotees who possess faith.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Different Types of Disciples.
Nārada said:
[I shall describe] the true nature of the practitioner (sādhaka), the preceptor (ācārya), the initiate bound by pledges (samayin), and the spiritual son (putraka).
O Blessed One, I desire to know from you the supreme characteristic. || 1 ||
What should one who knows the samaya do, and what should a *putraka* perform?
How indeed does a *sādhaka* abide, and what does an *ācārya* do? (2)
The Blessed One said:
[The characteristics of one who abides by the samaya: He who possesses supreme devotion to the mantra, is a celibate student, and has conquered his senses;
He who is truthful in speech, clever, wise, modest, faithful, and possessed of intelligence.
Firm in his vows, pure, and intent upon the service of his guru,
he should always perform auspicious deeds with a serene mind and pleasant speech.
Even one who has obtained permission and possesses the means should worship with a sacrifice;
likewise, having gone elsewhere, he should observe the sacrifice wherever it may be performed.
One should always listen to the scripture of Viṣṇu, honoring and satisfying it,
and one should observe all the rules (samayas) preceded by the recollection of the mantra.
Endowed with the forms and mudrās of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
one should worship him on the twelfth day and other such times without the use of fire-offerings.
One should constantly engage in recitation and listening, as well as worship, even without [external] offerings;
having understood the meaning of the scriptures according to the rules, one should be endowed with right conduct and proper behavior.
Protecting his own household and conducting virtuous worldly affairs—
one who is thus endowed with these characteristics should again entreat the Guru.
O Nārada, he who knows the *samaya* for the purpose of daily worship—having recognized him correctly through the signs of the *samaya* taught by the Guru—[should initiate him]. (10)
The expectation for which he was detained must be fulfilled;
he should endure the heat and the conduct required for the sake of staying in the teacher’s house. (11)

[The Description of the Characteristics of the Son] Having properly completed the mandala with the wealth belonging to him, using powders, leaves, flowers, and so forth, according to his means or lack thereof. (12)
Then the Guru should gradually initiate the disciple (or son) who knows the samaya;
from that time forward, he should perform the worship of Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, even at the risk of one's life, one should diligently protect [the mantra] from omission;
for him, no fire-oblation is prescribed for the sake of dharma, except for the purpose of worship. 14.
He who is devoted to daily worship and adorned with the previously mentioned qualities attains that excellence through hearing and reflecting upon the scripture. (15)
Janārdana, residing within his heart, bestows upon him a yearning;
thereafter, he should pray to the Guru regarding the practice of the mantra.
[The Description of the Characteristics of the Practitioner:
Supreme desire to hear with devotion, followed by transmission from the Guru;
endowed with qualities that are progressively superior, uniform in nature, and composed in mind—(17).

Appointed, possessing unwavering faith, with an intellect refined by the meaning of the scriptures, that great man should indeed perform sacrifice again through the ritual and recite the mantra for the attainment of his desired goal.
Having been consecrated and authorized, and endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm,
he should go to a solitary, uninhabited place, the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
One should stay far away from kinsmen and especially from wicked people,
as well as from a sacred field, a temple, and a mountain that is free from the pairs of opposites.
A forest or a grove that is provided with water, strewn with fruit, delightful, and situated near a cave; or one that is well-known and frequented by perfected beings (siddhas). || 21 ||
Free from craving for his circle of kinsmen, having bid farewell to those dwelling in the city,
he should dwell either in his own home— which is filled with Vedic study, purity, and contentment— or elsewhere.
Endowed with purity of being, one should practice the desired mantra while seated comfortably on a seat that has been meditated upon as all-pervasive. (23)
With a serene face and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while remaining fixed on the target.
Thus, the mantra becomes "territorialized" (kṣetrīkṛta) for the practitioner, regardless of where he may be situated.

O Sage, even if one has been excluded from the tip of the tongue by the act of turning away, one should still mutter the mantra for the sake of accomplishing its propitiation, having offered the arghya water.
O Nārada, from that time forward, one should offer [the oblation] with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra),
subsisting thereafter on either sacrificial porridge (caru), fruit, alms-food, or milk.
He should eat vegetables, roots, and tubers in such a way that he subsists on rice from the inner kitchen, free from visible salt and accompanied by clarified butter. (27)
Joyful, satisfied, and with a serene mind, one should begin the recitation as prescribed by Kāla;
practicing this every day, O best of sages. (28)
At the end of the night, having remembered the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa from his bed,
he should rise and place his left foot on the ground with his right shoulder.
Recalling the Astra-mantra at every step, he should go far away from the dwelling of the twice-born;
having discharged his excrement there, he should wrap it with a cloth.

One should not look toward the quarters or the sky; then one should go to a body of water, perform purification as before, and thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules.
O Nārada, having indeed used the tooth-stick,
one should then bathe according to the general rite and mutter the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī with the Astra-mantra.
Having recited it once, three times, five times, or seven times according to one's capacity,
one should then go to one's own hermitage and worship the mantra with flowers.
O Sage, having worshipped [the deity] seated upon the seat of the scriptures or residing within one's own body, one should perform the recitation for two full watches (praharas).
Having bathed above that as before, specifically according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform everything previously mentioned up to the conclusion of the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then, after completing the worship and the fire sacrifice, he should begin the recitation (japa) until the end of the day;
furthermore, O best of the twice-born, he should bathe again.
Having performed the twilight prayers according to the rules, one should then worship the deity;
having dismissed [the deity], one should always take food at the rising of the stars.
Having eaten, one should sleep on a bed or on the ground that is soft and smooth;
then, O twice-born one, one should rise at midnight or when only half a watch remains of the night. (38)
Having sipped water (ācamana), recollected the deity, and quickly performed worship as before,
one should perform recitation (japa) according to one's ability and then worship the Lord.
O Brahmin, protected by this, one indeed shall not fall away, even from those who are invisible beings—such as the Siddhas—who desire the success of the mantra-practitioner. (40)
Having thus offered [the flower] upon the bed, one should indeed cast off all fatigue;
for he who is intent on the propitiation of the mantra according to this procedure, || 41 ||
It is said, O tiger among sages: "He should indeed be known as a practitioner (sādhaka), yet he has no business anywhere in matters of cursing or bestowing grace. (42)
One should not disclose the mantra, the mudrā, or the samayas to anyone;
even regarding one's own practice, one should conceal every action from everyone else. (43)
The mantra must always be kept secret for the sake of the accomplishment of the mantra;
it should be understood by the practitioner of mantra as being endowed with the meditation on its pervasive presence. (44)

Having propitiated the Guru and the God, and having diligently studied the scripture, one who knows the Tantra becomes wise through the mantra; and by these two alone, O best of the twice-born, he becomes a hero.
[Now, the characteristics of the teacher:
When the accomplishment of the mantra has indeed been understood by him through the guru, then that disciple is to be consecrated (or: should be consecrated) by the guru out of grace. 46.
Having performed the fourth sacrifice with that wealth as before,
and having worshipped [the deity], he should summon the practitioner who possesses the required characteristics.
The worship should indeed be performed according to the ritual procedure proclaimed for the *layayāga*,
including everything stated regarding both the external and internal rites, just as before.
In the fire, however, one should complete the initiation called *nirvāṇa* as before;
then, having consecrated [the disciple] according to the rule, one should announce one's own authority.
Having received it, he must maintain the status of a guru toward others,
and always perform worship, fire-offerings, as well as recitation and meditation.
Indeed, he may cut through the doubts of his devotees even without the scriptures;
likewise, he may bestow grace or a curse, as well as initiate them into mantras and perform their consecration.
One should not bestow favor upon any living being, nor upon a deceitful person, out of greed, nor out of passion, nor for one's own self-interest, nor even for the sake of reputation. (52)
One should always effect peace through expiations for one who is frightened, humble, devoted, or afflicted, as well as for one who has fallen from right conduct.
O Nārada, the distinction among all those who bear the marks [of Vaiṣṇavas], such as the Vaikhānasas and others, must indeed always be understood.
Being well-pleased, he should consecrate the devoted and worthy disciple in many ways—for the sake of liberation, for the sake of sovereignty, and for the pacification of suffering. (55)
One should delineate the sacrificial pits, mandalas, lotuses, and so forth, as well as the images and other such forms;
likewise, one should show them to the artisans for the benefit of the disciples.
O twice-born one, one should perform the perfect consecration of the omnipresent God of gods,
and likewise the installation of other deities with an impartial vision.
Among mortals who are not Vaiṣṇavas,
even when requested by those devotees out of fear, he never [revealed] that teaching of the Gurus elsewhere.
O Brahmin, when requested, one should bestow grace upon all according to the ritual procedure prescribed for one's own Kalpa, as well as perform the sacrifice and the Pavitraka rite.
Free from greed, one should act toward one's own disciples and the disciples of others;
and toward others who are ignorant of the scriptures, one should remain established in the state of a guru.
One should not indeed engage in speculative reasoning, whether through logic or even through scripture;
nor, O Nārada, should one excessively accumulate wealth or provisions.
He constantly practices renunciation and contemplates impermanent existence;
one endowed with such characteristics is called an Ācārya.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Different Types of Disciples," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Empowerment" (Abhiṣekākhyāna).
The Blessed One [spoke on] the qualification for empowerment:
Then one should consecrate the disciple, who is endowed with all auspicious marks,
perfectly tranquil, clear-minded, self-restrained, and a worshiper of the deity.
The consecration should always be performed for one who is devoted to the guru, has conquered the senses, and abides by the previously mentioned commitments. || 2 ||
(p. 189) [The eligibility of a Brāhmaṇa caste preceptor for the consecration of all:
The preceptor [is authorized] for all castes as well as for all stages of life.
Likewise, [this applies] specifically to the three, beginning with the temporary [vows]. || 3 ||
He should be consecrated with sovereignty and for the sake of authority;
by him, too, the constant favoring of all living beings must be performed.
Being constantly well-pleased, he should grant the consecration;
the Brāhmaṇa, knowing the five times (pañcakāla), should bestow grace upon all.
[The eligibility of Kṣatriyas and others to perform the consecration for the benefit of disciples from their own or lower castes in the absence of Brāhmaṇas and others:
O best of the twice-born, in the absence of such [Brāhmaṇas], one who is peaceful in soul and absorbed in the Blessed One [is eligible].
He is one whose self is cultivated, omniscient, learned in the scriptures, and devoted to virtuous conduct.
Endowed with the threefold accomplishment and consecrated in the office of an Ācārya,
he is a Kṣatriya capable of bestowing grace upon those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes.
If such a person should be a Vaiśya, even though he lacks the status of a Kṣatriya teacher,
he must indeed always provide assistance to both of them.
By a Śūdra of the same caste, who is likewise possessed of great intelligence,
the acts of favor and consecration should always be performed for a Śūdra.
[The attainment of awakening for an ignorant person of the highest caste by means of skillful methods:

By means of skillful methods—whether through fear or through greed—an ignorant man, even if he be the best of the twice-born, must be led onto the true path by means of both scripture and practical action. (10)
Until he attains for himself the auspicious characteristic of perfect enlightenment—
[for him who has attained enlightenment, the accomplishment of his duty through time, preceded by the undertaking of all activities, without the thought of seeking favor].
Having worshipped Acyuta with a sacrifice according to the previously mentioned procedure, || 11 ||
O best of the twice-born, having gratified him with fire according to the prescribed rite and having bathed him,
all the funeral rites for him should indeed be performed with the intention of showing favor.
One should worship Viṣṇu with mantras once he has been requested and seated;
this should be done when he has fulfilled his purpose, either sequentially or after some time.

Through conduct, as well as through policy, scripture, and compassion— [this being the necessity for one to perform for oneself both the grace and the consecration by oneself alone, due to the non-availability of a teacher even from among one's own kin].
Likewise, having himself worshipped the Teacher of the World according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, || 14 ||

Having offered oblations according to the procedure taught in the scriptures and having worshipped the Lord Acyuta, one should personally perform the consecrations of grace and empowerment within oneself. || 15 ||
O Brahmin, in the absence of a preceptor of one's own caste,
one should perform this alternative rite (anukalpa) with those of the twice-born classes and others for the sake of accomplishing the purification of the self.
[The prohibition against performing it oneself when a guru is present:

While a guru of superior caste is present, or even if he has merely been heard of, or even if he is in another land than one's own, this [rite] must not be performed by one seeking auspiciousness. (17)

If one should cause a reversal even in his own country wherever it may be, he shall suffer the loss of his sons in this world; therefore, one should act according to what is declared in the scriptures.
[The lower caste has no entitlement to the rites of initiation and so forth for the highest caste:
One born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes should not initiate [a candidate] through the reverse order (prātilomya).
A twice-born person who knows the three principles (tritatva) may initiate [a candidate] according to the natural order (anuloma). 19.
[The Method for the Ritual of the Empowerment of the Knower of the Samaya:
Without the manifestation of its pervasive power through the recitation of the root mantra, the empowerment of the knower of the samaya must be conferred by the Guru. (20)
[The Procedure for the Consecration of the Son] Merely by the utterance of the mantra, devoid of meditative visualization and conscious awareness,
one should then contemplate the ninefold ladder of reality established upon the seed-syllable. (21)
Having worshipped and meditated upon that entire [deity] presided over by the single [seed-syllable] with the root-mantra in its entirety, according to the sequence of the creative dharma; 22.
But, O best of sages, the consecration known as the *tattva* should then be bestowed upon the spiritual son (putraka), either mentally or with various auspicious flowers. (23)
[The Method for the Initiation of the Sādhaka] I shall also describe, in due order, the procedure for the initiation of the sādhaka:
having meditated upon the ladder of the principles (tattva) through the yoga of withdrawal and emanation. (24)
Then, having sequentially deposited the ninefold series of mantras previously mentioned, which is divided into nine types according to the three categories beginning with the subtle (*sūkṣma*).

Right there, having worshipped the twofold creation— the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala)— by means of yoga according to the prescribed rite, [he should worship] separately in each of the jars.
Having recollected again and again, as before, the spiritual son (putraka) as the practitioner,
one should bestow the auspicious and great consecration of the principles (tattva-abhiṣecana), which brings about accomplishment.

O twice-born one, having thus bestowed the consecration of the practitioner— up to the limit of the *tattva-mantra*— and then the consecration of the preceptor (*ācāryābhiṣecana*) upon him who has attained perfection in the mantra, he [becomes] a guru. (28)
Listen to the beneficial consecration that should be bestowed upon him alone,
extending from Īśvara down to Acala, together with the adhibhūta and adhidaivata.
One should first recollect the entire garland of principles (tattvamālā) according to the method of emanation; there, one should place the extensive series of mantras previously mentioned.

Having worshipped [the deities] according to the prescribed rule in three ways, starting from the seven syllables up to the goad (aṅkuśa), one should afterwards proceed by means of the sequence known as withdrawal (saṃhāra).
O best of the twice-born, one should recite [the mantra] until speech ceases;
the Guru, established in his true nature, is directly the Supreme, which is manifoldly differentiated.
Then the consecration should be bestowed both mentally and according to one's capacity;
having meditated upon the limit of the supreme reality, one should consecrate the preceptor.
[The distinction of the festival days to be observed for the four types of initiates, beginning with the Knower of the Samaya:
For the Knower of the Samaya, the consecration should always follow the sequence of a general commander;
for the Son, the consecration is performed according to the rite of a Great Minister. (34)
The consecration of the practitioner should be performed according to the rite for a crown prince, while the consecration of the Guru is prescribed according to the royal protocol. (35)
[The Ritual Procedure for the Master’s Initiation:
On the initiation altar, the Guru, having drawn a svastika mandala with white powder, should create an auspicious mandala in its center. (36)
The eternal lotus should be two cubits in size, or else made from the wood of a sacrificial tree;
it should be well-crafted, very smooth, and eight finger-breadths high in every respect.
Upon its back is a deer skin, and above that a white cloth;
and above that, a white canopy with flowers, providing a clear overhead cover.
There, one should place full vessels and full jars and so forth in the various directions; one should offer eight lamps there and scatter parched grain and other items all around.
Having established [the materials] near the pedestal, moving clockwise in sequence:
white sandalwood, the arghya offering, dūrvā grass, and nutmegs. (40)
A betel-roll with its accompaniments, a staff, variegated sandals, and the four auspicious mudrās of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. || 41 ||
Two garments, a sacred thread, a silken cloth, a purifying ring, a water-clock, a small vessel, a cord, an offering bowl, and a water-pot. || 42 ||
Red ochre, mouth-fresheners, white clay, and likewise cow-dung;
the skin of the black antelope or the ruru deer, and also a tooth-stick. (43)
Then, for the sake of all administrative authority, he prepared a site of that kind in the northeastern direction, including the Saṃhitā manuscript and other such items.
And it was adorned with canopies and other ornaments; there, the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśvara) was first to be worshipped in the water-pot (kalaśa), and thereafter in the center of the mandala.
Then, having first worshipped the God residing within oneself, one should thereafter worship him repeatedly within the fire and within the body of the disciple. (46)
Having brought divine jars, characterized by the previously mentioned marks,
filled with all kinds of jewels and adorned with plantain fruits.
Having arranged them outside the mandala, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and provided with the previously mentioned decorations.

In the case of the Master (ācārya), the number [of vases] corresponds to the number of his own principles; however, there is a difference in the number of vases for the Initiates (sādhaka) and the Spiritual Sons (putraka).
One should indeed cast one [portion] into the liquid for the sake of one who knows the ritual procedure (samaya). || 49 ||
Having first prepared such pitchers (kalashas), consecrated with [mantras] beginning with Satya and so forth, according to the previously mentioned rule and sequence; || 50 ||
Having recited the mantras, performed worship, and meditated upon them in due order,
one should then [worship] in all directions starting from the east, sequentially with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped the all-pervading Lord of Mantras according to the previously described procedure,
he should then initiate the disciple by means of his own specific sequence.
Then, with the *caru* offering, one should worship in the sequence beginning with the support (*ādhāra*), and likewise the auspicious throne for consecration situated in the center of the altar. (53)
Having placed the disciple, whose body is the mantra, upon that which has attained the status of a Mantra-pīṭha and is adorned with a scattering of parched grain (lāja), [the teacher should proceed].
Then, having gone to the head of the assembly, the Supreme Lord should be informed:
"I shall exercise authority over those who have submitted to your command. (55)
O Brahmin, having obtained permission from you, I, who am devoted and equal to my own self, shall enter into dissolution within you, who are situated in the eastern direction. (56)
Having worshipped that water-pot with its own mantra and its own mudrā,
[the mantra] having been recited one thousand and eight times correctly.

Having recited the mantra one hundred times, and having visualized the Lord as radiant with jewels and filled with nectar, [one should worship] ten times starting from the Guru and proceeding in sequence. (58)
Having placed a consecrated jar upon his head,
he should then perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with all the jars in due order.
While auspicious *ṛc*, *sāman*, and *yajus* verses were being recited, and auspicious gifts were being presented accompanied by stringed musical instruments. (60)
With the sounds of conchs accompanied by drums and joined with shouts of victory,
one should perform the consecration of the preceptor according to this rite.
Having presented all the ritual implements for the mantra to him, one should speak while both hands are placed [upon the disciple] as he stands bowing down. (62)
One should meditate upon Acyuta, who possesses the luster of a thousand rays, situated in a lotus with infinite petals in his right hand, [conceived] by means of the solar seed-syllable (sūryabīja).
