Combined with the twelve *kalās* and the non-cruel vowels beginning with *a*, one should then meditate upon the origin of the substance for the sake of knowing the purification of the substance. (64)
One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa in the center of that white lotus, which is rich with a thousand petals and sixteen filaments, by means of the seed-syllable of the Moon (saum).
While performing the rite for the production of substances, one should display his form as flowing divine nectar, consisting of the elements, the subtle constituents, and the mantras.
The entire path of consciousness, experienced by oneself in manifold ways, must indeed be described in its various forms according to the sequence of places and characteristics. 67.
The auspicious modes of consciousness that have been explained in the book—having indeed sequentially integrated [the disciple's] mind with those, the Guru [proceeds]. (68)
Thereafter, he should cause those who are situated above to hear the auspicious commitments (samayas) of the Ācārya— namely, the special commitments not shared by the rank of an ordinary Ācārya—
for the sake of the devotees who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra regarding the Supreme Lord. (69)
One should illuminate this scripture according to the sequence of the treatise and in accordance with the prescribed rules;
whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, one should always remember the Blessed One.

One should worship Viṣṇu, who resides in the center of a lotus, with substances produced through acts of giving and by means of mantras and meditative states, in a region beset by the danger of thieves.
One should never abandon external ritual action out of pride;
rather, one should observe the rules of the Cāturmāsya period with self-restraint.
One must never indeed use a parasol, sandals, clothing, or other such items that have been used by another, especially by one who has been initiated.

Indeed, there is never any fault in failing to provide for one's own guru, those who have been initiated, or the teachers, even in times of misfortune or when their needs have already been satisfied. (74)
There would be no fault in consuming [food] that has been used, or even that which was taken from what was given by oneself;
for they are experts in devotion to the Blessed One, their minds fixed on Him, and solely intent upon Him.
Indeed, they should always be honored through action, mind, and speech;
they must be maintained and revered, and always addressed with sweet words.
Without abandoning the duties of his caste and likewise the tradition of his own teacher,
he should learn the knowledge prescribed by his own scriptures that he has not yet learned.
On one side are all religious observances (*samaya*) and all rules (*niyama*) taken together; on the other side is the Blessed Viṣṇu and those men who are devoted to Him. (78)
O son, having realized that this body is decayed and devoid of essence,
one should entrust one's own authority to a worthy successor and engage in wandering for the sake of spiritual practice.
Carrying a staff and wearing saffron-colored robes, he should say, "Obeisance indeed to Nārāyaṇa," preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava), while casting aside all his belongings.

At the conclusion of the fields, bases, and sacred fords, one should unite the reality of the self and the body with Brahman, or [dissolve them] into fire, or into the sky-farers and other such realms.

"By means of the yoga of the renunciation of reality (tattvasaṃnyāsa), through which there may be peace and non-falling," having thus spoken, the Guru himself should mentally contemplate [the bestowal of Viṣṇu’s hand] upon the right hand. (82) [The Bestowal of Viṣṇu’s Hand]
Having worshipped the supreme Viṣṇu, who is the essence of mantra and both with and without parts, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should place [the vessel] upon his head.
[The Disciple’s Duty of Consuming the Water from the Guru’s Feet:
Then, having offered a seat, the disciple should place his head at the feet [of the guru];
then, having washed the lotus-feet of the guru with water. (84)
Having sprinkled himself with that [water], he should then offer it with his joined palms;
then, as before, he should worship with devotion by means of himself and also with wealth. (85)

By this rite, one should perform the consecration of the preceptor; by this very same procedure, one should likewise consecrate the practitioner. (86) [This is the extension of the consecration for the practitioner.]
Whatever begins with the ritual anointing and ends with the cleaning of the teeth,
all its requisites should be provided without [the usual] restrictive observances.

[The specific items to be given at the initiation of a *putraka*: And the treatise on the authority of worship (*pūjādhikāraśāstra*) is bestowed upon the *putraka*. [The specific items to be given at the initiation of a *samayajña*:]
One should give the book of the scripture only to one who knows the rules.
And at the conclusion of the consecration, regarding the command in the Yoga-darśana:
[The consecration is the means for achieving various fruits, beginning with spiritual welfare].
He who, desiring welfare, bathes according to this rite shall attain welfare. (89)
Whether it be a king seeking victory, or an unfortunate man seeking good fortune, or a woman desiring a son, or a maiden desiring a husband. (90)
Whoever desires long life should bathe for the duration of a year;
consequently, his untimely death shall be destroyed without delay. (91)
For as many years as he performs [this rite], he remains free from disease, liberated from wrinkles and grey hair, fortunate, and possessed of enduring youth. (92)
One attains all desires and, at the end of the body, the eternal goal.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Consecration," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*. 18.

Now begins the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Signs of Mantra-Siddhi": O Nārada, having been consecrated, authorized, and having performed the recitation (jāpa) with a tranquil mind, one should perform the propitiation of the mantra according to this rite.

Having fashioned an image endowed with excellent characteristics— either in a secluded place or in one's own home, created through the aforementioned meditation, whether depicted on a cloth or made of metal— 2.

Having installed that [image] according to the prescribed rite— whether it be a palm-tree [liṅga] complete in all its parts or even exceeding a palm in height— one should always worship the mantra therein.
O best of sages, for the sake of attaining all desired prosperities and for the sake of liberation,
one should always worship according to the prescribed rule while remaining steadfast in the observances for twelve years.
Having become the very form of the mantra through pleasing flowers, fragrances that increase good fortune and health, and various recitations and fire-offerings; || 5 ||
Wearing white garments, adorned with garlands, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents,
he has a yellow sacred thread and is decorated with bracelets and armlets.
With his face purified by betel and well-scented with mouth-perfumes, adorned with a variegated tilaka, and possessing perfectly clean hair; || 7 ||
He was perfumed with all kinds of charming garlands and fragrances;
his feet were smeared with saffron, and his two hands were likewise prepared.
Adorned with the four mudrās of the forms,
bearing the purificatory thread and subsisting on sacrificial food, he should worship the King of Mantras.
Due to the absence of even the means of accomplishment, he has his hair and beard plucked out;
he wears whatever clothing is available and is free from lice and other such vermin. || 10 ||
One who is well-disciplined and devoted to friends, having propitiated the mantra with devotion through worship,
recitation, and fire-offerings, then the king of mantras becomes accomplished.
By means of that perfected [mantra], one should indeed perform various rites—
those desired by oneself as well as those desired by the worlds.
Nārada:
By what signs, O Lord, is one recognized as a *susiddha*, a sovereign of mantras?
The Blessed One:

For the practitioner engaged in the accomplishment of mantras, obstacles arise for three years; this applies to the practitioner whose purpose remains unfulfilled and who is devoted to constant practice. (13)
O Nārada, for one who is intent on propitiating [the deity] and remains steadfast in his observances, many obstacles arise frequently during the first three years. (p. 197) 14.
If the practitioner does not experience agitation through either action or mind,
then for him— whose mind is unassailed by obstacles— there is the attainment of auspicious signs such as being served by many disciples during the fourth year and subsequent years.
From the third year onwards, auspiciousness arises for him. || 15 ||
He is served day and night by many disciples who are free from sloth,
and practitioners serve him with devotion as his attendants.
They offer their entire possessions to the high-souled practitioner.
From the seventh year onwards, kings and other rulers [become his servants]. (17)
They entreat with persistence out of arrogance and pride:
"O Lord, please grant your grace for the sake of my deliverance. (18)
They behold him blazing with splendor and majesty;
therefore, O tiger among sages, they are unable to speak harshly.

[The Vision of Various Marvels from the Tenth Year Onward] From the ninth year onwards, the knower of mantras personally beholds within his heart various marvels consisting of laughter and bliss. (20)
O Brahmin, he who quickly bestows constant joy both externally and through direct perception remains inert for a moment and remains delighted for a moment. (21)
For a moment he would hear the sound of drums from the sky,
and for a moment sweet music accompanied by various songs.
For a moment he smells fragrances produced from camphor and musk;
for a moment he sees himself flying up by means of his own self.
O twice-born one, for a moment he should gaze upon the sky filled with the rays of the moon and sun,
and for a moment he should listen to the sounds of cows, horses, and elephants.
O twice-born one, for a moment he might hear the great turbulence of the water in a mountain torrent;
for a moment he might see the surface of the earth filled with flashes of lightning.
For a moment he beholds the entire circle of the earth filled with water, and for a moment he hears the sounds of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (26)
O Sage, for a moment the practitioner of the mantra perceives fierce yogins, the makers of stars, standing in the sky, variegated and afflicted by fear. (27)
For a moment he may hear the sound of joyful shouting along with the roar of fire;
for a moment he may see the rising of clouds, and for a moment night while it is day.
And at night, he beholds the daylight along with the sun for a moment, being fully endowed with power and a splendor like that of the sun. (29)
He was like the sun and moon in his splendor, like the king of birds in his gait,
and endowed with a voice that was both high-pitched and deep, characteristic of a great soul.
By eating very little, emaciation occurs, yet by eating much, it does not; furthermore, there is a reduction in feces and urine, and a great victory over sleep ensues. (31)
Devoted to recitation and meditation, observing silence, he indeed experiences no exhaustion even for more than a fortnight or a month without food and drink.
By such signs as these, which cause wonder in one's own heart, when they manifest, it should be understood that the King of Mantras has become gracious to me.
[The Non-disclosure of Mantra-Attainment:
O best of Brahmins, a sign produced by the grace of a mantra must never be disclosed by one who desires success, except in the presence of a guru. (34)
He who, out of delusion or excessive eagerness, reveals the bliss born of mantra,
finds that the accomplishments (siddhis) which were already in the palm of his hand depart far away from him.
Sufferings and various kinds of sorrows manifest themselves;
therefore, O Nārada, by every possible effort, one should seek the signs of spiritual perfection (siddhi).
"Those who desire their own prosperity should guard these [secrets] with great effort.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Signs of Mantra-Perfection," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*. 19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Consecration.
Nārada said:
For the benefit of practitioners, you have described the image that has been spoken of.
Therefore, O Lord, I desire to know how that is performed.
O Lord, tell me how even that [mantra] is established through its ritual application,
by the complete worship of which one may obtain these liṅgas.
The Blessed One said: (p.
199) [Now, the procedure for the icon on cloth: O Nārada, listen now to the procedure for the icon on cloth.
It brings about all accomplishments, is delightful, free from defects, and is not overly extensive.
The cloth, such as for painting and so forth, should be two cubits long and four-cornered, or even just one cubit;
it should be made of cotton or linen, new, white, and unwashed.
[The consecration of the cloth and the painter]:

O twice-born one, having washed the painter who knows the art of painting many times with the Astra-mantra and having bathed him, one should then meditate upon him together with the cloth by means of the procedure for generating heat. || 5 ||
Having outlined the seat, there [is] an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
[this is the measurement for the household image].
Situated in the center of the pericarp, however, it should be twelve finger-breadths in height.
Having drawn the image with its auspicious marks, measuring twenty-three finger-breadths,
it should be endowed with a retinue such as Lakṣmī and others, and surrounded by the scriptures of Lokeśvara. (7)
Having gathered [the materials] for the purpose of sacrifice today,
the measurement of that [site], which is greater than the house and located elsewhere, is above the twice-born.
One should construct the maṇḍapa outside the house, in a place beginning with a temple.
[The absence of fault even when a painted image exceeds one cubit in size for domestic worship]:
"Even when a painted image exceeding one cubit is established in the home, there is no fault for practitioners, provided it is not made of wood, clay, or stone. (9)

[Now, the measurement of the limbs of the image: O Sage, having divided the measurement of the image into nine parts according to its height, one should further divide each of those parts into twelve.
That [unit] shall be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) of the image; by means of that, the limbs and members [of the body] should then be made visible by the preceptor to the artisan in brief.
From the chin to the end of the forehead, the face shall be twelve finger-breadths in length;
O Brahmin, the head shall be three finger-breadths elevated above the forehead.
It is twelve finger-breadths wide and three times that in circumference;
the two ears are two finger-breadths wide and twice that measurement in height.
Know that the cavity within the ear is equal in size to the tip of the little finger;
its lower and upper portions, measured from the ear-lobe, are each recorded as half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula).
Outside the ear-opening, there should be a hollow (avaṭa) one finger-breadth deep in the middle of the ear;
its width from the two lobes of the ear should be three fingers, or it may be according to one's desire.
The creeper-like brow is like a crescent moon; four finger-breadths in length, half a finger-breadth in width, thick in the middle and slender at the ends. (16)

The space between the eyebrows should be equal to one finger-breadth; the nose should be four finger-breadths long, and from two finger-breadths below that, its tip should be fashioned in the shape of a sesame flower.
Know that the space between the two eyes is two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula), and the region of the eyebrows is likewise;
the eye is two finger-breadths in length and one finger-breadth in width.
One should fashion the *tāraka* in the center with one-third [of the measurement], that light being measured by those same three parts;
and below the nose, one should fashion it at exactly one finger-breadth less by a quarter.
O tiger among sages, the *gojikā* is one part; below that is the lower [part] called *uttara*, which is recorded as being one *aṅgula* in measurement. (20)
O Brahmin, the chin is proclaimed to be two finger-breadths in height;
know that its width is two finger-breadths, and the corners of the mouth are four finger-breadths.
The two earlobes should be measured at a slight distance from each other;
above the cheeks, they should be like the moon, and four finger-breadths apart in their middle.
One should make the cheeks of the face even, well-filled, and beautiful;
O Nārada, the height of the ears should be three finger-breadths, and that same measurement should be their width.
The circumference of the girdle is proclaimed to be three times eight finger-breadths;
it should extend from below the neck down to the chest, O twice-born one, reaching as far as the point of the pulsation.
The breast-region is always prescribed to be twelve finger-breadths in height;
it should be double that in width, measuring two finger-breadths.
One should fashion the two nipples with an eighth part of one's own finger-breadth;
and the distance between the two breasts should be twelve finger-breadths.
O Mahāmati, the two shoulders are recorded as being eight finger-breadths in width;
one should make the base of the shoulder elevated by six finger-breadths. (26)
In height, it reaches up to the navel; from the pulsation, it is indeed twelve finger-breadths [in circumference].
The perimeter of the region of the navel consists of five parts of four [units] each.
O Sage, one should make the navel cavity one finger-breadth deep, gradually increasing to two finger-breadths, turning clockwise between the navel and the penis.
Its height should be made perfectly level at twelve finger-breadths;
from the navel downwards, its belly should be made four finger-breadths wide.
O Sage, the remaining portion of the waist area should be the abdomen;
it should measure fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width, and its circumference should be three times that, which is beneficial.
The measurement of the waist is prescribed as being three times six finger-breadths in width;
the circumference of the waist is traditionally recorded as fifty-four finger-breadths.
The circumference of the base is traditionally said to be thirty-six finger-breadths;
O Brahmin, one should fashion the generative organ with a height of six finger-breadths.
The scrotum should be two finger-breadths wide and four finger-breadths long;
O twice-born one, the thigh-staffs should be fully formed with three or four testicles.
They should be made equal in height at twenty-four finger-breadths;
their bases and roots should gradually taper, being joined together like the trunk of an elephant. (34)
Alternatively, one may fashion the base of the thigh with a width of nine finger-breadths;
at the middle of the thigh, however, the circumference should be thirty-six finger-breadths.
O tiger among sages, at the end of the thighs, it is wrapped twenty-one times;
around the kneecaps, O tiger among sages, it is three finger-breadths wide.
Now hear from me concerning its width and height at the knees:
the elevation of the shank here is said to be twenty-four finger-breadths. (37)
The base of the shank is proclaimed to be six finger-breadths in width;
the circumference of those two at the middle of the shank is as follows. || 38 ||
O Sage, at the end of the shanks, the width should be known as five finger-breadths;
by tripling that very measure, the circumference of it is obtained. (39)
O Nārada, the height of the foot should be three finger-breadths below the ankle;
O best of the twice-born, it extends from the back of the heel as far as the tips of the toes. (40)
The foot should be fourteen finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in width, gradually raised like the back of a tortoise.
The thumb [of the handle] shall be four finger-breadths in length, and from that, the [other] finger [of the handle] two finger-breadths;
its circumference shall be three times [the width], and its length shall be more than one-quarter of that [circumference].
The little toe should be made to touch the region of the foot, with the other toes positioned near it;
the big toe should be equal [in length] to that, while the ring finger [of the hand] should be three-quarters of its size.
The ring finger is one-quarter shorter than the little finger;
know, O Nārada, that the measurement of the joints for all [the fingers] is one-third [of their length].
The auspicious nails should be made with half-joints, resembling the crescent moon;
the measurement from the back to the shoulder is recorded as thirty-six finger-breadths.
Or, the cow-mouth (gomukha) should gradually slope downward for twenty finger-breadths;
it should be wide from the middle region and rise gradually toward the backbone.
O Sage, it is remembered that the *kakṣā* (the space between the arms) is five finger-breadths wide, being very smooth, both undivided and divided, and joined like two fish closing their eyes.
The buttocks should be made perfectly round, sixteen finger-breadths in width,
well-proportioned, plump, auspicious, and resembling the frontal globes of an elephant.
Below the top of the shoulder, O best of the twice-born, the upper arm (bāhu) should be twelve finger-breadths;
know that the forearm (upabāhu) is eighteen finger-breadths. 49.
In that context, the region of the wrist (maṇibandha) is said to be three finger-breadths (tryaṅgula), extending from the base of the wrist up to the tip of the middle finger. || 50 ||
The shoulder-piece (skandha) should be twelve finger-breadths in measure and perfectly round;
it is recorded as being four finger-breadths wide and three times the thickness of the rim (paridhi).
O Sage, the forearm is said to be five finger-breadths from the base; its circumference is three times that, and one should gradually decrease it [toward the wrist].
O Sage, it should be shaped like a cow’s tail and measure three finger-breadths;
the region of the wrist, moreover, should be measured by its width and circumference.
The measurement of the hand is nine finger-breadths; hear now [the rest]:
know that from the jewel to the base of the fingers it is always seven finger-breadths.
The horizontal width is said to be five finger-breadths in measure;
one should make the palm deep and adorned with auspicious lines. (55)
In that regard, O Brahmin, know the middle finger to be five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula) long;
the two fingers on its sides are indeed half a finger-breadth shorter.
One should always make the little finger five parts less than that; the thumb is proclaimed to be three and a half digits and two joints.
The remaining fingers are known to have three joints, and the nails are said to be half a joint in length;
the fingers should be made like a cow's tail according to the measurement of the finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The smallest [size] should be one-quarter less; the fingers [should be] one finger-breadth, and so on by quarters of a finger-breadth.
Know that the circumference is three times the width according to its own measurement. (59)
All [the fingers] have nails like the shell of a tortoise, and their tips are shaped like a half-moon;
the measurement from the base of the [fingers], which has the form of a linga, is not fixed.
The measurement and beauty of the curls, teeth, and hair were fashioned with artistry;
a mass of curling locks adorned the forehead above. (61)
One should fashion the forehead so as to cover the upper fingers and endowed with three folds;
indeed, all the limbs should be made charming and possessed of auspicious marks.
O Brahmin, whether the proportions are equal or unequal, attached or unattached, one should especially fashion an image with auspicious characteristics according to this measurement.
O best of the twice-born, its height from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head is one hundred and eight finger-breadths measured by one's own fingers.
Adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, girdles, and a crown,
his stout central body was graced by symmetrical folds.
One should determine all else that has arisen from meditation—whether mentioned or not—as previously described.
[Now, the procedure for the materials of the image: One should fashion it according to this measurement, using either gold or silver. (66)
O Sage, for the purpose of propitiating the image, it may be made of brass, or of stone, clay, or wood, according to what is available.

[The prohibition of stone and other materials for a house for those desiring success: O Great-minded One, if one should construct a house made of stone, earth, or wood when better materials are available, his successes will manifest only after a long time.
(204) Therefore, liberation shall indeed be attained without obstacle by those who desire success;
for that reason, an image made of stone, wood, or clay should not be kept in the home.
[Now, the measurement of the pedestal:
Listen to how one should fashion the pedestal for the deity according to the measurement of the image and so forth.
[In this regard, there are two types of pedestals.]
Know that it is square, as well as circular and oblong.
[The Characteristics of the Square Pedestal] The pedestal should be equal in height to the image and its width should extend all around it;
one should make its height half of that—this is the general characteristic. (71)
O Great Sage, the characteristics of the square pedestal have been described;
now, attend to the measurement of the rectangular pedestal. || 72 ||
It is broad by half the measure of the bimba and elevated by that same measure;
it is equal in length to the deity and is rectangular in shape.
One should always provide the pedestal measurement for deities residing in lofty abodes;
however, for movable images and those installed in houses, the pedestal measurement is otherwise. (74)
One should fashion it equal in height to the [upper] trunk, or endowed with the measurement of the breasts;
[it should extend] from the feet up to the knees in both width and height. 75.
Alternatively, one may make the width and the height equal;
or, O best of Brahmins, the width should be half of the stated height. (76)
The height of the pedestal for a movable image is always prescribed as being four parts less than that [of the fixed image], or three parts, or even half. (77)
And because of the absence of the substance of the elements, it is indeed thus for those that are stable.
[Now, the definition of the upapīṭha:
Having made that, one should then construct the upapīṭha below it according to the proper measure. (78)

Then, the water-channel (praṇāla) should be at the center of the pedestal (pīṭha), measuring one-third [of its width]; it should be as long as that measurement, and furthermore, its front part should be according to its own [original] measure.
It should be three parts wide; from its center, one-third of that width should be excavated from the front toward the base, and there one should fashion the face of a makara.
Alternatively, it may have the face of a boar or a tortoise, or it may be entirely smooth;
one should divide the height into nine parts, and the mandala should be square.
One should perform the contact with the ground using two parts, known as the knees and feet;
above that, however, it should be circular in shape and raised by two parts.
Then, above the base (vṛtta), one should fashion a portion rising two parts in height;
that [portion] one should cause to enter completely around by one part. || 83 ||
O Brahmin, one should fashion the girdle (mekhalā) like a water-pot (kumbha), having it emerge with half a part and extending upward from that with one part, using half a part for its width.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be square with an upper portion measuring one and a half [units];
that is to be known as the water-reservoir (jalādhāra), and its height and width should be double [that measurement]. || 85 ||
One should have a pedestal for the scale (tulāpīṭha) excavated with a depth equal to one-quarter [of the height], using that which was dug out;
above that, one should fashion a lotus that is neither too deep nor too high.
The deities previously mentioned should be placed there upon the petals;
or, for the sake of worshipping them alone, one may simply employ a wide-open umbrella.
The lotus above that should be one-quarter of the height of the pedestal;
it may be separate if possible, but inseparable if a separate one is not available.
[The analysis of whether the pedestal and the image are of the same or different substances:
O best of sages, know that whatever pedestal is of the same substance as the image yields infinite fruit, bestowing security, health, and abundance. (89)
A pedestal that is separate from the image would be auspicious;
it bestows liberation and fame, yet it yields only limited fruit.
A beautiful pedestal for a golden image is made of silver;
it is said that for a silver one it may be made of copper, and for that [copper one], it is declared to be made of stone.
For an image made of stone, one made of stone is prescribed; for one made of wood, likewise one made of wood.
For an image made of clay, wood is prescribed, and for one made of wood, stone is also prescribed.

[Now, regarding the pedestal of the temple: O Nārada, the measurement of the wall of the temple is prescribed as one-fourth of the inner sanctum (garbha); that is, from the measurement of the sanctum including the walls. 93.
One should previously prepare a pedestal that is either circular or square, lacking one quarter [of its original size],
or indeed slightly less than the standard measure, or even a compact one, well-proportioned.
O Sage, having likewise prepared a level pedestal equipped with steps on the four sides, one should first either construct it or visualize it in this very manner. (95)
[Now, the characteristics of the palace: One should construct the palace accordingly; its characteristics are now described.
[Therein, the pedestal of the palace:]
O Brahmin, one should first contemplate the measurement of the deity, and then the measurement of the pedestal. || 96 ||
One should indeed construct the pedestal (pīṭha) all around the temple with a length equal to [the temple's];
the inner sanctum (garbhagāra) should be twice the width of the womb-chamber (garbha), according to the prescribed rule.
It was crowded with perfected Vidyādharas and graced by gods, brahmins, and kings;
it was adorned with [objects] produced from gardens, mountains, and oceans. 98.
Adorned with elephants, horses, lions, kings, and herds of deer,
one should construct an auspicious palace upon that pedestal.
[Varieties of palaces: It may be square with four doors, or circular, or even octagonal; it may have a single door, or be variegated, facing whichever direction is desired. || 100 ||
The height of that [pedestal] is twice the previously mentioned measurement of the site;
having thus completed the procedure for constructing the pedestal (pīṭha) of the temple, one should make the wall equal to one part, which is half of the temple’s base (pāda). || 101 ||

Having given that, O Sage, one should then perform the arrangement prescribed for the pedestal; having carefully raised the *jaṅghā* (the shaft) according to the measurement of height stated for the interior of the temple's *jaṅghā*. 102.
It is endowed with eight pillars, arranged as previously described,
filled with various leafy creepers, and adorned with clusters of flowers.
[The Construction Above the Pillar Base:

Then, O Mahāmati, having divided the remaining portion of the pinnacle (śikhara) into three and five parts, the construction above the pillar base (jaṅghordhvaracanā) should be executed with one part. 104.
One should indeed fashion there, in the four directions, excellent houses, celestial palaces, and temples of various forms.
[Now, the procedure for the five levels:
One should indeed fashion the group of levels with thirty parts.
Understand their contraction, elevation, and arrangement. (106)
O Sage, having previously unified the accumulation of portions belonging to all the stages, one enjoys them by means of ninety-one equal portions. (107)
The floor above the pigeon-hole (kapota) consists of thirteen components;
from that measurement, one should gradually decrease [the dimensions] by one unit up to the top.
O tiger among sages, as far as the ground extends upward, it becomes [purified] by one part through this procedure. || 109 ||
The rising and falling of the levels is called the contraction of the sides;
above the *kapotapāli*, the spire (*śikhara*) should extend all around.
By means of twenty-seven equal vertical lines, one part from the beginning at the base, prior to the *kapotapāli* (dove-cot), [is established]. 111.
Having purified [the mandala] all around, one should likewise purify each individual portion of the upper levels, continuing upward through the stages until the highest level is reached.
One should divide the ground into five parts in sequence according to unequal proportions;
on the single part situated at the bottom, three girdles (mekhalā) should be fashioned.
In this second part, however, the arrangement should be like that of a pigeon;
one should construct two girdles (mekhalā) in the third part and above that.
Thereafter, one should fashion the fourth [tier] with conch-shells, wheels, and lotuses;
however, only a single girdle (mekhalā) should be made on the upper portion of the fifth [tier].
Or else, O twice-born one, it may be fashioned with a girdle, leaves, flowers, and so forth;
alternatively, it should be made entirely smooth, perfectly round, and adorned with auspicious marks.
Having thus fashioned the auspicious structures for all beings,
that which is the fifteenth part situated above belongs indeed to the upper realm.
[Now, the procedure for the Amalasāraka:
One should fashion the Amalasāraka joined with the uṣṇīṣa;
having divided that uṣṇīṣa into three parts, one should indeed use the first part.
O twice-born one, it should emerge slightly from the top of the base like a covering;
it should be equal in height to the base, very smooth, and free from any carving.
Above that, having divided [the space] into nine equal parts, one should fashion the neck, broad at its center, with one part. (120)
The neck should be circular, measuring half a part on all sides;
one should make it elevated by a third part of the height of the neck.
In such a manner, one should fashion the auspicious staff-seat (daṇḍāsana) above the neck,
with prongs in the form of a pair of oyster shells made of stainless metal.
O best of the twice-born, one should construct the wheel above the amalasāraka; and above that,
a wheel endowed with a flagstaff, possessing twelve spokes and made of metal.
O Nārada, one should likewise construct fifty-two such subtle palaces in the corners of the ground.
[Now, the method for constructing the doors of the palace:
One should construct its door or doors according to the prescribed measurements, making them ten parts greater than the measurement of the pedestal and the image. 125.
One should construct the door elevated, with its width being half of its height;
however, one may also construct it at a measurement less than the full height of the door.
One should fashion two door-frames and two udumbara posts above and below them;
on the two udumbara posts, one should fashion a pair of branches provided with nine divisions.
[The Construction of the Pavilion at the Entrance]:
At the front of the entrance, a pavilion should be constructed here, provided with three doors; it should be square, equal in extent to the area of the temple's ground. || 128 ||
Extending as far as the *kapota* (dove-cornice) and elevated at its center,
one should provide twelve pillars there, accompanied by twelve walls.
O Nārada, the walls should be constructed according to the architectural principles for palaces;
thus, having built this supreme palace named Kaustubha, [one should proceed].
In the midst of that, one should firmly establish the eternal mantra-form [of the deity]. [The time for installation:
On an excellent and most auspicious lunar day of the bright fortnight, and during a great planetary conjunction. (131)
And when the lunar mansion is favorable, and likewise when a pure *lagna* is established,
in the months of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Caitra— wherever the sun may be situated— (132).

[The Procedure for the Adhivāsa Pavilion] To the east or north of the temple, one should construct a pavilion measuring thirty-two cubits by the span of two arms (or twelve cubits), provided it is otherwise [suitable]. (133)

[The arrangement of five altars in the center of the pavilion: In the middle of that, there should be five altars, square and elongated, surrounded by a space of five cubits, with an interval of one cubit between each. || 134 ||
Accompanied by a group of attendants moving clockwise and adorned with canopies and other ornaments,
one should construct a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed characteristics upon the altar situated in the north— [this being the specific application for each of the five altars]. 135.
Having placed all the implements for the fire sacrifice upon that [altar],
O Nārada, he should then open his eyes upon the western altar.
O best of sages, having spread out a variegated bed upon the altar in the center of the mandala, one should place a single lotus on the fourth day.
Then one should perform the ritual bath on the south side of the fifth [line]; [this is the commencement of the procedure for installation].
Having done this, one should bring the pedestal together with the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā). 138.
While reciting the Vārāha mantra and the Astra mantra, the preceptor,
having seated [the image] upon an auspicious seat placed on the ground at the altar, [should proceed].
Having appointed four teachers or practitioners,
one should worship them after they have performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva.
One should go to the work-sheds with garments and other items;
then, for the sake of purifying the form of the image, one should bathe it thoroughly with weapon-water.
Having had it raised by artisans using its own images and pedestals, or having brought it while situated upon a chariot, one should then diligently recite the Nārasiṃha mantra.
Having covered it with a cloth and placed it upon the pedestal, the practitioner should then place white mustard seeds,
consecrated by the Cakra-mantra, upon its head.
Having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and having worshipped the door as before,
he should enter and perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) with white mustard seeds and unbroken grains of rice.
One should complete the previously mentioned procedure for the initiation of the disciple (p.
210), as well as the consecration (*adhivāsa*) of all the ritual substances, such as the image and so forth, according to their respective positions. || 145 ||
Whether for his own sake or for the sake of others, the practitioner, being well-composed, should present the image of the God of gods like a disciple. (146)
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, I shall fashion this image for your worship after offering praise at the end of the night.

[The Ritual Procedure for Bathing to Destroy Artisanal Defects] Thereafter, having bathed himself at dawn, O Sage, he should bathe the image first in order to destroy the defects arising from the workshop. 148.
Having arranged twenty-five compartments as before, [one should perform the rite] with water alone consecrated by the recitation of the Nṛsiṃha mantra. || 149 ||
Then, having first placed eight jars starting from the east,
the practitioner should fill one with milk-water and the other with pure water.
The third [vessel] is with water from a jewel; another with water from the *homa* fire;
and yet another mixed with fragrance, provided with water containing fruits and flowers. || 151 ||
The eighth [vessel] is proclaimed to be filled with rice seeds and water;
[it is consecrated] respectively with the five mantras beginning with Satya and the three beginning with Siṃha.
O twice-born one, having consecrated each [mantra] seven times, one should place Darbha grass, clay, cow dung, and sesame seeds into each of the pitchers starting from the east.

Then, having placed eight directional jars (dik-kalaśas) outside of them, one should place water with Emblic Myrobalan (dhātrī-phala) in the east, and thereafter water with Chebulic Myrobalan (pathyā) in the west.
In one [vessel] a decoction of *galūci*, in another water from *vibhītaka* trees, in another water boiled with *kumārī*, and likewise water from *vyāghrī*. (155)
Water from a city well in one place and honeyed water in another—having consecrated these with the Cakra-mantra and the Hṛdaya-mantra and others; || 156 ||

Then, O Sage, one should bathe [the deity] in sequence with the jars previously mentioned and with the Gāyatrī; the rites of service performed by those stationed in the second enclosure should be done with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, one should sprinkle [the image] with water alone that has been consecrated with the Astra-mantra;
this is declared to be the bath for the purpose of destroying defects caused by the artisan. (158)
[The Procedure for Placing the Vase for the Purpose of the Enduring Bath:
Having drawn a sixteen-petaled lotus there in the northeast, one should place a quartet of vases upon its pericarp. 159.
O Sage, having likewise installed sixteen other jars, starting from the eastern leaf and extending as far as the region of the northeast (Īśāna).
Then, O Brahmin, having donned two garments, one lower and one upper, he should prepare a bed upon the second altar above [the first]. (161) [Now follows the ritual for opening the eyes.]
There, O twice-born one, he should cause the image to lie down with its head toward the east,
while he himself takes hold of a golden needle consecrated with the Astra-mantra.
O Nārada, having bathed, wearing clean garments, and being gazed upon by the preceptor, the practitioner should scratch his eyes with the Netra-mantra. (163)
The artisan should bring it to manifestation with a weapon consecrated by a mantra;
the pedestal (pīṭhikā) which is in front of it should be joined with the Brahma-stone.
Having placed the image upon a stable and auspicious throne, which is provided with the sequence of supports and the like, and which is always obtained and well-worshipped; || 165 ||
Then one should gaze upon the blazing image with the eye of wisdom;
having enveloped it with the armor-mantra, one should strike it with the weapon-flower.
[The minor ablution consisting of the opening of the eyes:

Then, with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should perform the ablution with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), then with clay and water, then with water infused with all medicinal herbs, and finally with pure water alone. (167)
Having wiped it with a well-washed, new cloth,
the knower of mantras should subsequently release the *kautuka* (protective thread) with the *cakra-mantra*. 168.
Having offered the *arghya* together with flowers and water upon the head,
and having purified it by means of meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇās*), one should contemplate [it] like the orb of the sun.

Having withdrawn [the deity] and placed it within the heart, one should then bathe the external [image] with pure, consecrated jars filled with ritual substances that have been worshipped. [This is the procedure for the preliminary consecration and bathing. 170.

(212) [The pillars] are provided with sandalwood, offerings of water (arghya), and fruits; they are adorned with tree sprouts, bear darbha grass leaves, and are decorated with silk ribbons, garlands, and perfumes. || 171 ||
O Brahmin, with sixteen heart-pleasing substances situated there in the north-eastern direction,
one should first fill the bathing jars with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) alone.
The second [ablution] is with cow urine, the third with cow-dung water,
O Brahmin, and the fourth with the ashes of the three sacred fires along with water.
Furthermore, with earth from the horns of an elephant, a cow, or a bull, from an anthill, from a field of rice, from the middle of a river, from a cluster of lotuses, and from a mountain; 174.
O twice-born one, the sixth jar should then be filled with earth;
the seventh with water and mustard seeds, and the eighth with all medicinal herbs.
Know that the ninth is with milk; the tenth is said to be with curd;
the eleventh is with ghee, O twice-born one, and the twelfth is with honey. (176)
The thirteenth is with all seeds; the fourteenth is with all fruits;
another is with all grains; and the sixteenth is with all perfumes.
Having first consecrated each individual pitcher with the heart-mantra,
one should then bathe [the deity] with the root-mantra, one by one, in due order.
O best of sages, having first wiped it with a valuable cloth moistened with water,
he should then rub it with the flour of lentils, black gram, and wheat.
[The Procedure for the Mantra-Installation on the Image] Having washed and worshipped it, one should then install the form-mantra (*mūrtimantra*) upon the head;
[it is installed] on the head, the mouth, the two eyes, the two ears, the heart, the navel, and the back. (180)
One should likewise place the remaining group of mantras at the base of the hips, the thighs, the knees, the ankles, and the feet, as before, except for the hand-assignment (nyāsa). || 181 ||
One should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as well as niṣkalīkaraṇa;
thereafter, O twice-born one, one becomes the self whose nature consists of both forms, in accordance with everything previously described. (182)
[The Bathing with Vases Situated on the Pericarp]:
Having bathed [the deity] with the vases situated on the pericarp while reciting the Satya-mantra and others, first with water and flowers, and then with fragrant golden water. 183.

Then, O Nārada, one should wipe [the image] with water containing all kinds of jewels or with a cloth; having offered the *arghya* consecrated with the root mantra upon the head, [one performs the worship beginning with the offering of *arghya* and ending with the formal petition]. (184)
Then, having anointed the image with ointments such as sandalwood paste, and having dressed it in two garments, one should adorn it according to the prescribed rite. (185)
O Sage, one should worship with divine ornaments such as crowns and anklets,
and with excellent flowers, incense, lamps, and the like, as well as with the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Then, with various kinds of food offerings, along with betel leaves and mirrors, and having formed the ritual mudrās, prostrated, and addressed the Supreme Lord: || 187 ||
[Now, the meditation on the pedestal as consisting of the entire path, together with the image:
O best of sages, having worshipped according to this rite the pedestal accompanied by the Brahma-stone, which was previously bathed along with the image; 188.
One should meditate upon the pedestal (pīṭhikā), which consists of the entire path and is endowed with a physical form;
one should remember it as being joined with the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) and extending down to the foundational power (ādhāraśakti). (189)
[The Covering of the Pedestal] Having subsequently covered the stone slab together with the pedestal with an auspicious cloth;
[then the lustration ceremony].
Having offered the water for sipping (ācamana) and the respectful offering (arghya), one should then perform the ritual waving of light (nirājana).
[Now, the procedure for the chariot procession:
Accompanied by the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" and cries of victory, together with the sound of Vedic chanting, the resonance of conchs and musical instruments, drums, and songs. (191)
O Brahmin, having mounted [the deity] upon a chariot as if it were an immovable mountain with most beautiful and incomparable [horses],
he then circumambulated the village, beginning with the temple.
One should then cause that chariot to enter the royal palace by way of the chariot-road;
first, one should offer water for the feet and the respectful *arghya* with devotion to him who stands before the gate.
[Now, the procedure for consecrating the bed:
On the following day, the fourth day, one should draw a svastika maṇḍala with colored powders or with flowers of four brilliant colors. (194)
There, having spread a layer of *darbha* grass, one should scatter parched grains (*lāja*) and other offerings in the center;
then, having placed [the image] together with its couch—smeared [with unguents] and provided with all necessary implements. (195)
Then, O Nārada, according to the sequence of the *pīṭhanyāsa*, one should place the worshipped water-pot, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, upon the region of the head.
During that night, one should likewise worship Śrī Ananta while he is asleep;
then, having slowly lowered the deity seated upon the pedestal, [one should proceed]. 197.

Having placed [the image] upon the bed with its head toward the east, one should cover it with a heart-mantra and provide a cloth covering perfumed with incense and other fragrances, while reciting the armor-mantra.
Then, one should perform the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of the deity situated upon the bed by means of the root mantra;
immediately thereafter, the manifestation of the circle of deities known as the "array" (*vyūha*).
O best of sages, having worshipped even the subtle [deity] at the feet, heart, and head with flowers, incense, and offerings, one should then prostrate with mudrās.
[The prescription for the fire-offering (homa) which constitutes the various ritual limbs such as the bathing and opening of the eyes:

Having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the fire-offering according to one's capacity with sesame seeds and clarified butter, beginning with a hundred oblations, throughout all the ritual activities. || 201 ||
Having recollected each individual rite, the performer,
empowered by the mantra, should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root-heart mantra.
Until dawn, for the sake of completing those rites,
O twice-born one, one should sprinkle the head of the image with water of pacification at the conclusion of the fire-offering (homa).
Then, O twice-born one, [the officiant] should sprinkle the water of pacification upon his own head at the end of the homa.
Then, having offered those eight [oblations] upon the head of the Bimba with the root mantra—
[which includes the recitation of the ritual mantras and the offering of the bali]—
one should perform the recitation of the ritual mantras according to one's capacity. (204)
Having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits (bhūtas) with the Astra-mantra as before,
one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) in the four auspicious pits (kuṇḍas) located in the four directions of the temple.
Alternatively, O Sage, the image-guardian (mūrtipa) should perform the fire-oblation (homa) starting from the east within the pavilion,
reciting each deity’s own mantra one thousand times, or one hundred and eight times.
And with those [mantras], the Guru should cause the water of pacification to be poured upon the head of the image. (p. 215) [Now, the consecration through meditation:
Then he should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) by means of the ritual action as seen in the rules. || 207 ||
O Brahmin, the mantra which has entered into the image, or likewise resides in a cloth painting, is always present through that which is called meditation—partless and pure. (208)
And it has not been withdrawn until it has first been entirely withdrawn by the Guru, the knower of reality, according to the method of the sequence of withdrawal. (209)
O Nārada, the Guru remains in his own nature, which is unchanging and pure,
having first established his own presence upon the lotus made of the rays of his own heart.

In this very way, having likewise contemplated the image as indestructible, devoid of parts, and possessing a body of enlightened consciousness (bodhivijñāna), one should indeed bring it to life. || 211 ||
Two paths consisting of the Suṣumṇā, blazing and radiant in appearance, are situated one on each side of the sphere of the heart-lotus. (212)
Just as [the two] are awakened in the radiance of the jewel, they abide as all-pervasive [both] above and below;
as it is in the self, so it is in the deity, and as it is in the deity, so it is in the self.
O Sage, having meditated upon this, one should then proceed by the southern path;
the divine heart should enter one's own body through the left channel.
Just as the Self is experienced within one's own heart as being indeed incomparable,
then one should remember the sphere of pure consciousness situated within that very heart.
Having seen that great [state], filled with bliss and inlaid with its own rays, which is solely intent on coming and going within the Śakti, the Brahman, and then the Self; 216.
Unity with the consciousness residing within the body of the deity must be accomplished until the duration of motionlessness is reached within one's own body. (217)
O Brahmin, that state which is experienced by the self alone, whether through the movement of time as a single essence or in a twofold manner, [is the supreme state]. (218)
Having thus [united] himself with the deity, the practitioner should then emerge;
he should enter by the right-hand path of the deity and by the left-hand path of himself.

O tiger among sages, this yoga consists of a heart of radiant form, overflowing with the nectar of primordial wisdom (jñāna), belonging to both the [inner] image and that which is produced from material substances. 220.
From the feet to the crown of the head, what is it that manifests the multitude of channels?
It is the concentration on the Lord (*īśvarasandhāna*), O Brahmin, by which sovereignty over all arises from this image. 221.
I shall now describe that yoga; listen with one-pointed attention.
The practitioner, free from mental fluctuations, should abide in the center of the lotus of the heart. (222)
By means of the application of the utterance of one's own mantra, as before, one should go upward through the flow toward the state free from affliction;
thus it proceeds further and further.
Though unwilling, untroubled, and unperturbed, he nevertheless undergoes agitation by his own will,
just as a lamp that is very close [to a flame] may flicker even when it is not shaking.
Just as a silkworm proceeds by taking hold of its own thread,
so too does consciousness, relying upon its own power, repeatedly [construct] the lotus of the heart.
Then, by means of his own *māyā*, the teacher should enter as before;
having beheld the lotus-heart of the deity together with him.
Then, having cultivated consciousness through the power of awakening, one should proceed from there;
having reached that "twelve-finger space" (dvādaśānta), which is called the object of knowledge, there is no further interval.
Then, by means of the reasoning previously stated, one should take refuge in the divine heart from that state;
thereafter, indeed, having entered one's own heart from the divine heart.
Having come from the heart along the path to its own eyeball, and having thus contemplated the Lord and gazed at one another; || 229 ||
One should contemplate oneself through the light of the deity and remember one's own spiritual attainment;
through the light of the self, one should meditate upon the Lord of Devas as pervading all things, yet distinct from them everywhere.
Know that this concentration on the Lord, which is distinct and characterized by single-mindedness, bestows all sovereignty at all times upon [those who worship] images.
[The Contemplation of Sound] Now, I shall describe the contemplation of sound, which reveals many wonders; for the mantra-nature itself attains unity with the reflected image. (232)
Having once again become the very nature of unshakable universal consciousness itself,
[he perceives] all those entities produced by words, which are subtle and even more subtle.
One should perceive them as having attained oneness through the word "non-perception of the universal," [perceiving them] as devoid of even the mere words arising from successive prior volitions.
O twice-born one, when that which has arisen from conceptualization approaches him directly as an object consisting of sound and form, its sound is the supreme [sound]. 235.
O Sage, know that to be the *madhyama* [speech] which, having ascended the path of conceptualization, clearly vibrates within and resides upon objects. (236)
He who resides in the pericarp of the heart-lotus and manifests within the paths of effort arising from the instruments of discernment.
In the form of the signified and the signifier, that sound is called "gross";
and furthermore, by virtue of its extreme grossness, it remains within the domain of speech. (238)
And it attains manifestation within both visible and invisible entities;
from that, sound becomes increasingly gross and is established in all worldly discourse. (239)
Therefore, having first made the thought "the body consists of sound" firm in their minds, practitioners should then meditate upon the image as being of that very nature.
Through the yoga of the withdrawal of sound, that Guru who is the essence of unshakable awareness and sound perceives his own body as united with the [divine] image.

O Brahmin, by means of the application of the sequence previously described, one should indeed behold that [Brahman], which has transformed from the nature of Śabdabrahman, gradually into the nature of the reflected image.
The image established by him bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having thus performed the investigation of the word "bimba," O Nārada, [one should understand its meaning]. (243)
[Now, the unification of mantras: Thereupon, one should indeed diligently begin the unification of mantras—the soundless yet consisting of sound, eternally arisen, and unstruck (anāhata). || 244 ||
One should visualize the mantra, joyful and situated within the lotus of one's own heart like a thread of resonance,
emerging through the central channel and entering into the interior of the *bimba*.
And [he is] in the form of a throbbing star, pervaded by all mantras;
he is the Lord of the World, whose nature is mantra, that image situated in the center of the lotus. (246)
The best of practitioners should remember Him as performing both creation and dissolution;
He alone is to be understood as the Supreme, most subtle, and partless (niṣkala).
The whole (sakala) and the partless (niṣkala), as well as that which consists of both, must be understood;
within the night of consciousness, it should be known as being permeated by the essence of sleep. [This is the manner of the Lord’s contemplation of sleep. 248.
(p. 218) [Now, the contemplation on the manner of awakening:
Then, at the dawn of the multitude of principles (tattva), upon the rising of the day of enjoyment (sambhoga), one should remember the awakened God descended from the supreme state (parātpada). (249)
[The contemplation of the identity of the image with the pedestal:
One should contemplate that the entire ground of the pedestal, which is the locus for the enjoyment of all the paths, has been stepped upon by Him;
for the power of the support (ādhāra-śakti) is indeed the abiding state of the All-pervasive Lord who consists of mantra. (250)
Therefore, one should contemplate the pedestal of the Brahma-stone and the image as unified.
[Now, the worship preceded by the ritual placement of mantras:
Thereafter, one should perform worship through the yoga of meditation and preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). || 251 ||

O Brahmin, having first performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) three times according to the previous sequence, one should perform the entire hand-placement (hastanyāsa) with a state of absorption, without [the preliminary ritual]. 252.
With water for the feet, with the arghya offering, with flowers, with incense, and with ointments;
with the madhuparka, with food, and likewise with various kinds of edibles.
With purifying drinks, heart-pleasing juices such as *rasāla* and other fruits, and with all kinds of sweet liquid essences, he offered manifold material enjoyments in embodied form. || 254 ||
With all the elements and seeds, with instrumental and vocal music in their entirety, with garments, umbrellas, and cloths, as well as mirrors, collyrium, and vehicles; || 255 ||
With sandals and wooden shoes, with fly-whisks and footstools, with gifts, betel leaves, garments, banners, and ornaments. (256)
With auspicious beds, seats, and all household furnishings, arranged within gardens, houses, and palaces; || 257 ||
With banners and canopies, with all manner of weapons and scriptures,
as well as with measures of land, cows, villages, cattle, and birds.
Having bound the wish-fulfilling mudrā, which consists of the enjoyment of one's own mantra, with infinite internal measures that are complete and uncontrived; (259)
Having offered each [oblation] with the *bhoga-mantra* and the *gāyatrī*, one should then praise Jitanta, offering incense again and again. || 260 ||
[The recitation of the Ṛgveda and other mantras by Brahmins standing in the four directions starting from the east, facing west and so on, respectively:
Having positioned the most excellent twice-born one seated in the east, facing west;
With flower garlands, as well as with uṣṇīṣas, ornaments, and finger-rings; || 261 ||
First, while looking toward the northern direction, one should have him recite the Ṛg-mantras;
then the preceptor should have him recite that collection of Vaiṣṇava Yajus-mantras.
One who knows the Sāmans, standing in the west, should sing the pure Sāman hymns;
the devotee, standing in the water, should recite [the Ṛgveda], and one standing in the south, facing north, should recite the Atharvaveda.
Likewise, having fully understood the mantras prescribed in his own Vedic branch along with their defining characteristics,
he should be surrounded by a group of disciples according to the sequence of those for whom he performs sacrifices.

[The recitation of the mantras of the Ekāyanīya branch by ascetics and others situated in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, together with those who follow the Āpta and other authorities:
"And those ascetics belonging to the Pāñcarātra who are devoted to the Blessed One..."
One should place [the vessels] joined with four trustworthy persons, such as Brahmins, in the direction of Īśa (the northeast).

O Brahmin, having seated those who are single-mindedly devoted, as well as those joined with the trustworthy (or untrustworthy?), located in the south-eastern direction, together with the Vaikhānasa ascetics who are devoted to the south-west.
Then, with four handfuls of water in the region of Vāyu,
he honored the Sārambhas and the Sātvatas, who at that time were absorbed in the Blessed One.
Furthermore, O Sage, four Śikhis are to be assigned to the four directions;
and because they follow them, there are likewise four Pravartins. (268)
O best of sages, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas,
and Śūdras [recite] the supremely purifying mantras arising from the Ekāyanīya Śākhā.
And he should cause trustworthy ascetics who follow the Pāñcarātra to recite their own mantras, which they mutter according to their own established practices, being firm in their vows. (270)
[The stationing of the Guru and others in the four directions starting from the east:
In the four directions beginning with the east and ending with the north, there are four [preceptors] beginning with the Guru;
they may be many, ending with those who know the *samaya*, or two, or even one, according to one's own capacity. (271)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and having their hands adorned with the meditation gesture (dhyānamudrā),
they should conceal their respective gestures from one another within their own garments.
Others were devoted to song and dance, while in front stood those reciting hymns; outside, there were groups of panegyrists as well as drummers.
Then the practitioner should perform the ritual action and a fire-oblation according to his capacity. (p.
220) In this manner, following the sequence of the initiation rite, he should purify the entire series of principles (*tattva*) within both the Brahma-stone and the pedestal. 274.
Having purified himself and being well-composed, the preceptor, abiding in the state of the Supreme Reality,
should offer oblations to that which is designated as Brahman by means of the Ādhāraśakti mantra.
O Nārada, having satisfied the pedestal with the Śaktyādhāra mantra,
the Lord, whose nature is dissolution, [is then worshipped] thereafter with abundant clarified butter.
[The Sprinkling with Peace-Water]:
One should bestow the peace-water upon the heads of all three in due order,
according to the ritual, using the root mantra recited from the heart.
Having thus addressed the Blessed One who resides within the image, the Guru should cause him to hear this mantra, which is present before him, with a perfectly pure mind. (278)
[The Prayer for Presence] "O Unstained One, O Aṭokṣaja, you must remain present here for the sake of the spiritual attainment of my ancestors who are devoted to you. (279)

Then that Blessed One, lotus-eyed and awakened by the mantra, having been raised up through the rites of *utthāpana* (rousing) and *saṃmukhīkaraṇa* (making present), should be meditated upon by the preceptor as being face-to-face. 280.
Having performed a prostration with the eight limbs, the practitioner,
through the procedure of absorption and enjoyment, should then bring down the deity residing in the sacrifice out of great eagerness and worship it. (281)

Then, having properly worshipped that which resides in the fire according to the previously mentioned procedure by means of the nature of absorption and enjoyment, and likewise having worshipped and fully gratified it in due order; || 282 ||
[The Procedure for the Peace-Offering (Śānti-homa):
Thereafter, the practitioner should perform the fire-offering (homa) consisting of four substances, for the sake of all the principles (tattvas) and the entirety of their manifestation. 283.
Of the array known as *sūkṣma*, of the mantra of manifold forms, of the power that transcends the mantra, and of the ten thousand Lords of Power (*śaktīśa*). || 284 ||
O Sage, having established the formation of a single connection even for those [deities], understand how their withdrawal occurs through the yoga of dissolution and maintenance. (p. 221) 285.
O Brahmin, having touched the two feet of the pervasive Lord Bimbātman with ghee,
one should offer that ghee into the fire one hundred and eight times.
Having placed his feet forward and [the vessel] above with a bundle of *darbha* grass, he should likewise perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with curd; then, touching his navel, he should proceed.
Then, when the heart region is touched, one should perform an oblation of milk;
thereafter, having touched the head, one should offer only honey.
Then, O Nārada, having unified everything into equal portions and having touched all the limbs, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa). || 289 ||

O Nārada, one should perform the oblation starting from the feet with mantras ending in the words "aniruddha" and "satyānta," and afterwards, having offered [the oblation] with ghee, one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra.
[The procedure for feeding with four substances such as honey at the conclusion of the peace-homa, and the giving of the sacrificial fee:
One should feed [the deity] with honey, clarified butter, ghee, and milk-rice, using the Mūrti-mantra.
And then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, such as gold and other items. || 291 ||
[Now, the method for passing the time while awaiting the moment of the *lagna*:
O twice-born one, as long as that auspicious moment (*lagnakāla*) does not arrive, he should pass the time with diversions, fire-offerings (*homa*), laughter, and recitations. (292)
[Now, regarding the manner of prayer to be performed first when the time for consecration has arrived:
O Brahmin, when the rising of the auspicious moment (lagna) has arrived, having restrained the Lord of the World, pray:
"O Blessed One, Omniscient One, Abode of Compassion, please grant me this moment's leave. (293)
I shall establish for you a Brahma-throne within the palace;
one should remember the Teacher of the World as he lies upon his bed, sleeping. (294)
[The Procedure for Pacifying Obstacles to Entering the Temple, etc.
Thereafter, O Nārada, the Guru, together with the bearers of the [deity’s] forms, should enter the temple; he should strike down the obstacles situated there with the *cakra* and the *astra*. 295.
Having washed it with the Astra-mantra, one should then meditate upon the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā),
O twice-born one— [the procedure for the installation of the Brahma-stone]— which is slightly less than the surface of the pedestal, level, smooth, and firm. (296)
Having first prepared a diagram of nine squares, one should properly draw a lotus within each square using a line, and then dig out the pericarp in all of them. (297)
O Nārada, one should then divide the temple into seven equal parts with level squares, extending from the door to the western wall for a single entrance.
O Sage, beginning from the location of the door and leaving aside four parts,
one should place the Brahma-stone in the center using two squares.
In the rite of installing a deity, the central area from the doorway must not be abandoned;
rather, having placed [the deity] in the center of a four-doored mansion, one should proceed.

When the site has been divided into three parts in the four directions, one should place a firm Brahma-stone there; once the Brahma-stone has been set down and the foundation (garbha) is established, the worship may commence.
Then, one should dig for the Brahma-stone at the distance of the span of both arms;
having moved that [stone] previously along the path of the thread, one should lead it toward the northern direction.
In the middle of that [pit] as well, one should fashion a beautiful cavity six finger-breadths deep;
and within that, one should place [an image] made of jewels, or of gold, or of copper.
Having consecrated with the heart-mantra and established with the Gāyatrī a conch-shaped vessel measuring four finger-breadths in size, || 304 ||
Having provided it with a lid and likewise applying a coating of lime on top,
one should place the Brahma-stone, which has been consecrated by mantras, after first offering [the preliminary rites].
Then, having taken recourse in pervasiveness, the Guru himself should meditate upon that stone as all-pervading, its form consisting of both the support and the supported.

There, one should contemplate the placement of all the upward-moving [deities] with the root mantra. Having thus established their presence, O twice-born one, thereafter [one should perform it] above that.
[The Installation of Jewels, etc.
Listen attentively to how one should perform the installation of the jewels and so forth:
one should install golden Agni, likewise Ananta made of silver, and the Earth made of gold. (307)
An eight-metal lotus is placed in the center upon the Brahma-stone;
then, in the cavities of the lotuses starting from the east and proceeding in order up to the northeast.
O best of sages, [the gems] are the diamond, the sun-stone, the sapphire, as well as the great sapphire, and beyond these, the pearl. (309)
Then, having placed a topaz in the northeast and a ruby beyond that, one should place a lapis lazuli in the northeast and a crystal in the center. (310)
Having placed silver, copper, tin, lead, iron, steel, and bell-metal in the east and other directions, and gold in the center; 311.
Tāla, realgar, turmeric, and kuṣṭha;
antimony from the stream, cinnabar, saurāṣṭra, and golden ochre. || 312 ||
In the center, however, one should place a royal stone (rājapāṣāṇa) and mercury on all sides,
as well as wheat, wild barley, mung beans, and likewise black gram.
O tiger among sages, having placed chickpeas, kuluttha beans,
and lentils in sequence within the eight [positions], one should place white mustard seeds and sesame seeds in the center.
Then [one should take] hrībera, rajanī, māṃsī, sahadevī, vacā, viṣṇukrāntā, balā, moṭā, śyāmāka, and śaṅkhapuṣpaka. || 315 ||
One should arrange the continuous sequence of the root-mantra starting from the east and ending at the center;
however, due to the absence of all other materials, one should employ gold everywhere.
In the absence of those [pearls],
however, one should place a bell and pearls that have already been soaked in ghee or milk.
O Brahmin, one should indeed apply a plaster in all the hollows,
and afterwards place upon it a new, pure white silk cloth.
[The Procedure for the Installation of the Pedestal upon the Brahma-stone] Then, having applied a smooth coating of lime, one should install the pedestal;
and having joined it with the stone as before, O Nārada. (319)
Then, O Sage, having placed my golden Garuḍa upon the hollow of the pedestal, [one should offer] milk, curd, clarified butter, parched grain, honey, flowers, and fruits. (320)
O best of Brahmins, one should meditate upon all perfumes together with all medicinal herbs upon the pedestal as before, endowed with the entire [set] beginning with Dharma.
Then, one should again place the pervasive presence consisting of the seat of consciousness (cidāsana) above that;
having consecrated each [element] individually with the Heart mantra and the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) for whichever specific rite one intends to perform,
up until the procedure for the placement on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa), one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
[Now, the awakening:
O Brahmin, when the rising of the auspicious moment (lagna) has arrived, one should awaken the deity who is lying upon his bed:
"O you whose self is the mantra, withdraw your own fiery form. (324)
O Supreme Lord, assume your gentle nature for the sake of stability;
salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, arise, O Supreme Lord! 325.
For the sake of showing me favor, ascend the ground of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
[The entry into the temple of the God:
Having been properly lifted up by the image-keepers (*mūrttipas*), the practitioner should enter behind or in front [of the deity]. (326)
While scattering many jewels for the sake of the offering,
O Nārada, he should then perform a circumambulation of the temple.
One should slowly cause the deity to enter so that it does not touch the upper part;
this is the door for both sides.
[Now, the installation of the deity upon the pedestal.]
Then, one should place [it] in the center of the seat. || 328 ||
O Nārada, by means of the root mantra joined with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya),
one should place him there in front, as well as at his sides and behind.
With the *vajralepa* mantra and the *gāyatrī*, the Guru, having first uttered the *tāraka*, should bring about the identity of the pedestal while his head is bowed in prostration. (330)
[The Petition: O Blessed One, you have been propitiated for the benefit of practitioners;
therefore, out of compassion, you should dwell here at all times. (331)
"O Lord, wherever you abide, there success is not far off for the best of practitioners;
this was indeed stated by you in the past. (332)
Therefore, O Great One, being forever content, supremely compassionate, and always intent on bestowing grace, remain thus as long as the moon and stars exist. 333.
Having spoken thus, one should then offer the *arghya* (water of respect) upon the head and the feet.
[Now, the establishment of the principles:
One should perform the establishment of the principles (*tattvasaṃsthāpana*) following the establishment of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). 334.

[He is worshipped] with the waves of consciousness and bliss, with the manifestations of the objects of knowledge, likewise with sounds that produce manifold delights, and with the various modes of conduct and so forth, extending from the base up to the head. 335.
One should perceive the image consisting of mantra, possessing many wondrous forms;
thus, in the source of all arising, it bestows the accomplishment of one's intentions.

[The visualization of the image as a mantra-tree: Having established the image as a mantra-tree with a stainless nature, its branch consisting of that very consciousness rises up pre-eminently through the power of illusion (or, from Māyā). 337.
O twice-born one, the practitioner should meditate upon [the goddess] who pervades the infinite sky, with abundant and indeed incomparable nectar. (338)
One should always meditate upon the tree consisting of the mantra-form as being full of sap,
O Nārada, [nourished] by the water of the earth and that which arises from the sky.
The *mandāra* flower-tree is indeed exactly like that and not otherwise.

[This refers to the procedure for worship by means of the rites of dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and so forth, of the mantra-wheel placed upon the *bimba*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and other such objects.]
Then, one should worship everything there through the sacrifice of dissolution (layayāga).
One should again worship the circle of mantras situated on the pedestal through the ritual of enjoyment (bhogayāga).
Having taken recourse to the base of the pedestal, one should install the world-protectors together with their weapons.
Then, O Nārada, one should worship the assembly of mantras belonging to the Pīṭhas in reverse order, up to the Ādhāraśakti, by means of the rite of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa).
[The bathing to be performed on the day of consecration, following the consecration: Having worshipped the deity, one should then bathe him [the worship of the four locations].
Furthermore, in the mandala, having performed worship according to the previous rule and following the sequence of the mandala, || 343 ||
Having performed the entire ritual up to the end of the oblation (homa), one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, having fashioned a conventional name ending with "Svāmī" (Master) as his own name, one should pronounce the benediction for its firm establishment.
Accompanied by the sound of cymbals, O Nārada, they all uttered the words "So be it! while scattering full handfuls of flowers and unbroken rice grains.
All those situated there should say: "The Blessed One is well-established.
[This is the proclamation of praise and victory.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, should be praised by everyone. (346)
Then, with a voice raised in victory, he cried out "Victory! Victory!"—for by that all-pervading Lord, who is the very soul of all and whose form is mantra, [he was thus addressed]. (347)
