Having offered water upon the layer of grass starting from the east in a clockwise direction, and having likewise offered the eight-fold oblation (balyaṣṭaka), one should first cast sesame seeds into the fire.
O Brahmin, first [he should offer] to the ancestors there in due order with the *hṛnmantra*,
and previously with the *gāyatrī* mantra joined with their own names and the word *svadhā*.
One should perform the offering of the bali-oblation with the right hand;
one should contemplate that power of those ancestors as being the same as before.
Then, O twice-born one, he should offer water with sesame seeds, using the heart-mantra at the beginning and end,
together with the word "svadhā," the syllable "oṃ," and the name accompanied by the lineage (gotra).
Then the king, with a mind purified by meditation on the qualities [of the deity],
[should worship] first upon the mantra-form, and then likewise in the fire, in due order.
[Now, the procedure for the distribution of food to the ancestors:
One should honor those who are seated with flowers, incense, and unguents, and having divided the food among them, [one offers] the sacrificial remains of the food offering. 54.
Whatever was previously accomplished, endowed with the fruits such as the *vyañjana* [mantras], by means of the root-mantra accompanied by *svadhā*, and adorned with the *mūrti* [mantra]. (55)
One should meditate on the vessel as being like the full moon, and within it, one should clearly recollect that Lord of Mantras, who has the form of nectar and produces great satisfaction. (56)
[The procedure for recitation and meditation while the ancestors are eating:
While they are thus eating, one should remember the weapon-mantra in the ten directions;
O great sage, one should recite and meditate upon the Lord of Mantras, Narasiṃha. 57.
[The Giving of the Dakṣiṇā at the End of the Meal:
One should please the Lord with devotion and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity.
O Nārada, the food offering (naivedya) should indeed be retained for that long. 58.

Until the completion of the act of eating, and having offered [the remainder] at its conclusion, one should indeed distribute the remaining food to everyone, including those who have arrived as guests. (59)
Or, having first distributed among them, one should set aside one portion right there—
that which was previously offered to Hari under the name of the grandfather.
The householder should give that [offering] to his wife for the sake of increasing her progeny;
then, having bid farewell to the God of gods, he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
And having first summarized it—
Nārada said:
"O Lord, this ritual procedure for the *kavya* śrāddha has been understood by me."
“I wish indeed to know, O Lord, that which is designated as the *aurdhvadehika* (rites for the deceased).
The Blessed Lord said:
“Having consecrated the deceased according to the rite prescribed by rule, [one should perform] the Vaiṣṇava [consecration]. (63)
[The Procedure for the Śrāddha of a Preta] [The Rite to be Performed on the First Day] Thereafter, his funeral rites should be performed either in one's own hermitage or by a body of water.
Having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Lion-mantra along with its weapon in the cardinal and intermediate directions, he should then proceed.
In that interval, one should meditate upon the hut with the armor-mantra and its own mudrā;
then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra.
p. 260) One should place the fire upon a hearth facing north using the Astra-mantra;
then, having washed and smeared a new pot with the Varma-mantra, [one should proceed]. (66)

O twice-born one, having filled [the vessel] with water from the heart-mantra and washed the rice with that very water, one should place it [on the fire], prepare it, and consecrate that sacrificial oblation (caru) with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then, having brought to completion the [preparation] mixed with honey, milk, and clarified butter,
one should withdraw it after consecrating it with those very mantras, from the base up to the [tip of the] weapon.
Gazing toward the direction of the fire, he should then smear a circle on the ground with the Astra-mantra, making it beautiful and free from hair and thorns.
Having prepared the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should then sprinkle [the area] with that water;
there, one should scatter sesame seeds and *darbha* grass mixed together while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
There, having brought down the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) consecrated with the weapon-mantra (astra),
one should prepare a mantra-throne either upon that [seat] or on the ground.
Then, one should worship the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśa) in his partless form (niṣkala) through the yoga of dissolution;
first, however, without the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), using offerings such as water for honor (arghya) and flowers.
The worship of the fire concludes with a ritual that is never overly elaborate;
it is performed using a vessel made of silver or copper, consecrated with the heart-mantra.
O Nārada, in the absence of a vessel, one should take up the food situated in the *caru* like a *piṇḍa*, and place it before the Goddess while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Then, one should [visualize] the heart-seed syllable situated in the midst of the food offering (naivedya), accompanied by the Praṇava, joined with the name of the deceased, and followed by the word of salutation (namaskāra). || 75 ||
Then, having meditated upon [the deceased] as having the form of a preta, one should worship him with his own name preceded by "svadhā" and ending with the word for the deity. 76.
With water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, as well as lamps, ointments, massages, and eye-salves;
with garments, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), food, and other such honors. || 77 ||
Then, having performed the libation with the proper measures and having prostrated before the Supreme Lord,
the Lord of Mantras who resides there as the partless (niṣkala) one remains thus established.
O best of Brahmins, one should then remember that dissolved body as slightly floating in the sky;
thereafter, [one should offer oblations] with sesame, honey, curd, food, and water.
Having filled the cupped hands or a silver vessel with water for the guest-offering (arghya),
one should scatter it outside all around the food offering (naivedya) by circling it from right to left (apasavya).
Having paid homage according to the rule, and having both forgiven and bound [the opponent],
O Nārada, with the previously mentioned mantra together with its mudrā.
O twice-born one, having filled the water-pot with water from the heart-vessel along with sesame seeds,
and having offered it to the Brahmin together with the food for the ritual meal (naivedya), [he should proceed].
Or [he may offer it] in cows; and in the absence of those, he should cast it into water.
Then, having offered water with sesame seeds while reciting the heart-mantra and the name [of the deceased], he should utter "svadhā."
Having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) immediately thereafter,
he should then withdraw the placement of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa) from the place of worship with water, O twice-born ones.
Having rinsed [the mouth] and smeared [the body with ashes], and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should enter the house;
then, having performed the protection (rakṣā) as before, one should eat light and purifying food. 85.
At the end of that, one should meditate upon Nṛhari and recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity.
At the end of the day, having scattered white mustard seeds with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the ritual for retiring to bed.
This entire procedure should be performed with diligence by a wise person for ten days, beginning from the second day until the tenth day, out of a desire to bestow grace upon the deceased. (87)
O Nārada, beginning from the head down to the weapon-mantras,
and then upwards from Aniruddha ending with Vāsudeva.
Having thus completed the ten-day period, when the eleventh day arrives,
one should indeed perform the rite of Śrāddha once the daily (Āhnika) duties have been accomplished. (89)
For that purpose, O twice-born one, one should request the Guru, or the Guru’s son, or in his absence, the Sādhaka, or the Putraka, or one who possesses the Samaya.
Either that which was previously described beginning with the ascetic (yati), or indeed the Vaiṣṇava alone;
having had him wash his feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then cause him to enter.
Having offered a seat and established him facing north,
one should then worship the deity, who is endowed with his powers, limbs, and constituent parts.
Then, O Brahmin, one should prepare an auspicious mandala for the teacher;
there, one should offer an excellent seat that has been worshipped and permeated by the [deity's] pervasive presence. (93)
Then, having placed it there consecrated with the name of the deceased, the ritual placement (nyāsa) and invocation (āvāhana) should be performed according to the previously stated procedure. 94.
Then, O Nārada, one should offer the *arghya* and *pādya* with the [guest's] name and lineage;
one should honor him with flowers, incense, and, according to one's ability, with garments and other such items. (95)
Having offered all the deceased's belongings to that very person and having obtained permission as before, one should commence the sacrifice for the sake of the ancestors (or the deceased). || 96 ||
According to the previously mentioned procedure, something further is also stated here:
having offered the food-oblation (*naivedya*) ball with the *Gāyatrī* mantra, it should be like a sphere of nectar (*amṛtagola*).
Having meditated upon that which stands above the three abodes, filled with delightful splendor,
one should [place it] in the center by means of the root mantra accompanied by the word *svadhā*.
One should meditate upon the form consisting of a preta, born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa;
there, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of dissolution for Lakṣmī and all others.
Then, one should worship him with the root mantra using offerings such as arghya and other enjoyments;
having formed the mudrā and performed the recitation, [one should offer it] into the fire situated before Hari.
One should perform everything on darbha grass with the tips pointing south, ending with the offering of water and sesame seeds; thereafter, one should feed the preceptor alone.
While that sage is eating, one should mutter the *nṛhari* mantra standing before him;
then, at the conclusion of that meal, one should do so before the seat of the mantra (*mantrapīṭha*).
O best of Brahmins, one should again offer water with sesame seeds using the arghya vessel;
then, taking the prepared food that remains from the meal, together with the arghya water— (103)
For the purpose of satisfying the spirits (bhūtas), one should scatter an offering (bali) as before;
and for the sake of the one who has been fully satisfied, one should [offer] with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) and nectar (amṛta) in front of him.
Having asked "Is it complete? with the mantra beginning with "amala" and ending with "namaḥ," joined by "parameśvarayuktena," he should then offer water for sipping (ācamana).
Having gathered up the remnants, one should sprinkle the ground with the Astra-mantra;
then, having indeed accepted the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should perform the propitiation of the Blessed One.
O twice-born one, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for the mantra residing in the fire;
[one should contemplate] within the center of the heart-lotus that great mass of light, radiant with a multitude of splendors.
Having withdrawn the Lord of Mantras into the center of the fire of the *piṇḍapīṭha* according to this rite, one should indeed perform it month after month, O great sage. (108)
[Now, the annual śrāddha that brings an end to the state of being a preta:
When the year has indeed been completed and the thirteenth month has arrived, one should perform the ancestral śrāddha for the sake of pacifying the state of being a preta. (109)
First, one should perform the daily rites of the twice-born, beginning with the bath and ending with the fire-oblation;
then, when the consecrated fire has been established, it should be saturated with ghee, milk, and honey.
Having summoned the devotees of the Blessed One and the preceptors devoted to ritual action,
he should seat them facing north, according to the sequence of the placement of the pedestal (pīṭhanyāsa).
Having placed two others with faces as before upon the two seats,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the four [deities] with the mantras beginning with Aniruddha.
One should then place the six root limbs one by one from the feet up to the head; with two [limbs], however, one should place the weapon (astra) throughout the body.

That very weapon-mantra, joined with its seed-syllable and adorned with its own name, should be placed on the hands and the body by those two for the purpose of performing the sixfold ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). 114.
The name of him for whose sake the *śrāddha* is performed is Aniruddha;
having assigned the name of his father, Pradyumna, who is of immeasurable soul, [to that purpose]. (115)
One should conceive of Saṅkarṣaṇa as the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśa) and as the grandfather (pitāmaha);
one should likewise conceive of Vāsudeva as the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha).
One should worship with water for the guest (arghya), flowers, and other offerings according to the rite known as the dissolution (āpyaya);
then, having requested permission from the Lord of Mantras residing in the image, [one should proceed].
Having honored him according to one's means with bathing water and other offerings, O high-minded one, as well as with sandalwood paste, ornaments, garlands, garments, incense, and collyrium; 118.
Immediately thereafter, [one should worship] with a lamp, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and a measured portion of excellent food,
as well as with hymns, mantras, prostrations, and flowers.
Having brought that very fire into the midst [of the vessel], one should worship it;
then, having extracted [the substance] with devotion from the vessels over which the Astra-mantra has been recited.
For the sake of accomplishing the union with the ancestors, there are four offerings of cooked food (naivedya),
accompanied by various side dishes and infused with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
Having sprinkled [the offerings] with the root mantra of the Lord by means of Aniruddha and the others,
one should present each one individually according to the sequence of reabsorption.
Then, one should bring forward each individual vessel of food previously consecrated;
one should meditate upon it in that form as divided into four parts.
From the many distinct powers of food, they have attained a state of progressive succession,
ranging from the divisions beginning with Aniruddha up to Vāsudeva.
O Mahāmati, that which is the power of *rasa* (taste/flavor) is Aniruddha;
Pradyumna is the power of *vīrya* (vitality/heroism); and from that [comes] Acyuta, the power of *dhṛti* (fortitude/steadfastness). || 125 ||
The power of bliss arising from the letter *Ā* is known as Vāsudeva;
having thus remembered and meditated upon him, one should [worship] with their respective individual mantras.
O twice-born one, know that for the deities whose bodies consist of food, the ritual placement (nyāsa) is as before,
beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon (astra), thus consisting of their forms.

Even when those four offerings of food have become liquefied and consumed, one should worship with the mantra using different types of food, such as the vessel for the *arghya* offering and so forth. || 128 ||
Then, as before, he should gratify the Lord of the Gods by means of his name, lineage, and so forth;
thereafter, in front of Acyuta who is stationed in the fire and has been previously satiated with clarified butter and other offerings.
In this very way, having divided the food-offering into four parts,
one should likewise perform the gratification of the Lord, the Master of the Ancestors.

Having drunk this ancestral offering (pitr-yāga) for your pleasure in my presence, it has been performed by me for you, who are the essence of the mantra—svadhā, oṃ, salutations again and again. || 131 ||
Then, with the heart-mantra, one should offer water with sesame seeds to each individual for the ancestors who are present before him in the form of food, being the very self of the mantra-body.
Furthermore, by this same procedure, one should meditate upon the ancestors— who consist of the potency of food—
as having attained a state of tranquility within the consciousness of the deities and mantras.
Understand how this is done through action, speech, and mind:
having first taken a little food from the *naivedya* with one's hand... (134)
When the morsel of food is held above that, one should first utter the previously mentioned *pitṛ-mantra*, including the name and lineage at its conclusion, and then join it [to the water]. 135.
Thereafter, having uttered the mantra of the Overlord (adhīśa) thus, accompanied by a salutation, go indeed to your own abode; then, one should meditate in this manner. (136)
The potency of food is dissolved into the self of Pradyumna, who is moon-bright;
he is the father, in the form of a star, the radiant Aniruddha.
O twice-born one, having thus prepared it endowed with the glory of the nature of consciousness,
one should then mix the food— which has been permeated by Pradyumna— according to this rite.
He [is merged] again into Vāsudeva, the great abode Saṅkarṣaṇa;
and the blessed Lord Vāsudeva likewise [merges] into the supreme, imperishable state.
Having thus performed the connection with the ancestors in the presence of Hari and near the fire, one who abides in that previously mentioned peaceful and infinite state shall not be born again.
O twice-born one, after they have been honored, he should first give them food;
then, in due order, he should ask them about their satisfaction with the meal.
Having sipped water for purification, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) before Viṣṇu;
with the heart-mantra, supreme devotion to Nārāyaṇa should be expressed by them. 142.
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and say, "O twice-born one, the King of Mantras should be forgiven.
[The giving of the remnants of the paternal food to the wife:
As before, the sacrificial offering (naivedya), consecrated with the root mantra, should be given to my wife. 143.
When his wife has purified herself, he should offer [the seed] infused with milk and clarified butter;
thus they attain perfection as a son and enter into her womb.
Then, by means of that very water, he— becoming a vessel for fortune and prosperity,
devoted to the performance of knowledge and dharma, and dedicated to the vow of truthfulness— [performed the distribution of the remaining food]. || 145 ||
One should indeed perform the assignment (*niyojana*) and other rites for the food offering (*naivedya*) as before.
[The method of dismissal of the ancestors:
Having first produced the vessel for the feet (*pādārghya-pātra*) with the heart-mantra (*hṛd-mantra*), 146.
One should remember all the ancestors present there, whether on earth or in the sky, with their respective mantras.
[Eye-cleansing: Then, with that very water and the eye-mantra, one should [cleanse] the two eyes. (147)
Having wiped away that water and cast it into a pure place, one thus performs the mantra-śrāddha, which bestows a favorable rebirth. (148)
[The Obligation of those who know the Samaya to perform the Śrāddha for the Guru and others:
Those who know the *samaya* and others should perform the śrāddha for their gurus for the sake of their own spiritual accomplishment;
likewise, it should be performed for one's ancestors by one's sons and gurus out of compassion. (149)
Even if a śrāddha rite would otherwise be required for disciples who have previously observed their vows and whose selves are purified, as well as for one who has been duly initiated; || 150 ||
There too, for the sake of attaining one's own welfare, one should perform the rite known as *kriyā*;
this *śrāddha*, equal to initiation (*dīkṣā*), bestows a good rebirth even from an evil state of existence. (151)
And always for those who are initiated in a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice or ritual,
therefore, with every effort, by whatever means available— || 152 ||
One should complete this śrāddha even with pure material offerings.
[Praise of the performance of śrāddha: O Nārada, even if it is performed with poor food, in an inferior place, or for unworthy recipients, [it is still meritorious]. (153)
Know that [the fruit] is eternal when accomplished through meditation, consciousness, mantras, and so forth;
how much more so when it is purified by faith, given at the proper place and time, and to a worthy recipient? 154.
A Vaiṣṇava is the supreme vessel; Hari’s temple is the sacred place;
and the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī) is proclaimed as the best of all times. 155.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Śrāddha," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Saṃskāras.
Nārada said:
Through your grace, I have heard [the rites for] the optional (kāmya), the funeral (preta), and the ancestral śrāddha.
Now I wish to hear about the funeral rites for those whose life-force has departed.
Speak in brief to those who have taken refuge in your teaching;
that which was previously uttered by you has not been clearly explained.
The Blessed One said:

"Having learned that the initiated one has met with misfortune, the Great Guru should be entreated, either out of affection or compassion, along with his disciples who have perfected their selves. (3)

Having performed his daily rites, especially having not yet eaten, the twice-born man should always go there after observing him with the previously mentioned gaze. (4) [The Procedure for the Funeral Rites]
Having given the command and raised up the corpse, one should first bathe the deceased with cow dung,
earth, and water consecrated by the recitation of the *astra-mantra*.
Having bathed him with fragrant *āmalaka* fruits and water infused with all medicinal herbs,
and having anointed him with sandalwood paste mixed with *bāhlīka*, O Nārada.
Having dressed him in two white garments, both lower and upper, which are free from impurity,
he likewise provides a new sacred thread along with an upper cloth.
There, two purifiers (pavitrakas) made of kuśa grass should be joined to the fingers;
having adorned them with flower garlands, they should be placed upon the yantra covered by a cloth.

[The Carrying of the Corpse to the Place of Cremation: Having taken hold of the corpse, whether by those of his own caste who are initiated or even those who are uninitiated, one should carry it to the place of cremation, which must be free from bones, charcoal, and the like. (9)
[Leveling the site for the funeral pyre: Having first smeared it with cow dung, one should level that site according to the prescribed rite.
[Carrying the belongings of the deceased, such as alms bowls and other items, along with his corpse:]
Likewise, the alms-bowl, the staff, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the rosary; || 10 ||
The two sandals, the seat, and likewise the yoga-band;
a wooden auspicious throne, an offering vessel, and a water-pot. || 11 ||
O best of sages, all the implements belonging to him [the image] should consist only of those materials;
[among them, the substances to be avoided are:
it must be devoid of gold, clothing, scriptures, and bells. (12)
That should be given at the time of the śrāddha for the sake of pleasing someone;
one should place flowers, water for the arghya offering, blossoms, and so forth before him, as well as the materials required for the funeral rites of the deceased. (13)
And whatever is to be employed there in the act of worship and the rite of fire-offering (homa)—namely, eight sharp stakes produced from the Aśvattha tree. (14)
O best of Brahmins, having himself obtained [the wood] from another ascetic without effort,
he should cut down an Aśvattha tree, or one of the Palāśa species in its absence.
A thread that is yellow or very white, made of linen or cotton;
all kinds of grains, black sesame seeds, and white mustard seeds.
Having prepared abundant dry fuel, such as that of the *pālāśa* tree and other purifying woods,
the preceptor should take his seat there, having reached the northeastern quarter.
[The Guru must also perform the placement on his own limbs according to the sequence of dissolution:
Having first adorned himself with the six-limbed rite by means of the mantra joined with the method of dissolution, starting from the feet up to the very top of the head. (18)

"The mantra that was performed by the deceased must first be used for worship; at the commencement, the twice-born should perform the worship with that which bears the name of its performer, or with that of another preceptor who remains. (19)
For a devotee established in the teaching, when the mantra is not known— [in that case,
the procedure for worship is performed] with the general mantra of the Great-Souled One, preceded and followed by the *praṇava* (oṃ). || 20 ||
First, there should be the syllable *Oṃ* for that fierce Nārasiṃha;
then, having uttered "Salutation to the Blessed One, Nārasiṃha. (21)
This twelve-syllable mantra is praised by all everywhere;
its first syllable, however, is modified by the six long vowels. (22)
One should join the *praṇava* (OM) at the beginning and end of those [mantras],
and having assigned the six limbs (*aṅga*) by means of the common designation.
[The Ritual Procedure for the Installation and Worship of the Vessel] Having first worshipped that which is within, one should thereafter worship that which is outside.
First, with the *praṇava* (Om), one should prepare the pedestal together with its base.
There, upon the honored back [of the deity], one should place a water-filled jar;
one should then install the mantra along with its ritual convention (*sāmaya*) by means of reciting it in reverse order. || 25 ||
One should place the six limbs, beginning with the weapon (*astra*), in the reverse order.
O Nārada, the weapon is placed in the heart and the heart in the weapon, as is appropriate. (26)
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the jar, one should then worship it according to the prescribed rite.
Therein, one should prepare the weapon-jar (*astrakalaśa*) and arrange the seat (*āsana*) there.
With the syllable *phaṭ*, however, one should place the wheel alone, bearing a purely red form;
it is devoid of a hub and rim, and above that, one should install a pitcher (*kalaśa*).
Having smeared [the area] with flowers, water-offerings (arghya), and incense, one should recite the Astra-mantra within that space,
beginning with the words "visarga" and "phaṭ," but in reverse order.

O twice-born one, having worshipped that [deity] at the conclusion of the offering of the sacrificial victim, one should then place an auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) in front of it; or, in its absence, [one may use] a mandala or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). Thus is the procedure for worship. 30.
Having placed the support (ādhāra) upon the ground with the syllable *praṇava*,
one should then place [the principles] beginning with Sovereignty (aiśvarya) and ending with Dharma above that.
O tiger among sages, one should fashion that great mass above it, resembling a heap of jewels, with the heart-mantra, and the remainder with the praṇava.
Having invoked the mantra from the heart onto its back, one should place it;
indeed, the body of dissolution alone [is established] according to the previously mentioned sequence of utterance.
[The Procedure for Offering into the Fire-pit (Kuṇḍa):
Having worshipped according to the rule, one should then prepare before it a single fire-pit, devoid of fixed dimensions and provided with a girdle (mekhalā). 34.
Having consecrated that [place] there in the past and having caused it to descend from the sky,
he [produced] a Vaiṣṇava fire by means of a sun-crystal gem (sūryakānta).
Because that [supramundane] state does not exist in the worldly realm, one should instead bring it forth and thus recollect it;
there, one should provide a layer of darbha grass in three directions, with the planets positioned in between.

Having consecrated the fire as before, he should then offer oblations with the mantra ending in "namaḥ," reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times with sesame seeds and clarified butter. [The Homa]
O Brahmin, having recollected the mantra by means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal until its end, one should then offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the water of the arghya offering.
[Now, the sprinkling and so forth of the corpse: Having sprinkled that corpse and struck it, and having gazed upon it with an eye full of knowledge and imbued with compassion, (39)
Having offered the arghya and flowers upon his head while standing at a distance and not touching him,
O best of the twice-born, he should then have him brought to his back and sprinkled with the two jars.
But when the seat has been drawn away, the Guru, remaining in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), sits down upon it after steadying his body with something and gazing at that [seat]. || 41 ||

But when one has died with prior karma purified, being exempt from the ritual of consecration (*saṃskāra*), the procedure for joining the soul to the corpse is performed preceded by an invocation; and the soul, having become solitary, has reached the state of proximity. (42)
Having summoned [the deity] with the mantra and placed it within the body, one should subsequently join it;
as before, however, into the corpse-mass, which possesses a radiance blazing like a jewel-lamp.
[The Mantra for Summoning the Life-force]:
One should join the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā-bīja) ending with the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by the name.
At the end of that, one should again place the seed-syllable of the crest ending with the Praṇava. 44.
Come, having entered this net, one should then apply it;
thus, having placed the life-force (jīva) here within the white [semen], it reaches its own place. 45.

[The procedure for uniting the soul, having been led to its own station, with the Supreme Reality: Endowed with the power of activity, like fire residing within wood, for this [soul], there is only the dissolution-oblation (*layahoma*) by means of the sequence known as initiation (*dīkṣā*). (46)
The preceptor should properly perform [the rite] according to the sequence beginning with earth and so forth;
then, having united [the soul] with the supreme reality (pare tattve), he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before.

[Now, the procedure for preparing the funeral pyre: Then, O Nārada, having sprinkled the ground to the south of oneself with water empowered by the *astra-mantra*, [one should prepare it] with sesame seeds, white mustard, and grains mixed together.
One should complete the Kālacakra, which is devoid of a hub and a rim;
outside of that, in front, is a triangle with twelve spokes turning counter-clockwise. 49.
Rich with flames the color of his body and endowed with three svastikas,
outside of that is a square city, radiant with five colors.
One should fashion [the mandala] endowed with five lines and adorned with eight vajras; one should cast the colored powder with the left hand in a counter-clockwise direction. (51)
One should construct a funeral pyre like a celestial chariot (vimāna) using wood previously gathered,
or with cow dung obtained from the forest by twice-born men and mixed with kuśa grass.
Then, starting from the southwest (antakāśāditaḥ) up to the southwest (nairṛtyāntam), the stakes (śaṅkavaḥ) are to be planted;
they should indeed be encircled with a thread wound three times.

[The casting of all the collected materials for worship into the fire of the sacrificial pit: O Nārada, having gathered all the materials for worship, including the food offerings (naivedya), one should then offer them as oblations into the fire situated within the sacrificial pit.
[The dismissal of the mantra from the locations such as the water-jar:

Having dismissed the mantra residing in the water-jar and that which is situated within the fire on the auspicious seat, one should dig the ground and sprinkle it with the water contained in the jar. 55.
Then, one should place the deceased's garment upon the funeral pyre and position the corpse thereon, facing the south.
One should place the yogapaṭṭa and other items upon specific locations of the corpse, such as its neck. || 56 ||
A spread yoga-band and a rosary in the right hand;
in the left hand, however, an arghya vessel, a praṇītā vessel, and a water-pot. 57.
One should place the two sandals on the left, and the parasol and the crown on the right;
in front, one should place the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) and whatever else, such as the conch and the ritual mudrās.
Having worshipped that funeral pyre with sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, and other offerings,
he should set it ablaze; then, using the fire contained within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he should ignite a bundle of *darbha* grass.
While gazing at that funeral pyre toward the southern direction,
the preceptor, standing facing it, should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Or one should cast [the remains] upon the head or into the opening of the mouth; there itself, one should discard the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. [This is the procedure for casting the weapon-vessel (*astrakalaśa*) into the sky, preceded by circumambulation of the funeral pyre.
Then, O twice-born one, taking the weapon-vessel from the direction of Varuṇa (the west), 61.
Scattering a spray of water, he should move around to the left;
then, holding the jar aloft toward the sky, he should cast it in the southern direction.
[Now, the procedure for bathing:
Having assigned guards there, the teacher should go to the body of water.
Entering the water with his clothes on, he should withdraw [his senses] by means of the mind. (63)
Then, having bathed according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the previously mentioned ritual placement of the body (vigrahanyāsa),
and after completing the bathing, sipping of water (ācamana), and other rites, one should offer a handful of water (jalāñjali).
Having emerged from the water and put on another garment that is pure and stainless,
O Sage, one should perform the rite of recitation (japa) with the Guru and others; standing upon a seat facing the east, one should meditate upon Nṛhari in the mind.
One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times with devotion, joined with meditation;
the carriers [of the palanquin] should recite half of that, and the bearers of the vessels half of that again.
[The necessity of performing the sacrifice for the Blessed One at night:
When it is night, or at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should especially worship Acyuta.
And at the end of the recitation and the fire-oblation (*homa*), the preceptor should then partake of food. (67)
Surrounded by his kinsmen and his own disciples for the sake of pacifying his grief,
he should perform the collection of the bones (*asthisañcayana*) when the third day has arrived. (68)
Having first worshipped Iṣṭāpūrtīśvarī with flowers, water-offerings, oblations, and incense, one should cast [the image] into pure water or into the unfathomable waters of a river. (69)
Once a pit has been dug in the ground, one should place [the bones] beneath it;
O best of Brahmins, one must not scatter the bones of those who have been initiated here and there.

Thus, this rite for the consecration of the body, which bestows the fruit of liberation, has been declared by me for all true devotees of Viṣṇu; indeed, it is a rite that must necessarily be performed by all upon the falling away of the body. (71)
Therefore, O high-minded one, the teacher must always perform this for his disciples, or the good disciples for their teachers, or likewise for women.

In the great sacrifice for those who have been initiated, all the purificatory rites and mantras are performed by the father or by the preceptor, without the need for a mother or other implements. (73)
Then, for the sake of destroying sins, it should be performed out of compassion by one's own son or wife—even by those who have not been initiated—with an intellect free from doubt. (74)
[The Specific Rite for the Cremation of Those Who Have Resorted to the Duties of an Ascetic] However,
for those who have resorted to the duties of an ascetic and for renunciants of action (*karmasaṃnyāsins*),
only cremation is prescribed, devoid of mantras and worship. (75)
[The Procedure for the Funeral Rites of Those Who Have Died in Absentia] Now the procedure for those who have passed away in absentia is described,
by which one who stands in either state attains the station of Viṣṇu. (76)
O best of sages, at the very moment one stands initiated in this teaching proclaimed by me, they have already attained my stainless state.

However, those *putrakas* who are initiates (*dīkṣita*) but have not previously fulfilled their commitment to constant worship, and who die while still ignorant of the rules (*samaya*), do so with their purpose unaccomplished.
They go under the power of their own karma to some impermanent abode,
and from there they return again after a long time with some kind of embodied form.
They are born at an auspicious time or an inauspicious one, in a favorable place or otherwise;
they perform meritorious deeds or evil ones, under the influence of that particular time and place. (80)
Through auspicious action one attains heaven, and through inauspicious action one goes below;
in this way, having withdrawn [the senses], the initiated person attains stability.
Moreover, when the teacher has passed away and is no longer present,
a capable and compassionate person must perform this great act of deliverance.
Understand how that occurred through the established nature of the body, after a certain devotee had previously recognized death according to the prescribed rule. (83)

At the conclusion of his own daily routine, however, he should worship the Lord in the images and other [media] with the specific rite prescribed for that purpose, ending with the fire-oblation (homa).
Then, having stirred white clay with the five products of the cow and water,
one should fashion an image twelve finger-breadths in height, according to that [deity's] form.
From the feet to the crest-lock, endowed with all limbs and members,
[one should fashion it] from the wood of the bark of the Palāśa or Aśvattha tree, or else from its sprout.
Having first placed that [image], which was fashioned on a yantra, in the location of Agni’s pit,
one should sprinkle it seven times with water while reciting the Praṇava along with the Astra-mantra.

Then, having struck [the vessel] twice with the three-syllable mantra ending in *phaṭ*—first in three ways and then in twelve ways using the *ātman* mantras—one should strike it again with the *arghya* rice grains. (88)
Then, with flowers or leaves together with a blade of darbha grass,
the knower of mantras should perform the rite of inspection with the eye of wisdom.
Then, having established the summary of reality— including the external world and the nature of the inner self—
exactly as before, in the sequence of creation.
The preceptor, following the path of meditation characterized by sequential stages,
should perform the fire-oblation according to the rule, using three, two, or one oblation.

Having understood that which is joined with the syllables of reality (tattvārṇa), conjoined with the root-mantra in a sealed union, and interspersed with the word "āyāhi," one should apply it for the sake of the intended purpose.
O Sage, one should [realize] reality after reality in due order according to the previously mentioned method;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the all-pervading mantra situated within the lotus of the heart.
For the purpose of bringing that [soul] back, it was properly equipped with a binding cord,
filled with compassion and bliss, and possessed the luster of a great ruby.
Having quickly made this known with the mind, and having recalled the threefold pure form from before:
"O Lord of Great Splendor, O Supreme Lord whose body consists of the six attributes! (95)
At the end of that, one should recollect the root mantra conjoined with the [deity's] form; then, having taken up any word whatsoever, one should remain established in it.
At the end of that, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable of nectar (Amṛta-bīja) adorned by Vyomeśa;
O twice-born one, the word "bring" (ānaya) should be joined twice, followed by its name.
One should indeed recite this mantra, accompanied by the salutation (namaskāra), externally;
one should remember it as completed by that [salutation], both what exists above and what exists below. 98.
Transversely, behind, and in front, reaching as far as the limit of the realm of Brahmā,
he draws in the soul— even if it is situated at a great distance— by means of his own splendor.
O twice-born one, quickly [consume] him with your own power, like a moth in a fire;
then you should assimilate that mantra together with the individual soul (jīva). 100.

Having purified the mantra within oneself, O Nārada, one should place the *jīva* into the image by means of the yoga of union (*sandhāna*), as previously described in the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Then, according to the prescribed rule, he should complete the initiation into reality (tattvadīkṣā) for him;
subsequently, by means of the yoga previously mentioned, he should unite him with the eternal state.
Then, by offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should burn the effigy;
and when the mantra has been raised from that very fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa). || 103 ||
Thereafter, one should perform all the previously mentioned rites, such as bathing;
then, for the sake of pacifying all defects, one should perform an expiation (prāyaścitta). || 104 ||
"O Brahmin, he may be healthy on another day, or perhaps capable on that very day.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Saṃskāras," in the glorious *Pāñcarātra-jayākhyasaṃhitā*. 24.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Atonement.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear the definitive rule regarding atonement."
For the pacification of all things done and undone, and for that of the devotee of Viṣṇu as well. || 1 ||
The Blessed One said:
"O tiger among sages, one who stands on the path but has abandoned right conduct falls downward; therefore, one must observe the conduct practiced by the virtuous. (2)
If a fault has arisen through fate, disease, or under the influence of delusion,
it should be washed away by recitation, as well as by giving gifts and performing fire-offerings.

O best of sages, having understood through austerity the strength and weakness of karma, [one should perform] the expiation for the omission of the *saṃdhyā*: in cases of omitting the initial *saṃdhyā*, the root mantra together with its limbs [should be recited]. (4)
One who is afflicted by disease should recite [the mantra] five times, endowed with the fivefold truth and so forth, each time;
one who is free from disease should recite the "seed of truth" one hundred and eight times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the twice-born should perform the entire ritual of the twilight (saṃdhyā).
Regarding the omission of the three twilights: if the three twilights are omitted, one who is free from illness should always perform the recitation as penance.
There are six hundred [mantras] for the root-mantra together with the form-mantra;
and for one who is afflicted by disease, there are three sets consisting of the root-mantra joined with the form-mantra and enriched by the six limbs.
One may recite [the mantra] daily for the sake of peace; otherwise, one incurs the fault of others.
[The expiation for the omission of the twilight prayers over many days:
When there is a lapse lasting for many days on the part of one who is afflicted by illness, [then this follows]. 8.
Having bathed, freed from disease, and having worshipped the Lord of the World, he should recite [the mantra] one thousand times, followed again by worship, fire-offerings, and libations. (9)

One should perform it with half the number of recitations for one who is free from disease; furthermore, the king of mantras may be recited twice, thrice, or for a single night, according to one's ability.
After reciting the mantra twenty thousand times, a special worship should then be performed;
one should offer one thousand oblations of sesame seeds sprinkled with clarified butter.
Thereafter, one should feed Vaiṣṇavas according to one's capacity, numbering three, two, or one.
[Regarding the expiation for consuming food touched by an impure person through negligence, or for serving another woman:
O best of Brahmins, if in the past it was consumed through negligence or unknowingly; || 12 ||
Furthermore, food and other items touched by those who consume liquor and the like, or by semen, urine, or feces, or licked by parrots, crows, or similar birds; || 13 ||
It is defiled by contact with village pigs, vultures, jackals, monkeys, and cocks, as well as by an outcaste, or rendered impure by the remnants of food from Śūdras and others.
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or having consorted with another's wife,
one should bathe, eat, and then perform the rite of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for a day and a night.
The wise one should recite the Siṃha-mantra a thousand times at each junction of the day;
for three days, he should eat only at night, bathe three times, and remain intent on meditation.
Having worshipped the deity, he should then perform a thousand oblations on the fourth day;
by providing food as before and eating only at night, the twice-born man is purified. (17)
[In that regard, the distinctions for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras:
One should prescribe this for a king whose mind is fixed solely on Nārāyaṇa;
however, bathing is declared to be twofold for a Vaiśya, and once for a Śūdra. (18)
The recitation for all of them is proclaimed to be double in successive order.
[The procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), which constitutes a limb of the aforementioned expiation:
milk, curd, ghee, cow urine, cow dung, and *kuśa* grass. (19)

Then, having placed water in a copper vessel and having consecrated it by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times for each [syllable], beginning with the root-mantra and ending with the weapon-mantra; || 20 ||
O Nārada, having bathed and drunk [the water], one should observe a three-night fast; then, whoever else might drink that [water] should meditate upon, chant the name of, and also worship Nṛsiṃha.
Even for him, the accumulation of great sins comes to destruction—whether it be theft, sexual union with the wife of a guru, the drinking of liquor, or whatever else. (22)
[The expiation for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa:
Having intentionally killed a Brāhmaṇa, one should remain in the midst of cows and recite the Siṃhamantra without weariness and incessantly for two years. (23)
Eating only food obtained unasked, bathing three times a day, and always acting as a trustee of deposits,
he should go to a sacred ford or a temple at the end of two years.
Then, according to one's capacity, one should perform a vow such as the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should indeed be initiated once again by means of the Navanābha rite.
He should give all his possessions to his guru and to his devotees by his command.
[The expiation for drinking liquor:
Having drunk liquor, he should recite the *Satya* mantra day and night at the end. (26)
Having fasted for three days, the wise man should drink water heated by a lion at the end;
then, staying in a temple of Viṣṇu, he should recite [the mantra] one thousand times.
[The expiation for stealing gold and so forth:

Having intentionally committed the theft of gold, land, or the like, one who is tormented by remorse upon realizing it should recite the *Kāpila-mantra* addressed to the Lord of Mantras (Maheśvara). || 28 ||

Staying in a secluded place, composed in meditation, and subsisting on water, roots, and fruits for a period of fifty thousand [years], one becomes pure at the conclusion of the worship and the fire-oblation.
One should intentionally renounce this collected wealth again;
and in its absence, one should perform twice as many recitations as previously prescribed.
[The expiation for approaching the wife of a guru:

Indeed, for unintentionally approaching the wife of a guru when no people are present, one should subsist on alms, observe silence, and recite [the sacred syllables] twenty thousand times for purification. (31)
If one is well-known, by repeating the mantra two hundred thousand times with desire, or even in secret with desire; or by repeating it twenty-five thousand times, one is purified, and not otherwise.
Having gone to a secluded place intentionally, one should recite it twenty thousand times;
but if done unintentionally in public, one should recite it forty thousand times.

Whether in public or in private, whether intentionally or unintentionally, one becomes pure only after performing recitation (japa), sacrifice (yāga), and oblation (homa) at the conclusion; not otherwise.

O best of the twice-born, due to the absence of the requisites for initiation and other such means, one who is attached to the wife of his guru is purified by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. (35)
[Expiation for eating food touched by a menstruating woman:
If one has intentionally eaten food touched by a menstruating woman, he becomes purified by reciting the Astra-mantra one hundred and eight times. || 36 ||
One should perform the recitation three times the usual amount, free from sloth.
[The expiation for eating food offered to the form of the Liṅga:
If a Vaiṣṇava indeed eats what has been offered to Rudra in the form of the Liṅga... (37)
If one touches it through negligence, one should recite the *siṃha-pañcaśata* [five hundred lion-mantras];
if intentionally, double that amount; and having bathed, one becomes pure through the performance of a fire-oblation (*homa*).
[The expiation for casting food offered to Viṣṇu in an unsuitable place or to an unworthy recipient:
Having consumed what was offered to Viṣṇu, if one should discard it anywhere or give it to an unworthy person, one should recite the Siṃha-mantra eight hundred times. (39)
[The Expiation for Consuming Food During Impurity:
O tiger among sages, having intentionally eaten food during a period of impurity caused by death or birth,
one should recite the Siṃha-mantra one thousand times.
If done unintentionally, one who is restrained and pure should indeed mutter half of that;
[this is the penance for eating the food of outcasts and the like].
O twice-born, this applies to the food of outcasts and of prostitutes as well. (41)
If food from a communal group has been eaten, one should perform the recitation of the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, and Kroḍa five, six, seven, or indeed a hundred times respectively.

[The expiation for eating food at the *sīmantonnayana* and other sacraments: He who eats during the *sīmantonnayana* rite should, when night falls, recite two hundred times the seed-mantra known as Aniruddha, remaining intent upon meditation.
During the sacramental rite known as naming, one should recite the Pradyumna mantra two hundred times;
during the sacramental rite of the first feeding of solid food, one should recite the Saṃkarṣaṇa mantra one hundred times.
In the remaining cases, one should repeat the seed-syllable known as Vāsudeva one hundred times.
[The expiation for eating food at a funeral feast (śrāddha) etc., held immediately after death:
He who eats the food of one who has passed away within the span of a year— 45.
Starting from the *sadyaḥśrāddha*, he should recite the *siṃha* mantra ten thousand times.
(p. 279) [Expiation for eating the food of a virtuous Śūdra:
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, from eating the food of a virtuous Śūdra— || 46 ||
A wise person should recite the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) one thousand and five hundred times in succession;
one should know that this [penance] is fourfold for eating the food of an unworthy Śūdra.

O twice-born one, having vomited, one should recite the Vārāha mantra three hundred times; then, having bathed and drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with that same mantra, [one is purified].
If one eats at the consecration of a non-Viṣṇu deity, or even at a sacrifice not dedicated to Viṣṇu,
one should indeed recite the Heart Mantra five hundred times.

[The expiation for eating in a garden, etc. In a garden, under trees, at a well, or outside a Sugata temple; at a water-station, a pond, or upon their release; at the ritual gift of a cow, or at the release of a bull (50).
If, on the occasion of a marriage or a formal selection of a bridegroom, one goes to another's house and eats there,
the practitioner of mantra should, without sloth, recite the Siṃha-mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having eaten in front of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times on the road.
[The expiation for eating the food of a naiṣṭhika, etc.
O twice-born one, if one intentionally eats the food of a naiṣṭhika or the food of a merchant, [one must perform the following]. 52.
Having eaten, one should recite the Mūrti-mantra a thousand times; if unintentionally, half that number. It is exactly the same for those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgins).
[The Expiation for Seeing Honey and Meat]:
If, due to negligence, one has seen honey or meat despite the prohibition, that fault shall be dispelled in a hundred ways by reciting the *siṃha* mantra eight hundred times. (54)

[Expiation for falling away from the observances: Because of the failure to maintain even the observances regarding sexual intercourse, food, drink, and so forth, one should recite one hundred and fifty weapon-mantras once the ritual placement (nyāsa) has been performed. || 55 ||
And likewise it is proclaimed that [this occurs] from greed for food obtained by begging;
one should mutter the Astra-mantra a hundred times for the loss of the resolve to sleep on the ground.
But when the expulsion of house-demons, piśācas, and the like has been accomplished,
one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times, encapsulated by the heart-mantra.
[Penance for performing dance, song, and so forth on occasions other than the attainment of knowledge, etc.

When the attainment of knowledge or consecration has commenced, during the vigil for Viṣṇu, when a temple or a sacred ford (tīrtha) has been reached, or regarding the scripture that reveals the true path—(58) p. 280).
Upon hearing of the death of his guru, when the tenth [lunar day] has arrived again,
he should perform dance and song without these [instruments] and recite the Satya-hymn one hundred times.
Then, out of necessity or affection, having performed rites for pacification and nourishment,
and having recited the Vārāha mantra three hundred times, one should worship the Lord of Mantras.
[The expiation for accepting worship during periods of birth or death, and during rites such as pacification.

O Nārada, if a practitioner of mantra should, out of desire, accept worship during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity, or at any time during rites such as pacification, [he incurs a fault]. (61)
One should recite the lion-mantra five hundred times here with devotion;
for the rite of atonement, one who is free from desire should recite it three hundred times.

[The expiation for performing rites such as eradication: O best of the twice-born, having intentionally performed rites such as eradication (uccāṭana) with a weapon-mantra, one must first recite it fifty thousand times; if done unintentionally, half of that amount.
A practitioner of mantra should never perform killing by means of a mantra.
Having performed the consecration of a deity and initiation at the three types of shrines (caityas) and so forth, [one must observe the following expiation]. || 64 ||
One should indeed rotate the three [deities] beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa in succession;
one should perform the fire-oblation and worship with one, two, and three hundred [oblations], plus eight.
[The expiation for accepting silk cloth and other items: Silk, cotton, wool, linen, bark-fiber, and even leather—if one accepts these anywhere at all— [one incurs an offense]. (66)
O Nārada, one should indeed recite the six [mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with the Weapon, starting from six hundred [repetitions] and decreasing by one in each successive case.
Whether done intentionally or unintentionally, the penance for each is half of what was previously stated.
[The penance for accepting milk and so forth:
O twice-born one, this applies to milk, curd, ghee, and whatever is produced from them. (68)
Having taken salt, honey, oil, and all products derived from sugarcane, one should recite the mantra three hundred times while joined with the Astra-mantra, [facing] the Boar (Varāha).
[Expiation for the appropriation of gems and so forth:
Having taken gems, silver, gold, coral, or likewise pearls, one should recite the Kāpila mantra three hundred times out of desire. (70)
And even if unwilling, one should recite that single [mantra] while devoted to meditation;
taking copper or other metals, or minerals such as those from royal mountains and the like. (71)

If one accepts a cow, a horse, a bull, an elephant, women, a she-ass, or a mule, the Nṛsiṃha mantra should be recited two hundred times if done intentionally, and one hundred times if unintentionally. [This is the expiation for accepting such gifts. 72.
O Sage, having taken it up, Nṛhari should be recited eight hundred times according to one's desire;
however, if without desire, he should recite it three hundred times while observing a fast.
[The expiation for accepting rice and other grains:
All types of grain, such as *śāli* rice, when accepted as gifts, require three hundred and two repetitions [of the mantra], whether done intentionally or unintentionally, while facing north. (74)
[The expiation for accepting a gift of land:
Having accepted even a small amount of land alone, one should recite the *Nṛhari* mantra a full thousand times, provided it is accompanied by fruits and rice. (75)
One should indeed perform this recitation twice as many times if done intentionally, and once if unintentionally;
the same applies to accepting a monastery, while for accepting a house, it is half that amount.
[The expiation for the commingling of sins:
O Nārada, when there is a commingling of even many sins, one should indeed recite the root mantra along with its ancillaries one hundred and eight times. (77)

Then, O twice-born one, having performed the five [limbs] beginning with *satya* through the process of transformation (*parāvṛtti*), one should mutter the seven-syllable mantra one hundred times, and then one hundred and eight times.
And due to the fault of mixing food, purification occurs at that very moment;
in the same way, one should perform recitation when a mixing of vessels has occurred. 79.
For the sake of purifying the confusion of lineages, one should recite the Truth three hundred times.
[The expiation for taking wood and so forth:
O Nārada, when there is the taking of wood, stones, grass, and the like— 80.
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, one should recite the *śikhā-mantra* one hundred times.
(p. 282) [Expiation for the theft of scriptures, etc.
O Sage, if knowledge or a scripture has been stolen from another through deception, || 81 ||
One should mutter the root mantra ten thousand times, with the form of the deity present.
[The expiation for reviling the teacher’s wife, etc.
Whoever, being deluded, reviles the wife or even the daughter of his guru— || 82 ||
One should recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times for each of the classes of deities in due order.
Regarding the expiation for killing living beings:
when a being with vital energy is killed, provided it is killed without leaving bones behind, [one should perform the following]. (83)
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, one should twice recite the Satya-mantra;
however, in the case of killing a mouse, one should recite it ten times, and in the case of a cat, indeed a hundred times.
For the killing of a dog or a jackal, the penance is double; likewise for a monkey or a cock, and also for the killing of serpents and other egg-born creatures, as well as for swans and other birds.
In the case of killing a lion or similar beast, or slaughtering a goat or other livestock,
one should recite the Nṛsiṃha mantra in sequence, from one hundred up to four hundred times.

[The expiation for being bitten by a dog, a jackal, or others: If one is bitten by any of these, such as a dog or a jackal, through negligence, one should bathe, stand in the midst of cold water, and recite the Gāruḍa mantra two hundred times.
[The expiation for accepting what is improper:
O tiger among sages, one who has accepted a gift—whether done intentionally or unintentionally, and whether with attachment or not—is purified by the recitation of the *siṃhajapa*. 88.
O Nārada, by bathing and meditating for three hundred [breaths], one is purified quickly;
[this is the expiation for touching] outcasts, barbarians, Caṇḍālas, Karaṅkas, and those who carry human skulls. || 89 ||
Upon touching a Soma-plant, a sacrificial post, a funeral pyre, a tree, or a Pulkasa,
one should bathe with one's clothes on and then mutter the Siṃha-mantra one hundred times.
[Expiation for reviling Vaiṣṇavas and others:
From reviling Vaiṣṇavas, and especially those who have been initiated,
from transgressing the command of the guru, and from neglecting the guru’s property— 91.
O best of sages, one should indeed mutter the *satya-bīja* mantra one hundred and eight times as an expiation for an ill omen,
as well as for the throbbing of the left limb or the sight of an evil dream. (92)
One should recite the mantra of Vāsudeva twenty-five times as an expiation for contemplating ill omens and for speaking untruths. (93)
One should recite the truth (the Gāyatrī) eight hundred times through action, speech, and mind.
[Regarding the expiation for the emission of semen:
When there is an involuntary emission of semen or similar fluids while one is asleep, [this is the penance]. 94.
Having previously bathed with one's clothes on, one should mutter the Astra-mantra a hundred times.
[Regarding the expiation for causing an abortion:
For an abortion caused intentionally, one should mutter the Nṛsiṃha-mantra ten thousand times.
[The expiation for killing a cow:
O best of sages, having killed a cow through negligence, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times or thirty thousand times;
one should bathe three times. If done intentionally, O best of sages, one should recite it twice that amount. 96.
Having performed a sacrifice as well as a fire-oblation (homa), one should give two cows to the preceptor.
[Regarding the expiation for cutting trees:
For the cutting of a tree, five, six, and so forth, in sequence, [are the penances]. 97.
O twice-born one, for every small cut, one should recite the mantra a hundred times;
for two hundred [cuts], one should diligently turn back the weapon-mantra.
If the mandala is broken on either the left or the right side, a twice-born man who has eaten there—whether intentionally or unintentionally—is [tainted] by the footprint of a Śūdra. (99)
One should likewise recite the Siṃha-mantra three hundred times and twice more for [the following]:
"Whoever causes distress to the Guru by deed, mind, or speech... (100)
Or one may engage in debate that likewise produces world-weariness;
having first spent three nights [in preparation], one should then recite the name of Vāsudeva within the heart.
O tiger among sages, one should perform this three hundred times daily during the three periods of the day.
As for the expiation regarding the voiding of urine and so forth in a temple or similar place:
"He who should void excrement or even urine in a temple... (102)

(284) Specifically regarding a temple or grove of a deity, and especially one belonging to Viṣṇu: [The expiation for taking leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth from such a grove for the sake of play:
"But for the taking of leaves, flowers, and fruits from that grove for the sake of play... (103)
O best of the twice-born, he who should do this must mutter the *siṃha* mantra one hundred and eight times.
[Regarding the expiation for performing a bath while naked:
Looking toward the sky and the quarters, he should bathe naked in the prescribed manner. (104)
That best of sages should then mutter the heart-mantra one hundred and eight times. [Regarding the expiation for disrespect toward elders and gurus:
This applies when in the presence of elders and gurus, or likewise upon their seat. (105)
Seated, one should recite the mantra of Pradyumna one hundred and eight times within the heart;
this applies when laughter at one's gurus has occurred or when vulgar speech has been uttered.
[The expiation for seeing the wife or daughter of one's guru with a wicked mind:
Having seen the wife or the daughter of one's guru with a wicked mind, the practitioner, having bathed, should indeed mutter the Siṃha-mantra five hundred times. 107.
[The expiation for killing a woman, a Śūdra, and so forth:

Having intentionally or even unintentionally killed a woman, a Śūdra, or a child, one becomes purified by reciting twenty thousand, ten thousand, and eighteen thousand [mantras] respectively, followed by a sacrifice. 108.
For the killing of a true Śūdra, the penance is double that previously mentioned in successive order.
[Regarding the penance for a Caṇḍāla entering a temple:
If someone who is a Caṇḍāla by birth should enter the temple, [the following applies]. 109.
One should discard all earthen vessels with the water used for rinsing weapons;
having performed the ritual bath with the *prokṣaṇī* water, one should remain there and mutter the *Kapila* mantra.
O Sage, twelve hundred [verses] are required there for everything to be purified.
[Regarding the penance for entering the house of washermen and others:
A washerman and a leather-worker [if one enters their house] whether intentionally or unintentionally... (111)
He should lie down after sprinkling himself with water consecrated by mantras and recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
[This is the specific teaching on immediate purification and other matters for the perfected one who is identical with Viṣṇu and established in disciplined practice.]
In both birth-impurity and death-impurity, there is no impurity for one who is eternally permeated by Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, for one who performs [the rite] along with its ritual application, immediate purification arises;
even in that case, one should mutter the mantra known as Vāsudeva five hundred times. (113)
One should avoid touching, eating with, or giving gifts to him for ten days; O great sage, through contact with him, even a perfected one (siddha) would incur fault.
[The Brahmins and others are unfit for the performance of recitation and other rites during periods of birth or death impurity:
Indeed, there is no entitlement to perform such rites;
a twice-born man remains so for ten days, a king for twelve days, and a Vaiśya until fifteen days have passed. (115)
A Śūdra must diligently refrain from recitation and meditation for one month;
this is the expiation for the contamination of food-leavings, even when the one who has been initiated into his own caste consumes what has been defiled by the leavings of another. 116.
O twice-born one, having bathed, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
for a person of mixed caste, such a recitation along with fasting is prescribed.

[The expiation for looking at one who is uninitiated: O twice-born, if an uninitiated person should see the Lord being worshipped, or his rosary, or a mudrā, he should then recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times. || 118 ||

[The Expiation for Taking an Oath in the Name of the Guru or the Deity: If an offense has occurred, one should not take an oath designated as being in the name of the Guru; nor should one take an oath designated as being in the name of the Blessed One (Bhagavat), even if it was performed through negligence. (119)
For that purpose, one should strive with effort to complete the worship, recitation, and oblations at the end;
for if the task is not brought to completion, the oath which was taken for its sake becomes void.
O Brahmin, for atonement one should mutter the three-syllabled mantra a thousand times;
one should perform a fire-oblation with half that number, along with worship while observing a fast.
If one, out of delusion, should take an oath when questioned by his teacher,
or if another, being evil-minded, should offer one, both of them shall go to hell.
[The expiation for mixed offenses: In all cases of mixed offenses, the practitioner of mantras should recite the Siṃha-mantra as the cause for purifying the mind, until the mind becomes serene. (123)

[Expiation for Theft and Other Offenses] O Nārada, in cases of theft and similar offenses, one should employ the *mūlamantra*; in cases of injury, the *siṃhamantra*; and likewise, the *astramantra* for all forms of purification. (124) p. 286)

O Nārada, one should employ the Heart-seed mantra in oaths, the Weapon-mantra in matters of what may or may not be eaten, the Vārāha-mantra in all acts of hostility, and the Nārāyaṇa-mantra in all rites for pacification.
The fourfold mantra of the Goddess is the cause for the purification of the mind;
by whatever contrary action has been committed here in this world, [it is purified by this]. (126)
O Brahmin, defilement arises within the self; for its pacification, one should recite [mantras], meditate, and perform oblations. Through this, the fundamental state (mūlabhāva) becomes serene.
As long as public censure persists, it continues until that [reputation] is purified;
through the stain of such censure, O Nārada, one falls into delusion.
By the power of the recitation of mantras, one's sin shall indeed depart a hundredfold;
or else, a living being may turn away from evil through meditation or through austerity.
Through the sacred bathing place, the recitation of mantras, worship, and burnt offerings,
he shines in the world like the sun when the clouds have cleared.
Therefore, for the sake of removing that cloud of sin, one should perform expiation;
in every way, for the sake of pacifying ill-repute and for the sake of the stability of dharma in the world. (131)
Nārada:
[Question regarding expiation when a mantra is impaired] When an impairment of the mantra occurs in the images and so forth belonging to householders, [an expiation must be performed].
[This applies] from the presence of kings, enemies, the waters, people, and thieves. || 132 ||

"O Lord of Gods, tell what must be done by devotees who are distressed by the fear of worldly existence, since you have stated elsewhere that the mantra is indicated by the scriptures and the rosary. (133)
Established upon a small bell atop an image, and situated among the supreme implements of sacrifice,
he was not worshipped according to the ritual prescribed in the Kalpa day after day.
But if she becomes enraged while pronouncing a curse, one does not attain success;
rather, it will produce many diseases, sorrows, blows, and anxieties. || 135 ||
The Blessed Lord said:

"The mantras that serve as the basis for the image and other supports, when installed, always bring about the presence [of the deity]—especially so for one who is devoted to the practice and whose mind is purified. (136)
Those mantras established as the foundation which were taught by the ancient teachers—when a calamity has arisen, one should always [perform] the rite of dismissal for them. (137)
By their own power and through their inherent capacity, they resort to their respective causes;
for indeed, when that support is impaired, the life-span of living beings perishes.
[The prescription for expiatory rites for the purpose of pacifying defects arising from the injury of an image that serves as the support for mantras:
O Sage, this must be performed for the sake of pacifying very great defects.
If this were to belong to that which is present and non-afflicted, then... || 139 ||
With diligence, one should begin the practice of self-restraint (yama) from that day;
or else, it should commence from the very day on which it was first understood. || 140 ||
Then, whether due to a lack of capacity or a lack of independence, one should nevertheless recite one's own mantra daily with devotion according to one's ability. (141)
Having reached each successive stage, one should perform it at the beginning of that day;
indeed, for ten days or one day, one should either abstain from food or consume only milk and clarified butter.

Or, eating only a small amount of fruits and roots, sleeping on the ground with his body cast down, he should—free from sloth—perform meditation, the mandala, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings. (143)
When the eleventh day has passed, one should worship ten and two preceptors who are absorbed in the Blessed One with devotion; thereafter, one should give twelvefold gifts.
And one should give everything according to one's capacity—the root of all—individually:
cows, food, gold, jewels, villages, silver, and sesame seeds. (145)
One should offer grain, elephants, horses, garments, and even the sweet and other tastes;
however, in their absence, golden and silver [images] may be used for the elephant and the horse.
This has indeed been prescribed for those who are capable, wealthy, and devoted;
however, for those with little means and lacking strength, a single meal at night is not satisfying.
An offering of curd, milk, and ghee, along with cows, Vaiṣṇava icons, and the like,
as well as the gift of gold and sesame seeds, should also be performed on those [days], specifically on the twelfth day.
Having given [the offering] in her presence, he should again perform the taking of the *mātrā* (measures), having received permission at that time according to the previously stated procedure. 149.
For those who dwell as celibate students (brahmacārins), forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), and ascetics (yatis),
[liberation] comes indeed solely from bathing, meditation, purity, and the recitation of mantras three times ten thousand times.
Otherwise, there would be purification; however, he falls into a state of degradation due to that sin.
For without sin, no loss of status can arise. (151)
The destruction of only that very sin accumulated in previous births occurs, by whose power a great mental anguish arises in the devotees. (152)

At the conclusion of the ritual for one who has died simultaneously [with the teacher], the preceptors born in the sacred field (kṣetra) should be honored; likewise, the Vaiśya should honor those who are masters of the three Vedas. 153.
One should recite [the mantra] twice as many times for each of the four watches of the night;
indeed, for whomsoever there is manifest fame in the world, having reached the assembly of the noble ones. (154)
This has been told to him for the sake of pacifying ill repute and misfortune, because public scandal is indeed censured by those who are self-restrained. (155)
O best of sages, what need has one who is perfectly accomplished for worldly things, since not even the slightest loss of his integrity is known in the world? (156)
He should then recite his own mantra three times ten thousand times in seclusion, following the very same rule prescribed for the student observing celibacy (brahmacārī). || 157 ||
One should perform the conjunction of the measures (mātrā) by which one may attain peace;
for if a measure has been lost, there may yet be a recovery. (158)
One should observe a period of residence for the sake of performing penance and other such efforts;
for even if all [the mantras] are lost, if at least one portion of a mantra is recovered again, [the purpose is achieved]. || 159 ||
"Having performed the purificatory rites, having attained [the state], having eaten, and having recited the mantra, one should then take it up.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation," in the glorious *Pañcarātra*, the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Sadhaka’s Practice of the Root Mantra.
Nārada said:
"The path to liberation has been proclaimed by you, as well as initiation for me in due order."
Now, please explain to me correctly the path of enjoyment (bhukti-mārga).
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O observer of noble vows, to the divine rites of the King of Mantras;
I shall describe them in brief for the purpose of accomplishing the rising from the netherworld (pātāla).
In the preparation of medicinal ointments such as *khaṭ*, *phaṭka*, *añjana*, and *kāśaṅgu*, as well as in the accomplishment of pills (*gulikā*) and other such rites—
[this is the rule regarding the distinction of locations and so forth in mantra-accomplishment]—
the practitioner, having become self-restrained and devoted to the vows of mantra, [should proceed]. (3)
Possessing great energy, virtuous conduct, and steadfastness, and endowed with all excellent qualities,
[he dwelt] in sacred fields, at holy fords, and at the confluences of rivers.
Endowed with pure food and avoided by those of mixed caste, he should take possession of a dwelling-place in locations frequented by sages and deities.
The wise and learned best of the twice-born, with his mind dedicated to the mantra, should perform three hundred thousand recitations according to the entire procedure previously described.
Having abandoned manifold ritual acts, one who has attained perfection bestows [boons];
when commanded, he swiftly performs the rites of subjugation, attraction, and killing.
It is the crusher of planetary fevers, poisons, and the like, as well as of malevolent spirits;
it is the leader of mantras for the subduing of all ḍākinīs.
Listen with a concentrated mind to how one should properly employ it.
[The method of application of the root mantra for pacifying spirits and other purposes:
Having prepared a divine mandala, one should place a water-pot there. (9)
Having worshipped the god Janārdana according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should place a pure and composed person upon a seat in front of him.
Having consecrated flowers together with white mustard seeds by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he should place them with both hands upon the patient.
One should meditate on a mandala in one's own hand, triangular and marked with fire; in its center, one should contemplate the Lord of the gods in the form of radiant splendor.
