Holding a blazing discus and mace in his hands, he should threaten all the wicked ones;
he should show that hand to the subject, which quickly causes possession. 13.
Seeing him, all beings enter [his presence] afflicted by fear;
as soon as they have entered, one should cause that Śaṅkhabandha to be performed.
The knower of mantras should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) here with ashes consecrated by the Astra-mantra, using the root mantra encased by the syllable *sāṃ*.
The wise one should strike [the disciple] with ashes over which the weapon-mantra has been recited;
furthermore, he should strike him with *kuśa* grass and white mustard seeds over which the mantra has been recited seven times.

He should offer incense of guggulu over which the mantra has been recited three times; or he should strike him with autumnal stalks [of grass] sprinkled with cold water, over which the mantra has been recited seven times. (17)
Then, having formed the Jayā mudrā, one should recite the mantra joined with the Astra-mantra;
and by means of this mantra, one may effect its subjugation as desired. || 18 ||
Should one strike Karna on the head with a mace for the sake of smearing his hands?
Or rather, one should fashion an image of the house out of cow dung.
If he does not release [the object] quickly, one should cut his limbs with a discus;
when he says, "I shall release it," one should always make him take an oath.
Having offered the bali-oblation, one should release the binding of the crest-lock and the directions;
likewise, one should release [the self] through action, mind, and speech as well. 21.
[The Method for Pacifying Poison]:
One should meditate on the mantra situated within the interior of the syllable *ṭha*, conjoined with the sixteen digits (*kalā*), resembling a lunar disc, and flowing with nectar. 22.
Having thus visualized it in the left hand, one should place it upon the head of the person to be treated;
and with that nectar, one should completely fill the body of the patient.
When employed according to this rite, it removes all poisons without exception.
[The method for subjugation: One should cause seven fragrant flowers, consecrated by recitation, to be given. (24)
O best of Brahmins, [one should touch] the right hand of women with one's left hand,
and the left hand of men with one's right hand.
By the power of this mantra, they immediately come under its control;
one should meditate on the mantra situated within the palm of the hand, in the center of a lunar disc.
To whomever one shows that hand, one shall quickly bring them under control.
Having performed the previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate a beautiful form.

Even if one stands before an angry person, one will quickly bring them under control; likewise, if a leaf, a flower, or even a fruit is given to someone after being consecrated with the mantra three times, [the same result follows].
By the power of this mantra, he quickly comes under one's control, whether using yellow pigment and saffron, or ashes and sandalwood. (29)
If one enters the royal court after reciting [the mantra] and applying the *tilaka*, one will receive great honor upon being seen; of this there is no doubt. (30)
[The Method of Exorcism:
One should meditate upon the mantra located within the realm of Vāyu, possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud;
situated within that, one should visualize the target (sādhya), supportless, emaciated, and immense. 31.
Wearing blue garments, dark yet equal in complexion to white, and light;
one should visualize the Lord being filled by the breath from the nose in the expanse of the sky. 32.
Being whirled about without support, he is quickly cast out; [this is the procedure for causing enmity].
He is situated within the realm of Agni and possesses a luster like that of a blue jay's wing. (33)
Having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras, one should quickly remember his two feet;
[one should visualize] the two objects to be accomplished, having the form of fire, looking at one another.
O Brahmin, by repeatedly and with great speed striking foot against foot, one creates hatred merely through meditation; of this there is no doubt. (35)
[The Attraction:
O twice-born one, one should meditate on the Lord of Mantras situated in the center of the solar disc, resembling a broken ruby, by means of the breath located at the tip of the nose. (36)
Drawing from a great distance the sādhya of radiant form, the Blessed One always performs this attraction through this very rite while meditating. (37)
Having drawn her forth, she bestows her entire abode upon the practitioner;
one should meditate on the mantra situated upon a white lotus, seated upon a bird-throne.
One should visualize those two objects of accomplishment (sādhya), appearing white and red in color, falling down from his two hands, having the same form as himself.
O best of sages, with a heart joyful, contented, and serene, one should lead [the disciple] along the path according to this procedure for the sake of his delight, by means of the king of mantras.
If even fire and water [cannot prevail], how much more so against human beings?
[Regarding killing:
One should visualize the Lord arisen as Cakra between the wind and fire cities. 41.
One should visualize the target as black and red, struck at the feet by him,
being violently crushed with the swift movements of his discus as if life were departing.
One should meditate upon him as having his power destroyed and with eyes closed; the practitioner by whom an adversary is thus targeted shall slay that opponent in no time at all. (43)
[The rite of] Stambhana:
[the deity] situated within the Maheśvara-maṇḍala, resembling water mixed with saffron, pressing with both feet upon the support established by the yantra. || 44 ||
The practitioner paralyzes whomever he desires in no time at all.
[The Ritual for Nourishment:
One should visualize the Lord, yellow in color and wearing yellow garments, situated in the center of a lunar disc. (45)

One should visualize that nectar, the ambrosia being vomited from the mouth of the Lord of Birds, entering the heart of the person to be accomplished through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). 46.
And one should visualize all the limbs as being pervaded by that [deity] stationed therein;
by this method, a person's limbs become perpetually nourished. (47)
[The Ritual for Pacification:
Having visualized two white lotuses situated within [the heart], complete and with the luster of the moon—
one above the Unborn (Aja) and the second positioned below— 48.
Resembling a spray of dewdrops, he stood freely in the midst, emitting from his body cool water that remained like milk. (49)
One should visualize the person to be acted upon (sādhya) situated beneath that [stream] being sprinkled;
for whomever you desire, O twice-born one, pacification (śāntika) is properly accomplished.
[The Ritual for Satisfying] O Brahmin, having first meditated upon the mantra— resembling saffron water, situated within a full moon, and vomiting nectar from its mouth— 51.
One should visualize it as white and yellow in color, situated at the tip [of the tongue], drinking either oneself or the patient with its two hands. (52)
Constant satisfaction arises through the power of the King of Mantras;
this is the fruit of the previously mentioned recitation, stated in brief. (53)
Even actions not explicitly mentioned are performed here when one is engaged;
and the word for action must be diligently applied in the context of preparatory rites (parikarman).
Performing it with repetition (*vīpsā*) and infused with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one shall attain success through a recitation (*jāpa*) twice that of what was previously stated. || 55 ||
[The Accomplishment of Vaikharī] Having reached the opening of the cavity, one should smear the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having worshipped the mantra according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with a concentrated mind. (56)
Furthermore, one may offer sesame seeds smeared with ghee, or indeed mahiṣākṣa resin,
or else fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood, or in its absence, stalks of dūrvā grass.
Indeed, when one hundred thousand oblations have been swiftly offered, one shall attain the perfection of Vaikharī;
having pierced through the mechanisms of the sattva, one shall enter the supreme aperture.
Having drunk this divine elixir, one shall possess the strength of Nārāyaṇa and sport with maidens until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the cosmic cycle.

[The Sadhana of the Sword] On a level patch of ground smeared with earth, one should draw a sword thirty finger-breadths long— clearly delineated with its parts, beautiful, and mixed with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma). (60)
Having worshipped Janārdana there according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should place the hand in the position of a fist and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind.
For one who is moderate in food and conduct, moderate in sleep, and free from weariness,
one should then cause the sword to be grasped by the fist as soon as it rises up.
Having grasped that, one shall become the sovereign of all vidyās;
one shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all the vidyādharas. || 63 ||
[The accomplishment of collyrium and so forth: One should worship the Lord of Mantras according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having taken yellow pigment (rocanā) in a conch-shell or mother-of-pearl with the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā), || 64 ||
One should recite the mantra for as long as it emits flames;
within those flames, a lovely maiden capable of assuming any form at will is seen.
She should say, "I am accomplished; perform whatever task you desire.
By this very procedure, one should accomplish the ointments and other such things.
[The Sadhana of the Pill] One should employ rocanā, saffron, yellow orpiment, realgar, and the medicinal herb marked with a wheel as the fifth ingredient therein. (67)
Having ground it finely and stirred it with the three sweet substances,
one should worship the Lord of Mantras within the mandala on the eleventh lunar day.
There, one should place that pill within the cavity of the yantra;
then, according to the ritual for white Arka, one should perform the recitation on the twelfth lunar day.
When that mantra has been recited ten thousand times, it becomes perfected;
with that [perfection] held in his hand, the practitioner of mantra, according to the rules, [attains power] within the expanse of the sky.
Whether in the netherworld, upon the surface of the earth, or in the cities of the world-protectors,
Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, is as unassailable by all the gods.
By the power of this mantra, a preeminent practitioner is born—
whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya— who is free from physical blemishes and endowed with auspicious marks. (72) [The practice of elixirs and so forth]
One should bring a single youth who has remained standing for a day;
having caused him to enter an empty house, one should then bathe and worship him.
Having worshipped the mantra in the mandala according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner, having placed a corpse seated there, should recite the mantra before it. (74)
One should strike it with one hundred and eight mustard seeds;
then, rising up with speed, it speaks these words while bowing down: || 75 ||
"What shall I do for you today? Let my command be given to me, O twice-born one; at your feet I have perfected the elixir of mercury and even the alchemical potion. (76)
Whatever else is desired by the mind, he grants it without hesitation. [The Sadhana of the Yakṣiṇī:
Having obtained a silk garment, one should draw the Yakṣiṇī upon it. (77)
Adorned with all ornaments, beautiful, and desired by the mind, one should worship the mantra as before according to the prescribed procedure. (78)
Having observed the fast, one should offer incense mixed with guggulu at midnight;
one should continue doing this for seven days and always recite the mantra ten thousand times.
For at the seventh watch, at midnight, the cloth [painting] vibrates with a sound;
O best of Brahmins, she remains visibly present, endowed with the splendor of her divine form.
But when the mantra-practitioner is not shaken, then she becomes accomplished for him;
she speaks, saying, "Which shall I be—your mother, your sister, or your wife? (81)
One should speak to her as one desires with a mind free from conceptual construction;
she, being perfected, swiftly accomplishes all the tasks of the mantra-practitioner. 82.
O best of the twice-born, she grants various desires in manifold forms according to one's wish, since she was formerly accepted as a wife. (83)
She eternally bestows inexhaustible treasures upon her state as a sister,
and she reveals the light between the worlds of Lokāloka without hesitation.
Then, for the sake of achieving peace, one should quickly prepare divine medicinal herbs, various essences, and diverse scriptures. (85)
When the time for battle has arrived, she who grants perfect success like a mother bestows excellent accomplishments; one should consecrate the weapons with mantras. (86)
Having consecrated mustard seeds with the previously mentioned mantra for the enemy's army,
using that very three-syllabled mantra enclosed by the *astra* [mantra], || 87 ||
Having gone forth with his eyes bloodshot with rage, he [struck] the enemy's army and weapons with a mantra and the power of fire, which was filled with garlands of flames. (88)
One should cast it into the midst of the army and destroy the enemy soldiers. [The immobilization of divine beings:
Combined with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), the name [of the target] should be interlaced with the mantra. (89)
One should draw [the diagram] in the center of the Kaustubha, endowed with sixteen digits (kalās);
for each individual digit, O Brahmin, was formerly joined with nectar.
And likewise, one should join above that the nectarine digits (kalās), which are established as the nourishment of the universe and possess a luster equal to the rays of the moon. 91.
Outside of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
one should write the goddesses and their limbs upon the petals within, according to the ritual worship.
One should paralyze all divine beings and ward off the sky-dwellers (khecaras) through worship,
fire-offerings, meditation, and the sprinkling of sandalwood water.
(296) [The Pacification of Portents:
Written upon birch bark and placed in milk and water, it shall destroy even the most violent portents accompanied by malevolent spells. 94.
[The Pacification of Fear from Poison, Weapons, and Other Dangers:
Having wrapped it with the three metals and written it out under the Puṣya asterism, or on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight when the sun has reached its meridian; 95.
For whoever always wears [this] on the arms, the neck, and likewise upon the head, no fear arises from poison, weapons, fire, or living beings. (96)

[The Accomplishment of the Wheel-Machine] One should fashion a wheel with twelve spokes, complete with a hub and a rim, upon birch bark or white cloth, using yellow pigment (rocanā) and sandalwood. (97)
In the center of that, one should fashion a lotus adorned with sixteen petals, using the root mantra consisting of three syllables in conjunction with the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa) of the name. || 98 ||
Having drawn that [diagram], one should write the twelve-syllable mantra outside it;
then, by means of the method of encircling, one should write it on each and every petal.
The seed-syllable of the goddesses is fourfold, extending as far as the filaments;
indeed, the number of these seeds reaches sixty-four when counted together in one place.
Then, O twice-born one, the Praṇava is written situated at the tip of all the petals;
beginning from the flower-petal, one should install the letters starting with 'ha'.

Then, sequentially up to the letter *ma*, one should write the head (*śiras*), the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the armor (*kavaca*) on the outside of the lotus, located in the three [sections] of the navel.
Then, O Brahmin, by means of the practice of encircling, one should write the weapons twelve times upon the spokes of the wheel, one in each interval.
O tiger among sages, one should apply the eye-mantra three times upon the rim of the navel-like circle; this yantra is the destroyer of all calamities.
Through retention, recollection, and meditation, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish. [The Conch Yantra:
Having drawn a twelve-petaled lotus situated within the belly of a conch shell, 105.
Having drawn [the diagram] with camphor and likewise with saffron,
one should write the three-syllable mantra together with the [deity's] form in the center of the pericarp.
By means of the arrangement in the shape of a circle, one should write [the name] in the center of that;
the three mantras beginning with Nārasimha are to be written upon the three petals. (107)
One should encircle the outer lotus again and again, four times,
in sequence with the mantras beginning with *padma*, according to the method of the "serpent-earring" (*sarpakuṇḍala*).
Then, on the area of the face of the conch, one should sequentially place the ten Lokeshvaras,
as well as the Astra-mantras and the female companions (sakhīs) of the conch.
O best of sages, this yantra is empowered by all mantras;
it is declared to accomplish all rites and destroy all calamities. (110)
It destroys all diseases and eliminates all ailments;
written under the Puṣya asterism, it correctly brings about all auspiciousness. (111) [The difference in results according to specific lunar days and asterisms.]
Then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the drawing for rites of pacification and nourishment by means of the procedure for consecration.
It should be employed everywhere and at all times for the protection against all beings.
[The difference in results arises from the difference in the substances offered as oblations and the difference in the number of oblations.
By the offering of one hundred thousand oblations of black-seeded sesame seeds, || 113 ||

O great sage, for as long as one year, at the conclusion of each fire-oblation, one should properly offer twelve hundred oblations of clarified butter with a sacrificial ladle while performing worship.
To him the Blessed One grants whatever is desired by his mind;
indeed, O Nārada, eleven thousand lotuses.
And whoever offers oblations of [these] soaked in ghee in a solitary, secluded place,
Lakṣmī immediately bestows her fortune upon him after she has been drawn forth from the water.
To him who offers ten thousand oblations of bilva fruits smeared with ghee, this Lord of Mantras quickly bestows abundant wealth. (117)
One should show villages, horses, and gold, both wrought and unwrought;
as well as long life, sons, health, and all-encompassing good fortune. (118)
Whichever deity one recites this Lord of Mantras before, she, being pleased, bestows upon him all his desires. || 119 ||
For when the mantra-king has been accomplished through meditative concentration, he brings about the attainment of mantras;
and when propitiated by worship and other rites, as well as by the fire-ritual, he likewise acts.
Even though some kind of ritual action exists on the ground, it quickly bestows everything upon practitioners through the power of recollection. (121)
[The Specific Majesty of the King of Mantras] O best of sages, listen to me as I declare this other matter:
the heroic power, the majesty, and the sovereign might of the King of Mantras. 122.
For one by whom he has been properly worshipped, known, meditated upon, and remembered even once, supreme success—both divine and human—comes forth. 123.
And there exists no mantra equal to this king of mantras for the sake of attaining happiness, good fortune, prosperity, and the realization of liberation. 124.
Having recited this Lord of Mantras, one who is devoted and full of faith, with his mind fixed upon Him in a solitary place, shall obtain all desires. (125)
O best of Brahmins, what need has he for hundreds of millions of other mantras, when this [mantra], which is like a wish-fulfilling gem, resides in his heart? (126)
Bestowing all desires immediately and granting liberation even at the end of the body,
one shall attain all desires by reciting this Lord of Mantras.
And there is no mantra equal to this, even by hundreds of millions of mantras.
Having thus obtained this supreme mantra, one shall shake off all that is fruit and non-fruit.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem in this world bestows everything desired, so indeed does this Lord of Mantras bestow [all desires] upon the practitioner. || 129 ||
When [the mantra] is always correctly propitiated, everything pertaining to this world and the next is attained—
even without worship, fire-offerings, and the like— once it has been recited one hundred thousand times, ten thousand times, or a million times.

O twice-born one, at the conclusion of the recitation, this king of mantras, when joined with breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and dedicated to concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna), bestows the supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā). || 131 ||
Without performing oblations or worship, one should remain reciting the mantra a hundred thousand times;
he directly beholds Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, in his supreme form.
O Brahmin, this [account] of the Lord of Mantras' ritual action has been told in brief for the sake of devotion by the foremost of practitioners, and not in excessive detail. (133)
There is nothing that the Lord of Mantras cannot accomplish when he is fully propitiated.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Practice of the Root Mantra for the Aspirant," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.

Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of the Mantras of Śakti," the Blessed Lord said: "O Sage, I shall now explain in due order the accomplishment of the mantras of Lakṣmī and the others."
And learn indeed from the mantras the various ritual actions. || 1 ||
[The commonality of the seat of Ananta and others for Lakṣmī and the rest:
And above that is Ananta, as well as the fourfold group beginning with Dharma;
this lotus, endowed with the three abodes, belongs to the entire host of mantras. (2)
Know that the general seat is always to be used at the time of worship. O best of sages, therein the door-sacrifice consists of the worship of Gaṇeśa and the other deities; this is common to all. (3)
The sacrifice to Lokeśvara and Astra is always prescribed everywhere;
however, in the case of the fourfold sacrifice to the Goddesses, it is performed with the six [limbs] beginning with Hṛdaya.
O twice-born one, one should worship [Viṣvaksena] during the sacrifices of Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, and Kroḍa;
however, Viṣvaksena is never to be worshipped elsewhere than in the sacrifices of Lakṣmī and others. (5)
[The ritual service for each respective mantra is performed with its specific heart-mantra:
Whatever mantra the practitioner, intent on attaining success, should worship, he should perform the ritual service for that very mantra using its specific heart-mantra alone. (6)

One should certainly not apply the previously mentioned secondary mantras; furthermore, in the rite of recitation (*japa*), the thread must not be obstructed by the root mantra. [The specific rule regarding the *japa*-thread. 7.
Having consecrated it with that mantra and previously joined another [to it], the incense bell and so forth are common to all mantras; the incense bell was described previously. (8)
O best of sages, I shall likewise describe the sacrificial hall, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), and the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva);
thereafter, I shall explain the six ancillaries (aṅga-ṣaṭka), beginning with the characteristics of Lakṣmī and the others.
The four seed-mantras of the four female companions,
and those of the four male attendants, are likewise situated in their proper order.
[The limb-mantra of Lakṣmī:
Having taken the Puṇḍarīka, one should place the Lord of the Earth (Dhareśa) beneath it;
having placed Anala beneath that as well, and having applied the sixfold [division], || 11 ||
One should gradually apply to these [the qualities of] bliss for the first [element],
and then Viṣṇu, vigor, sovereignty, the earth-sustainer, and the Supreme Lord.
One should place the lunar [syllable], conjoined with the Lord of the Sky (Vyomeśa), above all [the others].
Know that there are six [mantras], beginning with the Heart;
[this is the mantra of Lakṣmī’s companion].
Now hear from me about the friends. || 13 ||
Then, having taken up only the Truth (Satya), he placed Varuṇa upon it;
then Soma joined with Māyā, and Varuṇa adorned by Rāma.
Then, the lunar [power], pervasive, and the sequential [powers] should indeed be joined upon the heads of all;
Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Samṛddhi, and Vibhūti are her companions. 15.
[The mantra for the attendant of Lakṣmī:
The letter *la* resides in the primordial deity; then Soma is situated in the world. Having taken up nectar in two ways, it is conjoined with the earth-bearer (*bhūdhara*). (16)
As before, one should perform this fourfold rite for a long duration;
[the deities are] Lāvaṇya, Subhaga by name, and Saubhāgya as the third.
The fourth is mental joy (saumanasya), and these four are known as the attendants.
For all of them, the syllable Om (praṇava) comes first, followed by the name, and then "svāhā" or "namaḥ."
Having constructed a square maṇḍala with four gates as previously described for the city,
one should draw an eight-petalled lotus in its center, possessing a white and reddish luster. (19)
Having drawn four white lines and svastikas in the corners, one should first perform the placement (nyāsa) by way of pervasion, extending from the wrists, the face, and so forth. (20)
Having placed the root mantra solely upon the hands and the body,
one should subsequently, first of all, place the Lakṣmī mantra with both hands.
Then one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of its limbs, beginning with the heart and so forth, upon the hand and the body;
thereafter, one should place the quartet of goddesses that follows it. (22)

One should first place [the fingers] on the hand beginning with the index finger, then on the body, then on the head, in the center of the heart, and likewise on the two thighs and the two knees. (23)

O Nārada, having first placed the four [mantras] beginning with Lāvaṇya on the two hands starting from the nameless fingers (ring fingers) up to the thumbs, one should thereafter place them upon the body.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to rule upon the right and left shoulders as well as both wings, one who desires prosperity (śrī) should then worship in the heart through the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga). || 25 ||
Having performed the Lakṣmī-mantra alone by means of the application of the *layayāga*,
and having first performed the visualization (*avalokana*) and other rites, one should then place it externally.
[The purpose of the external sacrifice is the arrangement within the mandala:
O Nārada, the root mantra joined with the mūrti-mantra is placed upon the pericarp;
it is the Lord whose body consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and who is the essence of all mantras. (27)

And having brought down Lakṣmī, who was seated upon his lap, by means of his own mantra, he should visualize her according to the previously mentioned meditation for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (28)
Then, the four [mantras] beginning with the Heart are placed in the southeast, northeast, northwest, and southwest; the Eye [mantra] is on the filaments of the lotus.

One should place the four [deities], beginning with Śuddhā (or Ṛddhī), in sequence on its front, right side, back, and left petal; they have two arms and possess the same form as that [central deity].
Resembling a lotus in complexion, marked with the śrīvṛkṣa and the yak-tail whisk,
he was seated upon a lotus throne, gazing at his own face.
The group of four beginning with Lāvaṇyā is placed in the positions of the corners starting from the northeast;
they are yellow in color and possess four arms.
Clad in blue silk garments, he holds a lotus and a water-pot in his hands,
carries a lotus-stalk banner, and bears a mango tree laden with fruit.
Having assigned the weapons at the gates in the four directions and worshipped them as before,
O twice-born one, one should worship the goddess Lakṣmī, the bestower of fortune, accompanied by the root mantra— [this is the procedure for recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth]. 34.

Having performed the recitation (japa), one should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains mixed with ghee, as well as with *āmalaka* fruits, *śrīphala* fruits, parched barley flour (*saktu*), parched rice (*lāja*), and lotuses. || 35 ||

O twice-born one, at the conclusion of the fire-offerings, the practitioner, having become resolute and assuming the form of Lakṣmī, should perform [the rites] with innumerable offerings according to his capacity.
Having recited five hundred thousand times while maintaining a pure diet and subdued senses,
one should perform a fire-oblation at the conclusion of the recitation with bilva fruits and lotuses in their proper sequence.

O Brahmin, when an oblation is performed ten thousand times with offerings smeared with milk, honey, and ghee, the Supreme Goddess grants her vision at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice, bestowing the power born from the mastery of the Lakṣmī-mantra.
"O son, I have been accomplished for you; tell me what is desired in your heart. Perform all your desired rites with my mantra. (39)
"From this day forward, you shall be free from doubt and devoid of the afflictions of dualities.
Having spoken thus, that goddess departed for the place from which she had come.
Then the practitioner should indeed perform the rites prescribed by Lakṣmī;
when pleased, she bestows desired prosperity upon those seekers who long for wealth. (41)
When enraged, he can reduce a lord of the earth to poverty by mere word;
yet through a single act of meditation and the recitation of mantras, he can purify gold.
Having filled a water-pot with water, or with milk, or else with honey,
and having placed it in the right hand, one should place the left hand upon it.
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while endowed with meditation,
remaining focused on the placement of the vital breaths within the fluids, with a single-pointed mind and in a state of composure.

O twice-born one, the water brought into that vessel attains the state of the lord of mercury (rasendra); it becomes capable of piercing a hundred thousand targets and can [neutralize] weapons and the like.
He makes his body ageless and free from old age and disease;
first, he should take up a stone the size of the interior of a thumb.
Having consecrated with mantras two handfuls of jujube fruits— equal in size to a *badarī* fruit— held in his right and left hands, [he obtains] two hundred and sixteen [verses].
The stone situated on the right attains the state of a jewel, while that on the left becomes a pearl; both of these are indeed of great value.
Whatever one desires according to its species, that very jewel shall then become; likewise, whatever pearl appears to the mind, he creates that. (49)
Taking a bone produced from a cow, an elephant, or a horse with one's hand,
and having consecrated it fifty times with the mantra, it attains the state of coral.
Having consecrated tin, lead, and likewise iron one hundred times with mantras,
they become pure gold or stainless silver.
O best of Brahmins, whatever he takes up or whatever he desires—
whether in anger or in great satisfaction— he shall accomplish that very thing and not otherwise.
In this way, the distinctness of those made of stone is established;
for whatever manifestation the mind bestows upon anyone, that indeed comes to pass.
Having written [the mantra] on birch bark according to the sequence of sacrifice and ritual placement, he quickly bestows upon that person wealth, grain, cattle, and so forth.
O Nārada, he who always wears the Lakṣmī-mantra on his body, written with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma) and encased in gold, [attains prosperity].
There shall be a great increase in his lifespan and prosperity, serving as a refuge for all beings;
wherever he may dwell, he shall receive great honor.
This worship has been briefly proclaimed for those who desire prosperity.
Now, attend to me as I explain the ritual procedure for the Kīrti-mantra. (57)
O Brahmin, having drawn a lotus divided into six parts and situated upon a seat of fire, one should mark it with the head-mantra, O sage, according to the sequence of the group of limbs for Lakṣmī.
In all cases, one should avoid the insignia of the weapon-mantra.
[The mantras that are friends of fame (kīrti):
then Soma, which bestows peace, and then Mardana Śaṅkara. || 59 ||
Having drawn four [triangles] in sequence, situated within the fire of time (kālapāvaka),
one should then place the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī), the Lunar One (Cāndrī), and Māyā upon each of their heads.
Dyuti, Sarasvatī, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Kīrti constitute the circle of companions;
[these are] the mantras that follow Kīrti.
Furthermore, there is Varuṇa, endowed with bliss, and the immeasurable Kevala alone. (61)
The purifier mounted upon fire, likewise wearing a garland,
and overcome with bliss, is joined to the heads of the four.
The nourisher of all, the pervasive one—these are your successive attendants:
Vāgīśa, Abhaya, and the one known as Prasāda and Trāṇa.
[The procedure for the mandala and so forth is as before: Know that the ritual placement (nyāsa), the sacrifice at the heart-lotus, and everything else has been previously explained.
Having constructed the mandala described earlier, one should place white and yellow [colors] within it. (64)
However, one should indeed fashion a lotus and subsequently place it there; one should place Kīrti upon the lap of the Lord, and the heart and other limbs as before.
[The manner of meditation for the female companions and the attendants:
Now hear in sequence the meditation upon the female companions and also upon the attendants.
They have two arms, are golden in color, possess the form of Kīrti (Fame), and have smiling faces. (66)

One should meditate on them as having the color of the *kiṃśuka* flower, possessing lovely forms that captivate the mind; holding a fine book in their left hand and a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) in their right hand.
Then, one should contemplate within them the four attendant figures, four cubits in height and clad in white garments, with their primary left and right hands [held in specific gestures]. || 68 ||

Understand from me that the two supreme [goddesses] reside upon a great tree called kadamba, which shines like a hundred moons and conch shells, is covered in beautiful flowers, and is frequented by bees. 69.
O twice-born one, having meditated thus upon [the deity] resembling the full moon, holding a mirror in the left hand and a bright peacock-feather fan in the right, one should then perform worship.
[The Procedure for Homa and Japa:

Having properly offered the water for honor (arghya), flowers, and so forth, one should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to one's capacity, using sesame seeds sprinkled with clarified butter and accompanied by perfumes and incense. 71.
At the conclusion of the fire oblation, having assumed the form of the Goddess with flowers, collyrium, and garments,
one should remain in a solitary, secluded place, observing silence and subsisting on roots and fruits.

The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, O best of Brahmins, he should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) one hundred thousand times with rice mixed with sesame seeds.
O Nārada, with cow-derived ghee mixed with milk, one should likewise perform a thousand oblations for each of the substances beginning with ghee. (74)
Thereafter, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with milk mixed with clarified butter;
when the full oblation has fallen, the Supreme Goddess arrives. (75)
Standing before the practitioner, she indeed says, "Excellent! Excellent!
and [speaks]: "Come, come to the supreme abode; abandon this material city."
"Enjoy supreme enjoyments while situated in the midst of the stars, O great one!
O practitioner, perform all my ritual action with the mantra. (77)
Having spoken thus, that goddess shall then depart into the sky;
the practitioner, by means of the Kīrti-mantra, should perform whatever rite he desires.
Whatever he gives to anyone, that becomes inexhaustible for him;
by means of that, he attains fame as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. (79)
If one who stands as a mediator among fierce men awakens them, or says something in the assembly, he shall obtain vast renown. || 80 ||

Having overcome all people, he attains preeminence; and by chanting [this mantra], one obtains a vessel of prepared food, even when there is a scarcity of food at that time, however small it may be. (81)
O twice-born one, if one gives food according to the desires of people who have whatever they wish for,
continuously for seven days, that gift becomes inexhaustible.
One shall obtain great fame until the dissolution of all beings, even by giving a mere fragment of gold during a time of plenty. (83)
Having recited it a thousand times according to the prescribed rite,
it attains great power and is bestowed upon those who seek its benefit.
If one does not reach exhaustion for two weeks continuously, O twice-born one, he shall thereby attain great and eternal fame. (85)
O twice-born one, taking a water-pot from the abode of the lord of the nāgas, you should indeed travel to the desert land;
there, upon the low-lying ground, [you shall find it].
Or, having cast it upon the mountain peak after reciting the mantra a thousand times,
O twice-born one, that lord of serpents, accompanied by his attendants, [resides] there.
Guarding the water, he should remain standing as long as the earth endures;
by that means, O Nārada, he attains great fame in the world. (88)
But if, when it is the time for seeds to sprout, the god does not send rain, one should take a handful of earth from a pond that has been softened by water and hold it in the hand. (89)
Having recited that [mantra] three hundred times over one who is distressed by fear and indifference,
and having heated him with the breath from the mouth of Ka-Kha, one should recollect the mantra.
Just as that [water] would be cast into the sky and attain the state of a cloud, so too that cloud would fill the entire earth with water. 91.
By his command, that king of clouds shall dwell in that region for as long as it takes for all that is necessary for the rain to be fully accomplished.
By that, O best of Brahmins, he shall attain great fame throughout the three worlds;
he accomplishes whatever is desired by his mind.
By the power of the king of mantras and through the grace of Acyuta, [the mark] should be written as before and bound upon a cloth on the right arm. (94)
One shall attain great prosperity and complete fame as Sarasvatī;
this, O Nārada, has been declared in brief regarding the Kīrti-mantra.

[The Method for Accomplishing the Jayā-mantra] Now learn the unprecedented ritual procedure called Jayā, which bestows prosperity even upon one's lineage, intended for those who contemplate Viṣṇu. 96.
[The limb-mantra of Jayā:
Having taken the eternal [syllable] and divided it into six parts, one should place them in the fire in sequence;
as before, one should cause them to be stepped upon for the sake of accomplishing the six limbs. (97)
[The mantra of Jayā’s friend:
Ajita joined with Viṣṇu, Vārāha surrounded by Rāma, Vyāpaka, and then Kevala, as well as Soma accompanied by Rāma. (98)
O Sage, one should mark the four [directions] in sequence with the head as before:
Jayantī, Vijayā, and the third, Aparājitā. (99)
The fourth *siddhi* is to be known; listen now to the attendants.
(p. 307) [The mantra of the attendant of Jayā:
O twice-born one, Padmanābha is mounted [upon it], eternal and absolute. 100.
And one should apply these [syllables], including the *pradhāna* and the *uddāma*, in sequence; above which the *vaineya* is placed, accompanied by the moon and the sky. (101)
Pratāpin, Jayabhadra, and the third, Mahābala;
the fourth is named Utsāha—having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) as before. (102)
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, one should then perform worship outside [the enclosure].
[The Procedure for the Maṇḍala, etc.
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before, one should draw a lotus in its center. || 103 ||
And with pollen equal to a blue lotus, he should fashion an eight-petaled [lotus];
there, he should join Jayā, seated upon the lap of Viṣṇu, to his heart. 104.

One should perform the placements (nyāsa) of the remaining groups of mantras according to the sequence of each preceding one; now listen to a concise summary of the visualization for all of them. 105.
[The manner of meditating upon Jayā’s friends and attendants:
Regarding the heart and other centers previously mentioned in connection with the root mantra:
they are the color of blue lotuses, with serene faces and eyes. (106)
All the female companions wore yellow garments and golden earrings; they held white chowries in their hands and carried upraised leaves and fruits of various colors. || 107 ||
Gazing upon the faces of Jayā and Ajitā, they possessed the luster of jasmine buds, their lotus-like faces serene. || 108 ||
Wearing red garments, four-armed and possessed of great strength, they held bows and arrows in their hands, as well as maces and discs, O twice-born one. (109)
The four attendants, adorned with flower ornaments, should be meditated upon;
then one should worship them with devotion and subsequently perform the fire sacrifice (homa).

[The Procedure for the Homa and Other Rites] O best of Brahmins, at the conclusion of the homa, having fashioned an image consisting of victory with sesame seeds mixed with white mustard, clarified butter, and guggulu resin; 111.
Having perceived with his mind, "I am victorious," he approached the great *vīrasthāna* (hero’s station), which was solitary and free from people, remaining there without hesitation. (112)
Having performed the binding of the directions with the armor-mantra (varman) and the weapon-mantra (astra) for the destruction of evil,
he should thereafter begin the recitation (japa), always subsisting on milk, food, or fruit.
O Nārada, being disciplined with internal assistance, silent, and devoted to meditation, one should first prostrate with the head to Hari while reciting one's own mantra.
One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa).
The sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) should be one span (prādeśa) in length and made from red sandalwood.
One should perform ten thousand oblations of those [seeds] smeared with ghee;
O great sage, one should also offer twenty thousand *siddhārthaka* seeds mixed with honey.
Then one should offer thirty thousand oblations with black sesame seeds mixed with the three kinds of honey,
and at the end, three full oblations.
O Brahmin, one should perform the oblations in sequence with honey, milk, and clarified butter;
then, O Brahmin, the Goddess Jayā herself arrives.
[The grace of Jayā:
"I am well-pleased with you, my son; perform with my mantra whatever task you desire, free from doubt and devoid of anxiety. (119)
Having spoken thus, the Goddess, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, vanishes from sight.
Then one should perform various and manifold rites, born of the power produced by the mastery of the *jaya* mantra. (120)
Whatever things are desired in this world, whether for oneself or for another—even regarding those, I shall speak by way of summary; listen to them in truth, O Nārada. (121)
The practitioner should meditate upon the goddess seated on a throne of flames by means of her mantra;
indeed, he causes whatever object it may be to be raised up, in whichever matter it occurs.
Having conquered that enemy army— which is full of elephants, horses, and weapon-bearers, and is endowed with great strength— by means of justice, he indeed attains victory without effort.
Seeing another who had arrived in battle intent on killing him,
he consecrated his bow, sword, shield, and five arrows with mantras.
Having indeed bestowed this upon someone, he should urge him forward; having gone to the front of the army, even alone, he rends the enemy and attains eternal victory. || 125 ||
Having meditated upon the triangular mandala of fire situated in the right hand, one should contemplate the Goddess in its center, accompanied by her retinue. (126)
One should display [this mudrā] toward intoxicated elephants, lions, serpents, and thunderbolts;
upon seeing that palm of the hand, they quickly turn their backs and flee.
Having touched and taken up a pestle made of khadira wood, having empowered it with a hundred mantras, and having gone to the entrance of the cave accompanied by people of the four castes; 128.
O best of Brahmins, one should there gradually offer eight blows with a pestle,
using the mantra of the Goddess encased within the *astra-mantra*.
Then, with the syllable *phaṭ* at the end, the excellent practitioner, accompanied by all the people, should proceed downward to the underground mechanism (*bilayantra*). || 130 ||
Having shattered numerous mechanical devices and conquered the foremost of the Dānavas,
he remained there for a yojana with his groups of beloved women.
Having personally given him a drink consisting of nectar with his own hand, the one of great strength departed by that very same path along which he had come to his own abode.
O best of Brahmins, if the minister forms the resolve to conquer the three worlds, he will achieve victory without hesitation, rising up armed with mace and discus. (133)
Or else, holding a noose and a goad, one attains victory; it cannot be otherwise.
Having written [the mantra] with thick saffron on birch bark using the method of application, [one achieves this]. (134)
Having indeed performed the ritual of encapsulation (saṃpuṭīkṛtya) and having placed [the name] amidst the people, he always attains victory effortlessly through all divine means. || 135 ||
Having drawn [the design] with sandalwood paste, milk, and saffron, one who wears it on the neck, on a garment, or on the left or right arm, [attains the desired fruit]. (136)
O Brahmin, tiger among sages, he attains victory everywhere without hesitation through this mantra for the sake of victory, wherever it may be. (137)
The practitioner should constantly employ [this] here and there, and therein he shall obtain victory;
thus has the procedure for victory been briefly proclaimed. (138)
[The Method for Accomplishing the Māyā-mantra] Now I shall describe, exactly as it is, the ritual procedure known as Māyā.
(p. 310) [The Limb-mantra of Māyā]
Having taken up the sixfold primary [elements], it is established within the fire of time.
Then one should mark that [body] as before with the vowels, beginning first with the head;
know, O great sage, that these six are indeed the heart and the other [limbs], while the remainder is the rest.
[The Consort-mantras:
Then Pradhāna, Dhruvā, Rasthā, Padamānā, and Po’nalordhvagā; then all the Ādeyas, followed by Odanā and Ānandakā in sequence. (141)
Bhuvana, Yogaghātā, Vyāpinī, and Cāndrī are present in all four [elements], O great sage; as are Mohinī, Bhrāmaṇī, Durgā, and Preraṇī. (142)
These four, radiant with blood, are indeed known as the companions of Māyā;
[this is the method of meditating upon the companions] by means of their charm, heroism, beauty, and splendor. 143.
But those joined with the one called Māyā are clad in white garments and anointed with unguents;
holding chowries and goads in their hands, they remain seated in the lotus posture. || 144 ||
[The subsidiary mantras of Māyā:
One should indeed give that which is primarily endowed with concealment as it alone;
and one should give Śaṅkara and Kamala in sequence as they alone. 145.

O Brahmin, one should place the pervasive [syllable] of Brahmā and that of the Moon above all; and for each one previously [mentioned], one should place the syllable Oṃ at the end, joined with its own name.
Māyāmaya, Mahāmoha, Śambara, and Kalīśvara—these four attendants are indeed to be meditated upon as possessing the splendor of the Āli family. || 147 ||
[The mode of meditation for the attendants of Māyā: They have four arms and large bodies, with gentle faces and smiling countenances;
they are adorned with armlets and ornaments, and indeed wear yellow garments. 148.
Adorned with necklaces and anklets, decorated with various flowers, white as the dust of frost, they held aloft swords and nooses. (149)
Having thus duly extracted the arrow from the bow and the parasol from the two hands, one should perform the ritual salutation with the mantra of Māyā.
[The Ritual of Deposition (Nyāsavidhi):

Having performed the deposition on one's own hand as before, one should immediately thereafter perform it upon the body; having meditated upon [the deity] within the heart, one should then cause it to descend externally. (151)
[The Procedure for the Outer Sacrifice] All the limbs and other components should be deposited within the embrace of the mantras as before.
[The Procedure for the Mudrās]
Having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rule, he should then display his own mudrā.
That [mudrā] is taught as being common even to the four previously mentioned distinct [deities], and it is characterized by the friction and union of all the deities' mudrās. (153)
Know, O Nārada, that this is the root mantra, endowed with the limbs of the deity, and common to the sixteen female companions.
Pay close attention even to this single mudrā joined with its own mantra:
[the Mahāyonimudrā]. Having placed the two hands facing each other, they should likewise be fully extended. (155)
O twice-born one, one should join the pair of the little fingers and the pair of the ring fingers together at the tips of the nails, so that they appear as a single mass.
With three fingers in the middle of the palm without support, one should place the two thumbs like a staff, extended and touching the edges. || 157 ||
Having rested the four fingers up to the belly, one should diligently form the two index fingers like a serpent’s coil. 158.
O Great Sage, having extended the two middle fingers forward and joined them at their tips, it is brought back from the birth-place for a distance of two cubits. (159)
And one should join them very closely from the base up to the ends of the wrists, with the two hands barely touching the roots of the thumbs at the wrists. (160)
One should make it fully expanded; this is the mudrā called Mahāyoni, O best of sages, which was the mother of the three worlds in ancient times. (161)
If one should desire to bring the entire world under control, one should employ [this rite];
a woman devoted to its performance should bind [the object] and display it from a distance. (162)
They cause agitation in an instant even for sages who have abandoned all attachments;
or perhaps a man here, being incited, might show interest toward women. (163)
O Sage, even women whose passions have ceased are agitated when they are afflicted by desire; what then need be said of those who still possess desire? (164)
[The Anucara-mudrā] I shall now briefly describe the mudrā of the sixteen attendants, which is common to all and auspicious for the purpose of invoking their presence. 165.
Having placed the two hands joined behind the back, one should then release them;
likewise, the pair of index fingers and the pair of ring fingers [should be released]. (166)
O great sage, with those two [hands] facing clearly downward,
the two little fingers are joined at their middle, while the two index fingers are held apart.
One should hold the pairs of the middle and ring fingers together,
joined at a single point from the tip of the nail up to the middle joint.
O best of sages, with the face turned upward and the body held level by the earth, the two thumbs should hang down clearly, facing downward. (169)
When standing at a distance from one another, this mudrā grants all desires;
one should display it at the time of worship while joined with one's own mantra. (170)
And she resembles the four-armed [deity], bestowing the accomplishment desired by all.
Having thus displayed the collection of mudrās and recited the mantra immediately thereafter, || 171 ||
[The Procedure for the Homa and Other Rites] Thereafter, one should indeed perform the homa with sesame seeds mixed with white mustard,
along with rice and other grains saturated with saffron, ghee, and milk. 172.

Then, O Nārada, having resorted to the observance (*niyama*) and subsequently, through the practice of meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), one should transform oneself into the form of the Goddess. (173)

Accompanied by mature attendants and provided with his own seat, the observer of the vow should proceed to a place inhabited by twice-born men and perform seven hundred thousand recitations according to the previously mentioned rule.
Subsisting on milk, roots, and fruits according to the requirements of place and time, he likewise ate only a single alms-meal that was unasked for, or, in its absence, O Nārada, [he lived on water].
And food prepared by his own disciples, purified by mantras and free from salt, oil, and meat—even when the time of twilight has arrived—[he should eat]. (176)
Even if not yet satiated, the practitioner of mantras should eat the food consecrated with honey and clarified butter;
at the conclusion of the recitation, he should diligently perform the fire-oblation according to the rules.
Balā, modā, māṃsī, cakrāṅgī, nāgakesara, powdered kuṅkuma, sandalwood, and the powder of turmeric. (178)
One should mix white sesame seeds with honey, and likewise saturate them with ghee; thereafter, one should perform three hundred thousand oblations.
O Nārada, with the middle and ring fingers and the tip of the thumb,
one should perform the supplementary oblation (parihoma) with three ten-thousand fuel-sticks at the end.
First, ten thousand [oblations] of khadira wood originating from the rājārka tree;
after that, another [ten thousand] of suradāru wood; and then a third [ten thousand]. || 181 ||
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with a purified inner self;
when the final oblation has fallen, the Supreme Goddess arrives. 182.
Accompanied by her retinue, the Goddess spoke: "Excellent, excellent!
Now perform your desired task; go forth with the mantra. (183)
Having said this, the goddess would swiftly depart for the abode of Viṣṇu.
Then that best of practitioners [attains] various accomplishments and diverse powers. (184)
O Brahmin, listen briefly, O Nārada, to those things which one should always undertake with the mind, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others. (185)
Having recited [the mantra] over an *āmalaka* and a *bilva* fruit once, one should enter the king's palace;
having cast them before the treasury, one may remain wherever one wishes.
Whatever he desires as soon as it falls swiftly from the sky, O Brahmin—whether it be an ornament or whatever auspicious garment—[he obtains]. (187)
In this same way, one should cast a ball of rice, as well as sesame and rice,
into a full threshing floor, a granary, or a pit.
Likewise, wherever royal gold may be located, from there one obtains whatever grain, crop, or rice-filled produce one desires. (189)
Then, having consecrated the medicinal pill with mantras, it falls from the sky right before him, or wherever he desires; in this very manner, one obtains the food of the Siddhas.
Having cast it into the area of the kitchen, one should cause cooked food to rain down in an instant;
having made a pill from cow dung the size of a jujube fruit.
Having cast [the vessel] inside a cow-pen after consecrating it seven times with mantras, at the end of a mere moment of meditation, it becomes filled with curd, milk, and clarified butter. (192)
And wherever he may be standing, the observer of the vow should look back at his belongings; O Brahmin, having muttered [the mantra] over a jujube fruit or some other fruit, he should proceed. (193)
One should cast [it] into Madhuvana, and it brings about the drawing forth of fruits for the king;
furthermore, one should cast a single flower into the Puṣpavāṭikā garden.
Having recited the mantra three times, the practitioner of mantra should instantly attract flowers;
wherever those arising from his body are cast, they should be consecrated seven times with the mantra.
Once the resolve has been made, it shall remain in each respective place;
drawn according to one's desire, it shall go to that very place.
Nor does the excellence of the practitioner ever fail to manifest anywhere,
O Nārada, once he has performed the rite with a charcoal ember over which the mantra has been recited a hundred times.
One should cast into the midst of water a drop of water resting on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass that has been consecrated one hundred times; it is seen blazing [therein]. 198.
Having prepared it, one should cast it into a blazing mass of fire;
in an instant, that fire will appear like water.
Having seen a forest filled with sand and devoid of grass, one should cast there a blade of grass over which a hundred mantras have been recited.
One should make that place, strewn with flowers and leaves and crowded with foliage and sprouts,
surrounded by water and rice, equal to the Nandana grove.
It was filled with various kinds of birds, provided with city parks and groves,
complete with city walls, and endowed with temples for the deities.
Accompanied by the sounds of songs and celestial music, and graced by beautiful women—this wonder of kings is indeed always worthy of being beheld. (203)
Indeed, in forest regions devoid of dwellings and lacking moisture, they always obtain water, food, and various enjoyments according to their wish. (204)
O best of sages, when the host of enemies is standing face-to-face, one should perform [this rite] with eight lumps of earth and cow-dung consecrated by mantras. (205)
And if, while intent on killing out of anger, he remains alone, he should indeed recite [the mantra] properly, having formed a great resolve in his mind. (206)
O Brahmin, his own army, crowded with soldiers and weapons, will quickly become possessed of terrible prowess. (207)
Having seen his army—consisting of elephants and horses, resplendent with various weapons—turning its back, he [the enemy] retreats with his forces deprived of their vigor. (208)
Whatever a Brahmin does with his mind while reciting a mantra—whether it be false or true—it is perceived as being exactly so. (209)
Seeing a tree that is completely withered, one should strike it with one's foot while reciting the great mantra, until it becomes endowed with flowers and fruit. (210)
While reciting the mantra with both hands, the practitioner should squeeze the tree endowed with sap, flowers, and fruit; he then attains that which has been dried up.
O Brahmin, if one standing on a mountain peak recites the mantra for the purpose of destruction, it shall go downwards as far as the practitioner desires.
Being satisfied, he should thereafter raise the mountain again from the netherworld (pātāla).
One should write the mantra upon the interior of a lotus using sandalwood paste.
Then, on an auspicious day, having drawn the limbs upon the leaves and having worshipped them with water-offerings, flowers, and other articles, one should encircle them as before.
For one who maintains this great mantra, all prosperities shall manifest here in this world; moreover, he shall be free from all thorns.
He shall be very beautiful, long-lived, and attain auspiciousness in the hereafter;
this, in brief, is the collection of siddhis belonging to the four goddesses. (216)
A brief summary has been declared for the benefit of practitioners;
they bestow various kinds of divine and auspicious [attainments]. (217)
These deeds of incomparable power reveal the supreme state at the end,
especially for Vaiṣṇava devotees.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of the Śakti-mantra," in the Jayākhyasaṃhitā. || 27 ||
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of the Limb-Mantras.
The Blessed One said: "O best of Brahmins, listen to the great accomplishment of the limbs, which bestows success."
By the mere knowledge of which, the practitioner attains happiness. || 1 ||
[The Method for Accomplishing the Heart Mantra:
One should assign the heart mantra to both hands by way of pervasion;
having then assigned it to the body, one should worship that which resides in the center of the heart-lotus.
Then, having drawn outside [the mandala], in the center of the square with its four gates,
a very white eight-petaled lotus.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon its pericarp and meditated as before with the mantra,
one should worship according to the prescribed rite and offer oblations with well-purified sesame seeds.
At the end of that, having assumed the form of Hārdaka, one should go to a secluded place;
there, one should mutter [the mantra] three hundred thousand times and perform six hundred thousand oblations.
Then, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) of fragrant jasmine flowers that have been smeared with white sandalwood paste and likewise anointed with clarified butter.
One should behold the mantra residing in one's own heart with eyes wide open and awakened; having thus realized, "This Lord of my Heart is indeed accomplished," [one should proceed]. (7)
Then, O Nārada, one should perform the rites with that mantra— namely,
those for pacification and nourishment, as well as the discernment of auspicious and inauspicious dreams arising from the power born of the perfection of the heart-mantra.
Intent on accomplishing his own purpose, he gives instructions to the accused, as well as to kings and others in their dreams, and especially to women. (9)
Having placed her foot upon his heart, she should say, "Rise up, O evil-minded one!
Go and propitiate such-and-such a practitioner with wealth and other offerings. (10)
Having understood "So be it," and being awakened by that firm resolve,
he should go and entreat that practitioner of pure soul.
Having bathed with thick juices, one should place the name enclosed within the cavity of the heart in the center of the pericarp of a lotus on the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
Having risen at midnight, one should [anoint] the heart-mantra in its embodied form, together with the name, upon each petal with nocturnal water. (13)
Fasting and observing the vow, one should write [the mantra] with a blade of dūrvā grass under the Puṣya asterism, for the sake of pacifying all defects and for the increase of all happiness. (14)
For the sake of liberation from all calamities and for the attainment of all desired women, this sādhana of the heart-mantra has been narrated by me. (15)
[The Method for Accomplishing the Śiromantra] Now, O Nārada, I shall describe the method of accomplishment for the Śiromantra:
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the hands and likewise upon the body, and having worshipped it within the heart. (16)
Having drawn a mandala together with a lotus using a pigment soaked in lac juice,
one should then meditate upon the Śiromantra in its center as before and perform worship.
One should offer copper, gold, and sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
having become one who wears red garments and possesses a body formed by that mantra.
Having ascended to the middle of a mountain, one should indeed recite [the mantra] five hundred thousand times;
at the conclusion of that, the practitioner, with undistracted mind, should perform three hundred thousand oblations.
O Nārada, [this applies especially] to fragrant red and pale-red flowers that have been smeared with saffron and aloe-wood, and particularly those anointed with clarified butter.
Thereafter, he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with saffron and clarified butter;
then, he should behold the mantra, the Lord of the Universe, in its embodied form between his eyebrows.
Then, having attained realization, the excellent practitioner should indeed perform the rites;
he shall bring the entire world under his control, both by means of himself and through his wealth.

[The power born of accomplishment: Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times over a piece of Bāhlīka wood adorned with gold, one should rub it with night-water using the tips of the thumb and ring finger. (23)
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead with the ring finger;
below that, one should bind it at the heart with dust held by the thumb.
Reciting [the mantra] for three days according to the prescribed number, he should perform the three daily junctions (sandhyā).
When the fourth day arrives, the king becomes a master of the mandala.
318) Having approached him, one should pray: "O Lord, grant me your favor!
Accept my wealth, my kingdom, and my male and female slaves, elephants, and so forth. (26)
At the very end of that moment,
hundreds of Naga maidens arrive from the subterranean realm (rasātala), intent upon preparing elixirs (rasāyana).
"Drink this most beautiful drink and take your pleasure with us;
O Lord, from the fourth day onward, let this moment begin. (28)
We find no steadfastness there in Pātāla without you—not even the Kinnarīs, the Yakṣiṇīs, or the women of the Vidyādharas. (29)
Full of longing, they approach the practitioner and entreat him;
and he, O Nārada, being under their control, sports with them according to his desire.
And having drunk that excellent beverage according to one's own desire, one should prepare pure water in a vessel, consecrated with a hundred recitations of the mantra. (31)
Having worshipped with diligence this mantra here,
whoever has any doubt regarding the past, the present, or the future should reflect upon it.
O Nārada, in the rite of subjugation, the mantra reveals that very mantra situated within itself through its own clearly articulated syllables arising from its own place.
Or, for the sake of the accomplishment of attraction, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at sunrise;
O Brahmin, whatever man or woman is desired in the mind [shall be drawn]. (34)
By the power of this mantra, [the desired object] quickly comes at the end of the recitation;
one should write it with musk, milk, or saffron.
O Sage, at the break of day, upon a piece of white cloth, one should draw a three-petaled lotus situated within a triangular city using blades of dūrvā grass.
One should likewise place the name joined with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and so forth near it,
and join that with the mantra of its form on three leaves.
O best of Brahmins, whoever wears it—either encircled with a red thread on the arm or the shoulder, or hanging from the neck, or suspended upon the heart—[attains the fruit]. || 38 ||
Wherever he may be, his victory is certain and his worship becomes abundant;
[he remains unharmed] by beasts of prey, hunters, elephants, and even by thieves of terrible prowess. (39)
It cannot be overcome by virtue of the power of this mantra.
Thus, I have explained the ritual procedure for this mantra known as the "Head" (Mūrdha). (40)
[The Method for Accomplishing the Śikhā-mantra] I shall now describe the ritual manual (kalpa) for the crest-mantra (śikhā); listen briefly, O Nārada!
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the internal sacrifice (hṛdyāga), one should draw the mandala externally.
It is square, with four doors, adorned with five lines;
the doors are white in color, and the base is red in color.
In the center of that, one should fashion a lotus with a luster like crushed collyrium;
having brought it down from the heart and deposited it there, one should then perform worship.

Having completed the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), one wearing black garments should go to the ground at the edge of the mountain peak and then recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer thirty thousand red flowers there, combined with red sandalwood; and at the end of that, another thirty thousand [offerings].
O Nārada, one should offer oblations of sandalwood fuel sticks smeared with honey;
and at the end, one should present the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with sandalwood and ghee.
At the end of that, the King of Mantras should properly utter [the words] rising above the aperture of Brahma:
"Go, O Great-minded One, and perform various deeds! (47)
I am well-pleased with you because of your correct performance of the fire-oblation and recitation;
therefore, that preeminent practitioner may perform whatever rite he desires, [possessing the power born from the accomplishment of the mantra]. || 48 ||
One should recite the mantra named "The Best of Nagas," which is bound at the beginning and the end;
even the Lord of Serpents comes forth, holding an elixir in his hand.
He shall reveal the collection of locations where treasures are situated within the surface of the earth;
and by his command, he shall dwell indeed in a fortress upon a mountain peak.
He offered inexhaustible water, sweet and very cool;
and having clearly taken up a pair of tall milk-tree creepers, he [offered them]. (51)
O Brahmin, having bathed [the image] with water consecrated by mantras, one should bind it to those two jars,
or else to two pillars with blades of muñja grass and other such grasses over which mantras have been recited.
Having consecrated the guggulu incense seven times with the *śikhā-mantra*, one should offer it between the two creepers; [the disciple] should tremble very gently. (53)
In the midst of that, while reciting the mantra, one should hold a flower in the hand and, having grasped it, fix the mind upon whatever object pleases [the practitioner]. 54.
O best of Brahmins, if that flower which was in the hand were to be taken away by force, it would become a falsehood. (55)
When [the thief] has gone far away, having swiftly moved the two jars, and when the stolen goods have indeed been taken away by the spy, leaving only doubt regarding the lost property; || 56 ||
One should perform this "vine-work" (latākarma) for the purpose of piercing the vital spots of others;
or else, O tiger among sages, having seen [the victim] standing nearby.
Having mentally imagined two identical jars on the ground, of the same kind and possessing auspicious marks, with two creepers situated upon them; || 58 ||
Having formed this thought, the mantra-practitioner should recite while gazing at the two creepers; indeed, there, with the consciousness of the lost object, [he shall find it].
Having come together with one another for the purpose of making truth known, they enveloped themselves by means of themselves in order to make untruth known. 60.
O Brahmin, having bowed down, he should slowly touch the ground again and again;
or else, O Nārada, he should plant two pestles in the earth.
Having worshipped the object of accomplishment at a distance of exactly two cubits, one should offer incense;
O Brahmin, the two arrows mentioned previously are to be understood here as well. (62)
Having placed it on the ground, one should leave a space of one cubit in its center;
and having performed the consecration with those two for the sake of the aforementioned purification.
Having inscribed it, O Great-minded One, one should fill it with an iron nail;
it should be very clearly written with saffron alone, enclosed within the name-mantra.
Having cast the baked earthen shards anywhere for the sake of the funeral rite, one should place them in the midst of water and inform [the deceased] regarding the pot.
Having floated upon the surface of the water, one may dwell fearlessly beneath it;
furthermore, grains such as rice and the like should be consecrated seven times with mantras. (66)
To arouse suspicion in the thieves, one should place [the object] with the left hand;
then, one should cause their fist to grasp it in the right hand.
O Nārada, by reciting the mantra one hundred times, one shall remain [victorious];
the seeds and the hands of thieves are utterly consumed. (68)
One should wear it according to the previously mentioned rite on birch bark or a white cloth;
O Nārada, it grants the desires of devotees without any obstacle.
I have thus declared the ritual procedure for this mantra known as the *śikhā*.
Now, O Brahmin, listen to a brief description of the method for accomplishing the *kavaca* mantra. (70)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the sacrifice, one should then draw the mandala;
in its center, one should fashion a lotus with a brilliant yellow-black color.
Having caused [the deity] to descend into the center with dust mixed with that [earth],
one should worship according to the previously mentioned rule and then offer libations to the one situated in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having offered sesame seeds that are white, black, and copper-colored, and which have been consecrated with honey and clarified butter,
and having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should recite the mantra known as the Kavaca.
O Brahmin, one should go to an underground chamber, or a cave, or even a mountain retreat;
having recited [the mantra] two hundred thousand times there, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa).
With all the aforementioned substances infused with black agallochum (kṛṣṇāgaru),
one should then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with a quantity equal to half the number of recitations.
At the end of that, with ghee mixed with honey, he should behold the Lord of Mantras situated in the ten directions; and this he said to the practitioner: || 76 ||
"Go; you have attained success. Accomplish your desired rites.
Having placed that command upon his head, he should perform those things desired by his mind.
[The power born of mantra-siddhi:

Having gone to the edge of a forest or to the outskirts of a city, one should recite [the mantra] while holding white *siddhārthaka* seeds in the left hand, facing north for half a watch (three hours). 78.
One should cast them upon the forest ground, below, above, and even in the intermediate directions;
for then the forest deities arrive from all sides before him. (79)
"O knower of mantras, give me your command! For what purpose have I been tormented?
Bring these desired medicinal herbs by the thousands. (80)
For the sake of accomplishing all rites and for the cessation of hunger and old age, there are now the divine medicinal herbs that perform every function. (81)
Having taken it, the lord of practitioners should depart from the forest region,
carrying either a plantain leaf or a tamāla leaf.
One should draw the Lord of Mantras upon a spread-out birch-bark leaf;
whenever it is wrapped around [the body], it attains the state of armor. 83.
For the purpose of destroying the weapons of enemies, for the removal of flames of fire, for the sake of pacifying the heat of the sun’s rays, and for the destruction of cold things. (84)
Clods of earth, thorns, and gravel also become thickened;
and if one should lie down or sit upon that ground after having offered it [to the deity], [the same occurs]. 85.
Seeing before him the army of thieves with their excellent weapons raised,
he regarded it as a formidable lion, the king of beasts, or a great mass of deadly Hālāhala poison.
Or a lordly elephant intoxicated with rut, or a wild buffalo and the like, or a great creature such as a crocodile dwelling within a river or stream. (87)
And [he should do so] toward one who desires to kill the virtuous, always with the intent to seize him;
having placed that leaf upon the tip of his staff with his right hand.

One should cause that which stands at the summit of the half [of the body] to whirl; by the wind arising from that, which is like the wind at the end of an eon, everyone quickly goes here and there. || 89 ||
Alternatively, that lord of practitioners should contemplate with his mind a protection equal to a rampart by means of the armor whose nature is fire.
And the binding of the eyes of the wicked occurs at that very moment;
having recited that mantra while naked, one should give a banyan leaf.
Whether in the cold season or the summer heat, he attains the state of being clothed;
even when a great cloud has arisen over the entire village or the whole realm.
One should remember the weapon [mantra] on its blade; it goes to the back of the handle along with the leaf.
By the power of that mantra and its splendor, it is split into a hundred pieces along with the thunderbolt.
Having tied on the armor-mantra written upon a yellow cloth with milk and saffron mixed together— 94.
The mantra situated in the center of the pericarp is divided into two parts, with the designation at its end;
joined with the word for the ritual action, this mantra-form is placed upon each petal.
Having written [this] and wrapped it with thread, and having placed it inside a copper casket and bound it on the left arm, whatever the mantra-practitioner desires— (96)
Whatever he gives to anyone else, he attains that very thing; moreover, all planetary spirits, ghosts, and the like do not afflict that man. (97)
By the power of this mantra, it always bestows freedom from disease.
[The Method for Accomplishing the Eye-Mantra] Now I shall declare the procedure for the eye-mantra, which grants success. (98)
When the heart-sacrifice has been performed according to the previously stated procedure,
one should place within the mandala a yellow-and-red lotus.

Having summoned the Eye situated within the heart-lotus there into the center, one should worship it at the conclusion of the fire-oblation; the performance of the oblation with clarified butter is then recommended.
Having offered oblations with yellow *siddhārthaka* seeds mixed with copper-colored sesame until the vessel is full, one should then assume that form and go to a secluded place.
O tiger among sages, the observer of the vow, gazing day and night at the sun as it revolves through the circle of the directions, should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the practitioner of mantra should perform a fire offering (homa) with pure ghee alone,
or with the sap of the celestial tree (suradāru), for twenty thousand oblations.
Two others with honey-mixed [substances], one with white mustard seeds and sesame, and then, having completed the full oblation with equal portions of ghee and other ingredients. (104)
But at the conclusion of the full [lunar day], he should behold that Mantreśvara, whose eyes are blazing and who stands at the head of the path; then, having given his command, he shall depart.
Then, the practitioner of mantras should perform all rites upon the earth;
