having taken antimony from a mine and consecrated it two hundred times with the mantra, he should employ the power born from the perfection of the eye-mantra.
And having consecrated a golden probe seven times with mantras,
one should then apply that collyrium to one's own pair of eyes.
One shall see everything situated on the earth, whatever exists preceded by hidden treasures;
one also beholds the world of the Nāgas situated in the midst of the ocean waters.
If he should go to the world of the Nāgas to gather that entire collection of jewels, the water shall open up a fissure for him.
O Sage, he will soon behold that host of yakṣiṇīs situated between the stones and the trees, just as it is by his own [power]. (110)
Having entered, O twice-born one, he sports with them perfectly according to his will;
remaining invisible to those yakṣas, he gazes upon them.
O best of Brahmins, [I shall explain] all the medicinal herbs and their respective mantras in their entirety for those who constantly practice the yoga of the yakṣas.
Or [the flowers] are brought by himself from the presence of the beloveds of the Yakṣas;
and they emerge for those devotees who have sought refuge and whose souls are purified. 113.

For the practitioner bestows [the results] upon those who are incapable of performing the rite; by means of the power of the yakṣa-machines and yogas, they obtain whatever is desired in their minds. (114)
And they are drawn forth by the power of the practitioner;
furthermore, if one anoints the eyes again according to the previously mentioned procedure, [the result is as follows]. (115)
He beholds numerous hosts of Siddhas stationed within the expanse of the sky,
and they, in turn, worship that great-souled practitioner.
They grant whatever is desired or lead [the devotee] along their own path,
especially for the devoted Vaiṣṇava who has approached them in surrender.
O Sage, having consecrated collyrium one hundred times with mantras, whoever applies it to both eyes with a stick shall see everything.
And though situated in only one place, it perceives that entire object—even if it is separated by mountains and the like—endowed with the mastery of yoga. (119)
The host of ḍākinīs, bhūtas, and vetālas remained invisible;
yet, by the power of the practitioner, they became visible as soon as they were seen, filled with great joy. (120)
They bestow even more wealth upon one who remains indifferent;
having consecrated it seven times with the Netra-mantra, [one applies] collyrium.
A man situated between enemies should offer [this] into his own pair of eyes;
he shall constantly obtain a vision wherever he may go or wherever he may enter. 122.
Having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras,
if one who stands within the range of sight of others should employ it against another, even that person shall go out of sight.
What could a practitioner of mantra not accomplish on this earth when he has attained invisibility?
By rubbing collyrium mixed with *rocanā* with water from a night-blooming lotus, [he gains such power]. (124)

Having drawn it on a leaf of *barhi* grass with the name [of the recipient] as before, one should place the mantra in the center of the pericarp and according to the prescribed rule upon the petals. (125)
Having tied it on a ten-finger-long strip of cloth—whether square or circular—the practitioner of mantra should wear it; he will become beloved by everyone. (126)
This mantra, which brings about all prosperity, is to be meditated upon through the exclusion of anything else;
this most excellent procedure for the Eye has thus been fully described. (127)
[The Method for Accomplishing the Astramantra] Now, listen briefly to my [method for accomplishing] the King of Weapons (Astrarāja):
having first correctly performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), immediately thereafter, the mental sacrifice (hṛdyāga). 128.
O Great Sage, having fashioned a square with four doors for the sacrifice,
one should draw a lotus in its center using powder resembling royal stone (lapis lazuli).
Having placed the filaments with well-colored [red] [substance] and the pericarp with yellow [substance],
and having worshipped them there, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having offered an oblation of guggulu resin together with white and black sesame seeds,
and having subsequently performed the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should assume a body resembling that of the Weapon-mantra (astra).
The wise practitioner should go to a secluded place and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, the master of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice with two tens of thousands of pieces of guggulu resin.
One [fuel stick] shall be the size of a jujube seed or a mustard seed;
two ten-thousand [sticks] of fuel shall be made from the red sandalwood tree.
One should indeed offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter as the final full-offering (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, [one should meditate upon] the Lord of Weapons, who possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns, at the dvādaśānta.
Beholding him with a stainless gaze, that king of weapons spoke thus:
"Go, O best of practitioners; wander here as you please. (135)
O best of brahmins, performing all kinds of divine and mortal deeds many times over by his command, he also attained perfection.
Having recited [the mantra] over a piece of stone for a period of time known as a *ghaṭikā*,
while gazing at the surface of the earth, he should strike the ground with it.
Standing before the practitioner in her true form with yellow limbs,
she bestows immediately everything that he desires.
[The power born from the mastery of weapon-mantras:
All rice crops out of season, as well as fruits out of season, all flowers out of season, and even various fragrances [manifest]. (139)
There were countless and diverse openings to the subterranean chambers,
containing thousands of divine elixirs that could be taken at will from all sides.
Likewise, there are various kinds of objects situated in the seven netherworlds, as well as those in heaven and on the earth that are difficult to obtain by the thousands. (141)
O best of Brahmins, taking in his hand a staff made of khadira wood over which a hundred mantras have been recited, he likewise makes all of those things manifest.
One should forcefully strike with it a tree standing at a crossroads;
then the Śākinīs and Bhūtamātṛs emerge, rendered utterly distraught.
O sovereign of the best of practitioners, give whatever command you desire;
then, he shall impel the spirits even toward tasks that are impossible.
Having gone and ascertained everything concerning foreign affairs— both secret and overt— exactly as they truly are, he shall indeed return within a short time.
Afflicted by the mantra, the ḍākinīs report all of that;
the Mātṛs, becoming terrified, depart in an instant into the expanse of the sky.
Having understood whatever movement, action, or conduct belongs to those who travel through the sky, they quickly report it to the practitioner exactly as it occurred.
One should strike a person seized by spirits with a creeper or similar object;
then, one should bring [the spirit] and lead it to the creeper held before that person.
One may travel swiftly to a desired place and return in that very instant;
thus, having made the mother their vehicle, they go to distant lands.
Wherever the mantra-practitioner, having recited the mantra, casts white mustard seeds,
there the planets presided over by divine beings manifest their presence.
They bring whatever is desired, such as drink, food, clothing, and so forth;
having consecrated a weapon with the mantra, one should advance against the enemy force with that weapon. || 151 ||
If one casts that [mantra] into the midst of it, it quickly destroys the weapon—even if it be an indestructible vajra—by the power of the mantra recited over the weapon. 152.
In this way, others such as mountains and so forth undergo manifold division;
one should meditate upon [the weapon-mantra] situated upon the circle of the earth, surrounded by a garland of blazing flames. (153)
O Nārada, having consecrated an iron arrow with mantras, one should place it at whichever pillar is appointed for that purpose.
Causing that which is situated in the sky to whirl, he may arrest a downpour;
wherever he may direct his gaze with eyes bloodshot with anger, [there his power prevails]. (155)
Even a blade of grass consecrated with the Astra-mantra will fall there like a crane; likewise, having drawn [the figure] with saffron mixed with realgar, [it shall fall]. 156.

One who, with a disciplined mind, wears [this amulet] situated on the pericarp and so forth as before, accompanied by the eight vajras in the cardinal directions, shall be invincible everywhere. (157)
He obtains extensive worship as well as complete good fortune.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of the Limb-Mantras," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of the Mantra of the Mouth.
The Blessed One said:
"This procedure for the limbs has been proclaimed according to one's desire."
Listen; I shall now describe the ritual procedure (kalpa) for the Three-Faced One exactly as it is.

[The Sadhana of the Nṛsiṃha-Face Mantra] Listen now to the fourfold form endowed with the six limbs, which is that face of Nṛsiṃha possessing the radiance of ten thousand suns at the end of an aeon. (2)
Endowed with the fourfold power and possessing a brilliance equal to the fire at the end of an aeon,
he took up the limbs and mantras of Nṛsiṃha— the eternal sixfold [mantra] established in the recitation of the Sāmans. (3)
Then, one should join [the letters] with the two lords of the four states (caturgatidhara) situated within;
subsequently, one should mark them from top to bottom with the vowels as their limbs (aṅga).
Then one should adorn [the deity] with the Kaustubha gem in the center of the chest and Vyomeśa;
these, O best of Brahmins, are the limbs of the high-souled Nṛsiṃha.

[The Form-Mantras of Nṛsiṃha: Then, one should join the four—the Peak (kūṭa), the End (anta), Dhā, Mā, Ātman, and the one eternally abiding; as well as the Veda-Self (vedātman) and the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 6 ||
Now, that syllable which is the letter of Lokeśvara, situated within the subtle, abandoned by Lokeśvara, and joined with the letter known as Vyomeśa—[that indeed is it]. (7)
The four forms of the All-pervading Lord reside upon the four summits:
the first bestows the world of the Sun, and the second is the maker of light like fire.
The fourth is Viśvasūkara, the subduer of excessive pride.
[The method of meditation on the forms following Nṛsiṃha:
All the manifestations (forms) of Nṛsiṃha are to be meditated upon; all are four-armed. (9)
One should remember the mudrā called Vismaya with both hands for all [deities], which consists of striking with the nails and is the cause of the destruction of all worldly calamities.
One should meditate on the hand as intensely massaging the other hand;
therefore, O Sage, for those of exalted nature, this supreme mudrā is to be meditated upon.
One should meditate on [Nṛsiṃha], who has the luster of white, red, and gold, and whose form begins with the color blue;
thereafter, one should take up his form as fire, with eyes wide open. [The Śakti-mantras of Nṛsiṃha]. 12.
And one should place upon their heads the two radiant universal forms (Viśvarūpas),
which are the support of all worlds and adorned by Māyā and Vyomeśa.
One should place their seat as being devoid of Māyā and Vyomeśa;
it is the universal form of great splendor, like the flame of the fire at the end of an eon. 14.
The fourth is proclaimed by the name Jagatsaṃpūraṇī.
Now, listen attentively to the sequence of their colors according to their respective order. 15.
Their complexions were copper-red; they had two arms and beautiful earrings;
their limbs were prominent and their bodies were large; and they possessed tawny eyebrows and eyes. || 16 ||
And there were four others with six nostrils and protruding bellies, holding wheels and fly-whisks in their hands, seated in the lotus posture. || 17 ||
One should place the Praṇava at the beginning, the name, and the word of salutation for all [mantras];
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the method prescribed by the Root Śakti.
Having worshipped [the deity] within the heart-lotus, one should place the Supreme Lord upon the interior of an eight-petaled lotus situated outside the hexagonal mandala and perform worship.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the heart and the other limbs as before upon the four tips of the petals;
then, on the eastern petal and the others, one should place the collection of forms (mūrtis), and in the southeast and south, the powers (śaktis).
Then, having performed the sacrifice for the personified mantras, one should display their respective mudrās;
thereafter, [offer] the wheel of the fourfold fame, as well as guggulu and sesame.
But for grains that have had their awns removed, which are reddish in nature and especially freed from the defect of straw, when they are smeared with clarified butter— || 22 ||
Then, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) consisting of guggulu mixed with honey;
at that moment, he lets out a great roar that renders the three worlds inert.
The Man-lion (Nṛkesarin) emerges from within the fire from the sky;
by means of his mantra, he leaps swiftly into the sky with a great roar.
The preeminent practitioner should indeed act; he shall become joyful through his splendor.
Then that Blessed Lord, being thoroughly pleased, speaks in reply.
"Speak, O sovereign of practitioners, whatever resides in your heart.
Having said this, the Man-lion, whose form is the mantra, vanishes from sight. (26)
[The Power Born from the Accomplishment of the Nṛsiṃha Mantra:
Thereafter, O twice-born one, if the practitioner desires the eightfold sovereignty, he may accomplish it for himself or for another by mere word alone. (27)
Having seen a worthy recipient possessing auspicious marks— whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya—
one should mentally perform the act of entrustment with flowers, water for honor, and likewise with water.
Having worshipped him, once possessed while standing in the center of the arena, he would instantly speak of the past,
the present, and the future— whatever indeed appeared to his intuition.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras of those forms, he should then worship them with their respective mantras;
if he does so, even a child may speak of everything past and future.

Having caused the maiden to enter [into the state of absorption] by means of the four mantra-śaktis, even she who is very young and still in the state of childhood speaks according to her desire. (31)
While reciting the mantra of the Lord of Mantras, he should then withdraw it by means of that same mantra;
then, he may enter a village, a town, or a great city carrying white mustard seeds.
At that very moment, including the animals, humans, and gods, he undergoes agitation;
therefore, having assumed the form of a lion— || 33 ||

Having protected [the site] with ointments, ornaments, and so forth, the practitioner observing the vow should indeed go to the summit of the Lord of Mountains and recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times. (34)
Or ten thousand, or two hundred thousand; having performed the recitation, one should then offer oblations.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should enter the center, or remain in the presence of another.
O Nārada, when even a small portion of her is established, that city, together with its elephants, horses, and weapons, quickly falls into agitation. (36)
If one who has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Japan-mantra stands before her for even a moment,
she too becomes agitated and runs toward where that practitioner is.
O high-minded one, having reached the shore of the abode of sea-monsters,
whoever stands there in such a manner will surely agitate it before long.
If, while gazing at the sky, one should recollect the mantra,
that very moment the sky becomes free of clouds, stainless, and yet undergoes agitation.
With terrible thundering clouds accompanied by garlands of lightning and thunderbolts, the great forest, filled with trees and teeming with lions and tigers, [was shaken]. (40)
O best of Brahmins, by this rite, [the deity] quickly becomes agitated;
whomever the mantra practitioner agitates with the radiant lion-mantra, [that one is overcome].
Frightened by fear and out of devotion,
he offers his entire being to whomever he conceives in his mind, whether it be a yakṣa, a vidyādhara, or another.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the supreme mantra; he shall arrive swiftly and quickly carry out the command of the high-souled adept.
Then, at his command, one whose mind is filled with fear should return to one's own place;
having first drawn a twelve-spoked wheel, complete with a hub and a rim.
One should draw a six-pointed star together with a lotus upon the navel using saffron, water from a tree, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on a cloth.
The designation situated within the pericarp, with the mantra at its beginning and end, is restrained;
it stands amidst the ocean of nectar, all-pervading and joined with the lunar [digit]. (46)
This is one’s own form-mantra (mūrtimantra), which is [placed] on each and every petal;
and in the hexagon, the [mantras] beginning with the Heart (hṛdaya) are provided with the words "rakṣa" and "mukha."
O twice-born one, first, the two forms situated at the beginning and end of the name should be joined in two ways upon the nave of the wheel, and not within the spokes. (p. 331) 48.
By means of the connection between the intervals of the spokes, there is one [deity] for each of the six and six;
that which is indeed the first power here is endowed with the name of the syllable *rakṣa*. (49)
O twice-born one, that [line] should be applied in the intervals between the spokes as twelve single units;
and another, joined with the name, should be applied in three ways upon the rim of the wheel.
The third [power] is twenty-fourfold, and likewise in the expansions of the wheels;
the fourth power of the Lord is singlefold, situated outside the wheels.
Having wound the wheel seven times with that thread made of its own substance,
one whose self is purified by vows and fasting should perform worship as well as the fire-oblation.
On the twelfth lunar day of either the bright or dark fortnight, O Nārada, on a Thursday,
or else under the constellation presided over by Jupiter (Jīva), at an auspicious moment endowed with favorable omens.
Having drawn [the diagram] on the outer side, one should encircle it with white and red [pigments];
then, having placed it within three metals, O twice-born, whoever should wear this mantra— || 54 ||
For him there shall be long life, prosperity, health, good fortune, appropriate strength, contentment, splendor, fame, and all-encompassing victory. (55)
Whether it be a spell for destroying intelligence, a mantra employed through yoga, or that which is stationary, moving, terrible, known as "doubt," or likewise artificial; || 56 ||
Poison is destroyed; what need is there to mention [the effects on] household spirits? Moreover, one becomes beloved among women and may desire them. (57)
O Nārada, whatever desire one strives for, that very thing one obtains without effort through this mantra of Nṛsiṃha, which has become his mouth. 58.
[The Method for Accomplishing the Mantra of Kapila] The ritual procedure has been correctly explained; now that of Kapila is being told.
[The Limb-Mantra of Kapila]
It should be drawn as radiant and sixfold, encircled by fire above and below. || 59 ||
One should join these with the head in sequence, like the limbs of that Nṛsiṃha;
now hear indeed of his Ceṭakas, which are the limbs of Kapila.
[The mantras for the attendants of Kapila:

Having first placed the group of four ending with Varuṇa (Va), and having then placed the Lord of the Earth (La) mounted upon Fire (Ra) in sequence, one should place the Lord of the World (Sa) below each of these four. (61)
The all-pervading Viśvāpyāyakara is indeed to be placed above on all sides;
[then] Yogeśvara, Tattvajña, Brahmadatta, and Mahāmati. || 62 ||
White, red, and crimson, black, and with a tranquil body, he has four arms.
[This is the method of meditating on the form of the attendant Kapila:
All [the attendants] have their hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture and are seated in the *padmāsana* posture. (63)
Indeed, they have the form of an accumulation of consciousness; they hold rosaries of beads, possess the radiance of a thousand suns, and are adorned with divine garlands and garments. (64)
Their limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and they are adorned with divine ornaments.
[These are the Śakti-mantras of Kapila:
One should write the first four syllables in sequence, ending with the letter śa. (65)
One should place the fire-stationed [syllable] below all [others], and then place Soma;
one should then apply the Pervasive One (Vyāpin), the Lunar One (Cāndrī), and Māyā, ending with the dative case.
The powers (śaktis) are Vimalā, Karuṇā, Śakti, and the one called Jñānā. [This is the method of meditating on the powers of Kapila:
They are remembered as being yellow, dark, reddish, and white respectively, each having two arms. (67)
Having likewise performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of those with tawny forms, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness, one should thereafter worship them within the expanded lotus-heart.
Then, having fashioned a circular mandala resembling the full moon, with a single entrance and adorned with a lotus, and having caused [the deity] to descend into its center; || 69 ||
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the remaining limbs and so forth as before, and having placed [the mantra] within the petals of the Līlā lotus,
one should offer worship and display the Brahmāñjali and [other] mudrās to Yogeśā and the others.
Having placed the gestures of boon and fear on the principal limbs of the Śaktis as before,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) according to one's ability with sesame seeds drenched in clarified butter.
After offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then go to a secluded place and recite the mantra of the heart and the other limbs four hundred thousand times, O Nārada.
Then, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) gradually, offering one thousand oblations at a time;
subsequently, one should offer twenty thousand oblations with milk mixed with honey.
Then one should offer ten thousand oblations with water mixed with curd, and thereafter five times ten thousand oblations of *mālatī* flowers. (74)
One should offer one oblation of clarified butter alone with the *sruva* ladle;
then, one hundred and one oblations for each of all [the deities], having combined everything into one, should be offered.
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) filled with curd, honey, and clarified butter;
Adhokṣaja himself shall then appear, standing directly before one, having come by way of the path of the sun.
"Go, O practitioner; you have attained success. Accomplish everything by means of my mantra.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One departed from there along the path of the sun.
[The power born from the mastery of the Kapila-mantra:
Then, by means of that mantra, the practitioner of mantra (mantrin) may perform whatever rite he desires;
having applied the mantra to the lotus of the heart for a moment, he should employ it for those who are dull-witted. (78)
And they attain awakening through the mantra consisting of eight syllables, O Nārada, whose name is enclosed at the beginning and the end. (79)
If a practitioner of mantra should travel along a crowded path while reciting the mantra two hundred times, or if he should remain in a forest of asceticism while reciting the Lord of Mantras; 80.
Having attained satisfaction through their realized wisdom, those ascetics of tranquil minds prostrate at the feet of that high-souled master who knows the mantras. (81)

In front of the great king's palace, the practitioner of mantra should indeed meditate upon the Lord of Mantras; whenever the practitioner remains there for even a moment, the excellent king [perceives] him.
Having approached the base of the feet, the observer of the vow should report everything; indeed, having fixed whatever [intentions] in his mind, he should mutter the excellent mantra.
Having assembled there, O best of Brahmins, they diligently recounted their respective specialized knowledges to that high-souled master of mantras. (84)
The nāgas, vidyādharas, and yakṣas who indeed travel through the sky [all behold] the entire accomplishment of higher knowledge (vijñānasiddhi) of that great-souled one in particular. || 85 ||
Having given [the fruit] to the chief practitioner, they go back again to where they came from,
O Nārada, when the matter concerns the domain of consciousness, the attainment of siddhi, or a doubtful point.
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the mantra and recite it; he shall reach the state beyond doubt.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras in the navel, if one recites [the mantra] ten thousand times, [the result follows].
He knows everything—past, present, and future—without a doubt;
having recited [the mantra] two hundred and eight times, he places mustard seeds in the hollow of his joined palms. (88)
O best of Brahmins, one should bury them in the middle of the earth; they will themselves unite below, either at a place where treasure is located or at a site suitable for alchemy.
However, they provide a sign of its attainment there;
for in that treasure or elixir, no actual acquisition exists.
O twice-born one, from afar they fled hither and thither from that place,
while the minister remained seated in the lotus posture, established in the concentration on emptiness.
If one recites the mantra ten thousand times while meditating on [the deity] who eclipses the luster of a sapphire, one shall attain the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
O Brahmin, because it consists of a ten-thousandth part of the fourth state (turyāṃśa), resides in the path of the cavity of the palate, and destroys one's own or another's gray hair. 93.
If the practitioner of mantras recites the mantra residing within the city of Indra, then the tongue-tip of the Lord of the World becomes radiant like fire, and he is protected. 94.
Even he becomes mute; how much more so a man of small intellect?
[This occurs] by means of night-water, milk, thickened juice, and essence. (95)
Having drawn a great six-petalled lotus on birch bark or white cloth with abundant saffron, one should draw a twelve-petalled [lotus] outside of that.
Outside that, together with the hub and the rim, is the sixteen-spoked wheel, the king of weapons;
within the pericarp is the Lord of Mantras, joined with his name as before.
On the six petals, one should perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga) accompanied by the syllables and words of the name;
likewise, the limbs, the forms (mūrtis), and the powers (śaktis) are placed upon the three petals.
Having written those very same [syllables] repeatedly on other petals until the lotus is completed, one should again place the root [mantra] at the navel.
The seed-syllable of the Heart (hṛdbīja) is in the space between the spokes, and the seed-syllable of the Weapon (astrabīja) is on the spokes;
the remaining four limbs, as well as the forms (mūrtis) and powers (śaktis), are likewise [placed]. 100.
Then, O Great-minded One, having placed [the syllables] upon the rim of the wheel, the exterior of the wheel should be encircled nine times with the seed-syllable of Śakti.
One should insert the mantras for the peace of the hermitages, Varuṇa, and the assemblies;
or else, one should encircle that space in the sky with this thread. 102.
O Nārada, for that devoted person who places [this] in a casket of Jāmbūnada gold and wears it, knowledge together with realized wisdom (vijñāna) manifests. 103.
As he crosses rivers or traverses the ocean,
the multitudes of defects arising from the water and the waves are all stilled.
Wherever the sustainer of the *yantra* dwells, and where the lotus and the blazing reciter reside, there he leads [the practitioner] in no long time. (105)
Having established an unassailable position through the power of this mantra, thousands of terrible beings, such as those dwelling on the earth, enter [the site]. 106.
Therein, no divine obstacle arises, much less one instigated by the royal court;
instead, incomparable fullness, fortitude, prosperity, and boldness emerge.
Whatever is contrary to this indeed goes to total destruction;
for what in the three worlds is unattainable for this Lord of Mantras? (108)
Thus, for one who has propitiated [the deity] through rites seen in the injunctions, wherever and whichever mantra-lord the mantra-practitioner may employ, [that shall be accomplished]. (109)
Therein, one should worship the form of the power of the limbs (aṅga-śakti-mūrti), as well as perform oblations and recitations.
This has been declared regarding the Kāpila [Vārāha]; now that of the Vārāha [Purāṇa] is being told. 110.
[The method for accomplishing the mantra of Varāha; therein, the limb-mantra (aṅgamantra) of Varāha:
Having first taken Ananteśa in six ways, situated above the Pradhāna, one should place Dhareśa below that, conjoining them with the vowels arising from the limbs. 111.
[The mantras for the attendants of Varāha:
Govinda, Vibudhādya, Varāha, and Caturgati—one should assign these four in sequence, placing them below those [deities]. (112)
One should then place Dhareśa, Gadadhvaṃsī, Sūkṣma, and Varuṇa; thereafter, one should install Anala above them, placing these four in their proper sequence.
[The Power-mantras of Varāha] Now, having taken four syllables for the sake of the four powers:
Dhruva, Varāha, Anala, and Paramātman are for the one of great intelligence. (114)
O Sage, one should place the moon-seed (Soma-bīja), which has ascended, upon the seats of the four [deities], all of whom are adorned by Viṣṇu; then, from one's own heart— (115).
In the entire wheel of mantras, however, the lunar [power] pervades the head;
having performed the placement (nyāsa) as previously described and having worshipped within the sphere of the heart, || 116 ||
Having constructed an eight-sided city, complete with its constituent parts such as the gates and so forth,
one should place in its center a white lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having caused the Lord of Mantras to descend there, one should worship him with devotion;
then, as before, one should perform the [worship of] the heart and so forth, followed by the four subsequent [limbs]. 118.
Having meditated upon him as situated within a lotus petal, one should perform the placement; learn from me this method of meditation on the attendants of Varāha:
first, the Supporter of the Earth (Dharaṇīdhara), resembling the flax flower (atasīpuṣpa). 119.
The second earth-supporter has a luster like a fresh cloud;
the third earth-supporter is dark as a cluster of priyaṅgu blossoms. || 120 ||
One should meditate on the fourth [face], named Viśvadhṛk, which has the luster of a swarm of bees; all [the faces] have the face of a boar and hold a conch and a lotus raised in their hands. 121.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), they indeed grant boons and fearlessness;
their limbs are smeared with floral ornaments and covered with masses of frost.
[The Method for Meditating on the Śaktis of Varāha] Then, having meditated upon and meditated upon the four Śaktis, one should install them:
the first, who fulfills all worlds, has the luster of the color of a fresh campaka flower. 123.
One should meditate upon another [form] named Rājopalaprabhā, who sustains the universe;
and one should meditate upon the very powerful one called Ojā, who has the luster of a bandhūka flower.
And the fourth is the one named Sthiti, resembling the snowy mountain;
all have the faces of boars, possess two arms, and wear beautiful earrings. (125)
Holding maces and discs, and adorned with various flowers and garments,
one should then worship them and offer the mudrā to the host of mantras.
For the primary [mantras] such as the Heart-mantra and others, characterized by the previously mentioned marks,
one should employ the mudrās known as Varā (Boon) and Abhaya (Fearlessness), as well as the mace-mudrā, for the female deities.
Then the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations of black sesame seeds soaked in honey;
having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should assume his own form as Vārāha.

One should go to a secluded, solitary, and vast location near a body of water; having recited the mantra eight hundred thousand times there, one should perform oblations twelve hundred thousand times. (129)
One should likewise offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds, twenty thousand of cow's ghee, and again ten thousand of guggulu resin.
The mantra-practitioner should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and then the Lord Varāha, the bestower of boons, shall come within the range of vision while being praised by all the gods.
"Go; I am pleased with you, so quickly accomplish your desired goal.
Then that foremost of practitioners would accomplish what was commanded by the Lord.
[The power born from the accomplishment of the Varāha-mantra:

Having ascended to the very peak of a mountain summit and gazing toward the southern direction, one should recite the supreme mantra at night; at the end of the night, Antaka himself [will appear]. 133.
"Agitated, you come; what need have you of me? Tell me, who is this host of enemies against whom I am to exert my power today? (134)
Whether he be serene or dejected, whoever is [subject to] timely death shall not be afflicted from this day forward by my oath to you. 135.
"You are now a bearer of vows and have transcended death; of this there is no doubt.
I shall depart; give me leave to go," he should then say to him.
Having meditated upon the water contained within the jar and likewise recited [the mantra] one hundred and fifty times,
diseases such as those beginning with "donkey-fever" (gardabha) are pacified by that water.
O great sage, by bathing, drinking, and likewise sprinkling with night-water mixed with sandalwood and encapsulated by the name-mantra, [one attains purification] in an instant. (138)
Having drawn [the deity] together with its retinue upon a lotus and placed it in cool water,
the fever— whether quotidian or otherwise— departs at that very moment.
Having consecrated guggulu incense mixed with white mustard seeds, one who is fumigated with it at the end of a fever becomes completely well and happy at that very moment. (140)
Having taken earth and consecrated it with mantras, and having placed it in his left hand,
he should then stir it with water and smear it over that which is struck by the spider.
O best of the twice-born, it is quickly destroyed by the power of this mantra.
Having consecrated sesame oil mixed with ghee one hundred times [with the mantra], [it should be applied]. 142.
O twice-born one, by anointing [the body] with blue darbha grass held in the hand according to one's desired number, the destruction of all diseases is fully accomplished. (143)
Having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should place it on one's back while traveling through a great forest filled with the terror and fear of thieves. (144)
And following him dwells the lineage of Paiśācī Yakṣas;
though she bestows all happiness, she casts one onto the path of defects. 145.
Whatever a practitioner of mantra desires while staying on a path or at another sacred site (tīrtha), that very thing the yakṣas and others constantly bestow according to his wish. (146)
For the sake of that caravan’s satisfaction, he shall not undergo any fatigue;
indeed, other yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas stand before him. (147)
Merely by means of investigation, those who await his command—
when the practitioner of the vow, performing wonders, desires to go through the sky— 148.
Then, having taken honey and the great medicinal herb Subhagā,
and having combined them with mercury and Tuṣāra, place these within a copper crucible.
Then, having concealed it by means of mardana, one should again place it within a golden crucible;
having performed a thousand recitations, one should then fashion that [substance] into a pill.
Having placed it within the mouth, if one then falls into the sky, all the perfected Vidyādharas will come, overwhelmed by fear. 151.
O twice-born one, they serve as servants to the high-souled knower of mantras,
even if he has gone to the earth bounded by the seven continents and oceans.
By means of the intermediate space, the practitioner of mantra does not fall into delusion;
even if the practitioner has gone to the summit of Mount Meru, he wanders there without ceasing. 153.
If the celestial women there honor the ancient dwellers of heaven, the gods indeed worship him and bow down to him.
Having taken the pill and consecrated it twelve times with mantras,
[the practitioner summons] maidens born from the seven worlds and those originating from the seven nether regions.

If, having drawn her with the mind and made her one who accomplishes the welfare of both self and others, she is then seen [in reality], she appears cast down, her eyes rolling with intoxication. (156)
If the practitioner should depict elephants, buffaloes, tamed deer, lions, serpents, and so forth, as well as humans, kinnaras, and others; 157.
In an instant, those who have made a solemn pledge will undoubtedly rise up;
having applied a tilaka with honey combined with musk. (158) p. 339)
O best of sages, when this [mantra] is properly empowered one hundred times and applied to the forehead,
the king, together with his harem, will fall into a state of agitation at that very moment.
Having consecrated a mace made either of khadira wood or iron,
the mantra-practitioner should strike a portion of the earth that is entirely devoid of cavities.
Indeed, for the seven levels, there is a restraint of movement;
whatever desired accomplishment (siddhi) is in the mind of the practitioner, [that is attained]. 161.
By the power of that mantra, each [deity] is indeed perfectly accomplished without delay;
likewise, the goddesses arisen from the eight wombs, as well as the powers beginning with *aṇimā*. || 162 ||
O Nārada, by the power of the Lord of Mantras and of the practitioners, [this is achieved] with the milk of a tawny cow, as well as with yellow pigment and saffron. (163)
One should draw an excellent eight-sided figure on birch bark or cloth;
in its center, an eight-petaled lotus, and outside of that, a hexagon and a city-gate (fortress). 164.
Outside of that, however, is the twelve-spoked [wheel], joined with a hub and a rim;
in its center, it is joined with the mantra, situated within the seed-syllable of the name. || 165 ||
O best of Brahmins, by means of the application of the worship-nyāsa, the heart and other [limbs] are assigned to the petals;
furthermore, the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja) is assigned eight times to the three corners of the octagon.
Then, one should further apply the heart-mantra eightfold within those directions;
indeed, it should be applied sixfold in the six corners on the outside of the eight-pointed figure.
Having placed the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā) along with the armor (tanutra) and the eye (locana),
one should write the syllable "asaṃkhya" many times at the navel for the sake of fulfillment.
Through the application of six revolutions, there are four forms in the spokes;
that which is indeed the first power here is divided twenty-fourfold. (169)
One should place [the letters] in the intervals between the spokes; the second [letter] is on the circle of the rim.
However, that which is joined with the seed-syllable situated in the hub should be applied continuously. 170.
O twice-born one, by means of alternating placement, the remaining two powers should then be assigned to the spokes in the outer wheel.
Having wrapped it around the head with twelve strands, one should lead three [strands] forward;
one should encircle that yantra with Viṣṇu, using the color of Vyomeśa.
One should cast [the thread] with a five-colored thread into a golden casket;
a woman should place it upon her right arm, or between her two breasts. (173)
The practitioner constantly wins the affection even of his enemies;
he may effortlessly leap across rivers, streams, or even the oceans. || 174 ||
Due to its power, it possesses many benefits and one does not sink within the water;
furthermore, there is no fear for those born in the forest from the presence of wild beasts. (175)
The planets, though situated in adverse positions, become favorable;
even many kinds of terrible and most fearsome poisons do not cause affliction. (176)
May the collection of weapons of thieves and others not enter the joints of my limbs;
even if stones were indeed to fall from the sky upon me. (177)
O twice-born one, they become equal to or even greater than showers of flowers;
furthermore, the Bālagrahas and other such spirits abandon the child from afar and depart. (178)
Wherever this machine (yantra) resides, it indeed dwells within that body; and by wearing it, a woman whose fetus has become stuck gives birth with ease. (179)
A barren woman shall have sons, and a woman whose children have died shall have living sons; moreover, she shall receive eternal honor in the midst of the assembly of her co-wives. (180)
In battle, in the royal court, in gambling, in dispute, and in extreme peril, the bearer attains victory through the power of this mantra. (181)
Therefore, O best of sages, once the mantra has been mastered, a yantra—whether derived from this tantra or another—will indeed accomplish all rites. (182)
Bestowing all accomplishments and effecting the increase of all prosperity—this, O Brahmin, has been proclaimed to you as the secret of all mantras. (183)
This means of accomplishment is for great-souled practitioners who desire enjoyments;
one should not reveal it to the deceitful, the sinful, or those who lack devotion. || 184 ||

Never [should it be given] to those devoted to other philosophical systems, nor to those who are not disciples, nor to those established on an unjust path, nor to those whose souls are intent upon unrighteousness.
Whether in sport or on the path of the waters, or wherever else, he who proclaims the Dharma for the sake of gaining wealth, indeed without any spiritual elevation; 186.
For those who are attached to the pride of wealth, even if they have attained perfection, they fall downward;
therefore, this secret [should be kept] from those who seek both the seen and the unseen goals.
One who desires the highest good should speak thus to those who have understood according to the right method.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of the Mantra of the Speaker," in the glorious *Pāñcarātra-jayākhyasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Means of Accomplishing the Retinue.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Nārada, listen to the means of accomplishing the Kaustubha gem and the others in brief."
By the mere knowledge of which, one will accomplish whatever is desired. || 1 ||
The first syllable of one's own name, devoid of vowels and consonants, constitutes the physical signs (*āṅgika*);
the collection of marks (*lāṃchanacaya*) consists of six types, beginning with their respective designations.
This [method] is common to all for the accomplishment of the nine limbs;
now, the specific details regarding the Kaustubha and the others will be explained right here.
[The Kaustubha Mantra Sadhana]:
On the seat of the syllable of the gem (maṇi), the letters *ra* and *la* should be applied in sequence.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the body, one should worship it externally as circular like the sun.
Having fashioned a mandala with lotuses and having worshipped there, O Mahāmati,
and having performed recitation and oblations, one should then proceed to a mountain peak devoid of trees.
Afterwards, having performed two hundred thousand recitations, one should offer oblations of mandāraka flowers together with saffron, thoroughly saturated with honey and clarified butter.
Then, one should offer thirty thousand oblations of campaka flowers;
the Lord of Mantras will quickly be accomplished, and once perfected, he bestows a collection of excellent jewels.
Having wrapped three barley grains with a thread dyed in lac, it bestows, in no time at all, an increase in longevity and health. (8)
O Sage, having lit five wicks soaked in clarified butter, each four finger-breadths in length, with the mantra consisting of six limbs, one should perform the recitation.
Indeed, one hundred and fifty [yojanas] above the iron wheel,
there is a cave containing alchemical elixirs and wealth situated beneath the earth.
While reciting the mantra, one should walk about, leaping from wheel to wheel like a frog;
by the power of this mantra, the circles quickly fall into place.
O Brahmin, having dug at that spot, one may indeed ascend to the treasures that are the elixirs of life;
for the cavity thus made remains secluded as long as the moon and stars exist.
There, by the mere act of meditation, he [obtained] the entire kingdom of Narendra, as well as jewels, coins, and ornaments.
Indeed, he always bestows things that are difficult to obtain in this world of mortals. And whoever, with devotion, should wear this written [text] around their neck today—
reciting the Lord of Mantras in conjunction with the *padma* [mudrā]— [attains these fruits].
For the sake of accomplishing all his goals regarding every object of treasure, || 15 ||
This has been stated regarding the Kaustubha; now the Mālā-mantra is being told.
[The Practice of the Mālā-mantra] Now, from the syllables of one's own name, in sequence: the triad of *laya* (i.e., *ya-ra-la*). 16.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the group of limbs upon the body using the very same preliminary implements as before,
and having performed the internal sacrifice (hṛdyāga), [one should do so] externally within a half-moon mandala.
Having meditated upon and worshipped [the deity] within a six-petalled lotus, one should then perform oblations;
thereafter, having approached a forest grove, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should offer oblations of *jāti*, campaka, and *kadamba* flowers,
anointed with the juices of all medicinal herbs, ten thousand times each in successive order.
Or else, O twice-born, one should offer ten thousand oblations with pure honey alone;
at the conclusion of the homa, there shall be mastery over the mantra in both the divine and human worlds.
Having consecrated a garland of flowers with mantras, the practitioner should place it around his own neck or upon an image situated on the ground.
He does not suffer a loss of his status as long as he desires;
moreover, he performs the worship of Viṣṇu in a place devoid of flowers and fruits.
Out-of-season flowers fall swiftly from the sky there;
if one makes an offering with those flowers and then wears them, [the result follows]. (23)
Or, having further consecrated it two hundred times, the practitioner should place it on his head or at his throat;
he shall then become invisible, or attain the power of moving through the air like a bird, or like the wind.
Constantly carrying divine fragrances and displaying divine wonders,
he appears in form to be like the god whose weapon is the flower (Kusumāyudha).
O twice-born one, if the mantra-holding minister is indeed pleased with a florist regarding a flower garden within the entire multitude of women, [the result follows].
While reciting the mantra, the practitioner gazes [at it], and that which was withered becomes flowered;
even one who is angry, upon seeing a forest strewn with blossoms, acts [in the same way]. (27)
If he should desire it even more, he might reduce it to a state equal to that which has been utterly consumed by a forest fire during the months of the rainy season and spring. (28)
Whatever rare fragrances there may be, originating from heaven or the netherworld,
they waft wherever the mantra-holder Mālādhara resides.
He becomes beloved by all beings merely by being seen;
and except through his own defeat, he never suffers defeat anywhere. (30)
One who wears the garland shall quickly obtain both pacifying and nourishing rites without effort and in no long time, even merely by maintaining the mantra. (31)
[The Method for Accomplishing the Lotus Mantra] Now, this accomplishment of the garland (mālāsādhana) of the lotus is being described.
One should place the life-force (jīva), situated in the letter *va* (Varuṇa), upon the seat of the letters of the name. (32)
Having performed the previously mentioned consecration (saṃskāra) and having meditated upon him, one should worship him in the heart;
externally, within another lotus, there is a six-petaled lotus with twelve petals.
Having fashioned [the mandala] within a circular enclosure provided with a pericarp and filaments,
and having brought [the deity] down there and worshipped him, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds and other materials.
One should go to a lotus grove and then mutter the lotus mantra—
one hundred thousand times, O best of sages, accompanied by three tens of thousands.
O twice-born one, one should offer twenty thousand lotuses;
then ten thousand land-lotuses, and after that, ten thousand [lotuses] sprinkled with honey.
From that, there shall be the accomplishment of mantras for those who possess the fragrance of *nāgakesara*;
he shall obtain abundant fortune, being free from ailments and diseases. || 37 ||
He shall possess incomparable good fortune and most beautiful luster;
freed from wrinkles and gray hair, he will be endowed with wealth and grain.
O Nārada, having drawn a six-petaled lotus with saffron upon a birch leaf, one should place the mantra in its center through the application of nyāsa.
In ancient times, the lotus was accomplished and bestowed everything through its retention (dhāraṇā).
Now, this procedure for the lotus as well as for the conch is being described.
[The Method for Accomplishing the Conch Mantra] One should join the two *bala*s beneath the letter of one’s own bound [mantra];
having performed the ritual embodiment (*vigraha*) and the rite of complete integration (*sakalīkṛta*), when the sacrifice in the heart has been performed, [41].
O Nārada, having fashioned outside [the pavilion] a conch-bellied six-petalled lotus situated upon the mandala, one should worship the mantra there after performing the fire-oblation (homa).
O twice-born one, the practitioner of mantra should go to a secluded place provided with spring water and recite the mantra one hundred and eight thousand times, plus thirty thousand more.
One who is composed should offer six hundred thousand kumuda flowers;
at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, O great-minded one, the king of mantras is perfectly accomplished for him.
Through its power, the cognition of hearing from a distance proceeds;
one devoted to meditation and silent recitation shall likewise obtain the sounds of all living beings. (45)
By the power of the Lord of Mantras, one shall hear many sounds arising from the worlds of the gods and gandharvas, which are enchanting to the faculty of hearing. (46)
O high-minded one, wherever this mantra is employed according to the previously stated rule, it swiftly accomplishes that [purpose] through Vighneśa.
Whoever wears this mantra—whether on a cloth dyed with saffron, or on birch bark, or even on a surface adorned with frost, milk, lime, and sandalwood paste—[attains success]. || 48 ||
And the assembly for its accumulation proceeds to manifestation;
this procedure of Śaṅkha has been declared, and now that of Cakra is being told. (49)
[The Method for Accomplishing the Mantra of the Maṇḍala] Having first established the designation of the deaths above, and that which is their prior destruction,
one should make it richly adorned with its retinue for the sake of accomplishing the assembly of the limbs of the maṇḍala. (50)
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and the body, one should then worship [the deity] in the heart-lotus;
one should draw a wheel with twelve spokes, complete with a hub and a rim.
In that interval, however, is a six-petalled lotus, reddish-white in color;
and a wheel with white spokes, brilliant in its radiance, resembling a royal sapphire.
Having worshipped the wheel-mantra in the center of that, one should then perform the fire-oblation;
and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should enter the forest region.
Having written the mantra of the king of wheels— whether with saffron or otherwise—
with the realization "I am the wheel" established within oneself, O Nārada, (54).

Having stepped upon the axle of the wheel and assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), the mantra-practitioner should enter [the state] and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, together with the great medicinal herb marked by the wheel.
The observer of the vow, stationed at the center of the wheel, should perform one hundred thousand oblations according to this measure;
moreover, he should offer three oblations of clarified butter into an auspicious fire-pit marked with the wheel.

O tiger among sages, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the practitioner, having stepped upon the wheel and remaining absorbed in meditation, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; thereafter, the wheel shall fly up.
Having seized the practitioner indeed with speed, it goes to the station of the sun and leads him incessantly by force through all the other worlds. 58.
O Sage, if one does not indeed fall into delusion due to the exhaustion of the mantra-being, yet the latent impression persists with the thought "I am the wheel," [then it is so]. (59)
In this world of men, there is nothing that he cannot accomplish through mantra—
whether by action, mind, or speech, indeed through meditation or even mere recollection.
O Nārada, this is the procedure for the Cakra-mantra;
now I shall describe the method for accomplishing the Gada-mantra: one should place the syllables of that mantra upon the seat of the weapon called the Gada.

O twice-born one, having performed the placement (nyāsa) as previously described, the entire collection of limbs should be positioned above; then, perform the worship properly with the mind and externally.
One should fashion a lotus in the center, shimmering and surrounded by eight maces; there, one should worship the six-petaled lotus, golden-hued, and the mantra of the mace.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), O Brahmin, one should then proceed to the delightful cave;
there, one should mutter the mantra ten thousand times eight (eighty thousand) and subsequently perform the fire sacrifice.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one hundred thousand sticks of red sandalwood soaked in ghee,
when offered while reciting the mace-mantra, bestows perfect accomplishment.
Having first fashioned a two-cubit mace made of sandalwood, the practitioner of mantra should perform whatever is desired by his own mind, or that of others.
Having worshipped it and taken hold of it, and having empowered it one hundred and eight times with mantras,
the practitioner of mantra should destroy terrible and malevolent planets by striking them on the head.
Wherein various magical illusions, diseases, and other such obstructions, upon the whirling of the mace by her hand, pass into the power of her hand. (68)
Intoxicated elephants, as well as others such as dogs, fierce venomous serpents, mean creatures, and any others who are evil-minded, all perish [at its sight]. (69)
The observer of the vow, being fearless, should strike the surface of the earth ten times with blows consecrated by mantras, and he may traverse all the pathways to the netherworlds.
Whoever carries the gadā-mantra inscribed on birch bark and encased in three metals shall become a partaker of all happiness. (71)
O Nārada, this ritual of the mantra known as Gadā has been explained;
now, with one-pointed attention, quickly grasp the method for accomplishing the Garuḍa-mantra. (72)
But first, having assigned the phonemes, one should apply the essence of the Vedas;
then, one should again place fire above and below, joined with the vowels as before.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the mental sacrifice (hṛdyāga) within a square mandala,
one should fashion a six-petaled lotus of bright yellow color with a thunderbolt (vajra) at its center.
Having worshipped Garuḍa there and performed the fire-oblation according to the rules,
one should go to the peak of the excellent mountain and recite the mantra four hundred thousand times.
Thereafter, O Great-minded One, one should perform three hundred thousand oblations with a single-pointed mind, using sesame seeds mixed with *śyāmāka* rice and anointed with clarified butter.
Then the King of Birds grants him complete satisfaction and accomplishes the desired goal for the practitioner who has perfected himself. (77)
When the practitioner of mantra gazes upon the circle of the directions and proceeds clockwise,
he should recite the mantra while staying at night on the eighth day of the bright fortnight.
Then the eight Kulanāgas, accompanied by tens of thousands of hosts of nāgas, [offered] indeed the principal jewels and the preeminent elixir (rasāyana). || 79 ||
Seizing him and terrified, they stand before him; that country where the minister resides shall become free from serpents. (80)
What need is there to speak of stationary poisons and those that are internal, O Great-minded One, as well as those of spiders, pustules, and donkeys? (81)
There is no destruction of the name as long as its continuity persists;
one says "go, go at will" to one whose clouds have been consumed. (82)
He surely goes likewise to barren lands and deserts,
he who eats a thousand loads of poison at the time of its rising.
Having remembered that minister with devotion, or by uttering his various names, whoever bears the mantra upon their forehead with saffron; || 84 ||
Freed from all defects, he dwells in the sky like the king of birds;
and I have spoken this [mantra] of Garuḍa by way of summary. 85.

[The Method for Accomplishing the Pāśa Mantra] Now listen, O Nārada, to the majesty of the mantra called Pāśa, as well as its application (viniyoga) and its initial syllable: the letters *vi* and *śva*, with the fires (*ra*) beneath them. (86)
Then, having divided [the substance] into six parts as before, one should mark the head;
likewise, having placed it on the hand and the body, one should then worship it in the heart-lotus.
Having fashioned a six-petalled lotus within the interior of the noose upon a fire-mandala,
one should worship its mantra there and perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains.
Having recited the mantra eighty thousand times,
O high-minded one, one should offer oblations of white mustard seeds soaked in white mustard oil for half that number of recitations.
At the conclusion of that, O Nārada, one should perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds mixed with ghee ten thousand times; thereafter, the king of mantras becomes perfected.
O Sage, a practitioner situated in the world of mortals can attract those dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla),
and a practitioner situated in the netherworld can indeed attract all those residing in heaven.
When employed, this king of mantras brings about subjugation, attraction, and withering;
whether meditated upon or even merely written down, it accomplishes these—of this there is no doubt. (92)
O Great-minded One, one should employ the mantra joined with the *varapāśa*;
when propitiated according to the prescribed rite as before, one obtains those respective results without effort. (93)

O Nārada, whoever wears this [mantra] written with yellow pigment (rocana) and saffron (kuṅkuma) using water from the night [of the new moon], and wrapped around with a yellow thread, [attains success]. 94.
O gentle one, whomever he gazes upon with an exceedingly affectionate look, she shall become his follower until the end of death. 95.
O Brahmin, whether she has seen the practitioner or even heard of him from afar, she will abandon her own place and run to where he stays. (96)
Moreover, whether she be a Kinnarī woman, a Yakṣiṇī, a celestial maiden, a Vidyādharī woman, a Gandharvī, or one known as a Siddhā; || 97 ||
Having focused upon her with the mind, one should recite the excellent mantra at night;
at the end of the night, she remains as if agitated and drawn by a noose.
This has been declared regarding the noose; now the goad is described.
[The method for accomplishing the mantra of the goad:
One should join the syllable *a* with the letter of fire (*ra*) at the bottom and at the top. (99)
One should perform the appropriate rite with the vowels as before, having placed them and worshipped that which resides in the heart;
then, having fashioned the city in the shape of a crescent moon, one should place a lotus in its center.
In the center of that, one should place the heart [mantra], which has the luster of a mass of vermilion;
having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa). || 101 ||
With priyaṅgu, śyāmāka, and sesame according to one's ability,
I shall then become a goad, and he shall go to the mountain peak.
One should perform three hundred thousand recitations there, and thereafter one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of red arka flowers, and another hundred thousand of black ones.
O Great-minded One, one should then offer two ten-thousand oblations of khadira fuel-sticks soaked in pungent oil, followed by the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
And by means of fragrant clarified butter (ājya), the mantra then becomes effective;
from that time forward, one should perform all rites without exception. || 105 ||
By means of the Aṅkuśa mantra, the practitioner effortlessly and with ease accomplishes subjugation, attraction, and inciting enmity, as well as killing and expulsion. (106)
If the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) is meditated upon and drawn forth by this mantra, he indeed bestows all riches; and even Antaka (the God of Death) grants freedom from fear.
Śakra bestows sovereignty; Māruta grants swift movement; Īśa grants the proclamation of all sciences without exception; and Hutāśana grants splendor.
Varuṇa brings about peace and nourishment, and he performs summoning;
the Lord of Yakṣas grants the state of a Kinnara, and the Lord of Pannagas provides elixirs.
When drawn forth, Dhruva in the form of a Brahmin grants the power of flight;
the Vidyādharas grant a pill, and the Siddhas grant a great collyrium. (110)
Drawn forth by the power of this mantra, they always grant [their gifts];
and the aforementioned pill (gulikā) should be prepared for kings along with their retinues.
The practitioner should accomplish [the goal] by means of the goad-mantra (aṅkuśamantra) joined with meditation;
O Sage, through meditation, recitation, drawing, fire-offering, and worship.
Furthermore, others likewise state that the Aṅkuśa mantra accomplishes one's desired object;
and indeed, the Kaustubha and other mantras are said to be effective when accomplished through an unbroken ritual procedure.
Endowed with purity of intention, they bestow everything entirely,
according to the power of the age and by virtue of having good assistants.
This method for accomplishing the mantras has been declared by me for the Kṛta age;
know that it is twofold in the Tretā age, and is remembered as threefold in the Dvāpara age.
Furthermore, in the Kali age, the fruit for one who knows the true nature of reality, who is accompanied by love and devotion, and who is truly established in faith, is indeed fourfold.

Know that whatever recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth you perform, it should always, always be done with a single-minded disposition and devotion; therefore, O Nārada, fix your heart and devotion upon one alone. 117.
"Whether all the means of accomplishment are performed together at one time, equally, or not even so.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Means of Accomplishment for the Retinue," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*. 30.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Sadhana of the Upāṅga," [the method for accomplishing the Satya-mantra]. The Blessed One said:
O Nārada, having first fashioned a mandala shaped like a kadamba bud, adorned with various colors and containing a lotus, thereafter—
Having consecrated one's own self with the Truth-mantra (satya), one should worship within the heart;
then, having brought [the deity] down from the heart into the previously prepared maṇḍala.

O best of Brahmins, having performed sacrifices with various pure and delicious roots, fruits, and other offerings, and having offered oblations of sesame seeds and the like, one should then proceed to an auspicious forest.
In that regard, O Sage, four hundred thousand [recitations] should be muttered while remaining in one's own place and meditating; then, one should perform two hundred thousand fire-oblations.
Having combined sugar, honey, clarified butter, milk, sesame seeds, and rice into a single mixture, one should briefly form the *mṛgānanā* (deer-faced) mudrā.
[The Deer Seal (mṛgīmudrā):
By joining the tips of the three fingers—the middle, the ring, and the thumb—the index and little fingers are raised and slightly separated; O twice-born one! (6)
Having performed the mudrā for all the names during the prescribed oblation, one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti); thus, O twice-born, the Lord of Mantras becomes perfected.
Joined with the ritual procedure, he bestows divine accomplishment according to his own will;
the Lord makes manifest all the stages of higher knowledge.

[The Method for Accomplishing the Vāsudeva Mantra] In this very manner, O best of the twice-born, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon the body with the great-souled seed-syllable alone known as Vāsudeva, (one should proceed). 9.
Having worshipped [the deity] mentally, one should then prepare a large mandala externally, perfectly circular, resembling the full moon, and as white as the interior of a lotus petal.
Having caused [the deity] to enter there and having worshipped with white flowers and unguents,
one should offer various kinds of very white food offerings and perform oblations with milk-rice.
Then, having performed the recitation of the Satyokta mantra and the fire-oblation with milk, ghee, and rice, he should go to a delightful forest filled with trees bearing white blossoms.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, Vāsudeva indeed bestows all eternal perfections;
when properly employed, he grants his own state, which is the attainment of liberation.
The Supreme Lord, ever-gracious, reveals Himself.
[The method for the practice of the Saṅkarṣaṇa mantra:
O Sage, having first placed Saṅkarṣaṇa upon the hand and then upon the body... 14.
Having worshipped [the deity] within the heart-lotus, one should then construct a mandala externally with pale powder mixed with *sattva*, O Nārada. (15)
It was clearly visible, shining like a radiant orb, with the luster of the interior of a red lotus;
there, it was honored with offerings of reddish food, as well as flowers and unguents.
Having brought [the deity] down, one should worship with devotion and immediately thereafter perform oblations;
having offered sesame seeds sprinkled with clarified butter, one should proceed to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 17 ||
Having recited [the mantra] four hundred thousand times in the middle of an Aśoka grove, one should then perform a fire-oblation of red flowers exactly one hundred thousand times.
One should then offer a hundred thousand saffron flowers as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
thereupon the Lord of Mantras is perfected, and being perfected, he bestows success.
Even if not intentionally employed, whatever is pleasing to the mind is understood as the entire mantra-state known as deep sleep (sauṣupta). 20.
That Lord, the Divine One himself, manifests in his own abode through his partless nature and establishes his devotees upon the path to liberation.
[The Method for Accomplishing the Mantra of Pradyumna] Now, having formed oneself into the embodiment of the mantra by means of the Pradyumna-mantra,
and having performed the sacrifice within the heart-lotus in the mind; 22.
Having fashioned a lotus-mandala outside that has the luster of a *kadamba* flower and the appearance of gold due to its pollen, he summoned the Lord of the Universe there.
One should indeed worship with flowers and other offerings using the consecrated water;
one should offer clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds and combined with turmeric and full-moon rice.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should proceed into the interior of a grove of plantain trees;
having performed there the recitation (japa) in the previously mentioned number, O Nārada.
Having first prepared dehusked sesame seeds mixed with saffron and blended with fragrant śāli rice, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) measuring one hundred thousand [offerings].
O Sage, one should then offer three tens of thousands of measures of cow's milk that has been previously boiled and infused with saffron.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform ten thousand oblations of guggulu resin in the form of pills, each the size of a jujube fruit and smeared with clarified butter.
Then one should offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter alone;
afterwards, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and thereupon the Lord of Mantras becomes perfected.
He bestows the states existing within the seven worlds even upon those who have not applied themselves;
he then indeed joins them to the path of accomplishment and subsequently to the path of liberation.
[The Method for Accomplishing the Aniruddha Mantra:

Having first performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*) upon one's body with the Aniruddha mantra, and having duly performed the internal sacrifice (*hṛdyāga*), one should cast out the mandala externally. (31)
Resembling the flax flower in color, auspicious with its pollen, round like a kadamba bud, resting upon a lotus, and beautiful as honey; || 32 ||
There, having invited the Lord of the World, who possesses a splendor equal to the rising sun,
one should worship Him with pure and sanctifying offerings such as flowers and unguents.

Having performed the fire-oblation with black sesame seeds, one should go to a secluded forest at the conclusion of the oblation and perform recitation there according to the previously stated measure, O Nārada.
O Brahmin, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with half that amount [of materials], using black sesame seeds resembling the color of linseed flowers,
combined with black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru).
Thereafter, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti); then, O best of Brahmins, that Supreme Lord attains satisfaction, and being pleased, He grants everything.
One whose self is unobstructed should oneself unite [the mind] with the eternal state;
he shall then reveal everything, both external and internal, to the practitioner. (37)
By this, he shall have accomplished his purpose and become a partaker of infinite fruit;
what need is there for much speaking here? [The mantra] is endowed with the fivefold action.
[The Method for Accomplishing the Seven-Syllable Mantra:

O best of Brahmins, having first performed the seven-syllable mantra with the hand of a Brahmin, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of limbs), one should meditate upon the partless (niṣkala) form as before. 39.
Having worshipped within the center of the heart-lotus, one should then perform the recitation (japa) in a solitary,
secluded, and beautiful forest thick with trees.
O best of Brahmins, it measures seven hundred thousand [yojanas] and is endowed with three lengths,
even without external services such as fire-offerings (homa), worship (pūjā), and the like.
At the conclusion of the recitation, O tiger among sages, one shall obtain all desires,
as well as the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, and the six qualities such as strength and the rest.
He gives everything by his word alone, whatever is desired by the mind;
when pleased, he is the foremost of practitioners, but when enraged, he could burn the three worlds.
If even the gods, asuras, nāgas, and siddhas are vessels for liberation, then how much more so the deities perfected in yoga, who remain in a state of service? (44)
Endowed with the seven-syllable [mantra] of the Great-Souled Truth, he shall remain free from wrinkles and grey hair for as long as the moon and stars endure. (45)
O tiger among sages, the practitioner of mantra remains within his own body until the end; having then cast off the physical frame, he shall go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, that which, once gone, they do not return to this ocean of existence—the pentad beginning with Truth (satya), as well as the seven-syllable Piṇḍa mantra. (47)
He should be propitiated with half of that [effort] through auspicious recitations, fire-offerings, and so forth;
for a practitioner of mantra should not employ [the ritual] for the sake of ordinary accomplishments.
But when propitiated according to the prescribed rite,
he himself grants the desired objects to practitioners, and in the end, eternal liberation.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Practice of the Subsidiary Limbs," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Accomplishment" [the method for accomplishing the mantra of Vighneśa]:
That Vaināyaka mantra which was previously taught by me—
Now, O Nārada, hear the means for its accomplishment in brief.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual assignment (nyāsa) and worshipped within the heart-lotus,
one should then construct a mandala joined with three corners.
O twice-born one, one should draw three doors and, in their center, a three-petalled lotus according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having performed sacrifices and oblations, one should then properly assume one's own form;
O Sage, one should go to a forest region and recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times.
O best of sages, one should offer one hundred thousand flowers and specifically twenty thousand fuel-sticks of the white *arka* tree.
O Sage, one should offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter as the final full-offering (pūrṇāhuti);
then the god Vināyaka appears visibly before one’s eyes.
And he indeed says, "I am accomplished; perform whatever rite you desire.
Then that best of practitioners accomplishes everything in an instant.
[The power born from the accomplishment of the mantra of Vighneśa:
Having taken the root of the *rājārka* plant and having consecrated it one hundred times with the mantra of Gaṇeśa, one should then complete the rite by further consecrating it. 8.
(354) With a measurement of half a finger-breadth, one should place Vighneśa seated upon a lotus;
having deposited the mantra upon him once, one should then encircle it with *madana*.
Having placed it in a copper vessel, one should carry it upon the head during battle, in the royal court, at gambling, or even in dispute, O high-minded one. || 10 ||
The knower of mantras attains his desired goal without obstacle after performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) with Gaṇeśa [at the beginning] of whatever [rite] he undertakes. 11.
The knower of mantras who stands at the front shall then attain his goal without obstacle;
having consecrated with a hundred recitations a fruit or a flower belonging to the enemy, [he shall cast it]. 12.
If one places it in the hand everywhere, indeed an obstacle arises for him;
therefore, the practitioner, having ground realgar, should saturate it with water from the night.
Having wiped [the surface] with milk from a Kapila cow on a yellow cloth,
one should draw there the form of the Goddess of Vaighnesvara situated within the lotus of the heart.
One should impart the mantra of Vighneśa; it grants everything that is desired.
Indeed, wherever it remains in the house—in the northeast direction—it bestows all that is sought.
As long as he was not moved again and seen by anyone else,
so long did prosperity abound in that house, filled with wealth and grain.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade indeed bear fruit incessantly; yet the granary or the treasury would not [endure] if they were not accounted for again and again. (17)
Whether he makes an expenditure or gives a gift, that remains inexhaustible when spent;
or if he considers it to be the attainment of a region or the highest gain. (18)
Having prepared sweetmeats smeared with ghee and consecrated with mantras,
he who offers them as oblations becomes free from all affliction and goes wherever he may go.
Whether by night or by day, even when agitated by the fear of thieves and enemies,
he indeed proceeds, though possessed of garments, ornaments, and wealth.
Alone and free from obstacles, he travels for thousands of yojanas,
holding in his hand white mustard seeds that have been properly consecrated with mantras.
With a mind full of joy, he gives; he shall come under one's control.
If one performs oblations of black mustard seeds with the mantra of Vighneśa, [the same result follows]. 22.
Combined with pungent oil, it produces hatred in an instant; this applies even to those who are mutually affectionate, so what need is there to mention those who are already estranged? (23)
Facing the northwest, one should offer a thousand crow feathers into the fire while reciting the name of a person; that person will be expelled without delay.

O Great-minded One, having recited the mantra over buffalo-ash mixed with white mustard seeds, one should perform half of ten thousand oblations while uttering the name of the person [against whom the rite is directed].
Drawn from afar, the king of the gods approaches even at the conclusion of the oblation;
[one should offer] twenty thousand karavīra flowers combined with lac and alaktaka.
By offering oblations in the name of anyone, even one who is independent will indeed become submissive;
the practitioner of mantras should offer honey and clarified butter, or ten thousand sesame seeds, for each individual.
Powder made from nimba leaves, saturated with goat's blood and poison, quickly produces mutual affection among those who are hostile to one another. (28)

O Great-minded One, if one performs a fire-oblation at night on a Tuesday during the dark fortnight under the name of another, that person shall quickly meet his death at the conclusion of the oblation.
If one should indeed perform half of that with honey and ghee,
by means of ten thousand oblations in the fire-sacrifice, he shall restore him to life once again.
O high-minded one, through oblations of ghee, milk, and sesame seeds performed in sequence, the Lord of Mantras bestows peace, nourishment, and health without any obstacle.
