Whoever, for the sake of protection, wears this [mantra] written with yellow pigment (rocanā) upon birch bark on an eight-petaled lotus together with its ancillaries (sāṅga), shall attain liberation from all sufferings. || 32 ||
O Sage, those who cause him harm, including the foremost of the Brahmarākṣasas, are destroyed;
he who maintains this mantra shall slay epilepsy.
Other seizing spirits (*atigraha*) and the like, as well as the *skandagraha* and other such [demons], are destroyed by the mantra of Vighneśa through its recitation, meditation, and worship. (34)
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying all obstacles and for the sake of total prosperity, the mantra must be maintained by practitioners who long for spiritual success. 35.
O Sage, listen attentively as I describe this ritual arrangement for the mantra of Vaināyaka and that of Vāgīśvarī. (36)

[The Method for Accomplishing the Mantra of Vāgīśvarī] Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the root mantra in due order, one should first worship within the heart-lotus; thereafter, assuming the form of the moon and sun externally, [one should worship]. (37)

Having fashioned a mandala adorned with lotuses and having caused the Goddess to descend therein, one should worship her with all offerings such as white [garments] and the like, as well as food offerings, flowers, and so forth.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) with white sesame seeds and fresh butter, O Nārada,
and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should thereafter fashion a body in that [deity's] form.
One should go into the midst of a Kadamba forest with eyes cast upward;
one should mutter four hundred thousand [mantras] and thereafter perform the fire-oblation (homa).
O Sage, with white sugar measuring one hundred thousand units, as well as with fragrant śāli rice and indeed with fresh butter; 41.
O Sage, the mantra-practitioner should likewise offer ten thousand oblations of guggulu mixed with ghee and milk for each [deity] in succession, according to the mantra.
One should offer oblations and then present the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti); thereupon Vāgīśvarī herself, having approached, enters his mouth without delay.
That woman is perceived as if she were a stream of cool water—
[this is the power born from the mastery of the Vāgīśvarī mantra].
Then, in a very short time, he becomes a great poet.
The supreme practitioner is born, understanding the meaning of the scriptures without restraint, whether in Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Apabhraṃśa, or nasalized speech. (45)
By the power of that [knowledge], which arises from the distinction between various regions,
one knows the past and the future and simultaneously grasps what has not been heard.
The words of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas issued forth from the mouths of the twice-born;
what need is there to speak of the distinct differences between the three times? 47.
Or, as is appropriate, he effortlessly causes many masters of speech who possess superior intellects and are established in opposing positions to proclaim [the truth]. (48)

O Sage, O best of the twice-born, even if one were to describe the distinct form of each [of these] for a hundred years, they would not reach exhaustion by means of speech or the objects of cognition.

Alternatively, for those whose selves have been cultivated through the elements arisen from the counteragent, one should meditate on Vāgīśī, radiant red, residing upon the tongue and other [senses]. (50)
Standing in the midst of a vajra-fence, one should effect the paralyzing of speech;
one should meditate on [the syllable] located in the middle of the tongue of the person who has been confronted. 51.
[He saw her] standing in the center of the lunar disc, with the luster of a mass of snow,
pouring nectar from her mouth [and thereby filling] his body.
O Brahmin, by merely recollecting it while it is sprinkled [with water], one becomes a poet at that very moment.
Having placed a silver pitcher in the center of a mandala of flowers, || 53 ||
Having filled [the vessel] with honey, wine, and milk, and having worshipped the Supreme Goddess within it for seven days with white flowers and ointments, || 54 ||
On the eighth day, he who should offer three handfuls of water with his own hand for the purpose of drinking— having drunk it, that person shall become wise.
Through bathing in or immersing oneself in that [water], pacification (śāntika) or nourishment (pauṣṭika) arises for those of dull intellect, and especially for those who are unwell. (56)
O twice-born one, he who, having consecrated it with a hundred recitations of the mantra, eats vacā daily for seven days, shall become eloquent and wise. (57)
Having worshipped the Goddess for twenty-one days within the center of a white lotus,
he should devotedly offer milk-rice (paramānna) mixed with ghee, placed in a sacrificial vessel (caru).

Whether it be a child, a young woman, or a girl, whoever eats that which is combined with heat and is fully satiated until completely digested shall become a knower of the meaning of various scriptures. || 59 ||
Furthermore, O high-minded one, great scriptures issue forth incessantly from his mouth; even from afar, the power of the learned is diminished.
Having practiced this together with the assembly, both externally and internally,
even in the presence of one who is indifferent, ignorant, or a stranger.
Impelled by her command, he too should fetch those Vedas;
then the Goddess Vāgīśvarī, the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims, becomes perfected.
She bestows wealth upon one who desires wealth, sons upon one who desires sons;
she grants a kingdom to one who desires a kingdom, and enjoyment to one who desires enjoyment. (63)
She bestows victory upon one who desires victory; she bestows peace upon one who desires peace;
she bestows nourishment upon one who desires nourishment; and she bestows contentment upon one who desires contentment. (64)
She bestows knowledge upon one who desires knowledge; she bestows liberation upon one who desires liberation;
and she is the granter of all desires for those who have desires. (65)

[The Procedure for the Yantra of Vāgīśvarī] Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, the goddess together with her name is placed at its center; and when, as previously described, the sixfold set of the goddess’s six limbs is situated on the exterior— (66)
Outside of that is another lotus adorned with sixteen petals;
on each petal, one should place the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*) three times, reaching as far as the filaments.
Then one should apply the seed-syllable of the weapon to the sixteen petals;
outside the sixteen-petaled [lotus], one should draw a twelve-petaled lotus.
O Sage, one should assign the head, the vessels, and the armor to the half-petals and the petals; then, one should assign the eye-mantra situated within the petals twelve times.
One should write the Mātṛkā, from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', on the exterior of the lotus; then, by means of the Kuṇḍalī-yoga, one should encircle it with the head [of the letter 'ha'].
O tiger among sages, O high-minded one, the Supreme Self is sevenfold; moreover, outside of that, He exists in the eight directions together with Vyomeśa and Āhlāda.
Then, one should fill the space between the two *ya* letters of the Vāyavya-bhavana, which is adorned with eight *ya* letters, by joining them together. || 72 ||
O Nārada, it bestows sovereignty over the three worlds and is beyond numbering;
then, in the triangular abode, it is kindled by the śikhā-mantra.
O Brahmin, one should fashion [the seat] from the corners and the three directions, provided with svastikas, as the support of all worlds, accompanied by Vyomeśa. (74)
One should draw the number of *marīci* units outside the triangle;
outside of that, one should place the watery (*vāruṇa*) mandala, shaped like a half-moon.
One should draw [the diagram] joined with four-petaled lotuses;
therein, one should write the armor (kavaca) situated in the center of the pericarp, and the crest-lock (śikhā) on the petals.

One should fill the spaces between the lotuses with the syllable *vā* (varāha) joined with the Lord of Space (*vyomeśa*, i.e., *ha*). Outside of that is the earthly city (*pārthiva-pura*) associated with the moon.
It is joined with eight vajras and adorned with four finger-breadths;
the weapon (astra) is situated within the belly of the vajra, and further, it consists of rays by means of the weapon.
One should fill that entire outer square city;
having taken the juice of turmeric, as well as water from a cluster of lotuses. (79)
Having first worshipped Vāgīśa on an auspicious day with the juices of *rocanā*, camphor, and nocturnal water, one should then draw [the mandala].
O twice-born one, whoever wears this yantra— having inscribed it on birch bark, in the eye, or on cloth with a needle made of gold and encased in the three metals— [attains the highest goal].
O twice-born one, by the mere utterance of that [mantra], prosperity, wealth, honor, and the destruction of enemies shall swiftly belong to him;
indeed, he shall become inexhaustible in even the most terrible battle.
No fear exists for him from poison, snakes, fire, and the like;
it fulfills all desires through its retention, recollection, and so forth.
Therefore, a true Vaiṣṇava man who always desires victory at all times should indeed perform this with effort, either on his two arms or on his neck. 84.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Method of Accomplishment," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Yoga.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Thereafter, for the sake of the manifestation of yogic power, the Vaiṣṇava should indeed practice yoga."
In a well-concealed, solitary place, free from strife and possessing auspicious characteristics. || 1 ||
Having subdued pride and fixed his mind on the welfare of all beings,
he was devoted to the gods, the sacred fires, and his teachers, and was always intent upon the study of the true scriptures.
He who has abandoned malice toward living beings and whose senses are restrained sits upon a very beautiful seat endowed with auspicious marks.
But [an image] made from auspicious wood, twenty-four finger-breadths in length and twelve finger-breadths in height, should be wrapped in a well-washed cloth. (4)
Covered with soft kuśa grass and a sacred antelope skin,
seated there, he should constantly practice the limbs of yoga.

[The threefold nature of prāṇāyāma: By means of the four [stages] beginning with exhalation (recaka), distinguished by their respective measures (mātrā), that prāṇāyāma is proclaimed as the inferior, the middling, and the superior. || 6 ||
Then he should perform withdrawal (pratyāhāra), which is the restraint of the mind;
for the intellect (buddhi), the mind (manas), and the ego (ahaṅkāra)—these three are proclaimed to be the mind (citta).
Nevertheless, one should diligently practice the withdrawal of the mind;
it is taught that the fourfold mind is conquered through withdrawal (pratyāhāra). (8)
It remains upon the path of the target, and never otherwise;
meditation is the accomplishment of the target, and that is proclaimed as reflection (cintana).
Thereafter, however, the concentration (dhāraṇā) should be maintained in order to dispel cold and burning sensations;
it is fivefold, as before, according to the arrangement of each respective mantra.
One should perform the recitation (japa) with eyes closed, employing a mantra that is expressive;
it consists of syllables, seed-syllables, and words for the purpose of realizing that which is expressed.
That which was previously described according to the prescribed method is indeed declared to be threefold;
yoga also is said to be threefold—listen to that from me in its entirety.
The natural, the human, and sovereignty as the third;
reasoning is proclaimed as logic (tarka), and that is the investigation for the sake of establishing proof. (13)
Samādhi is the attainment of one's true self; it is proclaimed to be born from the self.
It consists of abandoning the object of focus and being devoid of the utterance of mantras. (14)
O Brahmin, it is always divided, being devoid of the rules regarding parts and portions;
when meditative absorption (samādhi) is fully perfected, one attains the Supreme Puruṣa.
Everything from the beginning of breath control (prāṇāyāma) up to the end of meditative absorption (samādhi) has been proclaimed;
it is established according to the distinctions of measures (mātrā), being twofold and even threefold.
Seated upon a yoga-āsana, one should perform the ritual exactly as prescribed;
one should bind the four yoga-āsanas with a yoga-band (yogapaṭṭa). || 17 ||
Having assumed one of these— either the paryaṅka, the kamala, the bhadra, or the firm svastika posture— one should keep the body straight and proceed with the sequence from above.
With clearly defined joints, broad thighs, and a well-formed neck, one should bring the two arms together and slightly bend the head. (19)
With the hands positioned like a tortoise at the navel or the middle of the hips,
the right hand should be placed upon the left, or alternatively, the left upon the right.
Having placed the two hands palms-upward, one should adopt the tortoise posture;
one should support the neck with effort, neither too rigid nor contracted. (20)
One should slightly close the eyes and gaze at the tip of the nose;
having closed the mouth, one should not let the teeth touch the teeth.
One should practice yoga either with the *garbha* (the internal focus) or without the *garbha*, remaining well-restrained.
Thereafter, one should agitate the wind known as *prāṇa*, which is conjoined with the mind. (23)
Prāṇāyāma is proclaimed to have four divisions, beginning with recaka;
one should always strive with effort to conquer the mind, which is difficult even for gods and dānavas to subdue. (24)
Even if the mind is restrained by force through practice and dispassion, one should nevertheless remain diligent and avoid that which depends on previous impressions.
They, however, should be known as twofold: those that are proximate and those that have entered the mind.
The proximate ones are situated in their respective locations and are produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the mind (or mental factors). || 26 ||
One should remain with eyes closed, free from all sensory engagement, in a place not infested by gadflies or mosquitoes, devoid of noise, and free from odors. || 27 ||
Thus, remaining firmly established in the true object of perception, one should completely renounce all limiting adjuncts born of proximity,
as well as the various [impurities] arising from latent impressions.
One should always withdraw the mind that is distracted among all objects; for that mind, which is ever-wandering, must be understood as being characterized by darkness (tāmasa). 29.
That [mind] which has moved toward passion and so forth due to habitual practice is known as rajasic;
however, the sattvic mind is said to be that which is closely attached to the sphere of the objective.
O ascetic, one should know that when [the mind] is thus withdrawn, it has transcended the qualities (guṇas);
in this manner, one should perform meditation with a "womb" (sagarbha) during the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
And it is further said that there are three types beneficial for yogins:
the Sakala (with parts), the Niṣkala (without parts), and Viṣṇu as the third, whose form is the Supreme.
Elsewhere, the knowable is to be understood as threefold: sound, space, and that which possesses form.
One should contemplate the form of the deity as having a manifest form. (33)
Thus has meditation been described: one should meditate upon the focal point as far as the very limits of space;
and one should continue to meditate upon the focal point as long as that focal point is not [fully] realized.
For when existence has reached non-existence, one's own nature is considered supreme.
One should first practice the gross, then the subtle, and after that, the beyond.
In this way, the mind dissolves along with the object of focus and its limiting adjuncts;
one should meditate upon the form of the God of gods within the sphere of the heart-lotus.
Then one should contemplate another object of focus, first gross and then subtle;
for one who practices in this manner, an excellence of qualities arises. (37)
The image consists of the moon, sun, and fire, resembling the solar disc;
it possesses a white form and bestows the excellence of the qualities (guṇas). || 38 ||
Then, one should know that point (bindu), subtler than the subtle, with a luster like a royal mung bean, which stands having ascended above all mantras. (39)
Then, one should gradually contemplate [the seed-syllable] the size of a royal kidney-bean;
furthermore, one should contemplate its producer, at the end of which the sound (nāda) is situated. (40)
Having dissolved that [subtle body], there arises one the size of a horse's hair,
which always moves through the sky and returns to the heart like the mind.
Then one should contemplate the subtle [channel] the size of a hair on the head;
by means of this, through the sprinkling of meditation, they quickly perceive the Brahma-nāḍī.
Then, having established himself in the practice of restraint, one should meditate on that which is the size of a single body hair, like a lotus fiber, and which illuminates the Brahma-nāḍī. (43)
Then that supreme channel, which is devoid of similarity, becomes visible;
by means of it, one should go to the supreme state through the path of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 44 ||
In this way, one should meditate upon the partless; he too becomes dissolved in the supreme state.
However, for one who practices further, the state of *unmanas* arises. (45)
Then, however, its own existence in the form of Brahman is manifested;
or one should meditate upon that which is both with parts and without parts as having the nature of sound. 46.
One should meditate upon the mantra consisting of Nārāyaṇa, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ";
for this entire Supreme Lord is composed of sound.
One should contemplate the single, partless syllable *kṣauṃ* or *hrīṃ*;
and even beyond that, the partless *bindu* situated upon its head, which contains the three deities.
That power (śakti), having arisen from that [Nāda], is half the measure of the Pramāṇa;
that power dissolves into Nāda, and Nāda goes to dissolution in the Supreme (Para).
For in this way, through the practice of meditation, they behold the supreme and eternal;
or else, one should contemplate after having expanded the two sounds "A" and "Lo. (50)
Wherever one has dissolved oneself, right there is the supreme state;
or else, the eternal reality, which is of the nature of space, should be meditated upon. (51)

One should always contemplate the triple space (trivyoma) situated both outside and within, which transcends the crest-lock (śikhātīta). Having meditated upon the supreme reality situated within the primary [space], one shall no longer be subject to worldly existence.
Meditating thus, liberation shall be attained; yet worldly enjoyment remains established in the Sakala [form].
The Sakala is the body of the God of gods, who possesses the form of Viṣṇu.
The God holds a conch and a lotus, adorned with a mace and a lotus;
he has four arms, four forms, four faces, and beautiful eyes. (54)
The one whose chest bears Lakṣmī, who is mounted upon a bird, adorned with all jewels, Kṛṣṇa, the supreme god, Viṣṇu, the victorious, the omnipresent, Hari. (55)
The Lord Hayagrīva, whose weapon is the thunderbolt; Hari, who assumes various forms;
Nṛhari; he who has the form of a boar; and Maheśvara, whose limbs are composed of power (Śakti). || 56 ||
Having thus undertaken this discipline, one should renounce the state of subsisting on alms-food,
after first thoroughly understanding the supreme characteristics of the cooked alms-food.

Having blocked the path of the vital junctions by means of the bodily breath, and having released it through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*) by means of the practice for departing (*utkrānti*), [one attains liberation]. 58.
If one who is devoted to constant practice should cast off the body after meditating [thus],
he attains the supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, the imperishable.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear from you in brief this definition of the fall of the body and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Nārada, for one who is disciplined in food and recreation, devoted to [spiritual] action,
regulated in sleep and wakefulness, and whose bodily constituents are always in equilibrium," (61)
The sound of the drum within the heart, which is the eternal Word, arises;
even as it creates cold and heat in due season, it does not perceive that heat or cold.
O Nārada, having meditated on the light between the eyebrows, it then sets at the dvādaśānta;
indeed, O Sage, the sound neither rises nor does it set.
When one established in meditative concentration does not perceive the joy within the lotus, the blood located in the limbs, characterized by phlegm, becomes parched. (64)
O Brahmin, when he no longer perceives the scent of the earth, whether external or internal, then it should be understood that his fall from the body will not be long delayed.
Established in the earth-element and concentrated in its meditative retention (dhāraṇā),
he no longer perceives the previously mentioned sound after five days, at the fifth moment.
Or, even while established in samādhi, these two—one cold and one hot—are not experienced;
the bodily aggregate (piṇḍa) falls away within four days, at the moment that [realization] is attained.
If, having attained the dhyāna of form according to the previously described method, [the deity] does not shine in the space of the heart or externally like the lord of luminaries; || 68 ||
For there will certainly be almsfood on the third day at that same moment, O Nārada, if the yogi is established in the Vāyavya Samādhi. (69)
He does not experience supreme bliss and trembles with thirst;
after two days, the falling of the physical body occurs at the second moment.
If one remains in the state of space according to the previously described method, one does not perceive various scents—whether auspicious or inauspicious—either internally or externally. (71)
On that very day, at the first moment of the morning, O tiger among sages, the yogi, with his mind solely intent on meditation, meditated thus: (72)
He himself ascends from the physical body (piṇḍa) and goes to the abode of Brahman;
or, joined by the process of unification (sandhāna), he may enter another body as previously described.

The time for the falling away of the body has been briefly described by its characteristics; now, the restraint of the vital wind (vāyu), which is the very essence [of that process], is being explained. (74)
Having extracted [the mantra] from its dwelling in the heart along with the seed-syllable (sagarbha), up to the edge of the blade,
one should employ that which is formidable and devoid of the immeasurable (aprameya).
The *pradhāna* [channel] at the pit of the throat does not go back to the heart;
one should remember the *pradhāna* within the cavity of the twice-born [teeth], devoid of the pervasive [element]. (76)
O Nanda, one should first avoid the path;
thus, for both the obstructed and the open paths, one should provide [the offering] on the right and the left.

Then, at the end of the mantra, one should meditate on the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, which is unmanifest yet radiant, located in the cavity of the mouth—namely, the eyes, nose, and face—or as existing solely within the oral cavity. (78)
O Sage, having abandoned this physical body which is as ripe as a fruit, one should proceed toward the Supreme Self and take refuge in the eternal state. (79)
Thus has this entire, supreme meaning of the Pañcarātra been told;
O best of Brahmins, it should be guarded with great effort as if it were one's own very life.
This compendium is the most excellent of all, a lamp illuminating all branches of knowledge;
it must not be told to men of wicked intellect or defiled souls.
Especially for those who are envious, lacking devotion, deceitful, acting with hypocrisy, and out of pride reviling the true substance of the scriptures. (82)
And [the destruction] of those who revile my devotees, whose souls are devoted to dry logic, who disparage the scriptures, and whose minds are conditioned by other philosophical systems. || 83 ||
It should be given to those of discerning intellect, whose souls are devoted to their own duty, who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, and whose souls are intent on devotion to me. 84.
O Sage, those who always behold those who have taken refuge in my teaching—possessing my nature and my disposition, and endowed with an exceedingly pure vision—[attain liberation]. 85.
For them, this scripture is to be taught after having performed initiation according to the rule, or after previously displaying the assembly of mantras or the worshipped mandala. (86)
Having first worshipped the scripture, one should recite the meaning of the scripture, by which various and eternal accomplishments quickly arise for both [the teacher and the student]. (87)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition on Yoga," in the glorious *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
This Jayākhyasaṃhitā is completed.
